questions.text: 24. As regards the oral cavity, all the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The posterior opening of the oral cavity proper is the oropharyngeal isthmus, framed by the palatoglossal arches; palatopharyngeal folds lie farther back.
options: Its roof is formed by the palate.
Its floor is supported by mylohyoid muscle.
The parotid duct opens in its vestibule.
The frenulum of the tongue is attached to its floor.
It is bounded posteriorly by the palatopharyngeal folds.

questions.text:
Question 41 :During surgical removing of a tumor in the infratemporal fossa, an
intense hemorrhage occurred. The surgeon clamped the main source of arterial
supply to the area.
questions.explanation: The maxillary artery is the main arterial trunk in the infratemporal fossa. The mandibular nerve is its major nerve, and chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve to carry taste from the anterior tongue.

subQuestions.text: a. Which artery did the surgeon clamp to stop the hemorrhage?
subQuestions.explanation: The maxillary artery is a major arterial source in the infratemporal fossa; tumors there can injure it, so clamping controls the hemorrhage.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The artery clamped to stop thehemorrhageis the maxillary artery.

subQuestions.text: b. Name the main nerve located in the fossa and its branches.
subQuestions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) traverses the infratemporal fossa and divides into anterior and posterior divisions; its branches distribute motor supply to mastication muscles and sensory supply to the lower face, teeth, and tongue.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
The main nerve located in the fossais the mandibular nerve.
Branches:
- From the trunk: nervous spinosus, nerve to medial pterygoid, tensor palate and
tensor tympani.
- From anterior division: buccal nerve, nerve to lateral pterygoid, nerve to
masseter and nerve to temporalis.
- From the posterior division:auriculotemporal nerve, lingual nerve and inferior
alveolar nerve. (ALI)

subQuestions.text: c. This patient complained of loss of taste, sensation from anterior part of the tongue after the operation. Can you account for this? Name the nucleus that receives taste sensation.
subQuestions.explanation: Chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds after joining the lingual nerve; the accompanying general sensation travels in the lingual nerve itself. Taste afferents ultimately reach the solitary nucleus.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
Loss of taste sensation due to affection of chorda tympani which joins the lingual
nerve.
-The nucleus that receives taste sensation is the nucleus solitaries.

questions.text: Case 1: A patient was asked to protrude his tongue outside the mouth cavity. The doctor observed that the tip of the tongue was directed to the left side. The facial muscles, as well as the rest of the body muscles, were normal.
questions.explanation: Left tongue deviation indicates left CN XII weakness: ipsilateral genioglossus is weak, so the intact side pushes the tongue toward the lesion. CN XII supplies tongue muscles except palatoglossus; sensation is divided by region among lingual/chorda tympani, IX, and internal laryngeal X.

subQuestions.text: 1. Name the injured nerve.
subQuestions.explanation: A unilateral hypoglossal (CN XII) lesion weakens ipsilateral genioglossus; on protrusion, the intact side pushes the tongue toward the injured side, here left.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Hypoglossal nerve.

subQuestions.text: 2. Mention the side of the lesion.
subQuestions.explanation: A unilateral hypoglossal motor lesion makes the protruded tongue deviate toward the weak side because the intact genioglossus pushes it across. Here that side is left.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Left side.

subQuestions.text: 3. Name the muscle responsible for the protrusion of the tongue.
subQuestions.explanation: Genioglossus is the chief protruder; unilateral weakness lets the intact side push the tip toward the weak side.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Genioglossus muscle.

subQuestions.text: 4. Mention the nerve supply of the tongue.
subQuestions.explanation: Tongue supply follows region: lingual nerve carries general sensation and chorda tympani taste anteriorly; CN IX supplies the posterior third and vallate papillae, while internal laryngeal CN X supplies the root. CN XII moves all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles except palatoglossus.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Nerve supply of tongue: Motor: All muscles of tongue are supplied by Hypoglossal nerve Except palatoglossus (supplied by granial accessory through pharyngeal branch of vagus). Sensory: Anterior 2/3: General sensation → lingual nerve; Taste → chorda tympani. Posterior 1/3 + vallate papillae: General & taste sensation → glossopharyngeal nerve. Most posterior part (including epiglottis & vallecula): General & taste sensation → internal laryngeal branch of vagus nerve.

questions.text:
Question 9:A patient when asked to protrude his tongue outside the mouth cavity
the doctor observed That the tip of tongue is directed to the left side the facial
muscles as well as the rest of body muscles where normal .
questions.explanation: A left hypoglossal nerve lesion weakens the left genioglossus, so the intact right side pushes the protruded tongue toward the weak side.

subQuestions.text: a. what is the diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: The tongue points toward a weak hypoglossal side on protrusion, so leftward deviation localizes to left CN XII.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: lesion in left hypoglossal nerve.

subQuestions.text: b. Name the muscles responsible for protrusion of the tongue .
subQuestions.explanation: Genioglossus pulls the tongue forward from its mandibular origin, so bilateral contraction protrudes it; unilateral weakness causes deviation toward the weak side.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Genioglossus muscle .

subQuestions.text: c. Mention the lymphatic drainage of the tongue .
subQuestions.explanation: The tongue has cross-drainage: its tip drains bilaterally to submental nodes, lateral margins mainly to submandibular nodes, and posterior third to upper deep cervical nodes, including jugulodigastric.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
• Tip of tongue bilaterally to submental L.N.s .
• Margins unilaterally & body bilaterally to submandibular and upper deep
cervical L.N.s
• posterior 1/3 bilaterally to upper deep cervical ( Jugulo-digastric and Jugulo-
omohyoid).

questions.text: Q2. Mention the extrinsic muscles of Tongue with its nerve supply
questions.explanation: Genioglossus, hyoglossus, and styloglossus receive CN XII; palatoglossus is the exception, supplied through the vagal pharyngeal plexus.
questions.modelAnswer: Genioglossus, hyoglossus and styloglossus: hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). Palatoglossus: cranial accessory fibres joining the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus, as stated in this edition.

questions.text: 28. Regarding the nerve supply of the tongue, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Palatoglossus is the exception: it is supplied through the vagal pharyngeal plexus, whereas the other tongue muscles receive hypoglossal motor fibers.
options: Its most posterior part is supplied by vagus nerve.
Its anterior 2/3 are supplied by lingual nerve.
Its posterior 1/3 is supplied by glossopharyngeal nerve.
Vallate papillae are supplied by glossopharyngeal nerve.
All its muscles are supplied by hypoglossal nerve.

questions.text: 2. Cancer in tip of tongue spreads to:
questions.explanation: The tongue tip drains bilaterally to submental nodes, so a tip lesion can enlarge them. More posterior and lateral regions have different submandibular or deep cervical drainage.

questions.text: 20. Taste sensations from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue are carried by:
questions.explanation: Chorda tympani carries anterior tongue taste with CN VII fibers that join the lingual nerve; lingual nerve alone carries general sensation.

questions.text: 49- metastasis to submental lymph nodes suggesting cancer in
questions.explanation: Lymph from the tongue tip drains first to the submental nodes, making them a likely early site of spread from a tip lesion.

questions.text: 9- taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue carried by
questions.explanation: Taste from the anterior two-thirds travels with chorda tympani (facial nerve), which joins the lingual nerve. The lingual nerve carries touch, pain and temperature from that region.

questions.text: 45- taste from tip of tongue is carried on
questions.explanation: The tongue tip is in the anterior two-thirds, whose taste fibers travel in chorda tympani, a facial nerve branch; CN IX serves posterior taste.

questions.text: 27. The muscle which protrudes the tongue is:
questions.explanation: Genioglossus is the main protruder: its fibers draw the tongue forward, unlike hyoglossus and styloglossus, which chiefly depress or retract it.

questions.text: 22- which of the following nerves carry taste from tip of tongue
questions.explanation: The facial nerve carries taste from the tongue tip through chorda tympani, which joins the lingual nerve. General sensation there is carried by the lingual branch of V3.

questions.text:
Loss of sensation from the posterior third of the tongue is most likely due to injury
of what nerve?
questions.explanation: CN IX supplies both general sensation and taste from most of the posterior third; anterior sensation uses lingual nerve and chorda tympani pathways.

questions.text: 15. The first lymph node receiving lymphatic drainage from the most posterior portion of the tongue is the:
questions.explanation: The posterior tongue drains chiefly to deep cervical nodes, especially the jugulodigastric node; the tip instead drains to submental nodes.

questions.text: 6. Loss of taste sensation from the vallate papillae is due to injury of:
questions.explanation: Vallate papillae lie just anterior to the sulcus terminalis but are supplied for taste by glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), like the posterior third of the tongue.

questions.text:
ANA1: Loss of sensation from the posterior third of the tongue is most likely due to injury
of what nerve?
questions.explanation: CN IX supplies sensation to the posterior third; anterior tongue sensation instead uses V3/VII pathways.

questions.text: 23- muscle that increase the convexity of dorsum of tongue
questions.explanation: The inferior longitudinal muscle shortens the tongue and curls its tip downward, increasing the convexity of the dorsum; superior longitudinal action curls the tip upward.

questions.text: 11. An ulcer at the tip of the tongue can cause the enlargement of:
questions.explanation: The tongue tip drains to submental nodes, often on both sides because lymphatic channels cross the midline. This explains nodal enlargement from a tip ulcer.

List the extrinsic & intrinsic muscles of the tongue
questions.explanation: Extrinsic muscles reposition the tongue; intrinsic longitudinal, transverse, and vertical muscles change its shape. CN XII supplies all except palatoglossus, which receives vagal plexus fibers.

questions.text: 42- only muscle in tongue Which is supplied by vagus
questions.explanation: Palatoglossus is the sole tongue muscle not innervated by CN XII; vagal fibers reach it through the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.text: 1. Sensations from the posterior 1/3 of the tongue are carried by:
questions.explanation: Glossopharyngeal nerve supplies both general sensation and taste to most of the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds use lingual nerve for general sensation and chorda tympani for taste.

questions.text: 46- tongue deviation to Rt side is suggesting for injury to
questions.explanation: Right tongue deviation on protrusion indicates right hypoglossal weakness: intact left genioglossus pushes toward the weak side.

questions.text: What is sensory supply of Ant. ⅔ / post. ⅓ and vallate papillae / most posterior part of tounge
questions.explanation: The tongue’s sensory territories reflect distinct cranial nerves: V3 lingual nerve for anterior general sensation, VII chorda tympani for anterior taste, IX for posterior third, and X at the epiglottic root.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior two thirds: general sensation by lingual mandibular branch; taste by chorda tympani facial branch. Posterior third and vallate papillae: both by glossopharyngeal. Most posterior part: vagus through internal laryngeal branch.

questions.text: 29-33. Match the muscle in the left column with its appropriate action in the right column:
questions.explanation: These actions reflect each muscle's pull: genioglossus protrudes, hyoglossus depresses, styloglossus retracts, and palatoglossus elevates the posterior tongue; intrinsic muscles alter its shape.

questions.text: 5. The nerve that carries taste sensation from posterior 1/3 of tongue is:
questions.explanation: CN IX carries posterior-third taste; chorda tympani carries anterior taste, and lingual nerve carries anterior general sensation.

questions.text: 26. Hypoglossal nerve supplies all muscles of tongue EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Palatoglossus is the exception because vagal motor fibers reach it through the pharyngeal plexus; the remaining intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles are supplied by CN XII.

questions.text:
Question 42 :A patient opened his mouth widely while yawing, after which he
couldn't close his mouth.
questions.explanation: The open-mouth position can displace the mandibular condyle anterior to the articular eminence, preventing closure. This is an anterior dislocation of the temporomandibular joint.

subQuestions.text: a. Name the joint affected and its type.
subQuestions.explanation: The mandibular condyle can dislocate anterior to the articular eminence during wide opening, locking the synovial TMJ open.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
The joint affected isT.M.J (tempromandibular joint)
Type: synovial, bi-condylar

subQuestions.text: b. List ligament of the joint which ligament is important right functionally?
subQuestions.explanation: The temporomandibular joint is reinforced by lateral (temporomandibular), sphenomandibular, and stylomandibular ligaments; the lateral ligament is the main stabilizing thickening of the capsule.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
Ligaments of the joint:
1. Tempro-mandibular ligament “the important right functionally”
2. stylo-mandibular ligament
3. Spheno-mandibular ligament

subQuestions.text: c. Mention the nerve supply of the joint.
subQuestions.explanation: The temporomandibular joint receives sensory innervation chiefly from the auriculotemporal nerve, with a contribution from the masseteric nerve, both branches of V3.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Nerve supply: Auriculotemporal& masseteric nerves.

questions.text: 21. The nerve supply of the palatopharyngeus muscle is the:
questions.explanation: Palatopharyngeus receives motor supply through the vagal pharyngeal plexus; CN IX chiefly supplies stylopharyngeus.
options: External laryngeal branch of Vagus nerve.

questions.text: 38. Paralysis of muscles of soft palate leads to:
questions.explanation: The soft palate elevates to close the nasopharynx during swallowing and speech; paralysis can therefore cause nasal regurgitation, dysphagia, and hypernasal speech.

questions.text: 47- muscle responsible for elevation of soft palate is supplied by
questions.explanation: Most soft-palate muscles are supplied through the pharyngeal plexus by vagal motor fibers (traditionally described as cranial accessory fibers joining CN X). Tensor veli palatini is the exception, supplied by V3.

questions.text: 44. Oropharyngeal isthmus is formed by:
questions.explanation: Palatoglossal arches form the anterior boundary of the oropharyngeal isthmus and approximate to narrow the oral passage.

questions.text: 39. The soft palate:
questions.explanation: The soft palate forms a movable partition between nasopharynx and oropharynx. Palatoglossus mainly narrows the oropharyngeal opening, and the horizontal palatine plates belong to the hard palate.
options: Is supplied by greater palatine nerves.
Is supplied by motor branches from glossopharyngeal nerve.
Contains the horizontal plates of palatine bone.

questions.text: The following muscles have the same nerve supply except
questions.explanation: Stylopharyngeus is the exception because it is supplied directly by glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); most other pharyngeal muscles receive vagal motor fibers via the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.text: 40. The muscle that winds around the pterygoid hamulus is the:
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini tendon hooks around the pterygoid hamulus, redirecting its pull to tense the palate and open the auditory tube.

questions.text: 11- tendon hooking around ptrygoid hammulous
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini tendon turns around the pterygoid hamulus, which acts as a pulley before the tendon spreads into the palatine aponeurosis.

questions.text: 14- most anterior part of palate is sensory supplied by
questions.explanation: The nasopalatine nerve supplies mucosa of the anterior hard palate behind the incisors. The greater palatine nerve supplies most of the remaining hard palate.

questions.text: 42. The scaphoid fossa gives origin to:
questions.explanation: The scaphoid fossa of the medial pterygoid plate gives origin to tensor veli palatini.

questions.text: 4. The palatine aponeurosis is the flattened tendon of:
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini tendon fans out as the palatine aponeurosis; its hamulus pulley redirects the tendon to tense the soft palate.

questions.text: 24- the muscle that close the oropharyngeal isthmus is innervated by
questions.explanation: Palatopharyngeus helps narrow the oropharyngeal isthmus by elevating the pharynx and drawing the palatopharyngeal arches together; its motor supply is via the vagal pharyngeal plexus.

questions.text: 36. Muscles of soft palate are supplied mainly by:
questions.explanation: In the classical terminology used by this key, cranial accessory fibers join the vagus and supply most soft-palate muscles through the plexus; tensor veli palatini is supplied by V3.

questions.text: 34. Palatine glands derive their parasympathetic innervation from:
questions.explanation: Preganglionic facial parasympathetic fibers synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion, then travel with palatine nerves to stimulate palatal glands.

questions.text:
Previous Essay Questions
1. List the nerve supply of the palate.
questions.explanation: The hard palate receives sensory input mainly through greater palatine nerve, with the anterior part via nasopalatine nerve; lesser palatine nerves supply soft-palate sensation. Most palate muscles are vagal via the pharyngeal plexus, except tensor veli palatini (V3).
questions.modelAnswer: Hard palate: greater palatine nerve, with the anterior part supplied by nasopalatine nerve. Soft palate: sensory fibres through lesser palatine nerves; motor supply to all muscles through cranial accessory fibres joining vagus, except tensor palati through the mandibular nerve (nerve to medial pterygoid). Taste from soft palate: greater petrosal nerve.

questions.text: 15- tensor palati supplied by which
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini is the exception: it receives V3 via the nerve to medial pterygoid, rather than the vagal pharyngeal plexus.

questions.text: 41. The palatine muscle that is not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus is:
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini is the exception: it receives motor supply from the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (V3), while the other palate muscles are supplied via the vagal pharyngeal plexus.

questions.text: 35. Taste from the palate is carried by fibers of:
questions.explanation: Taste from the palate travels with the greater petrosal nerve, a facial-nerve pathway. This differs from palatal general sensation, which is carried by branches of V2.

questions.text: 50- palatine apponeurosis is insertion of
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini spreads into and tenses the palatine aponeurosis; palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus arise from it.

questions.text: 37. The sensory nerves to mucous membrane of hard palate are derived from:
questions.explanation: The hard palate receives general sensation from the greater palatine nerve posteriorly and the nasopalatine (sphenopalatine) nerve anteriorly; lesser palatine nerves chiefly serve the soft palate.
options: Greater palatine nerve & lesser palatine nerve.

questions.text: 25- which of the following muscles takes origin from palatine apponeurosis
questions.explanation: Palatopharyngeus arises partly from the palatine aponeurosis and descends into the pharyngeal wall. Tensor and levator veli palatini instead have different origins and roles in palatal movement.

questions.text: 10- muscle responsible for closure of Oropharyngeal isthmus
questions.explanation: Palatoglossus approximates the palatoglossal arches to constrict the oropharyngeal isthmus.

questions.text: 43. Regarding pharynx, all statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The pharynx ends at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, around C6, where it continues as esophagus; C4 is too high.
options: It ends at the level of fourth cervical vertebra.
Its lymphatics drain into deep cervical lymph nodes.
Its constrictors are supplied by pharyngeal plexus.
Stylopharyngeus is supplied by glossopharyngeal nerve.

questions.text: 31. The muscles attached to the pterygomandibular raphe are supplied by:
questions.explanation: The raphe links buccinator anteriorly and superior pharyngeal constrictor posteriorly. Buccinator is supplied by facial nerve; the constrictor receives vagal motor fibers, historically attributed to the cranial accessory component.

questions.text: 3. Inflammation of the palatine tonsil leads to the enlargement of:
questions.explanation: Palatine tonsil lymph drains chiefly to the jugulodigastric node, a common enlarged node in tonsillitis.

questions.text:
Question 10A 54 years old man presented with a tumor in the posterior cranial
fossa. The neurologist wanted to check the integrity of the 9th , 10th and 11th cranial
nerves.
questions.explanation: The case tests CN IX–XI at the jugular foramen: vagal palatal movement, glossopharyngeal sensory branches, and the traditional cranial/spinal accessory descriptions distinguish the nerves and their functions.

subQuestions.text: a. How can you test for integrity of vagus nerve ?
subQuestions.explanation: Ask the patient to say “ah” and observe palatal elevation and uvular position. A vagal palsy weakens the palate on that side, so the uvula is pulled toward the intact side.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
examine arches of palate and uvula , In lesion there is ipsilateral flattening of
arches and uvula pointing to the normal side.

subQuestions.text: b. Enumerate sensory branches of glossopharyngeal nerve.
subQuestions.explanation: CN IX branches reach the tympanic cavity, carotid sinus/body, pharynx, posterior tongue, and tonsil; these branches explain the sensory territories tested.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
1) Tympanic branch: sensory to middle ear and auditory tube .
2) Carotid branch: to carotid body and sinus .
3) pharyngeal branch: to pharynx
4) Lingual branch: to posteriot 1/3 of tongue
5) Tonsillar branch: to palatine tonsil and soft palate .

subQuestions.text: c. Name the muscle(s) supplied by the accessory nerve
subQuestions.explanation: In the standard anatomy account, the spinal accessory component supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; cranial root fibers join the vagus and are described with vagal motor supply to pharynx, palate, and larynx.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
1) Cranial accessory nerve:
- muscles of palate, pharynx and larynx through pharyngeal and recurrent laryngeal
branches of vagus
2) Spinal accessory nerve:
- Trapezius muscle.
-Sternomastoid muscle

questions.text: 23. As regards the oesophagus, all the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The exception is incorrect: the cervical esophagus is supplied chiefly by inferior thyroid arterial branches, not superior thyroid arteries. It begins at C6 and is related to the recurrent laryngeal nerves.
options: It lies between trachea & prevertebral layer of fascia.
It begins at level of lower border of cricoid cartilage.
In the groove between it & trachea, lies recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Thoracic duct is related to its left side.
It is supplied by superior thyroid arteries.

questions.text: 47. The blood supply of the palatine tonsil is derived from:
questions.explanation: Tonsillar blood comes from several sources, including facial, ascending pharyngeal, and lingual branches, so “all” fits.
options: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

questions.text: 49. As regards the palatine tonsils, all are correct EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The tonsillar capsule is on its lateral (deep) surface, separating it from the superior constrictor; the medial surface faces the oropharynx and is crypt-bearing.
options: Reaches its maximum size during childhood.
Is related laterally to superior constrictor muscle.
Has a capsule on its medial aspect.
Drains into the jugulodigastric lymph nodes.

questions.text: 25. The lingual tonsil:
questions.explanation: The lingual tonsil is lymphoid tissue on the posterior third of the tongue, behind the sulcus terminalis. It is part of Waldeyer's ring.
options: Is found in posterior 1/3 of tongue.
Is found in posterior 2/3 of tongue.
Is found in anterior 2/3 of tongue.
Causes no irregularities of the overlying mucous membrane.

questions.text: 56- which of the following muscles Not inserted into posterior border of thyroid cartilage
questions.explanation: Stylopharyngeus ascends between the constrictors; the middle constrictor attaches to hyoid and stylohyoid ligament, not thyroid cartilage.

questions.text: 18. As regards the oesophagus, all the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The esophagus passes through the right crus at T10, not the central tendon; the central tendon is pierced by the inferior vena cava at T8.
options: It is crossed by the left main bronchus.
Has the left atrium as one of its anterior relations.
Pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm.
Crosses in front of the lower part of the descending thoracic aorta.
Has a portosystemic anastomosis in its lower part.

questions.text: .  Mention the components of the pharyngeal plexus.
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal plexus combines vagal motor fibers, glossopharyngeal sensory fibers, and sympathetic vasomotor fibers. Stylopharyngeus is supplied directly by CN IX rather than the plexus.
questions.modelAnswer:
1-Pharyngeal branch of Vagus (cranial accessory.): mainly motor.
2-Pharyngeal branch of glossopharyngeal: mainly sensory to mucosa of oropharynx.
3- Pharyngeal branch of sup. cervical sympathetic ganglion: mainly vasomotor

questions.text: 19. The pain from the palatine tonsil is carried by:
questions.explanation: CN IX carries tonsillar sensation and referred pain; its irritation can make tonsillitis pain radiate toward the ear.

questions.text: 46. As regards the palatine tonsil, all the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsil lies in the oropharynx and is related laterally to the superior constrictor, not the middle constrictor; its capsule is lateral and it forms part of Waldeyer’s ring.
options: It is related to middle constrictor of pharynx.
It drains into jugulodigastric lymph nodes.
It lies in lateral wall of the oropharynx.
Its capsule is confined to its lateral wall.
It forms a part of Waldeyer's ring.

questions.text: 19- salpingeopharyngeus muscle is innervated by
questions.explanation: Salpingopharyngeus is a pharyngeal muscle supplied by vagal motor fibers through the pharyngeal plexus. Stylopharyngeus is the notable CN IX exception.

questions.text: 18- longitudinal muscles of pharynx inserted into
questions.explanation: The three longitudinal pharyngeal muscles descend from the skull or styloid region and insert into the pharyngeal wall and thyroid cartilage, elevating the pharynx during swallowing.

questions.text: 22. As regards the oesophagus, all the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cervical esophagus begins at C6, at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, rather than C4. The other listed relations and its inferior-thyroid arterial supply are consistent with its anatomy.
options: It starts at level of 4th cervical vertebra.
It lies in the median plane at its beginning.
It is related to recurrent laryngeal nerve.
It is related, on its left side, to the thoracic duct.
It is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery in the neck.

questions.text: 59- Regarding Oropharynx select the incorrect statement
questions.explanation: The oropharynx is behind the palatoglossal arch at C2–C3 and is chiefly sensory via CN IX, making vagal sensory supply the incorrect statement.
options: supplied sensory by pharyngeal branch of vagus
supplied sensory by pharyngeal branch of glossopharyngeal

questions.text: ANA2: The following muscles have the same nerve supply except
questions.explanation: Stylopharyngeus is the exception: it is supplied by CN IX, whereas the other pharyngeal muscles receive vagal motor fibers through the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.text: 9. The artery that is most-likely injured if the tonsillar bed is pierced during tonsillectomy is:
questions.explanation: The facial artery gives the tonsillar branch that reaches the palatine tonsil and is a key vessel in the tonsillar bed. Injury there can cause substantial bleeding.

questions.text: 13. The nerve that lies between the middle & the inferior constrictors of pharynx is:
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and enters between middle and inferior constrictors, carrying supraglottic sensation.

questions.text: 55- Nerve in the gap between middle & inferior constrictors of pharynx (3rd) gap is
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve, a superior laryngeal branch of CN X, enters through the gap between the middle and inferior constrictors to supply laryngeal mucosal sensation.

questions.text: 52. Circopharyngeus muscle:
questions.explanation: Cricopharyngeus stays tonically contracted between swallows, preventing air from entering the esophagus during inspiration. It relaxes briefly to let the food bolus pass.
options: Is part of middle constrictor of pharynx.
Receives fibers from the external laryngeal nerve.
Acts as a sphincter for air.

questions.text: 44- all the following muscles supplied by pharyngeal plexus Except
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini is supplied through V3; the other listed soft-palate muscles receive fibers through the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.text: 27. A surgeon decides to divide the anterior vagal trunk (vagotomy) as it lies on the anterior surface the abdominal part of the esophagus as therapy for a chronic gastric ulcer not responding to medical treatment. Which of the following is likely to result from this procedure?
questions.explanation: The anterior vagal trunk carries parasympathetic fibers to gastric mucosa and glands; cutting it reduces vagal secretomotor drive, while the laryngeal branches leave higher in the neck.
options: A loss of secretomotor nerve supply to the mucosal glands of the stomach
Hoarse voice because of paralysis of the intrinsic muscles of the larynx on the left side
Increased heart rate because of decreased parasympathetic input to the cardiac plexus
Incontinence because of an absence of parasympathetic input to the bladder
Compromised input into the greater splanchnic nerves

questions.text: 14. The pharyngeal muscle attached to the oblique line of thyroid cartilage is supplied by the:
questions.explanation: The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage gives attachment to the inferior constrictor (thyropharyngeus). Its motor supply is vagal through the pharyngeal plexus, traditionally described as including cranial accessory fibers.

questions.text: 56. Mucous membrane of laryngopharynx is mainly supplied by:
questions.explanation: Internal laryngeal CN X supplies most sensation above the vocal folds, including laryngopharyngeal mucosa; recurrent laryngeal fibers serve below.

questions.text: 51. As regards the nasopharynx, chose INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx is roofed by the sphenoid and occipital skull base, not the cribriform plate; the latter forms part of the anterior cranial fossa floor.
options: It is the widest part of the pharynx.
It is roofed by the cribriform plate of ethmoid.
It receives the openings of the Eustachian tubes.
It communicates with the oropharynx by the pharyngeal isthmus.
Its sloping roof shows the pharyngeal tonsil.

questions.text: 50. Nasal cavity is closed off from oropharynx during swallowing by:
questions.explanation: During swallowing, levator veli palatini elevates the soft palate while tensor tenses it, sealing the nasopharynx so food does not enter the nasal cavity.
options: Contraction of tensor and levator palati muscles.

questions.text: 58- during tonsillitis pain is carried by
questions.explanation: Glossopharyngeal tonsillar branches transmit the characteristic sensory pain of tonsillitis.

questions.text: 48. Which of the following vessels is most liable to injury during a tonsillectomy operation:
questions.explanation: The paratonsillar vein lies close to the tonsillar capsule and is commonly encountered during tonsillectomy, so it is a frequent source of operative bleeding.

questions.text: 16. The sensory nerve supply of the oropharynx is the:
questions.explanation: The oropharynx receives general sensory innervation chiefly from CN IX via its pharyngeal branches. The nasopharynx is mainly V2 and the laryngopharynx mainly vagal.

questions.text: 18. Carcinoma of the lower end of the esophagus affecting both vagus nerves might cause serious disorders of gut motility as far as the:
questions.explanation: Vagal parasympathetic supply extends to the left colic flexure near the splenic flexure; pelvic splanchnics supply more distal colon.
options: Site of attachment of the vitello-intestinal duct.

questions.text: 17- muscle is important for preventing air entry to oesophagus
questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus forms the upper esophageal sphincter and stays tonically contracted between swallows, limiting air entry and reflux into the pharynx.

questions.text: 7. A structure that lies between the superior & middle constrictors of pharynx:
questions.explanation: Stylopharyngeus passes between the superior and middle constrictors as it enters the pharyngeal wall. Other structures pass through different gaps between constrictors.

questions.text: 55. Mucous membrane of nasopharynx is supplied by:
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal mucosal sensation is carried largely by the pharyngeal branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion (V2), unlike vagal laryngopharyngeal supply.

questions.text: 17. The sites of constrictions of the oesophagus include all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Normal esophageal narrowings occur at its origin, where the aortic arch and left main bronchus cross, and at the diaphragmatic hiatus; the descending aorta crossing is not a standard constriction.
options: Where the aortic arch crosses it.
Where the left bronchus crosses anterior to it.
Where it crosses anterior to the descending aorta.
Where it passes through the diaphragm.

questions.text: Case 2: A 50-year-old male started to complain from difficulty in swallowing few weeks ago. He had a computerized tomography scan on the neck done. It revealed the presence of a swelling (most-likely cancer) near the jugular foramen.
questions.explanation: A mass at the jugular foramen can affect CN IX and X, impairing pharyngeal sensation and most swallowing muscles; the traditional cranial accessory component joins X for motor supply. Pharyngeal sensation varies by level: V2 above, IX in the oropharynx, and X below.

subQuestions.text: 1. In this patient, which nerves could be involved & led to dysphagia?
subQuestions.explanation: A jugular-foramen mass can injure IX and X: IX provides pharyngeal sensation and stylopharyngeus motor supply; X supplies most pharyngeal muscles.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) and CN X (vagus), with the historically described cranial component of CN XI, may be involved at the jugular foramen. CN IX supplies pharyngeal sensation and the stylopharyngeus muscle; CN X supplies most pharyngeal muscles through the pharyngeal plexus. The cranial accessory component joins the vagus for pharyngeal motor supply. The spinal accessory component supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and does not itself provide this pharyngeal motor supply.

subQuestions.text: 2. Describe the motor & sensory nerve supply of the pharynx.
subQuestions.explanation: Pharyngeal motor innervation is predominantly vagal through the plexus, with stylopharyngeus as the CN IX exception; sensory territory shifts from V2 above to IX in the oropharynx and X below.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Motor: Pharyngeal plexus (CN X, historically incorporating cranial root of CN XI) supplies all muscles except stylopharyngeus (supplied by CN IX). Sensory: Nasopharynx (V2), Oropharynx (CN IX), Laryngopharynx (CN X).

questions.text: 45. The pharyngeal muscle innervated by glossopharyngeal nerve is the:
questions.explanation: Stylopharyngeus is the sole pharyngeal muscle supplied directly by CN IX. The constrictors and most other pharyngeal muscles are supplied through the vagal pharyngeal plexus.

questions.text: 54. Which of the following contribute(s) branches to the pharyngeal plexus of nerves:
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal plexus receives vagal motor, glossopharyngeal sensory, and sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion.

questions.text: List three structures lying anterior to the thoracic esophagus.
questions.explanation: The thoracic esophagus is anteriorly related to the trachea and left main bronchus above, then the pericardium and left atrium below; these relations help localize mediastinal compression.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Trachea.
2. Tracheal bifurcation.
3. Right pulmonary a.
4. Left main bronchus.
5. Oblique sinus of pericardium.
6. Diaphragm.

questions.text: 53. The middle constrictor of pharynx arises partly from:
questions.explanation: The middle constrictor arises in part from the stylohyoid ligament and hyoid bone. Its fibers sweep posteriorly to meet their counterparts in the pharyngeal raphe.

questions.text: 10. The tonsillar artery is a branch of:
questions.explanation: The tonsillar artery is the tonsil-directed branch of the facial artery; other arteries contribute separate branches.

questions.text: 36. The following structures pass through the esophageal hiatus in the diaphragm except:
questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus at T10 transmits both vagal trunks, esophageal vessels and lymphatics, but the left phrenic nerve does not pass through it.
options: Branches of the left gastric artery
A tributary of the portal vein

questions.text: 21- the oropharynx lies opposite to which vertebral level
questions.explanation: The oropharynx extends from the soft palate to the upper epiglottis and lies roughly opposite C2–C3. The laryngopharynx continues inferiorly.

questions.text: 12. The palatine tonsils derive its main blood supply from:
questions.explanation: The facial artery, through its tonsillar branch, is the principal source of palatine tonsil blood, though several arteries contribute.

questions.text: What are the relations of thoracic duct to the esophagus
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct ascends behind the esophagus on its right, crosses posteriorly near T5, then continues on its left toward the thoracic inlet.
questions.modelAnswer: Thoracic duct ascends right of oesophagus to T5, crosses behind it there, then ascends on its left.

questions.text: 8. Which group(s) of lymph nodes drain(s) the palatine tonsil?
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsil drains chiefly to the jugulodigastric (upper deep cervical) node. This node may enlarge during tonsillar infection.

questions.text: 57- muscle originated from oblique line of thyroid cartilage is supplied by
questions.explanation: The thyroid oblique line gives origin to thyropharyngeus, part of the inferior constrictor. Its pharyngeal plexus motor supply travels with the vagus; older course terminology calls these cranial accessory fibers.

questions.text: 4- structure separating parotid& submandibular glands
questions.explanation: The stylomandibular ligament separates the deep part of the parotid gland from the submandibular gland and helps define the passage between them.

questions.text: 36. The nerve from which preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland originate is:
questions.explanation: Preganglionic secretomotor fibers for the parotid originate with CN IX, then synapse in the otic ganglion; postganglionic fibers reach the gland via auriculotemporal nerve.

questions.text: 2. The parotid duct opens opposite the:
questions.explanation: The parotid duct crosses masseter, turns inward through buccinator, and opens opposite the upper second molar.

questions.text: 6. Which of the following is present inside the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve passes through the parotid and divides there, but does not provide the gland’s secretomotor supply; glossopharyngeal parasympathetic fibers reach it by another route.
options: Motor & parasympathetic parts of facial nerve.
Parasympathetic & sensory parts of facial nerve.

questions.text: 2- capsule of parotid supplied by
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve, from C2–C3, supplies sensation to the parotid fascia and capsule. It is not the gland's secretomotor pathway.

questions.text: 30- which of the following is Not content of parotid gland
questions.explanation: Facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery traverse the parotid; great auricular nerve runs superficially over it.

questions.text: 1- preganglionic parasympathetic to parotid gland carried by which of the following nerve
questions.explanation: Glossopharyngeal preganglionic fibers reach the otic ganglion through the lesser petrosal nerve; the auriculotemporal nerve carries the postganglionic fibers onward.

questions.text: 29- structure piercing posteromedial surface of parotid
questions.explanation: The facial nerve enters the parotid through its posteromedial surface and forms a plexus within it before dividing into terminal facial branches.

questions.text: 40- parasympathetic pathway to parotid gland doesn’t contain
questions.explanation: Parotid secretomotor fibers follow IX → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve; great auricular nerve is sensory.

questions.text: Mention structures within the parotid gland.
questions.explanation: Within the parotid, the facial nerve is most superficial, the retromandibular vein lies deeper, and the external carotid artery is deepest; this order matters during gland surgery.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. ECA (most deep) and its 2 terminal branches (= maxillary and superficial temporal arteries).
2. Retromandibular Vein: is formed inside parotid gland by union of maxillary and
superficial temporal veins. It divides into anterior and posterior divisions that leave the
gland through its apex.
3. Facial Nerve: (most superficial) enters through the posteromedial surface and divides
the gland into five terminal branches:
temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular and cervical.
4. Deep parotid L.N.: embedded within its substance.

questions.text: 17. Which of the following is related to the posteromedial surface of the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: The carotid sheath lies posteromedial to the parotid, alongside its deep relations. The gland also relates to the styloid apparatus and posterior belly of digastric in this region.

questions.text: 5. Relations of parotid gland.
questions.explanation: The parotid relates anteriorly to masseter, posteriorly to mastoid/SCM, and medially to pharynx; within it, facial nerve, vein, and artery lie superficial-to-deep.
questions.modelAnswer: Apex: posterior digastric belly; cervical facial-nerve branch between retromandibular vein divisions. Base: external acoustic meatus and temporomandibular joint, crossed by temporal facial-nerve branch, superficial temporal vessels and auriculotemporal nerve. Anterior border on masseter emits zygomatic facial branch, transverse facial artery, accessory gland, duct, buccal and mandibular facial branches. Posterior border relates to sternomastoid; medial border to pharynx. Superficial surface relates to skin and superficial/deep fascia. Anteromedial surface: mandibular ramus with masseter and medial pterygoid. Posteromedial surface: mastoid/sternomastoid/posterior digastric, styloid with stylohyoid/styloglossus/stylopharyngeus, and carotid sheath (ICA, IJV, vagus); pierced by external carotid below and facial nerve above.

questions.text: 28- all the following structures leave parotid gland from base Except
questions.explanation: The buccal facial branch exits along the gland’s anterior border, whereas superficial temporal vessels and the temporal branch approach or leave superiorly.

questions.text: 35. Regarding parotid gland, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The exception is the great auricular nerve: it carries sensory fibers to the capsule, not secretomotor fibers. Parotid secretion follows CN IX through the otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve.
options: It is the largest of the salivary glands.
Its anteromedial surface is related to mandible.
Its secretomotor fibers reach it through the great auricular nerve.

questions.text: 7. The secretomotor supply of the parotid gland is through the:
questions.explanation: CN IX begins the parotid secretomotor route; fibers relay in the otic ganglion and reach the gland via auriculotemporal nerve, while great auricular is sensory.

questions.text: 1. The most superficial structure inside the parotid gland is:
questions.explanation: From superficial to deep, the key intraparotid structures are facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery, placing the nerve at greatest surgical risk.

questions.text: 3. The deepest structure in the parotid gland is the:
questions.explanation: Within the parotid, the external carotid artery is deepest; the retromandibular vein lies between it and the more superficial facial nerve.

questions.text: 32. Regarding the parotid gland, all statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve supplies cutaneous sensation rather than secretion; parotid secretomotor fibers arrive via the IX–otic ganglion–auriculotemporal route.
options: Its duct opens in vestibule of mouth opposite upper 2nd molar tooth.
Facial nerve enters its postero-medial surface.
Is enclosed by deep cervical fascia.
Receives secretomotor fibers from great auricular nerve.
Is separated from submandibular gland by stylomandibular ligament.

questions.text: 14. Pain from capsule of parotid gland is carried by:
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies sensation over the parotid region and its fascia; auriculotemporal fibers mainly supply the gland and adjacent auricle.

questions.text: 31. Regarding the parotid gland, select the correct answer:
questions.explanation: Great auricular nerve supplies sensation over the parotid region and its capsule. The facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery are the principal structures traversing the gland.
options: It extends anteriorly to the styloid process.
Facial nerve enters its anteromedial syrface.
Auriculotemporal N. carries its preganglionic parasympathetic supply.
Great auricular nerve carry sensory fibers to its capsule.
Its duct lies above zygomatic arch.

questions.text: 8. The deepest structure within the parotid gland is the:
questions.explanation: External carotid artery is the deepest major parotid content, with retromandibular vein and facial nerve progressively more superficial.

questions.text: 12. Which of the following contains parasympathetic postganglionic fibers?
questions.explanation: After synapsing in the otic ganglion, secretomotor fibers hitchhike on the auriculotemporal nerve (V3) to reach the parotid gland.

questions.text: 16. All the following are present inside parotid gland EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve runs superficial to the gland, supplying skin and capsule, rather than passing through its substance. The facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery do pass within it.

questions.text: 2. Discuss the parasympathetic nerve supply of the parotid gland.
questions.explanation: Preganglionic IX fibers reach the otic ganglion through tympanic plexus and lesser petrosal nerve; postganglionic fibers hitchhike on auriculotemporal nerve.
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior salivatory nucleus → glossopharyngeal nerve → tympanic branch → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion (preganglionic relay) → postganglionic fibres in auriculotemporal nerve → gland.

questions.text: Case 2: A young inexperienced doctor opened a parotid abscess by making a vertical incision. After the surgery, the patient was unable to raise the eyebrow on the operated side.
questions.explanation: The eyebrow weakness localizes to the temporal facial branch crossing the parotid; parotid incisions should follow the branching nerve’s course, with the case also testing gland contents and duct landmarks.

subQuestions.text: 1. Which nerve was injured? Mention its branch that was cut.
subQuestions.explanation: Weakness raising the eyebrow localizes to the temporal branch of the facial nerve, which supplies frontalis. A parotid-region incision can injure these superficial terminal branches.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Facial nerve - temporal branch (that supplies the frontal bellies of occipito-frontalis muscle which raise the eyebrows).

subQuestions.text: 2. What could the doctor do to avoid the lesion?
subQuestions.explanation: The facial nerve branches fan across the parotid; an incision aligned transversely with their course reduces the chance of cutting vertically crossing branches.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The doctor had to make a transverse incision (to avoid the injury of the branches of facial nerve).

subQuestions.text: 3. What are the structures present within the substance of the parotid gland? Mention how they enter & leave the gland.
subQuestions.explanation: The parotid contains the facial nerve superficially, retromandibular vein centrally, and external carotid artery deeply; the nerve branches exit mainly anteriorly, while the artery divides into superficial temporal and maxillary branches.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Structures within parotid gland: a. Facial N. → enters from posteromedial surface → divides into its 5 terminal branches → Its temporal branch leaves from upper end, its zygomatic, buccal & mandibular branches leave from anterior border & its cervical branch leaves through its lower end. b. Retromandibular vein → is formed inside the gland & divides into 2 divisions inside the gland. The 2 divisions leave the gland at its lower end. c. External carotid artery → enters from posteromedial surface → divides into maxillary artery (which leaves from anteromedial surface) & superficial temporal artery (which leaves from upper end). d. Deep parotid LNs.

subQuestions.text: 4. Mention the surface anatomy of the parotid duct.
subQuestions.explanation: The duct is traced along the middle third of a line from the tragus toward a point between the nose and upper lip, then turns medially through buccinator to open in the cheek.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Middle 1/3 of line joining a point midway between ala of nose & upper lip & tragus of ear.

questions.text: 11. Anterior border of parotid gland lies on:
questions.explanation: The anterior parotid border overlies masseter, across which the duct travels before piercing buccinator.

questions.text: 3- which of the following cosidered as the deepest structure in parotid gland
questions.explanation: The maxillary artery is the deep terminal branch of the external carotid artery within the gland; the facial nerve is superficial and the retromandibular vein lies between them.

questions.text:
Question 45 :A young inexperienced doctor opened a parotid abscess by making a
vertical incision, the patient became unable to raise the eyebrow on the operated
side.
questions.explanation: The eyebrow weakness indicates temporal-branch facial nerve injury; parotid structures are arranged from superficial to deep as facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery. Incisions parallel to facial branches reduce nerve injury.

subQuestions.text: a. Which nerve was injured? Specifically, mention the branch that was cut.
subQuestions.explanation: The temporal facial nerve branch crosses the upper parotid toward frontalis; injury weakens forehead elevation and eyebrow raising.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The nerve injured: Temporal branch of facial n.

subQuestions.text: b. What could the doctor do to avoid the lesion?
subQuestions.explanation: Parotid skin incisions should run transversely or parallel to facial nerve branches, reducing the chance that a vertical cut crosses and severs them.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
The lesion could be avoided by making transverse incision & parallel to terminal
branches of facial n.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the structures present within the substance of the parotid gland? Mention how they enter and leave the gland.
subQuestions.explanation: The main intraparotid structures are facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery, arranged superficial to deep. The facial nerve enters posteromedially and branches within the gland; the artery divides there, while the vein forms and then exits inferiorly.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
The structures present within the sunbstance of parotid:
Facial n. (most superficial): enters through posteromedial surface & divides the
gland to superficial & deep parts forming pes anserinus plexus & then divides to 5
terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular & cervical.
Retromandibular v.: formed inside the gland by union of maxillary & superficial
temporal v. then divides into anterior & posterior divisions that leave the gland
through its apex
ECA (most deep): enters through posteromedial surface of the gland & divides at
the level of neck of mandible into 2 terminal branches, maxillary & superficial
temporal arteries
Deep parotid L.N.: embedded within its substance

subQuestions.text: d. Mention the surface anatomy of the parotid duct.
subQuestions.explanation: The duct runs about a finger breadth below the zygomatic arch, along the middle of a line from tragus toward the point between the nose ala and upper lip.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
The surface anatomy parotid duct:
It lies 1 finger breadth below the zygomatic arch, it corresponds to middle 1/3 of a
line drawn from the tragus of ear to a point midway between ala of nose & upper lip

questions.text: 33. All are true regarding the parotid gland EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The parotid occupies the space between the mandibular ramus and mastoid/styloid region, not trapezius; its duct does pierce buccinator and its gland encloses facial nerve branches and nodes.
options: Is wedged between trapezius and mandible.
Is covered by investing layer of cervical fascia.
Has lymph nodes buried in its substance.
Its duct pierces buccinator to enter mouth.

questions.text: 10. The anterior border of parotid gland is related to:
questions.explanation: The transverse facial artery runs across the face over the masseter near the anterior border of the parotid. The parotid duct also emerges from this border and crosses the masseter.

questions.text: Explain the nerve supply of the parotid gland.
questions.explanation: Parotid secretion is driven by IX: tympanic branch/plexus → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve. Sympathetic fibers travel on the external carotid plexus; gland and capsule sensation come via auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves, respectively.
questions.modelAnswer:
1) Sympathetic (Vasomotor) supply: from a sympathetic plexus around ECA.
2) Parasympathetic (secretomotor) supply: Inferior salivatory nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve gives preganglionic parasympathetic fibers
through tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) which forms the tympanic plexus in the middle ear from which arises the lesser
petrosal nerve then it relays in the otic ganglion to give rise to postganglionic parasympathetic fibers join the auriculotemporal nerve to reach the
parotid gland.
3) Sensory to:
a. Gland from auriculotemporal nerve.
b. Capsule from great auricular nerve.

questions.text: 31- which of the following muscles is related to posteromedial surface of parotid
questions.explanation: The posterior belly of digastric is among the posteromedial relations of the parotid; masseter is on its lateral/anterior aspect.

questions.text: 1. Enumerate the structures inside parotid gland.
questions.explanation: From superficial to deep, the parotid contains facial nerve, retromandibular vein, then external carotid artery. The vein is formed within the gland; the artery divides there into maxillary and superficial temporal branches.
questions.modelAnswer: External carotid artery (deepest), dividing into maxillary and superficial temporal arteries; retromandibular vein, formed by maxillary and superficial temporal veins and dividing into anterior/posterior divisions; facial nerve (most superficial), forming pes anserinus and temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular and cervical terminal branches; deep parotid lymph nodes.

questions.text: 5. The artery that lies above parotid duct is a direct branch of:
questions.explanation: The transverse facial artery arises from the superficial temporal artery and runs above the parotid duct across the masseter.

questions.text: 27-post ganglionic secretomotor parasympathetic to parotid gland is carried by
questions.explanation: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers leave the otic ganglion and travel with the auriculotemporal nerve to stimulate parotid secretion.

questions.text: 15. Parotid duct pierces:
questions.explanation: The parotid duct turns medially after crossing the masseter and pierces buccinator to open into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar.

questions.text:
Question 43 :A patient developed a benign swelling of the parotid gland (superficial
lobe) the doctor decided to excise it
questions.explanation: Protect the facial nerve because it traverses the superficial parotid and is vulnerable in parotidectomy; its temporal and zygomatic branches serve forehead/orbicularis muscles. Secretomotor fibers arise from IX and relay in the otic ganglion.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most important structure that would the doctor take care of?
subQuestions.explanation: The facial nerve divides within the parotid and lies superficial to the vein and artery, so it is particularly vulnerable during superficial-lobe excision.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
The most important structure is facial nerve because it is the most superficial
structure in the gland.

subQuestions.text: b. Mention the distribution of its upper two branches
subQuestions.explanation: The temporal branch supplies frontalis, while the zygomatic branch supplies orbicularis oculi and nearby facial muscles. Both are terminal branches of the facial nerve within the parotid plexus.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
distribution of upper two branches of facial is:
1. Temporal to frontal belly of occiptofrontalis m. &orbiculrisocculi.
2. Zygomatic to orbicularis occuli m.

subQuestions.text: c. Mention the cranial nerve carrying parasympathetic supply to the gland and the ganglion of relay
subQuestions.explanation: CN IX is the preganglionic source of parotid parasympathetics; fibers synapse in the otic ganglion before reaching the gland via auriculotemporal nerve.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
Cranial n. carrying parasympathetic is glossopharyngeal (IX) &ganglion of relay
is otic ganglia.

questions.text: Case 1: A patient developed benign swelling of the parotid gland (superficial lobe) & the doctor decided to excise it.
questions.explanation: Superficial parotidectomy risks facial motor branches because they run through the gland; its secretomotor pathway begins with CN IX and relays in the otic ganglion.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the nerve that the doctor should take care of?
subQuestions.explanation: The facial nerve divides within the parotid into branches that supply the muscles of facial expression. These superficial branches are vulnerable during surgery on the gland.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Facial nerve.

subQuestions.text: b. List its terminal branches.
subQuestions.explanation: The five terminal facial branches fan out from the parotid as temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical branches.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular & cervical.

subQuestions.text: c. Mention the cranial nerve that carries parasympathetic supply to the gland & the ganglion of relay.
subQuestions.explanation: CN IX carries the preganglionic parasympathetic pathway to the otic ganglion; postganglionic fibers then reach the parotid by joining the auriculotemporal nerve.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Glossopharyngeal nerve & otic ganglion.

questions.text: 4. Parasympathetic supply of the parotid gland does not involve:
questions.explanation: Parotid secretomotor fibers arise from CN IX and relay in the otic ganglion; they reach the gland via auriculotemporal nerve. Greater petrosal fibers instead supply lacrimal and nasal/palatal glands through the pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.text: 41- Regarding parotid gland select the incorrect statement
questions.explanation: The parotid’s posterior surface relates to mastoid process and sternocleidomastoid; buccinator is anterior/medial to the gland, so that posterior relation is incorrect.
options: its apex gives passage to cervical branch of facial nerve
its anterior border related to masseter
its anterior border related to TFA
its base gives passage to auriculotemporal nerve
its posterior surface related to buccinator

questions.text: 13. Which of the following structures is liable to be injured in case of incision of a parotid abscess?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve and its branches traverse the parotid superficially, making them vulnerable when an abscess is incised through the gland.

questions.text: 9. The middle structure inside the parotid gland is:
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein occupies the middle plane of the parotid contents: facial nerve is superficial to it and external carotid artery is deeper.

questions.text: 26- preganglionic secretomotor parasympathetic to parotid gland is carried by
questions.explanation: Preganglionic parotid fibers pass through the lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion; auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic fibers.

questions.text: 5- parotid duct pierces buccinator muscle at level of
questions.explanation: The duct pierces buccinator opposite the upper third molar, then runs forward beneath the mucosa to open opposite the upper second molar. Piercing and opening are different landmarks.

questions.text: The parotid duct opens into?
questions.explanation: Stensen's duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the crown of the upper second molar. It pierces buccinator after crossing the masseter.
options: vestibule of mouth opposite second mandibular molar tooth
floor of mouth at sublingual fold
floor of mouth at sublingual papilla
vestibule of mouth opposite second maxillary molar tooth

questions.text: 34. The following structures have part of their course inside the parotid gland EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein stays in the carotid sheath and does not traverse the parotid; external carotid branches and the retromandibular vein do.

questions.text: List structures within parotid gland
questions.explanation: The parotid’s key contents follow a depth sequence: facial nerve branches, retromandibular vein, then external carotid artery and its terminal branches, with intraparotid lymph nodes also present.
questions.modelAnswer: External carotid artery (deepest), dividing into maxillary and superficial temporal arteries; retromandibular vein, formed by maxillary and superficial temporal veins and dividing into anterior/posterior divisions; facial nerve (most superficial), forming pes anserinus and temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular and cervical terminal branches; deep parotid lymph nodes.

questions.text: 20. A muscle that can depress the mandible & elevate the hyoid bone is:
questions.explanation: When the mandible is fixed, digastric can elevate the hyoid; when the hyoid is fixed, it helps depress the mandible to open the mouth.

questions.text: 33- Regarding sublingual gland select the incorrect statement
questions.explanation: The sublingual gland rests on mylohyoid; the lingual nerve lies on its medial/superior side rather than between the gland and mylohyoid.
options: separated from submandibular gland by mylohyoid
separated from mylohyoid by lingual nerve
its ducts open in floor of mouth

questions.text: 38. Which of the following structures lie deep to hyoglossus muscle:
questions.explanation: Glossopharyngeal nerve passes deep to hyoglossus to reach the posterior tongue; the lingual nerve, hypoglossal nerve, and submandibular ganglion lie superficial to it.

questions.text: 51. Which of the following nerves supply the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Preganglionic secretomotor fibers reach the submandibular ganglion by chorda tympani, which joins the lingual nerve. Postganglionic fibers then supply the submandibular and sublingual glands.

questions.text: Superficial and deep part of the submandibular gland are continuous around which of the following muscles?
questions.explanation: The submandibular gland has superficial and deep parts that curve around the posterior free edge of mylohyoid, which separates them.

questions.text: Mention the relations of the superficial part of the submandibular salivary gland.
questions.explanation: The superficial submandibular gland wraps around the posterior mylohyoid border; its mandible-facing surface relates to the facial artery, while its medial surface meets mylohyoid and hyoglossus landmarks.
questions.modelAnswer:
The Superficial part of submandibular gland has 3 surfaces:
a. Lateral surface is related to:
i. Mandible (submandibular fossa).
ii. Insertion of medial pterygoid muscle.
iii. Facial artery separating the above-mentioned structures from the gland.
b. Inferior (superficial) surface is related to:
i. Skin, superficial fascia (containing platysma) & deep fascia.
ii. Facial vein & cervical branch of facial nerve .
iii. Submandibular lymph nodes.
c. Medial surface: (is divided into 3 parts, anterior, middle & posterior).
i. Anterior part: to mylohyoid (m., n. & a.).
ii. Middle part: to hyoglossus muscle & structures lying on its lateral surface.
iii. Posterior part: rests on wall of pharynx separated from it by 9th cranial nerve, styloglossus muscle and stylohyoid ligament.

questions.text: Sublingual gland is related inferiorly to?
questions.explanation: The sublingual gland rests on the mylohyoid, which forms the muscular floor of the mouth. It lies above that muscle and lateral to genioglossus.

questions.text: 6- all the following structures separating submandibular gland from hyoglossus muscle Except
questions.explanation: The lingual and hypoglossal nerves and submandibular ganglion lie between the gland and hyoglossus; the sublingual gland does not intervene there.

questions.text: 40. Hyoglossus muscle:
questions.explanation: Mylohyoid covers part of hyoglossus, forming the muscular floor of the mouth; the lingual artery lies deep to hyoglossus, whereas the lingual nerve and hypoglossal nerve are superficial.
options: Hypoglossal nerve runs along its upper border.
Has lingual artery on its superficial surface.
Has stylohyoid ligament superficial to it.

questions.text: Case 3: A patient had a painful swelling below the lower jaw on the right side. The swelling increased in size during chewing. The surgeon inspected the mouth and noticed pus oozing from a small papilla on each side of the frenulum of the tongue.
questions.explanation: A stone obstructing the right submandibular duct explains meal-related swelling and pus at the sublingual papilla. Wharton's duct opens beside the tongue frenulum, and chorda tympani fibers reach the gland via the lingual nerve and submandibular ganglion.

subQuestions.text: 1. Which salivary gland was inflamed in that case?
subQuestions.explanation: Pus at the sublingual papillae comes from the submandibular ducts, so meal-related painful swelling identifies an obstructed or inflamed submandibular gland.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Right submandibular salivary gland.

subQuestions.text: 2. Where does the duct of the gland open?
subQuestions.explanation: Wharton’s duct opens at the sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenulum; a stone can obstruct this outlet and cause meal-related gland swelling.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Submandibular duct opens on the summit of sublingual papilla on either side of root of frenulum of tongue.

subQuestions.text: 3. What is the nerve supply of the gland?
subQuestions.explanation: Sensory fibers reach the submandibular gland through the lingual nerve; sympathetics follow the facial artery plexus. Secretomotor preganglionic fibers travel in chorda tympani to the submandibular ganglion, where they synapse.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Nerve supply of Submandibular gland: Sensory: Lingual nerve. Sympathetic (vasomotor): Sympathetic plexus around facial artery. Parasympathetic (secretomotor): Superior salivatory nucleus → facial nerve → nervus intermedius → chorda tympani branch → joins lingual nerve → relays in submandibular ganglion → postganglionic parasympathetic emerge from the ganglion to enter the submandibular gland.

questions.text: 48. The following structures are situated deep to the superficial part of the submandibular salivary gland EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cervical facial nerve branch runs superficially in the neck, not deep to the superficial submandibular gland; mylohyoid, lingual nerve, CN XII, and ganglion are deeper relations.
options: Mylohyoid muscle, its nerve and vessels.

questions.text: 45. The submandibular salivary gland:
questions.explanation: The submandibular gland has superficial and deep parts that curve around the posterior edge of mylohyoid; the deep part lies against hyoglossus.
options: Has a deep part superficial to hyoglossus muscle.
Its main source of blood is from maxillary artery.
Its duct opens in the vestibule of the mouth.
Its secretomotor fibers come from the otic ganglion.
It is surrounded by the pretracheal fascia.

questions.text: 41. Choose the false statement concerning the mylohyoid muscle:
questions.explanation: Mylohyoid is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve from the posterior division of V3, not the anterior division. It forms the floor of the mouth.
options: It is called the diaphragm oris.
It is supplied by the anterior division the mandibular nerve.
It is related to both submandibular and sublingual salivary glands.
The geniohyoid muscle lies deep to it.
The anterior belly of digastric lies superficial to it.

questions.text: 30. In the submandibular region, the facial artery gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The facial artery gives submental, ascending palatine, tonsillar, and glandular branches around the submandibular gland; the angular artery is its terminal continuation near the medial eye.

questions.text: 4. Blood supply & nerve supply of submandibular gland.
questions.explanation: Facial and lingual arteries supply the gland; parasympathetic fibers travel from facial nerve via chorda tympani and lingual nerve, relay in the submandibular ganglion, then stimulate secretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Arteries: facial and lingual. Veins: common facial and lingual. Sensory: lingual nerve. Sympathetic: plexus around facial artery. Parasympathetic: superior salivatory nucleus → facial nerve/nervus intermedius → chorda tympani → lingual nerve → submandibular ganglion relay → direct postganglionic fibres to gland.

questions.text: 34-post ganglionic parasympathetic nerves carried by lingual nerve supply
questions.explanation: Chorda tympani preganglionic fibers synapse in the submandibular ganglion; postganglionic fibers hitchhike on the lingual nerve to reach the sublingual gland.

questions.text: 49. Regarding the submandibular duct, all statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve crosses the submandibular duct, but the lingual artery runs deep to hyoglossus rather than crossing over the duct; a stone blocks flow and causes meal-time swelling.
options: It is crossed superficially by lingual nerve and artery.
It lies between sublingual gland and genioglossus muscle.
It opens on top of sublingual papilla.
If blocked by a stone, the gland enlarges after meals.

questions.text: Describe Parasympathetic (secretomotor) supply of submandibular glands.
questions.explanation: Facial preganglionic fibers leave in chorda tympani, join the lingual nerve, and synapse in the submandibular ganglion; postganglionic fibers then supply the gland.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fibers begin from the superior salivatory nucleus, preganglionic fibers pass in the facial nerve in
chorda tympani branch and joins lingual nerve to reach submandibular ganglion (where
preganglionic fibers relay) and postganglionic fibers emerge from ganglion to enter
submandibular gland

questions.text: 22. The nerve which is more liable to be injured on ligating submandibular duct is the:
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve loops under the submandibular duct, passing from lateral to medial beneath it. That close crossing makes it vulnerable during duct ligation or stone removal.

questions.text: 7- which of the following muscles separating submandibular gland & sublingual gland
questions.explanation: Mylohyoid forms the muscular floor separating the superficial submandibular gland below from the sublingual gland above.

questions.text: 55. Which of the following statements regarding sublingual gland is correct?
questions.explanation: The sublingual gland lies lateral to the submandibular duct in the floor of mouth; its parasympathetic pathway is facial nerve to submandibular ganglion, not the otic ganglion.
options: Its duct opens on top of sublingual papilla.
It lies lateral to submandibular duct.
It lies inferior to mylohyoid muscles.
It is related to genioglossus muscle laterally.
It receives its parasympathetic nerves from the otic ganglion.

questions.text: 19. Facial artery:
questions.explanation: The facial artery takes a tortuous course across the mandible and face, allowing it to accommodate movements of the jaw and facial tissues.
options: Is a branch of internal carotid artery.
Enters face at anteroinferior angle of Buccinator.
Ends by anastomosing with supraorbital artery.

questions.text: 26. The sublingual salivary gland is related medially to the:
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve lies along the medial side and crosses the superior aspect of the sublingual gland, a key relationship during floor-of-mouth surgery.

questions.text: 36- all are deep to submandibular gland Except
questions.explanation: The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve high in the infratemporal region, while the submandibular ganglion and hypoglossal nerve are among structures deep to the gland.

questions.text: 56. Regarding sublingual gland, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The sublingual gland rests on mylohyoid, not between mylohyoid and digastric. Its other listed relations describe its position in the floor of the mouth.
options: Occupies the sublingual fold in floor of mouth.
Lies between mylohyoid and digastric muscles.
Secretomotor nerves travel via chorda tympani and lingual nerves.
Lies lateral to the submandibular duct.

questions.text: 54. The sublingual salivary gland is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The sublingual gland receives the sublingual branch of the lingual artery and contributions from the submental artery, so both sources apply.

questions.text: 21. A branch from the facial artery in the neck:
questions.explanation: The facial artery gives off the submental artery in the neck; the sublingual artery instead arises from the lingual artery.

questions.text:
Question 39 :A young man, while sucking a piece of lemon, noticed a painful swilling
below the mandible with a small nodule related to the swilling. Examination revealed
a stone in the right submandibular duct.
questions.explanation: A ductal stone causes painful meal-related enlargement because salivary secretion rises while outflow is blocked. The duct opens at the sublingual papilla, and the lingual nerve crosses under it from lateral to medial; parasympathetic supply relays in the submandibular ganglion.

subQuestions.text: a. Where does the duct open in the mouth?
subQuestions.explanation: The submandibular duct opens at the sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenulum; an obstructing stone causes swelling when salivary flow rises during sour-food stimulation.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
The duct opens bya narrow orifice on the summit of sublingual papilla at the side
of frenulum of the tongue.

subQuestions.text: b. Which nerve is intimately related to the duct?
subQuestions.explanation: The lingual nerve crosses beneath the submandibular duct, looping from its lateral side to its medial side as it proceeds anteriorly.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
The nerve related to the duct the lingual nerve hooks around it from the lateral
to the medial side.

subQuestions.text: c. What is the nerve supply of the submandibular gland?
subQuestions.explanation: The submandibular ganglion relays chorda tympani secretomotor fibers; its postganglionic fibers reach the gland. Lingual nerve carries general sensation, while sympathetics arrive along the facial artery plexus.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
The nerve supply of the submandibular gland is submandibular ganglion
which convey to the gland:
-sensory: from lingual nerve.
-sympathetic: from plexus around facial artery.
-parasympathetic: from chorda tympani.

subQuestions.text: d. Name structures related to the lateral surface of the superficial part of the gland.
subQuestions.explanation: The superficial submandibular gland rests against the mandible; the facial artery grooves its posterior part and crosses the mandibular border nearby.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
Structures related to the lateral surface of the superficial part of the gland.
-Mandible.
-Insertion of the medial pterygoid.
-facial artery.

questions.text: 3. Relations of submandibular gland.
questions.explanation: The gland’s superficial part sits in the submandibular triangle, while its deep part hooks around posterior mylohyoid between mylohyoid and hyoglossus; nearby lingual and hypoglossal nerves explain operative risk.
questions.modelAnswer: Superficial part: lateral surface relates to submandibular fossa of mandible and medial pterygoid insertion, separated by facial artery.
