questions.text: Which of the following increases maximally in pancreatic juice following the intravenous administration of secretin?
questions.explanation: Secretin acts mainly on pancreatic duct cells to increase bicarbonate-rich fluid, neutralizing acidic chyme in the duodenum.

questions.text: Mention four clinical consequences of liver cell failure ?
questions.explanation: Liver failure reduces clotting-factor and albumin synthesis, impairs detoxification, and weakens Kupffer-cell clearance, causing bleeding, edema, drug toxicity, and infection risk.
questions.modelAnswer: Bleeding from reduced clotting factors/platelet production; oedema from reduced albumin and oncotic pressure; drug toxicity from reduced detoxification; systemic infection from damaged Kupffer-cell bacterial clearance.

questions.text: Pancreatic secretion contains all the following except:
questions.explanation: Pancreas secretes enzymes and bicarbonate but no bile salts; bile salts are made by liver, stored/concentrated in gallbladder, and delivered to gut.

questions.text: 6. The enzymes produced by the exocrine pancreas include the following except:
questions.explanation: Enteropeptidase is a brush-border enzyme of the duodenum that activates trypsinogen; pancreatic acini do not produce it.

questions.text: 52. Pancreatic exocrine secretion is stimulated by the following except:
questions.explanation: CCK, secretin, and vagal input stimulate exocrine pancreas; enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen in the intestine rather than stimulating pancreatic secretion.

questions.text: Chemotrypsinogen in pancreatic juice is activated by:
questions.explanation: Trypsin cleaves chymotrypsinogen into active chymotrypsin after enteropeptidase initiates the intestinal protease cascade.

questions.text: 20. The secretion of the exocrine pancreas is increased by the following except:
questions.explanation: Noradrenaline generally suppresses exocrine pancreatic secretion, whereas vagal ACh, secretin, and CCK stimulate fluid or enzyme components.

questions.text: Concerning pancreatic juice:
questions.explanation: CCK from duodenal I cells stimulates pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion, while secretin chiefly stimulates ductal bicarbonate-rich fluid.
options: Gastrin is an important stimulant of secretion of bicarbonate by the pancreas.
Secretin inhibits the secretion of pancreatic juice.
Cholecystokinin (CCK) stimulates the secretion of pancreatic enzymes.
Sight or smell of food does not affect pancreatic secretion.

questions.text: The pancreatic secretion:
questions.explanation: Pancreatic duct cells supply bicarbonate-rich fluid, the main buffer neutralizing gastric acid as chyme enters the duodenum.
options: Is the primary source of HCO3- for neutralization of HCl in the intestine.
Is secreted by the pancreatic acini only.
Is the least important digestive juice.
Is associated with rise of the blood pH.

questions.text: Describe the effect of duodenal acidity on liver and pancreatic secretions
questions.explanation: Duodenal acid releases secretin, which stimulates bicarbonate-rich watery secretion from pancreatic ducts and bile ducts to neutralize chyme.
questions.modelAnswer:

Secretin, also, acts on pancreatic duct cells, increasing watery alkaline pancreatic secretion.

questions.text: 43. The exocrine pancreas secretes the following enzymes except:
questions.explanation: Lactase is a brush-border enzyme of small-intestinal enterocytes, not an exocrine pancreatic enzyme; pancreas secretes amylase, lipase, and protease precursors.

questions.text: Which is NOT true about pancreatic secretion:
questions.explanation: Pancreatic proteases are released as inactive zymogens to prevent autodigestion; amylase and lipase are secreted in active forms.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered the most powerful stimulation for the production of electrolyte-rich pancreatic juice
questions.explanation: Secretin is the strongest stimulus for electrolyte- and bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice from duct cells; CCK favors enzyme-rich acinar secretion.

questions.text: 61. Secretion of the acinar cells within the exocrine pancreas is not increased by:
questions.explanation: Acinar enzyme output rises with CCK and vagal acetylcholine; secretin mainly acts on ducts and bicarbonate itself is not a secretagogue.

questions.text: Mention the consequences of liver failure
questions.explanation: Liver failure impairs clotting-factor and albumin production, detoxification, glucose storage, and immune clearance, causing bleeding, edema, drug effects, and infection risk.
questions.modelAnswer:
Liver failure causes:
1.   decreased clotting factors --> bleeding.
2.   decreased plasma protein (albumin) --> deceased oncotic pressure --> edema

questions.text: The cells of the liver:
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes maintain blood glucose through glycogenesis, glycogenolysis, and gluconeogenesis, buffering glucose availability between meals.
options: Help to maintain the normal glucose level
Deaminate amino acids to form NH₄⁺ which is excreted as ammonium salts in the urine

questions.text: Loss of pancreatic secretion produces all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Without pancreatic enzymes/bicarbonate, fat digestion and absorption are most impaired, causing steatorrhea and loss of fat-soluble vitamins; other enzymes still digest some carbohydrate/protein.
options: Complete indigestion of carbohydrates and proteins
Decrease absorption of fat soluble vitamins

questions.text: Concerning pancreatic exocrine secretion:
questions.explanation: CCK released by fat and amino acids stimulates acinar enzyme secretion; secretin primarily stimulates ductal bicarbonate-rich fluid.
options: Bicarbonate-rich fluid is secreted by acinar cells
CCK augments secretion of enzymes after a meal
About 500 ml of pancreatic secretion are secreted per day.

questions.text: Case A female patient 45 years old presented to her physician complaining of pain in the right shoulder and sense of discomfort after fatty meals. On clinical examination, there was yellowish discoloration of skin & mucous membranes liver function tests were normal. questions.explanation: A common-bile-duct stone raises conjugated bilirubin, which is water-soluble and appears in urine; this produces obstructive jaundice.

questions.text: Case A female patient 45 years old presented to her physician complaining of pain in the right shoulder and sense of discomfort after fatty meals. questions.text: Concerning pancreatic secretion:

options: The inactive enzyme trypsinogen is activated to its active form trypsin by alkaline pH

During secretion of bicarbonate ions the pancreatic venous blood becomes alkaline

questions.text: Concerning regulation of pancreatic secretion

options: Secretin stimulate secretion of pancreatic juice rich in enzymes

Cholecystokinin stimulates bicarbonate secretion by the pancreatic duct cells
vagal stimulation increase pancreatic juice rich in bicarbonate.
vagal stimulation decrease pancreatic juice rich in enzymes

questions.text: Trace the pathway of formation, coagulation and excretion of bilirubin and explain how jaundice may be produced
questions.explanation: Bilirubin from heme is albumin-bound and unconjugated until hepatocytes conjugate it, then bile carries it to gut for bacterial conversion to urobilinogen/stercobilin. Prehepatic, hepatocellular, or obstructive defects raise bilirubin through different steps; obstruction raises conjugated plasma/urine bilirubin and reduces stool pigment.
questions.modelAnswer:
Bilirubin formation and excretion

-  In plasma: old RBCs (hemoglobin) → In macrophage → free bilirubin (protein-bound)in liver
   then→ in intestine conjugated bilirubin → urobilinogen by bacterial action → stercobilinogen →
    stercobilin (gives feces its brown color) by oxidation in air
-  some urobilinogen that is in plasma re-excreted by liver to intestine
-  in urine: some urobilinogen → urobilin (give urine its yellow color) by oxidation in air
    •  Free bilirubin combines with plasma albumin and transported into liver cells where it is
      conjugated acid forming conjugated bilirubin that is excreted from the hepatocytes into the bile
       canaliculi and then into the intestine
    •  Free bilirubin (indirect bilirubin) is albumin-bound and can’t be excreted into urine
    •  Conjugated bilirubin (direct Bilirubin) can be excreted into Urine

Jaundice (icterus)

-    It is a pale yellow discoloration of the body tissues, seen easily in the sclera (whiter of the eyes),
   mucous membrane and skin
-   Is caused by presence of large quantities of bilirubin fluid (>2 mg/dl plasma)

questions.text: The liver is NOT concerned with production of

questions.text: The following hormone stimulates pancreatic acinar secretion rich in enzymes and poor in HCO₃:

questions.text: Concerning obstructive jaundice:
questions.explanation: Obstruction prevents bile salts reaching gut, reducing micelle formation and fat absorption; unabsorbed fat causes steatorrhea and may carry fat-soluble vitamins.
options: Is accompanied by tachycardia and itching.
The colour of the stool is darker than normal due to high content of strecobilin.

questions.text: All of the following statements concerning pancreatic secretion are true except:
questions.explanation: Pancreatic secretion is regulated chiefly by secretin and CCK, with neural input modulating it; it is not primarily under neural control.
options: Its secretion is primarily under neural control
Contains protein digestive enzymes in an inactive form.

questions.text: All the following are true about liver functions except:

Liver cells detoxify drugs and chemicals

questions.text: All the following statements concerning pancreatic secretion are true except:

A fatty meal stimulates marked pancreatic enzymatic secretion through release of CCK
A Carbohydrate diet markedly increase pancreatic enzyme secretion
Contains enzymes which digest polysaccharides to disaccharides

questions.text: Concerning the pancreas, all are true EXCEPT:

questions.text: Lab report of liver function tests of a patient with jaundice showed increased levels of conjugated bilirubin. Which one of the following is the cause of this finding?
questions.explanation: A common-duct tumor blocks bile flow and raises conjugated bilirubin in blood; this water-soluble form is excreted in urine.
options: Acute hemolytic crises in sickle cell disease
Obstructive jaundice due to tumor of common bile duct

questions.text: Which of the following is considered the most powerful stimulation for the production of electrolytes-rich pancreatic juice
questions.explanation: Secretin is the strongest stimulus for pancreatic ductal bicarbonate and water secretion, neutralizing acidic chyme in duodenum.

questions.text: 38. Functions in the liver include production of:
questions.explanation: The liver synthesizes primary bile acids and conjugates them with taurine to form taurocholic acid; gut bacteria produce secondary bile acids.

questions.text: Pancreatic failure may lead to

options: Both a and d are correct

questions.text: Concerning regulation of pancreatic secretion:
questions.explanation: CCK stimulates enzyme-rich acinar secretion and potentiates secretin’s bicarbonate-rich ductal secretion, coordinating digestion with chyme arrival.
options: Presence of food in the stomach directly increases pancreatic secretion.

CCK augments the action of secretin in producing pancreatic secretion rich in HCO3-.
Pancreatic secretion is entirely under hormonal control.

questions.text: Pancreatic lipase activity is increased by:
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify dietary fat and, with colipase, help pancreatic lipase act at the lipid–water interface; salts alone do not directly activate the enzyme.

questions.text: The stimulation of release of pancreatic secretions normally involves all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine, CCK, and secretin are main neural/hormonal pancreatic secretagogues; histamine is not a major physiologic driver.

questions.text: One of the following items is NOT synthesized by the human liver :-
questions.explanation: Plasma cells produce gamma globulins (immunoglobulins), whereas the liver synthesizes hepcidin, clotting factors, albumin, and most cholesterol.

questions.text: Trypsinogen in pancreatic juice is activated by:
questions.explanation: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal brush border cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin; trypsin then activates additional pancreatic zymogens.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about pancreas is correct?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic juice is alkaline because duct cells secrete bicarbonate to neutralize gastric acid and create a suitable intestinal enzyme pH.
options: The endocrine pancreas comprises 98% of the gland
The exocrine pancreas is stimulated by the sympathetic nervous system
The pH of the pancreatic juice is alkaline

The pancreatic juice contains enzymes that complete the digestion of only carbohydrates since other food stuffs are digested earlier

questions.text: Which of the following increases maximally in pancreatic juice following the intravenous administrator of secretin?
questions.explanation: Secretin stimulates pancreatic duct cells to release bicarbonate-rich fluid, so juice bicarbonate concentration rises markedly.

questions.text: 7. The secretion of the exocrine pancreas is increased by the following except:
questions.explanation: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and reduces cholinergic stimulation of acinar and duct cells, unlike vagal/ACh, secretin, or CCK stimulation.

questions.text: The exocrine pancreatic secretion:
questions.explanation: Bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion moves H+ into blood, producing an alkaline tide in venous blood; duct cells secrete the enzymes and islets secrete hormones.
options: Is secreted by islets of Langerhans

Rich in bicarbonate is stimulated by CCK hormone
During its secretion the pancreatic venous blood becomes acidic

questions.text: "The liver acts as an endocrine organ". Explain this statement ?
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes release thrombopoietin, hepcidin, and IGF-1 into blood, regulating platelet production, iron availability, and somatic growth.

questions.text: Liver failure is likely to cause all the following, except:
questions.explanation: The failing liver makes less urea from ammonia, so plasma urea tends to fall rather than rise. Severe hepatic dysfunction can instead increase ammonia and toxic metabolites.

questions.text: The following statements about pancreatic failure are true except:

options: There is moderate impairment of protein digestion.
There is moderate impairment of carbohydrate digestion.
There is marked decrease in digestion and absorption of fat.

Vitamin K absorption is decreased leading to bleeding tendency

questions.text: Mention 4 hormones produced by the liver and their functions?
questions.explanation: The liver acts endocrinologically by releasing thrombopoietin for platelet formation, hepcidin to reduce iron export, IGF-1 for growth, and erythropoietin mainly during fetal life.
questions.modelAnswer:
1- Thrombopoeitein hormone -->platelet production
2- Erytherpoeitein hormone--> erythropoiesis
3- Insulin Like Growth Factor--> growth of bones & soft tissues
4- Hepcidin--> inhibits Ferroportin

questions.text: Case A female patient 45 years old presented to her physician complaining of pain in the right shoulder and sense of discomfort after fatty meals. questions.text: Acute obstruction of the common bile duct produced experimentally will produce which of the following changes in plasma and urine bilirubin levels: [Column order: Free bilirubin Plasma; Conjugated bilirubin Plasma; Conjugated bilirubin Urine]
questions.explanation: Obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin in plasma and urine because water-soluble bilirubin backs up from bile ducts; unconjugated bilirubin may remain near baseline.

questions.text: The majority of bile salts produced by the liver are:

questions.text: The bile salts:

questions.text: Describe the role of bile salts in fat digestion and absorption.
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify fat droplets and form mixed micelles that carry fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins to the intestinal surface for absorption.
questions.modelAnswer:
Digestion of fat by:

   a) Emulsification of fat = detergent action: bile salts change large fat globule into small fat
       globules to increase surface area for enzymes action

Absorption of fats:

    1.  Bile salts form micelles with fats which help fat absorption
    2.  Micelles are minute cylindrical aggregation
    3.  In the center there is fatty acids, monoglycerides & cholesterol facing the non-polar part of bile
        salts while the polar parts are outside
    4.  Micelles are water soluble structures that can transport fat and fat soluble vitamins to reach to
       intestinal villi while they are absorbed

questions.text: Illustrate the chemical regulation of bile salts secretion ?
questions.explanation: Bile salts returning through enterohepatic circulation stimulate hepatocytes to secrete more bile; secretin and vagal input also contribute to hepatic secretion.

questions.text: Mention the most potent hormone affecting gall bladder emptying and illustrate its physiological mechanism ?
questions.explanation: CCK is released by fatty/protein chyme and contracts gallbladder while relaxing sphincter of Oddi, delivering bile when digestion requires it.
questions.modelAnswer: CCK is the most potent hormone for gallbladder emptying. Duodenal fat/protein products release it from intestinal mucosa; blood carries it to contract gallbladder and relax sphincter of Oddi, releasing concentrated bile to assist digestion/absorption of the nutrients that initiated the response.

questions.text: Which of the following acts as cholagogue
questions.explanation: CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, promoting bile expulsion into the duodenum.

questions.text: Discuss the function of gall bladder and its evacuation.
questions.explanation: The gallbladder stores and concentrates hepatic bile, then contracts when CCK rises after a meal to deliver bile into the duodenum.
questions.modelAnswer:
-  Function
1.  Storage of bile: “main function”
    Bile is formed in liver and stored in gall bladder till needed
2.  Concentration of bile:
   By absorption of sodium actively and H2o passively from stored bill
   H2o absorption will increase concentration of cholesterol and bile salts
    **ca++ is not absorbed
3.  Acidification of bile:
   By absorption of HCO3 which change PH from 7.8 to 7 “relatively acidic”
    this keep cholesterol and bile salts soluble not precipitated

Evacuation:

There are 2 factors affect emptying:

    a.  Nervous (10%): By vagus nerve cause wall contraction and sphincter of oddi relaxation this
      causes evacuation.
    b. Hormonal (90%): By cholecystokinin which is a cholagogue that cause contraction of gall

questions.text: Obstructive jaundice:

questions.text: What is meant by enterohepatic circulation of bile salts. Dedicate effect of its interruption ?
questions.explanation: About 95% of bile salts are reclaimed, mainly in terminal ileum, and returned via portal blood for hepatic resecretion. Ileal loss shrinks the bile-salt pool, impairing micelles and fat-soluble vitamin absorption and promoting steatorrhea and cholesterol stones.
questions.modelAnswer: After intestinal action, about 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed (mostly actively in terminal ileum), return through portal blood and are resecreted by liver; about 5% are lost in faeces and replaced by synthesis. 2) Compare between segmentation and migrating complex of
small intestine.
questions.explanation: Segmentation consists of alternating ring contractions that mix chyme without much net propulsion; the migrating motor complex is a fasting sweep that clears residual material between meals.
questions.modelAnswer: Segmentation is alternate ring-like contraction and relaxation that mixes chyme with juice, exposes it to absorptive mucosa and slowly moves it forward. Pacemaker slow waves trigger spikes at threshold. Frequency is 12/min in duodenum and 9/min in ileum; this gradient gives slow net forward propulsion over 3–5 hours. Stretch, gastrin and parasympathetic activity increase intensity; sympathetic activity decreases it. It is vigorous after meals and slight or absent between meals. Migrating motor complex is a fasting peristaltic pattern starting in stomach and migrating toward terminal ileum in cycles about every 90 minutes. Motilin initiates and increases it; eating inhibits motilin and replaces it with segmentation. It clears food remnants, mucosal debris and bacteria into colon as an intestinal housekeeper.

questions.modelAnswer: After meals, apical Na+ cotransport with glucose/amino acids and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase provide absorption. Between meals, coupled apical Na+/H+ and Cl−/HCO3− exchange gives electroneutral NaCl uptake, with Na+/K+-ATPase pumping Na+ basolaterally. Chloride also passively follows the electrical gradient. Water moves passively by osmosis; Na+ accumulation in lateral intercellular spaces raises osmotic pressure and draws water from lumen, then elevated hydrostatic pressure drives it into capillaries.

questions.text: 17) Give an account on the intestinal absorption of vitamins.

questions.text: 12) Give an account on the intestinal absorption of iron.
questions.explanation: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum: heme enters by a dedicated carrier, nonheme Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ and transported by DMT1; ferroportin exports iron to transferrin.
questions.modelAnswer: Absorption is adjusted to iron need (about 0.5–1 mg/day in men and 1–1.5 mg/day in women). Heme iron enters by energy-dependent heme carrier protein 1 and iron is released within the cell. Inorganic ferric iron is reduced at the brush border and ferrous iron enters via DMT1. Unneeded iron remains as ferritin and is lost with shed enterocytes; needed iron exits through basolateral ferroportin and travels in blood bound to transferrin. Liver hepcidin controls ferroportin: high blood iron increases hepcidin, causing ferroportin internalization and lysosomal degradation, limiting iron entry to blood.

questions.text:
23) Explain the process of absorption. What function do the
lacteals have in absorption?
questions.explanation: Absorbed long-chain lipids are packaged into chylomicrons and enter lacteals, then lymph and thoracic duct; lacteals carry fat rather than most sugars/proteins.
questions.modelAnswer: Absorption transfers small digested nutrients, water and electrolytes from gut lumen into blood and lymph. Carbohydrates enter blood principally as monosaccharides glucose, galactose and fructose (the book notes only a small disaccharide fraction). Apical SGLT1 cotransports glucose/galactose with Na+ down the Na+ gradient established by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase. They exit basolaterally by facilitated diffusion. Fructose crosses apical and basolateral membranes through facilitated-diffusion carriers independently of Na+ cotransport. Absorbed carbohydrate travels by portal blood to liver. Proteins enter enterocytes as free amino acids and di-/tripeptides. Most amino acids use apical Na+ cotransport driven by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase gradient; a few use facilitated diffusion. They leave through basolateral amino-acid transporters into blood. PepT1 cotransports di-/tripeptides with H+; intracellular peptidases hydrolyse them to amino acids which then exit basolaterally. Both ingested and endogenous proteins are absorbed (about half each in this account); portal blood carries amino acids to liver. Free fatty acids and monoglycerides are carried inside bile-salt/lecithin micelles to the brush border, leave the micelles and diffuse through the apical lipid membrane. Inside enterocytes they are reformed into triglycerides and coated with lipoprotein as chylomicrons. Chylomicrons leave by basal exocytosis, enter central lacteals and lymph, then reach systemic blood through the thoracic duct. Small amounts of short/medium-chain fatty acids pass directly into portal blood without chylomicron formation. Central lacteals take chylomicrons into lymph, then thoracic duct/systemic blood; they allow large fat particles to leave villi.

questions.text: 22) Briefly describe the process of protein digestion.
questions.explanation: Pepsin starts protein breakdown in the stomach; intestinal enteropeptidase activates trypsin, which activates pancreatic zymogens, and brush-border enzymes finish digestion.
questions.modelAnswer: Gastric pepsin initiates proteolysis in acid. In duodenum, enteropeptidase activates trypsin, which activates more trypsinogen and other pancreatic protease precursors. These release amino acids and peptides; brush-border aminopeptidases and enterocyte intracellular peptidases complete hydrolysis.
