questions.text: 42) About absorption from small intestine:
questions.explanation: Long-chain fatty acids leave enterocytes as chylomicrons into lacteals and lymph, reaching systemic blood via thoracic duct rather than portal veins.
options: Absorbed proteins pass to central lacteals.
Absorbed carbohydrates must be diluted in general circulation before reaching the liver.
Absorbed fats pass to liver through portal circulation for their processing.
Absorbed fats pass to general circulation through lymphatics.
All absorbed nutrients reach the liver through the portal circulation.

questions.text: 13) List the factors affecting iron absorption.
questions.explanation: Ferrous iron, acid, vitamin C, and increased iron demand aid uptake; ferric form, alkali, dietary chelators, iron excess, and inflammation reduce it.
questions.modelAnswer: Increased absorption: ferrous iron, acidity/HCl/vitamin C, solubilizing sugars/amino acids, iron deficiency and increased erythropoiesis. Decreased absorption: ferric iron, alkalis/antacids, precipitating phosphate/oxalate/phytate, iron excess, reduced erythropoiesis and infection.

questions.text: 35) Absorption of glucose in the small intestine-:
questions.explanation: Glucose enters duodenal/jejunal enterocytes apically through SGLT1 with sodium and exits basolaterally through GLUT2.
options: Depends on the presence of Ca++.
Is absorbed in the duodenum by a co-transporter.
Absorbed from lumen to enterocytes to lacteals.

questions.text: Absorption of Na⁺ from the small intestine is important for absorption of all the following, EXCEPT :
questions.explanation: Sodium uptake drives chloride and water absorption and powers glucose/amino-acid cotransport, but calcium uses distinct regulated transport pathways.

questions.text:
18) In what form are carbohydrates absorbed into the
bloodstream?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are digested to monosaccharides—glucose, galactose, and fructose—which cross enterocytes into portal blood.
questions.modelAnswer: Glucose, galactose and fructose (monosaccharides); the book notes only a small fraction as disaccharides.

questions.text: 50. The stomach has the ability to absorb:
questions.explanation: Alcohol is a small molecule that can be absorbed through gastric and small-intestinal mucosa; most nutrient absorption occurs later in the small bowel.

questions.text: 14) Give an account on hepcidin hormone
questions.explanation: Hepcidin from liver binds ferroportin on enterocytes/macrophages, causing its internalization and reducing iron export into plasma.
questions.modelAnswer: Hepcidin is the primary regulator of iron homeostasis, synthesized by liver. Increased blood iron stimulates its release; it binds ferroportin, causes its endocytosis and lysosomal destruction, reducing iron exit from enterocytes. Without hepcidin, ferroportin transfers iron into the body without this control.

questions.text: All of the followings are absorbed by Na dependent 2ry active transport except:
questions.explanation: Glucose, galactose, amino acids, and vitamin C can use Na-linked uptake; B12 instead requires intrinsic factor and ileal receptor-mediated uptake.

questions.text: 53) Which of the following statement is wrong-;
questions.explanation: The stomach mainly absorbs water, alcohol, and some drugs; glucose and protein digestion products are absorbed predominantly in the small intestine.
options: Vitamin B12 absorbed from the terminal ileum.
Glucose and protein absorbed from the stomach.
Bile salts absorbed from the ileum.
Folic acid absorption is active, Na+-independent.

questions.text:
49) Which of the following increase iron absorption
from small intestine:
questions.explanation: Solubilizers keep iron available for uptake; low pH and vitamin C aid nonheme iron absorption, while phytates, phosphates, and antacids reduce it.

questions.text: Regarding the absorption of amino acids, all the following statement are correct except-:
questions.explanation: Amino acids enter apically through Na-coupled secondary active carriers and exit basolaterally by facilitated transport; ATP is used indirectly to maintain the Na gradient.
options: Needs Co-transport at the brush border.
Simple facilitated diffusion at the basolateral border.
Depends on the Na+ in the duodenum.
Does not depend on the presence of glucose in the duodenum.

questions.text: Absorption of glucose in the small intestine-:
questions.explanation: Glucose uptake uses sodium-dependent SGLT1 at the apical membrane and basolateral GLUT2 to reach portal blood.
options: Is depends on the presence of Ca++.
Is absorbed in the duodenum by a co-transporter.
Absorbed from lumen to enterocytes to lacteals.

questions.text: 9) Give an account on the intestinal absorption of fats.
questions.explanation: Dietary fatty acids and monoglycerides enter micelles, diffuse into enterocytes, are re-esterified to triglyceride, and exit as chylomicrons through lacteals.
questions.modelAnswer: Free fatty acids and monoglycerides are carried inside bile-salt/lecithin micelles to the brush border, leave the micelles and diffuse through the apical lipid membrane. Inside enterocytes they are reformed into triglycerides and coated with lipoprotein as chylomicrons. Chylomicrons leave by basal exocytosis, enter central lacteals and lymph, then reach systemic blood through the thoracic duct. Small amounts of short/medium-chain fatty acids pass directly into portal blood without chylomicron formation.

questions.text: List the enzymes found within the brush border of the small intestine epithelial cells.
questions.explanation: Brush-border enzymes complete digestion at the epithelial surface: enteropeptidase activates trypsin, disaccharidases split sugars, and peptidases cleave small peptides.
questions.modelAnswer:
• Enterokinase
• Disaccharidases as maltase, sucrase &lactase
• Peptidases as aminopeptidases

questions.text:
19) The brush border of the small intestine contains all
of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Trypsin is a pancreatic protease delivered into the lumen, not a brush-border enzyme; brush-border enzymes include peptidases and disaccharidases.

questions.text: About fat absorption from small intestine:
questions.explanation: Chylomicrons leave enterocytes by exocytosis into villus lacteals; long-chain fats use lymph, whereas short-chain fatty acids can enter portal blood directly.
options: It is decreased by bile salts.
Long chain fatty acids are absorbed passively.
Deficiency of fat absorption leads to poor absorption of vitamin B complex.
Chylomicrons are extruded into lacteal by exocytosis.
Absorbed fats pass to liver through portal circulation.

questions.text: 6) Give an account on: lactose intolerance.
questions.explanation: Undigested lactose retains water osmotically and reaches colon, where bacterial fermentation produces gas and acids that cause diarrhea, bloating, and cramps.
questions.modelAnswer: Lactase is adequate in children under 4, decreases with age and is reduced or absent in many adults. In lactase deficiency, lactose remains undigested in the intestinal lumen, raises osmotic pressure and draws water in, causing osmotic diarrhoea. Colonic bacteria ferment it to CO2 and methane, producing cramping abdominal pain.

questions.text:
30) Absorption of Na ions from small intestine across
the luminal border occurs by the following except:
questions.explanation: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is basolateral and maintains the sodium gradient; apical sodium entry occurs through cotransporters and exchangers.

questions.text:
34) The following are true statements about absorption
of carbohydrates from small intestine except:
questions.explanation: Fructose uses facilitated diffusion, not sodium cotransport; glucose and galactose use apical SGLT1, but basolateral exit is carrier-mediated.
options: Glucose is absorbed at luminal border by a Na+-dependent mechanism.
Galactose is absorbed at luminal border by a cotransport mechanism with Na+.
Fructose is absorbed by facilitated diffusion.
All monosaccharides have Na+ independent carrier mechanism at basolateral border.
The mechanism of all carbohydrates absorption is 2ry active.

questions.text:
54) The volume that is absorbed by small intestine per
day is about:
questions.explanation: The small intestine absorbs about 7.5 liters daily from intake and digestive secretions, leaving only a small volume for the colon.

questions.text: PHY13: Which of the following nutrients is absorbed into lymph vessels?
questions.explanation: Long-chain dietary fat is packaged as chylomicrons in enterocytes and enters intestinal lacteals because the particles are too large for blood capillaries.

questions.text: Which of the following decrease iron absorption from small intestine:
questions.explanation: Alkali and antacids raise luminal pH and precipitate iron, reducing its soluble nonheme form available for uptake.

questions.text: PHY12: Which of the following is correct about absorption of Na+ by electroneutral Na Cl mechanism?
questions.explanation: Electroneutral NaCl absorption is most active between meals via parallel Na/H and Cl/HCO3 exchange, distinct from nutrient-coupled Na uptake.
options: It includes exchange of Na⁺ with Cl⁻.
It provides minor role for Na⁺ absorption.

questions.text: 41) About fat absorption from small intestine:
questions.explanation: After enterocyte re-esterification, triglycerides are packaged into chylomicrons and released by exocytosis into lacteals.
options: It is decreased by bile salts.
Long chain fatty acids are absorbed passively.
Deficiency of fat absorption leads to poor absorption of vitamin B  complex.
Chylomicrons are extruded from enterocytes by exocytosis.
Absorbed fats pass to liver through portal venous circulation.

questions.text: The following are true statement about hepcidin hormone except:
questions.explanation: Hepcidin regulates iron export by binding ferroportin, not transferrin; high hepcidin traps iron in cells, and low hepcidin permits overload.
options: It is the primary regulator of Fe++ absorption.
Released from liver in conditions of excess body Fe++.
Binds to transferrin and inhibits Fe++ transport in blood.
Its decrease leads to Fe++ overload.

questions.text: If the ileum of a patient is completely resected, the following occurs:
questions.explanation: Terminal ileum absorbs intrinsic-factor–B12 complexes; extensive resection therefore causes B12 deficiency and can also impair bile-salt recycling.
options: Deficiency of fat content of the stool

questions.text: The ileum is the principle site for the absorption of:
questions.explanation: Bile salts are actively reclaimed in terminal ileum and recycled through portal blood to liver, preserving the enterohepatic pool.

questions.text:
26)
State the volumes that reach each of the small and the large
intestine per day. Discuss the causes of differences in these values
questions.explanation: Roughly 9 L/day enters small intestine from drinks/food and digestive secretions, while only 1–2 L reaches colon because small bowel absorbs most fluid.
questions.modelAnswer: About 9 L/day enters small intestine: 2 L ingested food/fluid plus 7 L digestive juices derived from plasma. About 1–2 L/day enters colon. The difference reflects extensive small-intestinal absorption; failure to recover the secreted juices depletes plasma volume/BP and can cause circulatory shock.

questions.text:
20)
Briefly describe the process of carbohydrate digestion.
questions.explanation: Amylases reduce starch to short sugars, then brush-border disaccharidases release monosaccharides, the only major forms absorbed into blood.
questions.modelAnswer: Salivary amylase begins carbohydrate digestion in the mouth. In the small intestine,pancreatic amylase digests starch and glycogen into maltose and trisaccharides. Brush-border disaccharidases complete digestion: maltase yields two glucose molecules,sucrase yields glucose and fructose,and lactase yields glucose and galactose. The final absorbable products are monosaccharides.

questions.text: Absorbed proteins from small intestine do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Absorbed protein generally appears as amino acids and small peptides; intact dietary proteins are not normally absorbed in appreciable amounts.

questions.text: 35) Absorption of glucose in the small intestine :-
questions.explanation: Glucose enters duodenal enterocytes through apical SGLT1 with sodium; insulin does not drive intestinal uptake and nutrients enter blood, not lacteals.
options: Depends on the presence of Ca++.
Is absorbed in the duodenum by a co-transporter.
Absorbed from lumen to enterocytes to lacteals.

questions.text: Absorption of Cl- ions from small intestine occur by the following mechanisms except:
questions.explanation: Chloride absorption follows electrochemical gradients or exchanges with bicarbonate; it is not directly pumped by a primary active chloride transporter.
options: 2ry active transport in exchange with HCO3.
By electrical gradient created by Na absorption.

questions.text: 48. The brush border enzymes of the small intestine digest:
questions.explanation: Lactase is a brush-border enzyme that splits lactose into glucose and galactose for transport into enterocytes.

questions.text: 10) Give an account on the intestinal absorption of proteins.
questions.explanation: Amino acids use sodium-linked carriers and di-/tripeptides use H+-linked PepT1; intracellular peptidases convert peptides before portal blood carries amino acids to liver.
questions.modelAnswer: Proteins enter enterocytes as free amino acids and di-/tripeptides. Most amino acids use apical Na+ cotransport driven by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase gradient; a few use facilitated diffusion. They leave through basolateral amino-acid transporters into blood. PepT1 cotransports di-/tripeptides with H+; intracellular peptidases hydrolyse them to amino acids which then exit basolaterally. Both ingested and endogenous proteins are absorbed (about half each in this account); portal blood carries amino acids to liver.

questions.text: 21) Briefly describe the process of fat digestion.
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify dietary fat, and pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides; micelles then carry products to the epithelial surface for uptake.
questions.modelAnswer: Bile salts emulsify fats in small intestine. Pancreatic lipase hydrolyses triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids; micelles carry the products for absorption.

questions.text: PHY13: Which of the following nutrients is absorbed into lymph vessels?
questions.explanation: Chylomicrons enter lacteals and travel via lymph to the thoracic duct before reaching systemic blood, bypassing initial portal circulation.

questions.text:
7) Give an account on: malabsorption syndrome and gluten
enteropathy.
questions.explanation: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy flattens villi and damages brush border, reducing absorptive area; removing gluten allows mucosal recovery and improves malabsorption.
questions.modelAnswer: Malabsorption is impaired intestinal absorption. Loss of absorptive area after removal of more than 50% of small intestine or villous damage reduces uptake. In gluten enteropathy, sensitivity to wheat gluten produces T-cell-mediated villous injury and mucosal flattening, lowering surface area and absorption of all nutrients. Treatment is to remove wheat flour and use rice or corn flour.

questions.text:
20) Briefly describe the process of carbohydrate digestion.
Physiology Digestive System MCQ 16 pg.
questions.explanation: Starch is hydrolyzed by salivary and pancreatic amylase, then brush-border enzymes finish the process so monosaccharides can be absorbed.
questions.modelAnswer: Salivary amylase begins carbohydrate digestion in the mouth. In the small intestine,pancreatic amylase digests starch and glycogen into maltose and trisaccharides. Brush-border disaccharidases complete digestion: maltase yields two glucose molecules,sucrase yields glucose and fructose,and lactase yields glucose and galactose. The final absorbable products are monosaccharides.

questions.text:
20) Proteolysis in the small intestine is caused by all
of the followings except:
questions.explanation: Pepsin works in the acidic stomach; it is inactivated when the pancreatic bicarbonate raises small-intestinal pH, where pancreatic proteases take over.

questions.text:
5) Discuss adaptation of the small intestine for absorption
functions.
questions.explanation: Folds, villi, and microvilli multiply absorptive area; capillaries carry water-soluble nutrients to portal blood, while central lacteals collect long-chain lipid chylomicrons.
questions.modelAnswer: Circular folds increase surface area about 3-fold, villi 10-fold and microvilli 20-fold, producing about 600-fold total enlargement. Brush borders provide digestive enzymes and specialized carriers; each villus has blood capillaries and a central lacteal. The intestine has a large absorptive reserve; removal of 50% except terminal ileum does not disturb digestion/absorption as stated in the book, whereas terminal ileal loss impairs B12 and bile-salt absorption. Crypt stem cells renew the epithelial lining, with high brush-border enzyme and absorptive capacity at the villus tips.

questions.text:
45) Vitamin C is absorbed from small intestine by a
mechanism similar to the absorption of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C uptake uses a sodium-dependent transporter, like glucose; fructose instead enters by facilitated diffusion.

questions.text:
19) What must happen to fat before it can be chemically
digested?
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify fat into small droplets, increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase; they are not enzymes and do not hydrolyze triglycerides themselves.
questions.modelAnswer: Fat must be emulsified into small droplets by bile salts, increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase; the salt coating keeps droplets from recoalescing.

questions.text:
31) Absorption of Cl- ions from small intestine occur by
the following mechanisms except:
questions.explanation: Chloride is absorbed passively with sodium or via Cl−/HCO3− exchange; intestinal epithelium does not use primary active chloride pumping as the usual mechanism.
options: Active transport in exchange with HCO3.
By electrical gradient created by Na absorption.

questions.text: Water absorption from the small intestine occurs by:-
questions.explanation: Water follows absorbed solute down an osmotic gradient from the lumen through epithelial and paracellular pathways into interstitial fluid.
options: osmotic gradient from the intestinal lumen to intercellular spaces.
hydrostatic pressure gradient from intestinal lumen to intercellular spaces.
osmotic gradient from the intercellular spaces to capillaries.

questions.text: Fructose is absorbed from small intestine by:
questions.explanation: Fructose crosses the apical enterocyte membrane by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5, unlike glucose and galactose, which use sodium-coupled transport.

questions.text: Concerning absorption:
questions.explanation: Steatorrhea is excess fat in stool from failed fat digestion/absorption, as in bile obstruction or severe pancreatic enzyme deficiency.
options: Short-chain fatty acids are absorbed through lacteals.
Bile salts of no importance in fat digestion and absorption.
Steatorrhea means increased protein content in stool.
Steatorrhea occurs in obstructive jaundice & severe pancreatic disease.

questions.text:
18) The intestinal brush border helps digestion and
absorption by the followings except:
questions.explanation: Brush-border microvilli provide enzymes and transporters and expand absorptive surface, but do not propel intestinal contents.
options: Increasing surface area of intestinal mucosa.

questions.text: Explain briefly how micelles are formed and mention their role in fat absorption ?
questions.explanation: Bile salts and phospholipids form micelles with a hydrophobic lipid core and hydrophilic exterior. Micelles ferry digestion products through the watery lumen to the brush border.
questions.modelAnswer: Bile salts and lecithin assemble with lipid-soluble portions inward as a hydrophobic core and charged water-soluble portions outward as a hydrophilic shell. Fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol and fat-soluble vitamins dissolve in the core. The water-soluble shell carries these products through intestinal fluid to the absorptive surface; lipids leave the micelle and diffuse into enterocytes.

questions.text: The major site of absorption of vitamin B12 is:
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 binds intrinsic factor and is absorbed in terminal ileum, where specific receptors recognize the complex.

questions.text: What is the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion?
questions.explanation: Mechanical digestion changes food size and mixing physically, while chemical digestion uses enzymes to cleave molecules into absorbable nutrients.
questions.modelAnswer: Mechanical digestion physically breaks and mixes food, as in chewing and gastric retropulsion. Chemical digestion is enzymatic biochemical cleavage of large nutrient molecules into small absorbable units.

questions.text: 21. The jejunum is the main site for absorption of except:
questions.explanation: Vitamin B₁₂ is absorbed in the terminal ileum bound to intrinsic factor; the jejunum is not its principal site.

questions.text: Vitamin C is absorbed from small intestine by a mechanism similar to the absorption of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C uptake shares sodium-dependent cotransport with glucose-like absorption rather than lipid diffusion or passive transport alone.

questions.text: 25. Micelles:
questions.explanation: Mixed micelles are bile-salt-coated carriers containing fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol, and other lipid products; enterocytes later package absorbed fat into chylomicrons.
options: Are emulsified fat globules in the duodenum
Are packets of pro-enzymes found in pancreatic acinar cells
Are dead enterocytes leaving the tips of villi
Are "flickering clusters" of cholesterol and fatty acids coated with bile salts and 2 mono-glycerides
Are the triglyceride particles formed by enterocytes and transported in the lymphatic system

questions.text: 15) Give an account on the intestinal absorption of calcium.
questions.explanation: Calcium enters enterocytes through apical channels, binds calbindin, then exits via Ca²⁺ pumps/exchangers; paracellular absorption also occurs, and vitamin D enhances uptake.
questions.modelAnswer: Calcium absorption is adjusted to body need. Ca2+ enters apically down its electrochemical gradient through calcium channels, is carried intracellularly by calbindin and leaves basolaterally by Ca2+-ATPase and Na+/Ca2+ exchange. Active vitamin D increases channels, calbindin and ATPase. Low plasma calcium increases PTH, promotes renal vitamin-D activation and thereby increases intestinal absorption.

questions.text: 53) Which of the following statement is wrong ;-
questions.explanation: Glucose and proteins are chiefly absorbed in small intestine, not stomach; B12 requires terminal ileum/intrinsic factor and bile salts are reclaimed in ileum.
options: Vitamin B12 absorbed from the terminal ileum.
Glucose and protein absorbed from the stomach.
Bile salts absorbed from the ileum.
Folic acid absorption is active, Na+-independent.

questions.text:
4) Describe digestion of different types of food in the small
intestine.
questions.explanation: Small-intestinal enzymes finish carbohydrate and protein breakdown at the lumen/brush border; bile salts emulsify fat so pancreatic lipase can hydrolyze triglycerides.
questions.modelAnswer: Pancreatic amylase hydrolyses starch/glycogen into maltose and short sugars; brush-border maltase, sucrase and lactase complete carbohydrate digestion into glucose, fructose and galactose. Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen; trypsin activates other pancreatic proteases and together they produce amino acids/small peptides. Brush-border aminopeptidases and intracellular peptidases finish protein digestion. Fat digestion occurs in the intestinal lumen: bile salts emulsify fats, and pancreatic lipase hydrolyses triglycerides into free fatty acids and monoglycerides.

questions.text: 16) List the factors affecting calcium absorption.
questions.explanation: Calcium uptake rises with active vitamin D, low calcium intake, and acidic conditions; phytate/oxalate binding, vitamin D deficiency, and some dietary factors reduce availability.
questions.modelAnswer: Absorption increases with active vitamin D, low blood calcium and protein in the intestine. It decreases with excess blood calcium and intestinal phosphates/oxalates forming insoluble calcium salts.

questions.text:
25) State the volumes that reach each of the small and the
largeintestine per day. Discuss the causes of differences in
these values
questions.explanation: About 9 L/day enters small intestine but only 1–2 L reaches colon because the small bowel absorbs most ingested and secreted water/electrolytes.
questions.modelAnswer: About 9 L/day enters small intestine: 2 L ingested food/fluid plus 7 L digestive juices derived from plasma. About 1–2 L/day enters colon. The difference reflects extensive small-intestinal absorption; failure to recover the secreted juices depletes plasma volume/BP and can cause circulatory shock.

questions.text: All of the following are causes of constipation EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Rapid intestinal transit limits water recovery and causes diarrhea, whereas slow transit, low motility, and withholding promote constipation.

questions.text: Concerning large intestine:
questions.explanation: Colonic bacteria break down nitrogen-containing substrates and can generate ammonia. They also make vitamin K and gases and contribute to stool pigment.
options: Distention of proximal colon initiates defecation.
Ammonia can be formed from bacteria.
Digestion of cellulose occurs in human.

questions.text: Colonic mass movement is:
questions.explanation: Colonic mass movements propel feces toward rectum and are triggered by gastrocolic responses after meals.

questions.text: 59. The mucosal cells of the human colon perform the following functions:
questions.explanation: Colonic epithelial cells absorb sodium and water, concentrating stool; bacteria perform bile-acid conversion and bilirubin metabolism in the lumen.
options: Converting primary bile acids into secondary bile acids

questions.text: Vibrio cholera causes diarrhea by:-
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin persistently activates adenylate cyclase in enterocytes, raising cAMP and driving chloride-rich fluid secretion with reduced sodium absorption.
options: Creating an osmotic load in intestinal lumen
Decreasing cAMP level in the enterocyte
Multiplying in the enterocyte leading to its destruction.

questions.text: A preparatory reflex for defecation is:
questions.explanation: Gastrocolic reflex increases colonic motility after stomach filling, helping move contents toward rectum and preparing for defecation.

questions.text: 57) Diarrhea may be caused by:
questions.explanation: Undigested lactose retains water in the intestinal lumen and is fermented by bacteria, producing osmotic diarrhea and gas.
options: Decrease intestinal motility by bacterial toxins.
Increase osmotic forces in small intestine as in lactose intolerance.
Damage of neural reflex of defecation.
Mechanical obstruction of intestine by tumor.

questions.text: 58) Harmful effects of severe diarrhea do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Severe diarrhea causes dehydration, potassium loss, and bicarbonate loss, tending toward metabolic acidosis rather than alkalosis.
options: Loss of energy due to loss of nutrients.

questions.text: Functions of haustration movements of large intestine do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Haustral mixing supports absorption and storage and promotes bacterial fermentation, but large intestine does not digest food enzymatically.

questions.text: 60) Cholera toxin does not produce:
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin drives chloride and water secretion but leaves sodium–glucose cotransport intact, which is why oral rehydration solutions remain effective.
options: Increase fluidity and frequency of defecation.
Increase loss of fluids from the body.

questions.text: The most important colonic secretion is:
questions.explanation: The colon secretes alkaline mucus that lubricates feces and protects mucosa; it also absorbs water and electrolytes.

questions.text: PHY14: Mass movements help:
questions.explanation: Mass movements are powerful propulsive colonic contractions that shift feces over long distances toward the rectum.

questions.text: In the colon, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic activity reduces colonic motility; parasympathetic and enteric activity generally promote propulsion.
options: Bacterial synthesis of vitamin K is of vital importance.
More than half of the water that enters the colon is absorbed from the contents.
Sympathetic stimulation results in enhanced motility.
The secretion lacks significant digestive enzymes.

questions.text: Defecation spinal center is present in:
questions.explanation: The sacral defecation center lies in S2–S4, coordinating parasympathetic rectal contraction and internal sphincter relaxation.

questions.text:
25)
Discuss diarrhea, its causes, effects and treatment.
questions.explanation: Diarrhea occurs when secretion/motility exceeds absorption; infections, osmotic solutes, and mucosal injury cause fluid loss, while glucose–sodium cotransport preserves oral rehydration uptake.
questions.modelAnswer: Diarrhoea is frequent passage of highly fluid faeces because intestinal fluid absorption is insufficient. Causes include rapid motility from microbial irritation or emotional stress; osmotic particles such as magnesium sulphate, retained lactose from lactase deficiency or glucose/galactose from SGLT1 deficiency; and cholera toxin driving crypt water/electrolyte secretion. It eliminates harmful material but also loses nutrients, Na+, K+, water and bicarbonate, causing dehydration, reduced plasma volume/BP, shock, metabolic acidosis and chronic hypokalaemia. Oral glucose/NaCl rehydration works because Na+/glucose cotransport and Na+/K+-ATPase remain functional: coupled Na+/glucose uptake promotes osmotic water absorption.

questions.text: Which sentence about colonic mass movement is NOT true:
questions.explanation: Colonic mass movements are powerful propulsive contractions triggered by gastrocolic reflexes; they do not exist to promote bacterial growth.
options: It is long distance propulsive movements.
It occurs as strong simultaneous contractions.
Increased by gastric distension and release of gastrin hormone.

questions.text: The diarrhea due to lactose intolerance is:
questions.explanation: Unabsorbed lactose retains water in the intestinal lumen and is fermented by bacteria, producing osmotic diarrhea with gas and cramps.

questions.text: 11. The intestinal flora is:
questions.explanation: Most gut microbiota reside in the colon, where slow transit and nutrients support dense bacterial populations.

questions.text:
55) The volume that enters the large intestine per day is
about:
questions.explanation: About 1.5 liters of fluid enter the colon daily after most small-intestinal water absorption.

questions.text: Which sentence is NOT true about haustration movements of large intestine:
questions.explanation: Haustral contractions are slow local mixing movements that occur in response to colonic filling; they are not a continuous propulsive pattern between meals.
options: It is the primary movement of colon.
It is similar to segmentation, but less frequent.
Myogenic and its pace maker is BER.

questions.text: 59) Diarrhea due to cholera toxin is called:
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin raises enterocyte cAMP and drives chloride/water secretion, producing high-volume secretory diarrhea despite intact mucosa.

questions.text: Mass movement in the colon is decreased by:
questions.explanation: Mass movements require intact enteric neural circuits; destroying the intrinsic plexus disrupts coordinated propulsion.
options: Destruction of the intrinsic nerve plexus.

questions.text: Cutting the pudendal nerve that controls the external anal sphincter result in:
questions.explanation: The pudendal nerve carries voluntary motor control to the external anal sphincter; cutting it removes voluntary continence, though the internal sphincter remains.
options: Paralysis of sacral spinal control on defecation.
The voluntary control of deification is abolished.

questions.text: 13. The defaecation reflex:
questions.explanation: Rectal distension initiates the defecation reflex through sacral spinal segments (S2–S4); voluntary sphincter control can delay it.
options: Is initiated by stretching the anal canal
Is integrated in a control center in the lumbar spinal cord
Is integrated in a c ontrol center in the sacral spinal cord
Is controlled by the vagus nerve
Involves contraction of the sigmoid colon

questions.text: Haustration movements of large intestine are:
questions.explanation: Haustrations are slow mixing contractions paced by colonic basic electrical rhythm; mass movements are the longer-distance propulsive events.
options: Simultaneous strong contractions of a large portion of colon.
Myogenic and its pace maker is BER.

questions.text: Large intestinal secretion is stimulated by:
questions.explanation: Colonic secretion responds to local mucosal irritation and enteric/parasympathetic stimulation; these coordinated signals support mucus and electrolyte-rich fluid release.

questions.text: PHY14: Mass movements help:
questions.explanation: Mass movements propel colonic contents toward rectum, unlike haustrations that mix and slowly absorb water.

questions.text: Cholera toxins cause diarrhea by:
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin activates crypt chloride secretion, drawing sodium and water into the lumen and causing high-volume secretory diarrhea.
options: Activation of intestinal crypts secretion of water and electrolytes.

questions.text: 10. The functions of the colon include the following except:
questions.explanation: The colon chiefly absorbs water, sodium, and chloride and secretes potassium; calcium absorption is primarily a small-intestinal function.

questions.text: Defecation:
questions.explanation: Meals trigger gastrocolic activity and rectal filling, making defecation more likely afterward; external sphincter control can defer it.
options: It is under voluntary control in infants.
During rest, the rectum is distended.
It is delayed by gastro colic reflex.
It occurs more likely just after meals.

questions.text: 29. The primary motility of the large intestine is:
questions.explanation: Haustral contractions are the colon’s routine mixing pattern, while mass movements occur intermittently to propel feces over longer distances.

questions.text: Colonic bacteria perform all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Colonic microbes synthesize some vitamins, generate gases and ammonia, and help create stool color; urea is produced mainly by the liver, not bacteria.
options: Give the stool its brownish color.

questions.text: 42. Major constituents of feces include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Feces include water, bacteria, cellulose/undigested residue, and mineral salts; glycogen is normally digested and absorbed rather than excreted.

questions.text: About defecation:
questions.explanation: Rectal distension by feces activates intrinsic and sacral defecation reflexes; voluntary external sphincter control determines whether evacuation proceeds.
options: It is initiated by distention of rectum with feces.
It is facilitated by inhibition of pelvic nerve.
It is under voluntary control in infant.
It is inhibited by stimulation of stretch receptors in the colon.
It occurs due to sympathetic stimulation to rectum.

questions.text: PHY15: Which of the following gut hormones is released by glucose in the duodenum?
questions.explanation: Duodenal glucose stimulates K cells to release GIP, which augments glucose-dependent insulin secretion after oral nutrients.

questions.text: Gastrin hormone-:
questions.explanation: Gastrin can increase colonic mass movements after a meal as part of the gastrocolic response; low gastric pH suppresses gastrin instead.
options: Has no effect on growth of the mucosa of the stomach.
Is secreted when PH of the antral mucosa is below 2.

questions.text: Which of the following substances is NOT released from the duodenal mucosa in response to acidic food:
questions.explanation: Acid in the duodenum stimulates secretin and other enteric responses, but histamine is not a duodenal hormone released for this stimulus.

questions.text: The Secretin hormone:
questions.explanation: Secretin is released from duodenal S cells by acid and stimulates pancreatic duct cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich watery fluid.
options: Is released by the pyloric mucosa.
Increases the pancreatic Secretion of water and HCO3

questions.text: Secretin hormone:
questions.explanation: Secretin is released by duodenal S cells in response to acid and stimulates pancreatic duct bicarbonate secretion.
options: Stimulates bicarbonate secretion by the pancreas.
Its secretion is stimulated by food digestive products.

questions.text: 41. The functions of gastrin include the following except:
questions.explanation: Gastrin stimulates gastric acid, pepsinogen, motility, and mucosal growth; bicarbonate-rich bile-duct secretion is mainly a secretin response.
options: Increased production of histamine in the gastric mucosa
Stimulation of the growth of intestinal mucosa
Increased secretion of HCO 3 - by biliary duct cells

questions.text: Regarding the GIP hormone all the following statements are true except-:
questions.explanation: GIP from duodenal/jejunal K cells is released by glucose, fatty acids, and amino acids from protein digestion; it promotes insulin and slows gastric activity.
options: It is secreted by the K cells in the duodenal mucosa.
It inhibits the gastric motility and secretion.
It is known as the glucose - dependent insulin trophic peptide.
It stimulates the pancreas to secrete insulin hormone.
Released in response to proteins in the duodenum.

questions.text: The only GIT hormone that stimulates appetite and food intake is:
questions.explanation: Ghrelin from the stomach rises before meals and stimulates hunger and food intake, unlike satiety-promoting CCK.

questions.text: Concerning secretin hormone, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Secretin is released by duodenal S cells and acts on pancreatic ducts to increase bicarbonate secretion; it is not secreted by the pancreas.
options: Augments the action of CCK in producin pancreatic secretion rich in enzymes.

questions.text: The most powerful gastric inhibitory enterogastrone hormone is:
questions.explanation: CCK is the strongest enterogastrone signal for slowing gastric emptying after fat/protein enters duodenum, allowing time for digestion.

questions.text: Describe the mechanisms concerned with the release of gastric hormones. What are their functions?
questions.explanation: Protein peptides and vagal GRP release gastrin; acid releases somatostatin, which inhibits G and ECL cells. ECL histamine stimulates parietal acid, ghrelin rises before meals, and duodenal acid/fat release secretin/CCK to brake gastric activity.
questions.modelAnswer: Gastrin is released by G/TG cells in response to protein products and vagal GRP; it increases acid/pepsinogen secretion, gastric/ileal motility, colonic mass movements, relaxes ileocaecal sphincter and is trophic to stomach/intestine. Somatostatin is released by D cells in response to luminal acid, acts locally to inhibit gastrin and parietal/ECL activity, and decreases gastric acid and motility. Histamine is a gastric paracrine from ECL cells stimulated by ACh/gastrin; it activates nearby parietal H2 receptors to raise cAMP and acid secretion. Ghrelin comes from oxyntic mucosa before eating and stimulates feeding. Duodenal acid/protein products release secretin, while fat/protein products release CCK; both inhibit gastric activity as chyme enters the intestine.

questions.text: Maximum secretion of CCK is by the
questions.explanation: CCK is released chiefly from duodenal I cells in response to fats and amino acids, then contracts gallbladder and stimulates pancreatic enzymes.

questions.text: The hormone VIP affects the salivary glands by:
questions.explanation: VIP supports salivary secretion by enhancing cholinergic parasympathetic effects on glandular acini and blood flow.
options: Enhancement of the effect of acetylcholine and parasympathetic.

questions.text: Regarding the somatostatin hormone all the following statements are true except-:
questions.explanation: Somatostatin inhibits insulin release; pancreatic delta cells release it, and acidity stimulates its release from gastric D cells.
options: It is secreted by the D cells in the pancreas.
It is secreted by the D cells in the gastric mucosa.
It is secreted due to high acidity.
It stimulates the pancreas to secrete insulin hormone.
It inhibits the secretion of all other hormones.

questions.text: Oral glucose stimulates the release of :-
questions.explanation: Glucose in the small intestine stimulates K cells to release GIP, an incretin that enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

questions.text: Which of the following tract hormones is most directly concerned with motility of the small intestine?
questions.explanation: Motilin drives fasting migrating motor complexes that sweep the small intestine between meals; feeding interrupts this housekeeping pattern.

questions.text: About CCK, all the following is true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: CCK contracts gallbladder and stimulates pancreatic acinar enzymes, while secretin mainly acts on pancreatic ducts to release bicarbonate-rich fluid.
options: It causes contraction of the gallbladder wall.
It produces a pancreatic secretion rich in enzymes.
It potentiates the action of secretin on the pancreas.
It inhibits both gastric and intestinal motility.

questions.text: Secretin hormone causes:
questions.explanation: Secretin slows gastric motility and acid secretion as acidic chyme enters duodenum while stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate output.

questions.text: Presence of fat in the duodenum mainly causes secretion of
questions.explanation: Fat in the duodenum stimulates CCK release, coordinating gallbladder contraction, pancreatic enzyme secretion, and slower gastric emptying.

questions.text: The hormone secretin stimulates which of the following:
questions.explanation: Secretin augments pancreatic duct bicarbonate and water secretion; CCK chiefly drives enzyme-rich acinar secretion.
options: enteropeptidase enzyme Secretin, stimulates the pancreatic duct cells resulting in marked increase in the aqueous, alkaline pancreatic secretion into the duodenum. Secretin also inhibits gastric motility and acid secretion

questions.text: Enumerate the gastrointestinal hormones and describe the release and function of one of them.
questions.explanation: The gut hormone set includes gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP, VIP, somatostatin, motilin, and ghrelin. CCK responds to fat/protein, stimulates pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder emptying, and slows gastric delivery.
questions.modelAnswer: The book lists gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP, VIP, somatostatin, motilin and ghrelin as gut hormones/paracrines. Example: CCK is secreted by I cells in upper small intestine and nerves in distal ileum/colon in response to duodenal fat and protein products. It stimulates pancreatic enzymes, augments secretin-induced alkaline juice, contracts gallbladder and relaxes Oddi, inhibits gastric motility/secretion, stimulates intestinal secretion and pyloric contraction, promotes exocrine-pancreas growth and satiety.

questions.text: The GIP hormone has all of the following effects except-;
questions.explanation: GIP is an incretin that enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion and can slow gastric activity; it does not produce hyperglycemia as a normal action.
options: It is released in response to glucose and fats in dodenum.
Has no effect on gall bladder.
It inhibits both gastric motility and secretion.
It stimulates the pancreas to release insulin hormone.

questions.text: As regards gastrin hormone, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Gastric acidity suppresses gastrin release through antral D-cell somatostatin, whereas vagal GRP, distension, and peptides stimulate G cells.
options: Presence of acid in the stomach stimulated its release.

questions.text: The VIP hormone has all of the following actions except:
questions.explanation: VIP relaxes smooth muscle, suppresses gastric acid, and promotes intestinal water/electrolyte secretion; it is a potent vasodilator, not a vasoconstrictor.
options: It stimulates the intestinal secretion of electrolytes and water.
It causes relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.
It causes inhibition of the gastric acid secretion.
It potentiates the effect of acetylcholine on salivary secretion.

questions.text: Protein digestion products directly stimulate:-
questions.explanation: Peptides and amino acids in the stomach stimulate antral G cells to release gastrin, increasing acid secretion and gastric motility.

questions.text: Regarding CCK hormone, all the following statements are correct except-:
questions.explanation: CCK contracts gallbladder and relaxes sphincter of Oddi; it does not directly stimulate hepatic bile formation, a choleretic action of bile salts/secretin.
options: It exerts trophic effect on the pancreas.

questions.text: Inhibition of gastrin release will
questions.explanation: Gastrin stimulates parietal-cell acid output, so blocking its release reduces its contribution to cephalic-phase secretion.
options: decrease Hcl secretion in cephalic phase
not affect Hcl secretion in cephalic phase
not affect Hcl secretion in gastric phase

questions.text: Regarding CCK hormone, choose the false statement-:
questions.explanation: Duodenal acidity chiefly releases secretin, whereas CCK release is stimulated mainly by fats and protein digestion products.
options: Secreted in response to high acidity in the duodenum.
Causes contraction of the gall bladder.
Causes secretion of pancreatic juice rich in enzymes.
Is one of the enterogastrones that inhibit gastric motility and secretion.

questions.text: All the following statements about cholecystokinin (CCK), are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: CCK contracts gallbladder and relaxes sphincter of Oddi, facilitating bile flow; contraction of Oddi would impede emptying.
options: CCK is released by fat in the small intestine.

questions.text: About some GIT hormones(true or false): Gastrin is released as a result of stomach distension and vagal stimulation.
questions.explanation: Stomach stretch activates local reflexes, and vagal GRP stimulates antral G cells; both increase gastrin release.

questions.text: Regarding the ghrelin hormone all the following statements are true except-:
questions.explanation: Ghrelin rises with fasting and promotes hunger and food intake; it does not potentiate somatostatin's inhibitory effects.
options: It is secreted by the gastric oxyntic mucosa.
In excess amount, it causes obesity.
It potentiates the effects of somatostatin.

questions.text: The hormone secretin stimulates which of the following:
questions.explanation: Secretin stimulates ductal bicarbonate secretion, not gastric motility, acid, enteropeptidase, or acinar enzyme output.

questions.text: About some GIT hormones(true or false): Secretin stimulates the pancreatic acinar cells to secrete enzymes.
questions.explanation: Secretin primarily stimulates pancreatic duct cells to release bicarbonate; CCK and vagal input mainly stimulate acinar enzyme secretion.

questions.text: Which of the following GIT hormones does not stimulates insulin secretion:
questions.explanation: Somatostatin suppresses pancreatic beta-cell insulin release, while incretins such as GIP and GLP-1 enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

questions.text: VIP causes(true or false): Peripheral V.C.
questions.explanation: VIP relaxes vascular smooth muscle and produces vasodilation, so peripheral vasoconstriction is false. Its smooth-muscle relaxation also contributes to sphincter relaxation.

questions.text: State the mechanisms concerned with the release of gastrin hormone. What are the major actions of this hormone?
questions.explanation: Gastrin rises with antral peptides, distension, and vagal GRP, while acid and somatostatin suppress it; it promotes acid, motility, and mucosal growth.
questions.modelAnswer: Gastrin is secreted by antral G cells and TG cells in stomach/upper small intestine. Products of protein digestion directly stimulate G cells; vagus acts through gastrin-releasing peptide (bombesin), so atropine does not block this vagal release. Acid in the antrum inhibits it directly and through D-cell somatostatin; somatostatin, secretin, GIP and VIP also inhibit release. It increases HCl directly and through ECL histamine, increases pepsinogen, stimulates gastric and ileal motility, relaxes the ileocaecal sphincter, induces colonic mass movements and promotes growth of stomach and small-intestinal mucosa.

questions.text: The passage of gastric contents to the duodenum may cause all the following, except:
questions.explanation: Acid in duodenum stimulates secretin, CCK, and pancreatic bicarbonate secretion; CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, so Oddi contraction is the exception.
options: Copious secretion of pancreatic juice rich in bicarbonate
Contraction of the sphincter of Oddi

questions.text: Regarding the somatostatin hormone all the following statements are true except-:
questions.explanation: Somatostatin inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretion, motility, insulin, and other GI hormones; acid stimulates its release, so the statement that acidity inhibits it is false.
options: It inhibits gastric motility and secretion.
It inhibits insulin secretion from pancreas.
Its secretion is inhibited by duodenal acidity .

questions.text: The gastrin hormone has all of the following properties except-;
questions.explanation: Gastrin stimulates ECL-cell histamine release, amplifying parietal-cell acid secretion; it does not inhibit histamine.
options: It is a polypeptide hormone secreted by the G and GT cells.
It has a trophic effect on the gastric and duodenal mucosa.
It inhibits the release of histamine.

questions.text: PHY15: Which of the following gut hormones is released by glucose in the duodenum?
questions.explanation: Duodenal glucose stimulates K cells to release GIP, which enhances insulin secretion only when glucose is present.

questions.text: 14. A tumor producing large amounts of gastrin DOES NOT include:
questions.explanation: Gastrinoma-driven gastrin causes acid hypersecretion, parietal/ECL stimulation, mucosal growth, and recurrent ulcers, but not lymphocyte hyperplasia.
options: Histamine secretion in the gastric mucosa

questions.text: Gastrin secretion is decreased by:
questions.explanation: Low antral pH activates somatostatin feedback that suppresses G-cell gastrin release.

questions.text: VIP causes(true or false): Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.
questions.explanation: VIP is an inhibitory enteric neurotransmitter that relaxes smooth muscle, including the lower esophageal sphincter.

questions.text: Gastrin secretion is increased by:
questions.explanation: Gastric distension activates vagovagal and local reflexes that stimulate gastrin release; antral acidity and secretin inhibit it.
options: Acid in the lumen of stomach

questions.text: The only GIT hormone that stimulates insulin secretion in response to glucose in duodenum is:
questions.explanation: GIP is an incretin released by duodenal/jejunal K cells in response to oral glucose and nutrients; it enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

questions.text: Which of the following substances is NOT released from the duodenal mucosa in response to acidic gastric juice:
questions.explanation: Duodenal acid releases secretin and promotes other gut responses, but histamine is not released as a duodenal hormone.

questions.text: Secretin hormone:
questions.explanation: Secretin from duodenal S cells augments CCK-driven pancreatic enzyme secretion and bicarbonate flow; it suppresses gastric acid and motility.
options: Augments the action of CCK on the pancreas
Is secreted by the antral mucosa.

questions.text: Enterogastrone hormones do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Secretin, CCK, VIP, and GIP inhibit gastric activity as chyme enters the small bowel; gastrin instead stimulates gastric secretion and motility.

questions.text: Secretin mainly stimulates
questions.explanation: Secretin from duodenal S cells stimulates pancreatic duct cells to secrete high-volume bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralizes gastric acid.

questions.text: Regarding secretin hormone, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Secretin is released by duodenal acid and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate; CCK is the primary gallbladder contractile hormone.

questions.text: Which of the following substances is released from the duodenal mucosa in response to acidic gastric juice:
questions.explanation: Acidic chyme stimulates duodenal S cells to release secretin, which promotes bicarbonate secretion to neutralize acid.

questions.text: Discuss the physiology of gastrin hormone.
questions.explanation: Gastrin comes mainly from antral G cells, stimulated by peptides and vagal GRP and inhibited by acid/somatostatin. It increases acid, pepsinogen, gastric motility, and mucosal growth.
questions.modelAnswer: Gastrin is secreted by antral G cells and TG cells in stomach/upper small intestine. Products of protein digestion directly stimulate G cells; vagus acts through gastrin-releasing peptide (bombesin), so atropine does not block this vagal release. Acid in the antrum inhibits it directly and through D-cell somatostatin; somatostatin, secretin, GIP and VIP also inhibit release. It increases HCl directly and through ECL histamine, increases pepsinogen, stimulates gastric and ileal motility, relaxes the ileocaecal sphincter, induces colonic mass movements and promotes growth of stomach and small-intestinal mucosa.

questions.text: CCK hormone-:
questions.explanation: CCK release is triggered by fatty acids and amino acids in duodenum, then increases pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction while slowing stomach emptying.
options: Produces relaxation of the gall bladder.
Stimulates aqueous secretions in pancreatic juice.
Its secretion is stimulated by the presence of fatty acids.
Its secretion is stimulated by acid chyme.

questions.text: As regards cholecystokinin (CCK), all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: CCK contracts the gallbladder and promotes enzyme-rich pancreatic juice, but generally slows gastric emptying and reduces gastric secretion.
options: Products of protein digestion stimulate its release.
Causes contraction of the gall bladder and relaxion of sphincter of Oddi.
Causes secretion of pancreatic juice rich in enzymes.

questions.text: VIP causes(true or false): Inhibition of gastric Secretion.
questions.explanation: VIP inhibits gastric acid secretion and motility through enteric inhibitory pathways; it also relaxes sphincters and promotes intestinal secretion.

questions.text: Which of the following is not produced by a GIT hormone?
questions.explanation: GIT hormones do not directly cause salivary secretion; cranial parasympathetic reflexes control salivary glands.
options: Increased production of pancreatic juice rich in enzymes
Increased acid secretion in the stomach
Decreased acid secretion in the stomach

questions.text: The only GIT hormone that inhibits all secretory and motor GIT activities is:
questions.explanation: Somatostatin is a broad inhibitory signal that suppresses endocrine secretion and gastrointestinal motility.

questions.text: All the following statements about cholecystokinin (CCK), are trur EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: CCK contracts gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi; it does not contract the sphincter, allowing bile to flow into duodenum.
options: CCK is released by fat in the small intestine.

questions.text: The CCK hormone:
questions.explanation: CCK coordinates fat/protein digestion by stimulating pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder emptying; it slows gastric emptying and is not itself choleretic.
options: Stimulates both bile and pancreatic secretion.
Increases both the gastric secretion and motility
Induce atrophy of the pancreatic acini.

questions.text: The vasodilator substance of GIT blood vessels is:
questions.explanation: VIP dilates splanchnic vessels while relaxing smooth muscle and increasing intestinal water/electrolyte secretion.

questions.text: Describe the functions of cholecystokinin.
questions.explanation: CCK inhibits gastric emptying, stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic juice, relaxes Oddi, contracts pylorus/gallbladder, and supports pancreatic growth and satiety.
questions.modelAnswer: CCK inhibits gastric motility and secretion; stimulates pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion; augments secretin-induced alkaline pancreatic juice; contracts gallbladder and relaxes Oddi; is trophic to exocrine pancreas; promotes satiety; stimulates small-intestinal secretion; and contracts the pyloric sphincter.

questions.text: The hormone secretin is mainly released due to:
questions.explanation: Duodenal acid is the main stimulus for S-cell secretin release; secretin then drives pancreatic bicarbonate secretion.
options: Peptones in the gastric chyme entering the duodenum

questions.text: Regarding the motilin hormone all the following statements are true except-:
questions.explanation: Motilin is released cyclically during fasting and stimulates migrating motor complexes; food suppresses its release.
options: It is secreted by the Mo cells in the stomach, intestine and colon.
It is secreted by the enterochromaffin like cells.
It stimulates contraction of smooth muscles of stomach and intestine.
It is the 1ry regulator of migrating motility complexes.

questions.text: About some GIT hormones(true or false): Secretin causes excessive gastric Secretion and accelerates gastric emptying.
questions.explanation: Secretin inhibits gastric acid secretion and slows gastric emptying while stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate; its effects oppose, rather than accelerate, gastric delivery.

questions.text: Regarding the motilin hormone:
questions.explanation: Motilin coordinates fasting migrating motor complexes that sweep residual contents through the stomach and small intestine.
options: It is secreted by the S cells in the duodenal mucosa.
It stimulates the pancreas to secrete insulin hormone.
It contracts the gall bladder to empty its bile in duodenum.

questions.text: One of the following is not true about hormonal regulation of GIT function:
questions.explanation: CCK relaxes sphincter of Oddi while contracting gallbladder; the paired actions direct stored bile into the duodenum.
options: Gastrin is released from G-cells the antral and duodenal mucosa
Secretin is a hormone that is released from the duodenum in response to HCl
CCK contracts the sphincter of Oddi.
GRP is involved in vagal-gastrin secretion

questions.text: 14. Which of the following hormones stimulates insulin release after a protein meal?
questions.explanation: CCK release after protein can promote insulin release, while GIP is the major incretin response to glucose and also responds to amino acids.

questions.text: VIP causes(true or false): stimulation of the intestinal cells to secrete water and electrolytes.
questions.explanation: VIP acts on intestinal epithelium to stimulate chloride and water secretion, contributing to luminal fluid movement.

questions.text: The only GIT hormone that stimulates motility between meals is:
questions.explanation: Motilin triggers migrating motor complexes that clear the small intestine between meals, the principal fasting motility pattern.

questions.text: The Neurotransmitters involved in relaxation of smooth muscles are:
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide and VIP are inhibitory nonadrenergic, noncholinergic transmitters that relax GI smooth muscle.

questions.text: Extrinsic nerves of the GIT are NOT:
questions.explanation: The enteric nervous system generates gut contractions intrinsically, so extrinsic autonomic nerves modulate activity but are not required for every contraction.
options: Affect the GIT through the enteric nerves.
Affect the GIT through GIT hormones.
Coordinate activity of different parts of GIT.
The only mechanism that makes the GIT respond to external stimuli.

questions.text: Secondary esophageal peristalsis:
questions.explanation: Secondary peristalsis is triggered by esophageal distension and can be generated by intrinsic myenteric circuits in the smooth-muscle lower esophagus, so it can return after vagotomy.
options: Reappear in the lower esophagus after vagotomy
Reappear in the upper esophagus after vagotomy.
Disappear in the lower esophagus after vagotomy

questions.text: The tone of the lower esophageal sphincter is:
questions.explanation: Tonic LES pressure is a barrier against reflux; reduced tone permits gastric acid to reach esophagus and cause heartburn.
options: Lesser than the tone in the middle esophagus
A major factor in preventing heartburn

questions.text: Gastric Mixing of food:
questions.explanation: Antral contractions are strongest because this region has thicker circular muscle and grinds food before controlled pyloric passage.
options: Is weak in the body due to thick muscle layer.
Is strongest in the pyloric antrum.
Occurs in the form of segmentation movement.

questions.text: Swallowing of food induces receptive relaxation in the stomach through:
questions.explanation: Swallowing activates a vagovagal reflex with inhibitory vagal fibers to the proximal stomach, allowing it to relax and accommodate food without a large pressure rise.
options: Conditioned reflex through the cerebral cortex.

questions.text: Receptive relaxation of the stomach
questions.explanation: Vagal pathways mediate most receptive relaxation, while enteric inhibitory neurons execute the response; vagotomy therefore partly reduces accommodation.

questions.text: The hormone secretin is mainly released due to:
questions.explanation: Duodenal acid stimulates secretin release from S cells; the hormone then prompts pancreatic bicarbonate-rich secretion.

questions.text: In the stomach:
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid cleaves pepsinogen into active pepsin in the stomach; pepsin then begins protein digestion.
options: Pepsinogen is converted to pepsin by HCl
Ferrous iron is reduced to ferric iron by HCl
Acid secretion is inhibited by gastrin

questions.text: Bile salts:
questions.explanation: Bile salts are synthesized from cholesterol in hepatocytes, then secreted into bile and recycled through enterohepatic circulation.
options: From micelles with carbohydrates in the small intestine
Are essential for protein digestion and absorption

questions.text: All the following is correct about Bile salts EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Most terminal-ileal bile salts are actively reclaimed by sodium-coupled transporters, then returned to the liver in portal blood.
options: Are absorbed passively from the terminal ileum.
Form micelles in the small intestine and gall bladder

questions.text: About fat absorption from small intestine:
questions.explanation: Enterocytes reassemble long-chain lipids into triglycerides, package them as chylomicrons, and exocytose them into lacteals.
options: It is decreased by bile salts.
Deficiency of fat absorption leads to poor absorption of vitamin B complex.
Chylomicrons are extruded into lacteal by exocytosis.
Absorbed fats pass to liver through portal circulation.

questions.text: Absorption of glucose in the small intestine:
questions.explanation: Glucose enters duodenal enterocytes through sodium-coupled SGLT1, using a cotransporter rather than passive diffusion.
options: Is depends on the presence of Ca**.
Is absorbed in the duodenum by a Co-transporter.

questions.text: Vibrio cholera causes diarrhea by:
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin raises enterocyte cAMP and drives chloride-rich fluid secretion into the lumen, producing secretory diarrhea.
options: Creating an osmotic load in intestinal lumen
Multiplying in the enterocyte leading to its destruction.

questions.text: Which of the following is paired correctly?
questions.explanation: CCK stimulates pancreatic acinar cells to release enzyme-rich juice, complementing secretin's bicarbonate-rich duct secretion.
options: Secretin - relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi
Cholecystokinin Stimulation of pancreatic secretion rich in enzyme
Secretin - Stimulation of pancreatic secretion rich in enzyme

subjects.name: Histology
lectureNames: Histology of Taste bud, palate and pharynx

questions.text: 30. One of the following is true about the circumvallate tongue papillae:
questions.explanation: Circumvallate papillae are surrounded by a trench/furrow that holds tastants near taste buds on their lateral walls.

questions.text: 2. The vermilion zone is found at:
questions.explanation: The vermilion zone is the transitional red margin where external skin meets the oral mucosa of the lip.
options: the junction of the hard and soft palate
the junction of oropharynx and laryngo-pharynx
the junction of cardiac and fundic region of the stomach
the junction of the inner and outer surface of the lip

questions.text: 1. Which of the following is lined by stratified squamous keratinized epithelium
questions.explanation: Gingiva is masticatory mucosa exposed to friction, so its surface epithelium is keratinized stratified squamous.

questions.text: site & structure of Fungiform papilla
questions.explanation: Fungiform papillae cluster at tongue tip and edges; a vascular connective-tissue core beneath thin epithelium gives them a red appearance and they contain taste buds.
questions.modelAnswer:
Less numerous,
      o More on the tip & edges of tongue.
      o Resemble mushromes with narrow base and broad apex.
      o Covered by nonkeratinized st.sq.epith.
      o Carry taste budds.
       Fungiform papillae appear as red spots on tongue surface
       Because:

questions.text: 8. Which type of papillae on the tongue is not well developed in man?
questions.explanation: Foliate papillae are rudimentary in humans compared with other mammals; filiform, fungiform, and circumvallate papillae are better developed.

questions.text: 3. free margin of lip (vermilion zone) is characterized by having
questions.explanation: The vermilion border has thin epithelium over tall vascular connective-tissue papillae, making capillaries visible through the surface and giving the lip its red color.

questions.text: 28. The fungiform papillae:
questions.explanation: Fungiform papillae have a richly vascularized connective-tissue core, visible through their thin covering epithelium.

questions.text: 1. The outer surface of the lip is covered by:
questions.explanation: The external lip surface is ordinary thin skin with hair follicles and sebaceous/sweat glands, while the red margin lacks these appendages.
options: Thin skin with no hair follicles.
Thin skin with no sebaceous glands.
Thin skin with hair follicles, sebaceous & sweat glands.

questions.text: 72. Filiform papilla of tongue:
questions.explanation: Filiform papillae have keratinized epithelium for friction and food manipulation; they lack taste buds and are not at the sulcus terminalis.

questions.text: 33. One of the following is true concerning the Foliate papillae:
questions.explanation: Foliate papillae form parallel folds/ridges separated by grooves on the posterolateral tongue, with taste buds in their sides.
options: The most numerous papillae in humans
Have mucous glands in the lamina propria

questions.text:
6. Which of the followings characterize the shape of fungiform
papillae?
questions.explanation: Fungiform papillae have a narrow base and rounded broad apex; their vascular cores give them a red appearance and they contain taste buds.
options: They have wide base and pointed apex.
They have constricted base and broad apex.
They have constricted base surrounded by deep groove.
They are conical structures rich in taste buds.

questions.text: 3. The lining epithelium of the oral mucosa is
questions.explanation: Most lining oral mucosa is nonkeratinized stratified squamous to remain flexible and moist; masticatory mucosa of gingiva and hard palate is keratinized.

questions.text: 31. The circumvallate papillae are:
questions.explanation: Circumvallate papillae are large and few, arranged just anterior to terminal sulcus; nonkeratinized sides contain many taste buds and serous glands.
options: Covered by non ker. St. sq. epithelium

questions.text:
44. All of the followings about the masticatory mucosa is true
EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Masticatory mucosa on gingiva and hard palate is keratinized and has dense lamina propria; it still contains nerves and blood vessels.
options: It is found on the gums and the hard palate.
Its epithelium is stratified squamous keratinized.
Its lamina propria contains thick papillary layer of loose connective tissue
Its lamina propria contains reticular layer of dense connective tissue
Its lamina propria does not contain blood vessels and nerves.

questions.text:
8. Asses the value of

- Striated muscle in Different directions in the tongue
- Von Ebner’s gland in circumvallate papillae
- Filiform papillae on tongue surface

questions.explanation: Tongue muscle bundles cross in three planes beneath specialized dorsal papillae; the lip’s red margin appears vascular because thin transparent epithelium overlies deep capillary-rich papillae.
questions.modelAnswer:
The Tongue is formed from bundles of Skeletal Muscle Fibers covered by Mucous Membrane.
The Sk. Ms. Fibers are arranged in three directions: Longitudinal, Vertical & Transverse.

Its Mucous Membrane is smooth&loosly atteched to the muscle
It's formed of:
A St. Sq. Non-Keratinized Epithelium.

2-Dorsal surface:
Its Mucous Membrane is rough& to the muscles
It's formed of Parakeratinized St. Sq. Epithelium.
It's divided by a V-Shaped groove called Sulcus Termnalis into:
Pharyngeal Part (Posterior One Thirds):
A-covered with stratified squamous non keratinizie epitelium
B-The epithelium forming short crypts in between the follicles
C-The base of the crypts receives opening of the mucous glands which clean the crypts continously.
D- Containing lymph follicles with germinal centers
E -Containing Linguial Tonsil& covered by Non-Keratinized Epithelium
Oral Part (Anterior Two Thirds):
Carrying small projections of Mucous Membrane called Lingual Papillae
(4 types)
Are formed of C.T. core covered with St. Sq. Epithelium
According to their shape they are classified into
Historical response table (physical page3):
Foliate Papillae (Rare)
Site: Poorly Devolped in Man but well devolped in Rabbites in the basolateral area
Shape: Parallel ridges separated by deep clefts of C.T.

Tast bud: Numerous (in rabbits)

Shape: Large Dome-Shaped with narrow base & broad tip. -surrounded by trench or vellum(deep groove) -kept clean &flushed by von-Ebner's gland (serous)
Covered by: - Dorsal Surface is ParaKeratinizd - Lateral Surface is Nonkeratinizd
Tast bud: Numerous (250 around each papillae
Fungiform Papillae (Less Numerous)
Site: Scattered between the Filifirm Papellae (More in Tip & Edges)
Shape: Fungi-Shaped with narrow base & broad apex. -epit.surface doesn't follow the contouof 2ry papillae(unlike filliform) -red in life (blood vessels very close to the surface epit -The surface epith relatively transparent
Covered by: Nonkeratinized St. Sq. Epithelium
Tast bud: Occasional
Filiform Papillae (filium –thread) (Most Numerous)
Site: Anterior 2/3 of the Dorsum of Tongue (Arrenged in oblique transverse rows parallel to the Shaped Sulcus) Towards the base of the tongue
Shape: Conical in shape 2ry papillae may extend from the 1ry papillae towards the surface.
Covered by: Parakeratinized St. Sq. Epithelium
Tast bud: No (but contain many touch receptor)
The free margin of the lip is red
Due to the transparency of epithelium & the rich blood supply due to the presence of numerous high very vascular dermal papillae.

questions.text: 55. Lamina propria of hard palate is formed by:
questions.explanation: Hard-palate lamina propria is dense and firmly attached to underlying bone periosteum, providing a stable chewing surface.

questions.text: 15. The lining epithelium of the nasopharynx is:
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal respiratory mucosa is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells, supporting mucociliary clearance.

questions.text: 9. The cells of taste bud are ___, ___ & ___
questions.explanation: Taste buds contain gustatory receptor cells, supporting cells, and basal progenitor cells that replace the short-lived sensory cells.

questions.text: Give short account on the structure of taste buds
questions.explanation: Taste buds are barrel-shaped epithelial structures with supporting, receptor, and basal stem cells; apical microvilli pass through a taste pore and basal receptor processes synapse with afferents.
questions.modelAnswer: Taste buds are barrel-shaped sensory structures perpendicular to epithelium in tongue dorsum, soft palate and laryngeal epiglottis. Peripheral curved columnar supporting cells have dark cytoplasm/light nuclei and apical granules. Central gustatory cells have pale cytoplasm/dark oval nuclei, apical microvilli extending through taste pores into supporting-cell glycosaminoglycan material and basal afferent connections. Basal stem cells replace receptor/supporting cells. Saliva-dissolved tastants stimulate receptors via pores.

questions.text: 34. The following organ has no taste buds
questions.explanation: The hard palate has no taste buds; the soft palate, pharynx, epiglottis, and taste papillae can contain them.

questions.text: 17. The lining epithelium of the laryngeal pharynx is:
questions.explanation: The laryngopharynx carries food and is exposed to abrasion, so its lining is nonkeratinized stratified squamous rather than respiratory epithelium.
options: Pseudostratified columnar ciliated with goblet cells.

questions.text: 6. The soft palate is formed of ___and is covered on its superior surface by ___ and its inferior surface is covered by ___
questions.explanation: The soft palate has a striated-muscle and connective-tissue core, respiratory ciliated epithelium above, and nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium below where food contacts it.

questions.text: 7. The hard palate is formed of ___ And is covered by ___
questions.explanation: Hard palate is a bony roof covered by keratinized masticatory mucosa that withstands pressure from food.

questions.explanation: Wharton's duct drains the submandibular gland; Stensen's duct drains the parotid, opening opposite the upper second molar.

questions.text: 19. Which of the following is a character of parotid salivary gland?
questions.explanation: Parotid is a serous acinar gland with intercalated and striated ducts; adipose tissue commonly increases in adult stroma.
options: Mucous acini are the predominant type of acini
The main duct is lined by simple columnar epithelium
It has a few striated duct inside the lobules
It has adipose connective tissue in its stroma

questions.text:
16. Compare between:
The mucous acini & serous acini
Pancreas & parotid gland
Sublingual & parotid gland
questions.explanation: Mucous acini are pale with wide lumens and flattened nuclei; serous acini are darker, protein-secreting units. Pancreas is pure serous with centroacinar cells and no striated ducts, parotid is pure serous with striated ducts, and sublingual is mostly mucous.
questions.modelAnswer: Serous acini: small diameter/narrow lumen; pyramidal cells, indistinct borders, rounded nuclei, basal basophilia/apical acidophilic zymogen; abundant basal RER, Golgi and spherical secretory granules, lateral interdigitations/junctional complexes; less prominent myoepithelium; serous secretion. Mucous acini: larger/wider lumen; cuboidal/columnar cells with distinct borders, flat basal nuclei and pale foamy basophilic cytoplasm; larger Golgi/mucin granules, no lateral interdigitations; prominent myoepithelium; lubricating glycoprotein secretion. Pancreas versus parotid: Pancreas has thin capsule/delicate reticular stroma, mixed endocrine/exocrine gland with pure serous acini, centroacinar cells and no myoepithelium or striated ducts; main pancreatic duct has simple columnar epithelium and opens into duodenum. Parotid has thick capsule/septa with adipocytes, pure serous acini with myoepithelium and prominent striated ducts; main parotid duct has stratified columnar then nonkeratinized stratified squamous lining and opens in oral vestibule. Both have intercalated and excretory ducts. Sublingual versus parotid: Parotid: thick capsule/septa with fat and lymphocytes/plasma cells; pure serous acini/prominent striated ducts, 25% saliva. Sublingual: thin less-developed capsule, developed septa, predominantly mucous mixed acini; few less-developed intercalated/striated ducts, 5% saliva. Both compound tubuloalveolar.

questions.text:
31. The basic functioning secretory unit of the salivary glands is

questions.explanation: A salivary acinus is the secretory end-piece; ducts modify and convey its product, so they are not part of the basic secretory unit.

questions.explanation: Parotid has prominent striated ducts that modify electrolytes; pancreas lacks them and instead has centroacinar cells/intercalated ducts.

questions.modelAnswer: Serous acini: small diameter/narrow lumen; pyramidal cells, indistinct borders, rounded nuclei, basal basophilia/apical acidophilic zymogen; abundant basal RER, Golgi and spherical secretory granules, lateral interdigitations/junctional complexes; less prominent myoepithelium; serous secretion. Mucous acini: larger/wider lumen; cuboidal/columnar cells with distinct borders, flat basal nuclei and pale foamy basophilic cytoplasm; larger Golgi/mucin granules, no lateral interdigitations; prominent myoepithelium; lubricating glycoprotein secretion. Parotid: thick capsule/septa with fat and lymphocytes/plasma cells; pure serous acini/prominent striated ducts, 25% saliva. Sublingual: thin less-developed capsule, developed septa, predominantly mucous mixed acini; few less-developed intercalated/striated ducts, 5% saliva. Both compound tubuloalveolar.

questions.text: 47. The sublingual gland is

questions.text: 36. Basket cells are characterized by:
