questions.explanation: Scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency, which impairs collagen hydroxylation and weakens connective tissue and blood vessels.

questions.text: For patients treated with Isoniazid, which of the following vitamins is used as a supplementation
questions.explanation: Isoniazid can deplete or inactivate pyridoxine, so vitamin B6 supplementation prevents peripheral neuropathy.

questions.text: Pellagra (with its 3 D clinical manifestations of ___, ___, and ___, and if uncorrected will → the 4th D: ___).
questions.explanation: Pellagra classically causes diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia; untreated deficiency may progress to death, the fourth “D.”

questions.text: Which of the following is an antioxidant vitamin?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is a water-soluble antioxidant that donates electrons to neutralize reactive species and also supports collagen synthesis.

questions.text: BIO4: Which of the following diseases is caused by the deficiency of Niacin?
questions.explanation: Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, classically with dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia; other choices have distinct vitamin causes.

questions.text: Which of the following vitamin deficiency causes Pellagra
questions.explanation: Niacin deficiency reduces NAD/NADP availability and causes pellagra, especially with poor intake or impaired tryptophan conversion.

questions.text: Which of the following Coenzymes is Carrier for Amino acids
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6, carries amino groups during transamination and other amino-acid reactions.

questions.text: In preterm infant with very low birth weight, we give which of the following vitamin
questions.explanation: Very-low-birth-weight preterm infants may receive vitamin E to protect vulnerable red-cell membranes from oxidative injury.

questions.text: The requirement for vit. E increases as the intake of ___
questions.explanation: Vitamin E needs rise with PUFA intake because polyunsaturated lipids are more vulnerable to peroxidation and require antioxidant protection.

questions.text: Consumption of large amounts of raw egg whites (20 eggs or more) can induce:
questions.explanation: Raw egg white avidin binds biotin tightly and prevents its absorption. Eating very large amounts over time can therefore cause biotin deficiency.

questions.text: Weakness in muscles and increase in the fragility of red blood cells (hemolytic anemia) is caused due to the __________.
questions.explanation: Vitamin E deficiency weakens antioxidant protection of erythrocyte membranes and can cause hemolytic anemia and muscle weakness.

questions.text: Macro-minerals mean
questions.explanation: Macrominerals are required at approximately 100 mg/day or more; smaller daily needs define trace and ultratrace minerals.

questions.text: Metallothionine ins liver is rich in which amino acid
questions.explanation: Metallothionein binds metals through cysteine thiol groups, allowing cells to store or buffer copper, zinc, and other metals.

questions.text: Selenium is the cofactor for which of the following enzymes
questions.explanation: Glutathione peroxidase contains selenium and reduces hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides, limiting oxidative tissue damage.

questions.text: What is the main source of natural fluoride?
questions.explanation: Drinking water is the principal natural fluoride source for many populations, though concentration varies by location.

questions.text: Wilson disease is characterized by the following except :
questions.explanation: Wilson disease causes copper accumulation in liver and other tissues, with increased urinary copper and usually low serum ceruloplasmin. Low hepatic copper is the false statement.

questions.text: (which of the following minerals is a component of glucose tolerance factor (GTF
questions.explanation: Chromium was historically proposed as a component of glucose tolerance factor and may support insulin action.

questions.text: In a normal muscle contraction, Ca is a relaxant and Mg is a stimulant.
questions.explanation: Calcium triggers skeletal-muscle contraction, while magnesium supports relaxation and modulates neuromuscular excitability; the statement reverses them.

questions.text: Kinky hair syndrome
questions.explanation: Menkes disease impairs copper transport, reducing copper-dependent lysyl oxidase activity. Defective collagen cross-linking helps explain the abnormal hair and connective-tissue findings.
options: Is due to mutation of Atpase transporter in liver
Decrease activity of lysine hydroxylase enzyme
Decrease activity of lysyl oxidase enzyme.

questions.text: Mitochondrial superoxide dismutase contains
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2) uses manganese to convert superoxide radicals into hydrogen peroxide.

questions.text: Phenocopy of cutis laxa
questions.explanation: Maternal penicillamine exposure can disrupt fetal copper-dependent cross-linking and produce a cutis-laxa-like phenotype without an elastin mutation.
options: Is due to mutation of gene encoded elastin
Occur in fetuses of pregnant women treated with penicillamine.

questions.text: Phosphorus (P) is important for pH regulation
questions.explanation: Phosphate is a major intracellular and urinary buffer, helping regulate acid-base balance. It also participates in ATP and phosphorylation reactions.

questions.text: In Wilson disease, all the following are true except
questions.explanation: Wilson disease impairs copper excretion, increasing free and tissue copper; ceruloplasmin is typically reduced, not increased.

questions.text: Molybdenum is a cofactor for which of the following enzyme
questions.explanation: Molybdenum is incorporated into the molybdenum cofactor used by xanthine oxidase and several other oxidoreductases.

questions.text: All the followings are true about Menke's disease except
questions.explanation: Menkes disease reflects defective ATP7A copper export from intestinal cells, causing low copper and reduced copper-enzyme activity. A liver copper-transport defect instead suggests Wilson disease.
options: Deficiency of Cu transporter ATPase protein in liver

questions.text: Mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD) needs
questions.explanation: Manganese is the catalytic metal in mitochondrial SOD2, which detoxifies superoxide formed during oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.text: In the liver Cu is stored bound to___ .
questions.explanation: Hepatic copper binds metallothionein for intracellular storage; ATP7B normally exports copper into bile and loads ceruloplasmin.

questions.text: Copper is mainly excreted in
questions.explanation: The liver eliminates excess copper mainly by secreting it into bile and then feces. Urinary copper rises in Wilson disease but is not the main normal route.

questions.text: Wilson's disease is an example of _______and Menkes' syndrome is an example of __________ .
questions.explanation: Wilson disease causes copper accumulation; Menkes disease impairs copper absorption and distribution, causing copper deficiency.

questions.text: The highest concentration of Mn present is
questions.explanation: Bone is a major storage site for manganese, which also accumulates in liver and other tissues; the choice reflects the largest body store.

questions.text: Which of the following mineral is involved in the enzyme -controlled energy yielding reactions of metabolism?
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is present in ATP and other phosphorylated intermediates that capture and transfer energy in metabolism.

questions.text: All of the following minerals are constituent of metallo-enzymes except :
questions.explanation: Zinc, copper, and manganese serve as cofactors in metalloenzymes, whereas fluoride is not generally a metalloenzyme constituent.

questions.text:
Minerals are divided into ___ ,
___, ___
questions.explanation: Minerals are grouped as macrominerals, trace (microminerals), and ultratrace elements according to required amounts.

questions.text: Copper is a cofactor for all the following enzymes except
questions.explanation: Copper is required by cytochrome c oxidase, ferroxidase, Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase, and lysyl oxidase. Lysyl hydroxylase instead requires iron and vitamin C.

questions.text: Wilson's disease is an example of __________ and Menkes' syndrome is an example of __________ .
questions.explanation: Wilson disease causes copper toxicity from impaired biliary excretion; Menkes disease causes systemic copper deficiency from defective transport.
options: Vit D toxicity; Vit D deficiency

questions.text: Which mineral important for glucose metabolism (a component of glucose tolerance factor (GTF) :
questions.explanation: Chromium has historically been described as part of glucose tolerance factor and linked to insulin action, though its essentiality in humans is debated.

questions.text: selenium is important cofactor for which of the following enzymes
questions.explanation: Glutathione peroxidase is a selenium-dependent enzyme that reduces hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides using glutathione.

questions.text: Copper is a cofactor for all the following enzymes except
questions.explanation: Copper-dependent ferroxidases oxidize ferrous to ferric iron; ferroreductases reduce ferric iron and do not use copper as their cofactor.

questions.text: Cytosolic superoxide dismutase (SOD1) needs
questions.explanation: Cytosolic Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase requires both copper at its catalytic site and zinc for structural stability.

questions.text: Menkes Syndrome-Kinky hair syndrome is characterized by the following except :
questions.explanation: Menkes disease causes low serum copper and ceruloplasmin because intestinal copper export is impaired; high serum copper is therefore the exception.
options: Decrease enzymatic activity for the Cu- depending enzymes
mutations in the gene for the Cu binding protein

questions.text: which of the following minerals is needed by xanthine oxidase
questions.explanation: Xanthine oxidase contains molybdenum and catalyzes purine oxidation to uric acid.

questions.text: Dietary deficiency of iodine leads to ___ of the thyroid gland.
questions.explanation: Iodine deficiency chronically stimulates TSH and enlarges the thyroid, producing goitrous hypertrophy.

questions.text: The need for Sulfur is satisfied by essential ___ .
questions.explanation: Methionine supplies dietary sulfur and can be used to synthesize cysteine. These sulfur-containing amino acids support proteins and compounds such as glutathione.

questions.text: All the followings are true about Wilson's disease except
questions.explanation: Wilson disease impairs hepatic copper excretion, causing copper accumulation in liver and increased urinary copper; serum ceruloplasmin is usually low.
options: Increase copper in urine & copper in liver
Decrease Excretion of Cu from liver to bile
Deficiency of Cu transporter ATPase protein in liver

questions.text: Cu is a cofactor of many metalloenzymes as:
questions.explanation: Copper is a cofactor for lysyl oxidase, cytochrome c oxidase, Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase, and ferroxidase, so all listed enzymes qualify.

questions.text: Which serum enzyme elevation is diagnostic in obstructive jaundice?
questions.explanation: Cholestasis raises serum alkaline phosphatase because bile duct obstruction induces release from biliary epithelium.

questions.text: Kernicterus can occur with
questions.explanation: Kernicterus is bilirubin neurotoxicity associated with severe unconjugated neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, when immature binding/barrier protection is overwhelmed.

questions.text: A patient presents with dull right sided abdominal pain, fever from the 7 days, loss of appetite, pale stool and jaundice . Blood biochemistry reveals, mixed hyperbilirubinemia i a, high SGPT (ALT) but near normal alkaline phosphatase levels. What is the cause of jaundice?
questions.explanation: Marked ALT elevation with relatively normal alkaline phosphatase favors hepatocellular injury such as viral hepatitis over obstruction, which usually raises cholestatic enzymes and causes pale stools.

questions.text: The catabolism of hemoglobin:
questions.explanation: Heme breakdown oxidatively opens the porphyrin ring to form biliverdin, releasing iron and carbon monoxide; bilirubin follows reduction.
options: Involves the oxidative cleavage of the porphyrin ring.
Results in the liberation of carbon dioxide.
Results in the formation of protoporphyrinogen.
Is the sole source of bilirubin.

questions.text: BIO9: Biliary obstruction leads to major elevation of the blood level of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Biliary obstruction prevents excretion of conjugated bilirubin, so water-soluble direct bilirubin refluxes into blood and rises markedly.

questions.text: 2. Illustrate the reaction of Bilirubin conjugation in Liver.
questions.explanation: In hepatocytes, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase adds glucuronic acid to unconjugated bilirubin, producing water-soluble bilirubin diglucuronide that can be excreted in bile.
questions.modelAnswer: Bilirubin + 2 UDP-glucuronic acid → bilirubin diglucuronide (conjugated/direct bilirubin, cholebilirubin) + 2 UDP, catalysed in the liver by glucuronyl-transferase. Conjugation makes bilirubin water-soluble for biliary excretion.

questions.text: A patient has been diagnosed with carcinoma of the head of the pancreas. Which serum enzyme is expected to be much higher than normal for this patient
questions.explanation: A pancreatic head mass can obstruct the common bile duct, causing cholestasis and a marked rise in serum alkaline phosphatase.

questions.text: 6. A female patient has a bile stone, her stool is pale clay color & bulky, she is diagnosed to has jaundice.
questions.explanation: Bile-duct obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin in blood and urine; retained bile salts cause itching, and absent bile/stercobilin causes pale bulky steatorrheic stool, unlike hemolysis with indirect bilirubin and dark stools.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the type of jaundice in this patient?
subQuestions.explanation: In the described jaundiced patient with pale stools, obstruction prevents bile from reaching the intestine, producing post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: This is post-hepatic jaundice (obstructive jaundice).

subQuestions.text: b. Did this patient have itching & why?
subQuestions.explanation: Cholestasis allows bile salts to accumulate in skin and stimulate sensory nerve endings, producing pruritus.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Yes, because of bile salts that irritate skin.

subQuestions.text: c. Why stool is bulky?
subQuestions.explanation: Without bile salts, intestinal fat digestion and absorption decline; unabsorbed lipid makes stool bulky and pale because stercobilin is absent.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Bulky because of steatorrhea in this patient as it can’t digest lipid due to deficiency of bile in intestine and stool is pale clay color due to absence of stercobilin.

subQuestions.text: d. What is the color of urine? why?
subQuestions.explanation: In the described patient with biliary obstruction, conjugated bilirubin refluxes into blood and is filtered by kidneys, darkening the urine; reduced intestinal pigment also pales stool.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Dark tea color because conjugated bilirubin secreted in urine (choluric urine)

subQuestions.text: e. compare in two points between this type of jaundice & hemolytic jaundice
subQuestions.explanation: Hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and urobilinogen without bilirubinuria; obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin and causes pale stools and dark urine.
subQuestions.modelAnswer:
Table: Anatomical site of defect | Pre-hepatic jaundice | Post-hepatic jaundice
According to underlying cause: Hemolytic jaundice | Obstructive jaundice (cholestatic)
Example of underlying disease: 1-Sickle cell crisis; 2-Rh incompatibility; 3-G6PD deficiency; 4-Pyruvate kinase deficiency | “most severe > 30mg/dl”; Obstruction of bile duct: Gall stone, Hepatoma, Cancer head of pancreas
Type of Elevated serum bilirubin: Indirect (unconjugated) | Direct (conjugation) The liver “regurgitates” CB into the blood
Presence of bilirubin in urine: Absent (Acholuric) | Present (choluric) urinary bilirubin
Urobilinogen in urine: ↑ | Absent
Stercobilin in stool: ↑ | Absent
Stool color & consistency: Normal | Pale clay color; Bulky (steatorrhea “lipid in stool)
Urine color: Normal | Dark urine
Serum bile salts: - | Present (itching)
ALP: Normal | ↑↑↑
cholesterol: Normal | ↑↑↑
hemoglobin: Low | Normal
Reticulocytes: Elevated | Normal

questions.text: Gilbert's syndrome is the genetic disorder of bilirubin metabolism. Which of the following form of bilirubin is elevated in this disease?
questions.explanation: Gilbert syndrome mildly reduces bilirubin conjugation, so unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises while conjugated bilirubin remains normal.

questions.text: Gilbert's syndrome is the genetic disorder of bilirubin metabolism and the defect lies in the uptake of bilirubin.Which of the following form of bilirubin is elevated in these subjects
questions.explanation: Gilbert syndrome reduces hepatic uptake and conjugation of bilirubin, so unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises. Conjugated bilirubin is typically not elevated.

questions.text: Which pathway of glucose metabolism is directly linked to bilirubin excretion
questions.explanation: Bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid derived from the uronic acid pathway, making it water soluble for biliary excretion.

questions.text: Steatorrhea can occur with
questions.explanation: Obstruction deprives the intestine of bile salts, impairing fat digestion and causing steatorrhea; isolated unconjugated disorders do not.

questions.text: Acholuric jaundice is
questions.explanation: Hemolysis increases unconjugated bilirubin, which is albumin-bound and not filtered into urine, producing acholuric jaundice.

questions.text: Which serum enzyme elevation is most diagnostic in obstructive jaundice
questions.explanation: Alkaline phosphatase rises disproportionately in cholestasis because bile duct epithelial injury and obstruction increase its release.

questions.text: Impaired Glucuronyl transferase activity is observed in all of the followings except
questions.explanation: Gilbert, neonatal physiologic, and Crigler–Najjar jaundice involve reduced conjugation; pyruvate kinase deficiency causes hemolysis instead.

questions.text: The increase in bile salts in plasma and urine is suggestive of:
questions.explanation: Biliary obstruction causes bile salts to accumulate in plasma and spill into urine because they cannot flow normally through the ducts into intestine.

questions.text: Hemolytic jaundice is not characterized by
questions.explanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered into urine; bilirubinuria points to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia instead.

questions.text: A patient with decreased hepatic conjugation of bilirubin. A. Increased "Indirect" bilirubin in patient's blood B. Increased "Direct" bilirubin in patient's blood
questions.explanation: Reduced hepatic conjugation leaves bilirubin water-insoluble and albumin-bound, increasing indirect bilirubin rather than direct bilirubin.

questions.text: Conjugated bilirubin is formed in the intestine.
questions.explanation: Bilirubin conjugation occurs in hepatocytes before secretion into bile; intestinal bacteria later convert bilirubin products to urobilinogen and stercobilin.

questions.text: 5. Life span of RBCs is:
questions.explanation: Red cells circulate for about 120 days before senescent cells are removed and their hemoglobin is recycled by macrophages.

questions.text: What are the enzymes responsible for Heme Catabolism
questions.explanation: Heme oxygenase opens the heme ring to biliverdin; biliverdin reductase then converts biliverdin to bilirubin.

questions.text: Choluric jaundice is/are:
questions.explanation: Choluric urine contains conjugated bilirubin, which is water-soluble. It occurs in hepatocellular and post-hepatic jaundice, but not uncomplicated hemolysis.

questions.text: The enzyme that catalyzes the formation of bilirubin diglucuronide is
questions.explanation: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase transfers glucuronic acid to bilirubin, forming water-soluble bilirubin diglucuronide for biliary excretion.

questions.text: Impaired Glucuronyl transferase activity is observed in all of the followings except
questions.explanation: Obstructive jaundice raises conjugated bilirubin through impaired bile flow, not deficient UDP-glucuronyl transferase activity.
options: Physiological jaundice of the new born

questions.text: A rise in serum "direct" bilirubin would be expected in:
questions.explanation: Biliary obstruction blocks excretion of conjugated bilirubin, causing direct bilirubin to reflux into blood. Hemolysis and conjugation defects primarily raise indirect bilirubin.
options: Absence of glucuronyl transferase as in the newborn.

questions.text: Phenobarbital is effective in treatment of all the following diseases except
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital induces residual UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity in type II Crigler–Najjar syndrome, but type I lacks the enzyme.

questions.text: Crigler Najjar syndrome is the inherited metabolic disorder of bilirubin metabolism due to a defective enzyme
questions.explanation: Crigler–Najjar syndrome reflects deficient UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, reducing bilirubin conjugation and increasing unconjugated bilirubin.

questions.text: 1. Illustrate the reaction of Heme oxidation in RES.
questions.explanation: Heme oxygenase opens the porphyrin ring in reticuloendothelial cells, releasing iron and carbon monoxide while forming biliverdin. Biliverdin reductase then produces bilirubin.
questions.modelAnswer: In reticuloendothelial cells of liver, spleen and marrow, microsomal heme oxygenase uses molecular O2 and NADPH + H+ to cleave the methenyl bridge between pyrrole rings I and II of heme, producing biliverdin with release of CO and iron. The figure also shows formation of NADP+ and water.

questions.text: Which pathway of glucose metabolism is directly linked to bilirubin excretion
questions.explanation: Bilirubin conjugation uses glucuronic acid from the uronic acid pathway, enabling secretion into bile.

questions.text: Urine analysis of a patient reveals the presence of Bilirubin and urobilinogen. which serum enzyme is expected to be elevated much higher than normal
questions.explanation: ALT rises in hepatocellular injury because damaged hepatocytes release this cytosolic enzyme; bilirubinuria and urobilinogen help characterize the pattern.

questions.text: 48. Conjugated bilirubin is:
questions.explanation: Conjugated bilirubin rises in viral hepatitis because impaired hepatocyte excretion allows it to reflux into blood. It is water-soluble and may appear in urine.
options: Transported in blood bound to albumin
Reduced in serum in biliary obstruction
Elevated in blood in viral hepatitis

questions.text: Urobilinogen is oxidized to form a colored product and these give the characteristic color of urine and feces. In which type of jaundice, the stool color is clay-colored because of absence of urobilin
questions.explanation: Without bile pigments reaching the intestine, little urobilin is formed and stools become pale or clay colored in obstruction.

questions.text: 5. Both indirect and direct bilirubin are increased in case of hepatitis, Why?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis can impair bilirubin conjugation while swelling and canalicular inflammation impede excretion, raising both unconjugated and conjugated fractions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Increase unconjugated bilirubin as a result of decreased conjugation.
Increase Conjugated bilirubin due to Inflammatory oedema of hepatocytes will compress the intracellular canaliculi “mild obstruction”.

questions.text:
(1625) Encircle True or False:
Haemolytic anaemia is associated with increased serum bilirubin. ( T - F )
questions.explanation: Hemolysis increases heme breakdown and unconjugated bilirubin production, so serum bilirubin rises if hepatic conjugation cannot keep pace.

questions.text: A patient presents with dull right-sided abdominal pain, fever from the 7 days loss of appetite, pale stool and jaundice. Blood biochemistry reveals, mixed hyperbilirubinemia, high SGPT "ALT" but near normal alkaline phosphatase levels. What is the cause
questions.explanation: Fever, abdominal discomfort, high ALT, and mixed bilirubin elevation with near-normal ALP favor hepatocellular viral hepatitis over obstruction.

questions.text: BIO8: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for making bilirubin more water soluble:
questions.explanation: UDP-glucuronyl transferase adds glucuronic acid to bilirubin, making it water-soluble for secretion into bile.

questions.text: b)What is jaundice? …………………………………………….
questions.explanation: Jaundice is yellow discoloration of skin and sclera from elevated bilirubin, usually visible once serum levels rise above roughly 2–2.5 mg/dL.
questions.modelAnswer: yellowish discoloration of sclera, conjunctiva and skin. secondary to hyper-bilirubinemia (bilirubin level exceeds 2-2.5 mg/dl).

questions.text: All the following statements about Type I Crigler-Najjar Syndrome are true except
questions.explanation: Type I Crigler–Najjar lacks functional UDP-glucuronosyltransferase; phototherapy can help, but phenobarbital cannot induce absent enzyme.
options: Increase unconjugated bilirubin more than 20 mg\dl

questions.text: Hemolytic jaundice is not characterized by
questions.explanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and cannot enter urine; conjugated bilirubin can, so its urinary presence argues against isolated hemolysis.

questions.text: In which type of jaundice, the stool color is clay - colored?
questions.explanation: Obstructed bile flow prevents stercobilin formation in the gut, so stools lose their brown pigment and become pale or clay-colored.

questions.text: Reduction of biliverdin produces bilirubin.
questions.explanation: Biliverdin is reduced to bilirubin by biliverdin reductase during macrophage heme breakdown.

questions.text: Which of the following is a marker of intravascular hemolysis
questions.explanation: Increased urinary urobilinogen reflects increased bilirubin delivery to gut and conversion by intestinal bacteria, a common feature of hemolysis.

questions.text: Crigler Najjar Syndrome is the inherited metabolic 9. disorder of bilirubin metabolism due to a defective enzyme
questions.explanation: Crigler–Najjar syndrome results from deficient UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, impairing bilirubin conjugation and causing severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.text: Which serum enzyme elevation is most diagnostic in obstructive jaundice?
questions.explanation: Obstructed bile flow causes cholestatic enzyme induction and leakage, so alkaline phosphatase is more diagnostic than aminotransferases.

questions.text: Urobilinogen is converted to……. which is excreted in the feces
questions.explanation: Intestinal bacteria convert bilirubin-derived urobilinogen into stercobilin, the brown pigment that colors feces.

questions.text: Which one of the following molecules is more hydrophobic:
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is less polar and more hydrophobic than bile acids or their salts. Hydroxyl groups and conjugation make bile salts amphipathic and more water-compatible.

questions.text: The modification to bile salts that Increases the working pH range and amphipathic nature of bile salts is
questions.explanation: Conjugation with glycine or taurine forms bile salts with improved water solubility and amphipathic detergent behavior at physiologic pH.
options: Conjugation and Formation of salts with sodium and Potassium

questions.text: BIO7: Which of the following molecules is normally used to conjugate bile acids?
questions.explanation: Primary bile acids are conjugated with glycine or taurine before secretion, increasing solubility and supporting bile-salt function.

questions.text: The bile acid is converted into secondary bile acids ( eg . deoxycholic acid) by:
questions.explanation: Intestinal bacteria deconjugate primary bile salts and remove the 7α-hydroxyl group, converting cholic acid to deoxycholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid to lithocholic acid.
options: Enzymes present in the gall bladder.
Bacterial oxidation in the small intestine.

questions.text: 1. Mention Two mechanisms of cholesterol excretion
questions.explanation: Cholesterol leaves the body mainly after conversion to bile acids and through direct fecal loss, including bacterial conversion to coprostanol.
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Conversion to bile acids and bile salts.
b) A small percentage of which is excreted in feces as coprostanol which is a reduced form of cholesterol modified by bacteria in the lower intestine.

questions.text: 7. Mention two main functions of bile salts.
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify dietary fat and form micelles that carry lipids and fat-soluble vitamins to the intestinal surface.
questions.modelAnswer:
1) The only significant mechanism for the elimination of excess cholesterol.
2) Bile acids and phospholipids solubilize cholesterol in the bile, so prevent the precipitation of cholesterol in the gallbladder.
3) They facilitate the digestion of dietary triacylglycerols by acting as emulsifying agents that render fats accessible to pancreatic lipases.
4) They facilitate the intestinal absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.text: Ratio of glycine to taurine forms in the bile is 3:1.
questions.explanation: Bile acids are conjugated more often with glycine than taurine, commonly approximated as a 3:1 ratio. Conjugation increases their solubility at intestinal pH.

questions.text: 3. Illustrate the rate limiting step of Bile synthesis, mention the organ and Coenzyme needed.
questions.explanation: Hepatic cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase catalyzes the rate-limiting first step in bile-acid synthesis, using cytochrome P450, oxygen, and NADPH.
questions.modelAnswer: In liver, the first and rate-limiting reaction is cholesterol → 7α-hydroxycholesterol by cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (a monooxygenase). It requires O2, cytochrome P450 and NADPH; hydroxylation is at C7. Bile salts downregulate enzyme expression.

questions.text: Which out of the following statements is incorrect about bile salts
questions.explanation: Glycocholate is often the predominant human bile salt; taurocholate is a valid conjugate but is not generally the major species.
options: Taurocholate is the major bile salt
Bile salts are highly effective detergents

questions.text: * Primary bile acids are conjugated to taurine forming: ___
questions.explanation: Conjugating primary bile acids with taurine forms taurocholic acid and taurochenodeoxycholic acid, which are secreted in bile as bile salts.

questions.text: BIO7: Which of the following molecules is normally used to conjugate bile acids?
questions.explanation: Glycine is a common amino-acid conjugate of bile acids, forming glycocholate and glycochenodeoxycholate.

questions.text: Which of the following is secondary bile acid
questions.explanation: Lithocholic acid is a secondary bile acid produced by intestinal bacterial modification of primary bile acids.

questions.text: The process by which bile acid sequestrants lower serum cholesterol level is
questions.explanation: Bile acid sequestrants bind bile acids in the intestine and increase fecal loss. The liver uses more cholesterol to synthesize replacement bile acids, lowering serum cholesterol.
options: Divert cholesterol metabolism towards bile acid formation

questions.text: * Primary bile acids include: ___
questions.explanation: Cholic and chenodeoxycholic acids are the primary bile acids synthesized in the liver from cholesterol.

questions.text: All of the following are functions of bile salts except:
questions.explanation: Bile salts act on lipids, not carbohydrates: they aid fat digestion, vitamin absorption, and cholesterol solubilization/excretion.
options: facilitate the intestinal absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.
Facilitate the digestion of dietary triacylglycerols.
Allows solubilization and elimination of cholesterol.
Increases emulsification of carbohydrates in the small intestine.

questions.text: 4. Mention the name of primary bile acids and secondary bile acids.
questions.explanation: Cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid are the primary bile acids made in liver; gut bacteria convert them to deoxycholic and lithocholic acids, respectively.
questions.modelAnswer:
Table: Primary bile acids | Secondary bile acids.
Cholic acid (OH 3,7,11) | Deoxycholic acid
Chenodeoxycholic acid (OH 3 &7) | lithocholic acid

questions.text: * Cholestyramine is used for treatment of: ___
questions.explanation: Cholestyramine binds bile acids in the intestine, interrupting enterohepatic recycling and increasing fecal cholesterol loss.

questions.text: The modification to bile salts that Increases the working pH range and amphipathic nature of bile salts Is
questions.explanation: Conjugating bile acids with glycine or taurine lowers their effective pKa and increases water solubility across intestinal pH conditions.
options: Formation of salts with sodium and Potassium.

questions.text: Compare between 1ry and 2ry bile acids regarding names , structure
questions.explanation: Secondary bile acids are bacterial products of primary acids: deoxycholic from cholic and lithocholic from chenodeoxycholic, each losing the 7α-hydroxyl group.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary acids are cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid, synthesized from cholesterol in liver. Secondary acids are deoxycholic acid (from cholic acid) and lithocholic acid (from chenodeoxycholic acid), produced by intestinal bacterial deconjugation and removal of the C7 hydroxyl. All have 24 carbons and a terminal carboxyl side chain. Cholic has three hydroxyl groups; chenodeoxycholic has two; their secondary derivatives each lack the C7 hydroxyl.

questions.text: * Primary bile acids are conjugated to glycine forming: ___
questions.explanation: Primary bile acids conjugated with glycine form glycocholic and glycochenodeoxycholic acids, which are more water soluble.

questions.text: * Secondary bile acids include: ___
questions.explanation: Deoxycholic and lithocholic acids are secondary bile acids formed when gut bacteria modify primary bile acids.

questions.text: Which is the following is the end product of cholesterol in stool when excreted with bile
questions.explanation: Gut bacteria convert some cholesterol to coprostanol, a poorly absorbed sterol excreted in feces along with bile-derived products.

questions.text: Which out of the following statements is incorrect about bile salts ?
questions.explanation: Glycocholate is generally the most abundant bile salt because humans conjugate bile acids with glycine more often than taurine.
options: Taurocholate is the major bile salt.
Bile salts are highly effective detergents.

questions.text: Cholic acid is converted to secondary bile acid called
questions.explanation: Gut bacteria remove a 7α-hydroxyl group from cholic acid to produce the secondary bile acid deoxycholic acid.

questions.text: Which of the following enzyme is the rate - limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1) catalyzes the rate-limiting first step of the classic bile acid synthesis pathway.

questions.text: 6. Give a short account on mechanism of action of cholestyramine
questions.explanation: Cholestyramine sequesters intestinal bile acids, increasing their fecal loss and driving hepatic conversion of cholesterol into replacement bile acids.
questions.modelAnswer:
Bind bile acids in the gut; prevent their reabsorption; and, so, promote their excretion.
They are used in the treatment of hypercholesterolemia because the removal of bile acids relieves the inhibition on the bile acid synthesis in the liver.

questions.text: . In the conversion of cholesterol to bile salts, which of the following statements best describes the process
questions.explanation: Primary bile acids are synthesized in liver from cholesterol; conjugation to glycine or taurine occurs before secretion, not in the gallbladder.
options: The side chain can be conjugated with glycine or Taurine
The hydroxyl group at 3 carbon remains in the beta position

questions.text: Which is the following is the end product of cholesterol in stool when excreted with bile
questions.explanation: Gut bacteria reduce cholesterol to coprostanol, which is poorly absorbed and leaves the body in feces.

questions.text: What is the ratio of taurine to glycine conjugates?
questions.explanation: In humans, glycine conjugates outnumber taurine conjugates by about three to one, so taurine:glycine is approximately 1:3.

questions.text: 2. Mention Two organic components of bile
questions.explanation: Bile contains organic acids/salts, phospholipids, cholesterol, and bilirubin conjugates; bile salts are the principal emulsifying agents.
questions.modelAnswer:
Bile acids.
Bile salts.
Lecithin.
Cholesterol.
Bile pigments (bilirubin glucuronides).

questions.text: Primary bile acids are:
questions.explanation: Primary bile acids have both hydrophilic hydroxyl/carboxyl regions and a hydrophobic steroid face, making them amphipathic detergents.

questions.text: The rate limiting enzyme of Bile acid synthesis is
questions.explanation: Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase catalyzes the rate-limiting step of classical bile-acid synthesis in the liver.

questions.text: 1ry Bile acids are synthesized in the intestine by Cholesterol- 7-a-hydroxylase.
questions.explanation: Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase in liver initiates primary bile-acid synthesis; intestinal bacteria instead convert primary acids to secondary ones.

questions.text: In the conversion of cholesterol to bile salts, which of the following statements best describes the process
questions.explanation: Before secretion, bile acids are conjugated at the side-chain carboxyl group with glycine or taurine, producing more water-soluble bile salts.
options: The side chain can be conjugated with glycine or Taurine
The hydroxyl group at 3 carbon remains in the beta position

questions.text: 5. Mention two amino acids used in bile conjugation
questions.explanation: Bile acids are conjugated with glycine or taurine, both amino-acid products; taurine is derived from cysteine metabolism.
questions.modelAnswer:
Glycine or taurine (end product of cysteine metabolism).
Glycine : Taurine conjugates ratio is 3:1.

questions.text: 6’ mercaptopurine
questions.explanation: 6-mercaptopurine inhibits purine synthesis and nucleotide interconversion; reduced AMP production reflects blockage of the IMP-to-adenylate branch.

questions.text: Which of the following is the rate liming enzyme of Pyrimidine synthesis
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II is the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo pyrimidine synthesis; it uses cytosolic glutamine and bicarbonate.

questions.text: 2. Illustrate PRPP synthetase reaction, Mention its regulation
questions.explanation: PRPP synthetase activates ribose-5-phosphate using ATP, and feedback inhibition by purine nucleotides limits excessive nucleotide synthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: Ribose-5-phosphate + ATP → 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP) + AMP, catalysed by PRPP synthetase. ATP supplies pyrophosphate to activate the pentose. Inorganic phosphate activates the enzyme; purine nucleotides inhibit it by end-product feedback.

questions.text: In the catabolism of CTP:
questions.explanation: Pyrimidine degradation opens the ring and releases nitrogen as ammonia; purines, unlike CTP, are degraded to uric acid.
options: uric acid is an end product.
nitrogen will be released in the form of ammonia (ammonium ion).
the nitrogen-containing ring will be oxidized.
the final product will have the same type of nitrogen-containing ring as CTP.

questions.text: ___is structurally similar to IMP, so used as anticancer (competitive inhibitor for conversion of IMP to either AMP or GMP)
questions.explanation: 6-mercaptopurine resembles hypoxanthine and inhibits purine synthesis after activation, reducing IMP-derived AMP and GMP production in proliferating cells.

questions.text: Regarding conversion of Inosine mono phosphate to other nucleotides which statement is true:
questions.explanation: Glutamine donates an amide nitrogen in GMP synthesis from XMP; AMP synthesis instead requires aspartate.
options: To Adenosine mono phosphate (AMP) is inhibited by Guanosine mono phosphate(GMP)
To AMP requires uridine mono phosphate (UMP)
To Guanosine di phosphate (GDP) requires ribonucleotide reductase

questions.text: 15. Which of the following is the rate-limiting step of purine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase catalyzes the committed, regulated step of de novo purine synthesis, inhibited by AMP, GMP, and IMP.

questions.text: 5. Illustrate deoxyribonucleotide synthesis reaction, Mention its coenzymes, and regulation
questions.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase converts ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxy forms using thioredoxin as the reducing system. ATP activates overall activity, while dATP signals sufficient pools and inhibits it.
questions.modelAnswer: Ribonucleoside diphosphate + reduced thioredoxin → 2′-deoxyribonucleoside diphosphate + oxidized thioredoxin + H2O, catalysed by ribonucleotide reductase. NADPH + H+ regenerates reduced thioredoxin through thioredoxin reductase. The reductase is an allosteric two-subunit enzyme: ATP activates it and dATP inhibits reduction of all four nucleoside diphosphates.

questions.text: The first intermediate with a complete purine ring is ____________
questions.explanation: IMP (inosinate) is the first intermediate with a complete purine ring and branches toward AMP or GMP synthesis.

questions.text: Which base derivative can serve as a precursor for the synthesis of two of the other pyrimidine base derivatives ?
questions.explanation: UMP supplies the pyrimidine pathway for CTP and dTMP synthesis; purine nucleotides cannot serve as their direct precursors.

questions.text: The ring of pyrimidine is derived from 2 AAs ___ and ___ And one carbon unit in the form of___
questions.explanation: Pyrimidine-ring atoms come from aspartate and glutamine, with carbon dioxide supplying one carbon. This contrasts with purines, assembled directly on PRPP.

questions.text: Hydroxyurea is a drug used in treatment of leukemia, because it inhibits DHF reductase enzyme so, inhibit DNA synthesis
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, reducing deoxyribonucleotide supply; dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate.

questions.text: 1. Illustrate the rate limiting step of purine synthesis, Mention its regulation
questions.explanation: PRPP amidotransferase transfers glutamine’s nitrogen onto PRPP to make 5-phosphoribosylamine, the first committed purine intermediate.
questions.modelAnswer: Glutamine + PRPP + H2O → 5-phosphoribosylamine + glutamate + pyrophosphate, by glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase. This is the committed step of purine nucleotide synthesis. AMP and GMP inhibit the enzyme; intracellular PRPP concentration controls the reaction rate.

questions.text: 3. Enumerate three amino acids used in purine synthesis
questions.explanation: Glycine contributes three atoms to the purine ring (C4, C5, N7), while glutamine supplies N3 and N9; aspartate contributes N1.
questions.modelAnswer:
Aspartate → N1
Glutamine → N3 & N9
Glycine → C4, C5 & N7

questions.text: Which of the following is the degradation product of pyrimidines?
questions.explanation: Pyrimidine ring breakdown yields beta-alanine from uracil and beta-aminoisobutyrate from thymine; purines instead yield uric acid.

questions.text: All deoxyribonucleotide is synthesized by the ribonucleotides.
questions.explanation: All deoxyribonucleotides are made by reducing the corresponding ribonucleotide diphosphates; thymidylate is then formed from dUMP.

questions.text: Impaired Thymidylate formation is due to the deficiency of-
questions.explanation: Folate supplies one-carbon units needed to convert dUMP to dTMP. Deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and can cause megaloblastic anemia.

questions.text: Phosphorylation of AMP to ADP is promoted by ____________
questions.explanation: Adenylate kinase catalyzes the reversible reaction 2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP, allowing phosphate transfer between adenine nucleotides.

questions.text: List the names of the enzyme and coenzymes required for the biochemical reaction of the synthesis of deoxyribonucleoside diphosphate from ribonucleoside diphosphate.
questions.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase uses thioredoxin electrons to reduce NDPs to dNDPs; NADPH and thioredoxin reductase regenerate reduced thioredoxin.
questions.modelAnswer: Ribonucleotide reductase reduces ribonucleoside diphosphate to the corresponding deoxyribonucleoside diphosphate. It requires reduced thioredoxin and NADPH + H+ to regenerate reduced thioredoxin through thioredoxin reductase.

questions.text: PRPP Synthetase enzyme is allosteric activated by which of the following
questions.explanation: Inorganic phosphate allosterically activates PRPP synthetase, increasing PRPP supply for nucleotide synthesis. Purine nucleotides provide feedback inhibition.

questions.text: 7. Illustrate thymidylate synthesis reaction, Mention its coenzymes
questions.explanation: Thymidylate synthase converts dUMP to dTMP using N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF, which becomes dihydrofolate; DHFR and NADPH regenerate THF.
questions.modelAnswer: dUMP + N5,N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate → dTMP + dihydrofolate, catalysed by thymidylate synthase. N5,N10-methylene THF supplies the methyl group and becomes DHF; DHF reductase regenerates THF using NADPH + H+.

questions.text: An amino group donated by glutamine is attached at C-1 of PRPP, this results in ____________
questions.explanation: Glutamine’s amide nitrogen replaces pyrophosphate on PRPP, yielding 5-phosphoribosylamine and committing ribose to purine-ring assembly.

questions.text: 4. There is balance in denovo synthesis of both types of purine nucleotides, How?
questions.explanation: Purine branches use reciprocal energy requirements: ATP drives IMP-to-GMP synthesis and GTP drives IMP-to-AMP synthesis, balancing the two nucleotide pools.
questions.modelAnswer: Reciprocal control for balance.(ATP is required for GMP synthesis & GTP is required for AMP synthesis).

questions.text: Which of the following is the coenzyme for the synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides catalyzed by an enzyme ribonucleotide reductase?
questions.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase reduces ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides; thioredoxin supplies the reducing equivalents and is regenerated using NADPH.

questions.text: The first intermediate with a complete pyrimidine ring is ____________
questions.explanation: Orotate is the first intermediate with a complete pyrimidine ring; the ring is assembled before attachment to PRPP.

questions.text:
8. Mention the name of enzyme inhibited by the following drugs:
a) Methotrexate b) Hydroxyurea c) 5-flurouracil
questions.explanation: Methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase, hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, and 5-fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthase, limiting DNA precursor synthesis.
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Methotrexate inhibits Dihydrofolate reductase.
b) Hydroxyurea inhibits Ribonucleotide reductase
c) 5-flurouracil inhibits Thymidylate Synthase

questions.text: Which of the following serves as the cofactor for the denovo synthesis of purine metabolism?
questions.explanation: Folate derivatives donate one-carbon units during de novo purine synthesis; N¹⁰-formyl-THF supplies two carbons of the purine ring.

questions.text: Which of the following contributes nitrogen atoms to both purine and pyrimidine rings ?
questions.explanation: Aspartate contributes nitrogen to both purines and pyrimidines, though it enters at different steps in each pathway.

questions.text: A 7 - year - old boy suffers from mental retardation and self mutilation and has an increased levels of serum uric acid . These symptoms are characteristic of Lesch Nyhan syndrome, which is due to defective
questions.explanation: HGPRT normally salvages hypoxanthine and guanine. Its loss causes Lesch–Nyhan syndrome with excess uric acid and neurologic features, including self-injury.

questions.text: BIO11: As regards Methotrexate, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate is a folate analogue used as an anticancer drug; it inhibits mammalian dihydrofolate reductase and limits nucleotide synthesis.
options: It Inhibits mammalian synthesis of folic acid.
It Inhibits bacterial synthesis of folic acid.
It is used as an anticancer drug.
It is the structural analogue of para amino benzoic acid.
It acts as an irreversible noncompetitive inhibitor.

questions.text: Inhibitors of dihydrofolate reductase, such as methotrexate, will inhibit DNA replication because they prevent
questions.explanation: Methotrexate blocks DHFR, depleting reduced folate needed by thymidylate synthase to convert dUMP into dTMP for DNA synthesis.
options: recycling of nucleoside bases into nucleotides
formation of the RNA primer required for DNA synthesis

questions.text: How to regulate the De novo synthesis of purines
questions.explanation: Purine synthesis is feedback-regulated at PRPP production and the committed amidotransferase step; AMP and GMP inhibit their own branch products, with reciprocal ATP/GTP use balancing output.
questions.modelAnswer: PRPP synthetase is activated by inorganic phosphate and inhibited by purine nucleotides. Glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase is inhibited by AMP/GMP and controlled by PRPP concentration. Conversion of IMP into AMP or GMP is inhibited by the corresponding end product. Reciprocal control balances the branches: GTP is involved in AMP synthesis and ATP in GMP synthesis.

questions.text: Which of the following statement is correct as regard reciprocal regulation of purine nucleotides:
questions.explanation: AMP synthesis uses GTP, while GMP synthesis uses ATP; each purine branch is promoted by the other nucleotide’s energy input.
options: GTP is involved in AMP synthesis
ATP is involved in GMP synthesis
Rate of AMP production increases with increasing concentrations of GTP
Rate of GMP production increases with increasing concentrations of ATP

questions.text: Orotic aciduria is an inherited genetic disorder caused by a deficiency of the following enzyme:
questions.explanation: UMP synthase deficiency blocks the last steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis, causing orotic aciduria with megaloblastic anemia.

questions.text: Orotic aciduria is due to deficiency of which of the following enzyme
questions.explanation: Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase is one activity of UMP synthase. Impaired conversion of orotate to pyrimidine nucleotides causes orotate accumulation and megaloblastic anemia.

questions.text: Methotrexate inhibits which of the following enzyme:
questions.explanation: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing regenerated THF needed for thymidylate and purine synthesis.

questions.text: BIO12: In Orotic aciduria, which of the following is not correct?
questions.explanation: Classic hereditary orotic aciduria is due to UMP synthase deficiency and responds to uridine; dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is not the defective enzyme.
options: It could be treated by uridine administration.
It’s due to defective dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
It can occur secondary to ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC) deficiency.
It’s due to defect in UMP synthase enzyme.

questions.text: CTP is formed from UTP by the action of ____________
questions.explanation: CTP synthetase converts UTP to CTP by adding an amino group from glutamine and using ATP. The enzyme is also called cytidylate synthetase.

questions.text: Treatment with hydroxyurea, a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor is begun. The normal functioning of this enzyme is to do which of the followings ?
questions.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase converts ribonucleotides into deoxyribonucleotides, supplying the precursors needed for DNA synthesis.

questions.text: 6. Illustrate the rate limiting step of Pyrimidine synthesis, Mention its regulation
questions.explanation: CPS II is the cytosolic, regulated entry step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis; PRPP activates it and UTP provides feedback inhibition.
questions.modelAnswer: Glutamine + CO2 + H2O + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate + glutamate + 2 ADP + Pi, catalysed by carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase II. This is the regulated step in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. PRPP activates CPS II; UTP inhibits it.

questions.text: In humans, uric acid is the end product of catabolism of:
questions.explanation: Humans degrade purine nucleotides to uric acid because they lack uricase. Pyrimidines are instead broken down to soluble products.

questions.text: A 1-year-old female patient is lethargic, weak, and anemic. Her urine contains an elevated level of orotic acid. The administration of which of the following compounds is most likely to alleviate her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Orotic aciduria from UMP synthase deficiency is treated with uridine, which bypasses the blocked de novo pyrimidine pathway.

questions.text: in de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides
questions.explanation: Purine rings are assembled stepwise directly on PRPP, whereas pyrimidine rings are completed as orotate before attachment to ribose phosphate.
options: the purine ring is assembled first , and then linked to ribose phosphate
the purine ring is built on PRPP

questions.text: Fluorouracil is an anti-tumor agent that binds and irreversibly inhibit which of the following enzyme
questions.explanation: 5-fluorouracil is converted to FdUMP, which forms a stable inhibitory complex with thymidylate synthase and blocks dTMP production.

questions.text: Ribonucleotide reductase It is an allosteric enzyme ,which ___acts as an allosteric inhibitor ,while ___ Is an allosteric activator
questions.explanation: ATP activates ribonucleotide reductase when deoxynucleotide pools are low; dATP signals abundance and allosterically inhibits the enzyme.

questions.text: Thioredoxin is involved in the:
questions.explanation: Thioredoxin supplies reducing equivalents for ribonucleotide reductase, which converts ribonucleotides into DNA-precursor deoxyribonucleotides.
options: conversion of a ribonucleotide to a deoxyribonucleotide.
inhibition of xanthine oxidase as a treatment for gout.

questions.text: The biological value of nucleotides are: to produce nucleic acid as ___ and___ Structural component of some coenzymes as ___ And ___ Signal transduction such as ___ And ___ Which are 2nd messengers.
questions.explanation: Nucleotides form DNA and RNA, are parts of coenzymes such as CoA, FAD, and NAD+, and serve as signaling molecules such as cAMP and cGMP.

questions.text: The formation of dATP for DNA synthesis occurs primarily by:
questions.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase converts ADP to dADP using thioredoxin-derived reducing power; phosphorylation then yields dATP for DNA synthesis.
options: de novo synthsis beginning with dPRPP.
salvaging adenine using a nucleoside phosphorylase and dR 1-P.
converting ADP to dADP using thioredoxin.
converting dIMP to dAMP using 5,10-methylene THF.

questions.text: What substances required for both purine and pyrimidine synthesis
questions.explanation: Both nucleotide pathways use glutamine, aspartate, and PRPP; CO₂ also contributes atoms, while folate transfers one-carbon units.
questions.modelAnswer: Both pathways require glutamine, aspartic acid and PRPP as essential precursors; CO2 is a ring-atom source for both. Tetrahydrofolate is required for purine synthesis and also for pyrimidine thymidylate synthesis.

questions.text: The conversion of lnosine Mono phosphate
questions.explanation: IMP becomes GMP through IMP dehydrogenase and GMP synthetase; the latter uses glutamine as the nitrogen donor and ATP for energy.
options: To Adenosine mono phosphate (AMP) is inhibited by Guanosine mono phosphate(GMP)
To AMP requires uridine mono phosphate (UMP)
To Guanosine di phosphate (GDP) requires ribonucleotide reductase

questions.text: What is an activator of the enzyme “Glutamine: Phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase” a committed step of de novo biosynthesis of purines?
questions.explanation: PRPP activates glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase, the committed enzyme of de novo purine synthesis; purine nucleotides inhibit it by feedback.

questions.text: List the names of the enzyme and coenzymes required for the biochemical reaction of the synthesis of deoxyribonucleoside diphosphate from ribonucleoside diphosphate. (1mark)
questions.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase converts ribonucleoside diphosphates into their deoxy forms, using thioredoxin and NADPH-linked regeneration.
questions.modelAnswer: Ribonucleotide reductase reduces ribonucleoside diphosphate to the corresponding deoxyribonucleoside diphosphate. It requires reduced thioredoxin and NADPH + H+ to regenerate reduced thioredoxin through thioredoxin reductase.

questions.text: Orotate phosphoribosyl transferase and orotidylate decarboxylase are 2 catalytic (sites) of a single bifunctional enzyme called ___
questions.explanation: UMP synthase is bifunctional: its orotate phosphoribosyltransferase domain makes OMP, and its orotidylate decarboxylase domain converts OMP to UMP.

questions.text: 5’ Fluorouracil is an anticancer which inhibit the synthesis of
questions.explanation: 5-fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthase, reducing dTMP (thymidine nucleotide) production needed for DNA synthesis.

questions.text: A biological structure formed of pentose sugar , nitrogenous base and P is called ___ , while the same structure without P called___
questions.explanation: A nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base, pentose, and phosphate; removing the phosphate leaves the nucleoside.

questions.text: in de novo purine synthesis how many of the C and N atoms of the purine ring system would be provided by glycine and glutamine together
questions.explanation: Glycine contributes three atoms to the purine ring and glutamine contributes two nitrogen atoms, totaling five ring atoms.

questions.text: All the following are Mitochondrial Cytochrome P450 functions except.
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial CYP enzymes support steroid, bile-acid, and vitamin-D metabolism; polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon hydroxylation is chiefly microsomal.

questions.text: Nicotinamide is conjugated with which of the following for excretion
questions.explanation: Nicotinamide is methylated, principally by nicotinamide N-methyltransferase, to water-soluble metabolites that can be excreted.

questions.text: Glucuronic acid is produced from glucose by
questions.explanation: Glucuronic acid is formed by oxidation of glucose’s C6 primary alcohol group to a carboxyl group.

questions.text: Which statement is incorrect as regard the biochemical basis of NAFLD?
questions.explanation: In NAFLD, hepatic fatty-acid uptake and triglyceride synthesis can exceed VLDL export capacity; the problem is insufficient export relative to lipid load, not excessive lipoprotein production.
options: increase in serum FFAs and liver uptake.
More TAG synthesis and accumulation in the liver.
excessive lipoprotein production by liver to accommodate the high FFA influx.
TAG produced by liver is beyond the capacity of VLDL export from liver.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true about cytochrome P450 enzymes?
questions.explanation: Cytochrome P450 enzymes are heme-containing monooxygenases with iron at the catalytic center, not magnesium. Their genetic variation can alter drug metabolism.
options: They belong to a general class of enzymes called monooxygenases.
There are over 30 different cytochrome P450 enzymes.
Variation in cytochrome P450 enzyme profile between individuals can explain individual variation in drug susceptibility.

questions.text: In Alcohol addict patient, all the following statements are true Except.
questions.explanation: Ethanol metabolism raises NADH, favoring lactate and triglyceride synthesis and suppressing fatty-acid oxidation; stimulation of oxidation is the false statement.
options: Shift oxaloacetate to malate, so increase Acetyl CoA
Shift Dihydroxyacetone Phosphate (DHAP) to glycerol 3-P. so increase TAG synthesis.

questions.text: Lipids are mainly exported from the liver in the form of:
questions.explanation: The liver exports endogenous triglyceride in VLDL; chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride from intestine.

questions.text: patient was given warfarin as anticoagulant, then he take phenobarbital
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital induces hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes, increasing warfarin clearance and shortening its half-life. A higher warfarin dose may be needed with monitoring.
options: the catabolism of Warfarin is decreased
we have to decrease the dose of warfarin
phenobarbital decreases rate of monooxygenase synthesis
the half-life of warfarin is decreased

questions.text: 2. Mention three causes for each category:
questions.explanation: Plasma free fatty acids rise with starvation, high-fat intake, or uncontrolled diabetes. Fatty liver can follow impaired apoprotein/VLDL synthesis or secretion, reducing triglyceride export.
questions.modelAnswer:
Raised levels of plasma free fatty acids: 1- Starvation. 2- Feeding of high-fat diets. 3- Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.
Metabolic block in the production of plasma lipoproteins: 1. Block in apolipoprotein synthesis “may be due to satvation”. 2. Block in the synthesis of the lipoprotein. 3. Failure in the secretory mechanism itself of VLDL. 4. Some toxins & Drugs: antibiotic puromycin, lead, arsenic. 5. Failure in supplying of phospholipids

questions.text: all the following is true about Cytochrome P450 Except
questions.explanation: Cytochrome P450 enzymes are heme monooxygenases that insert one oxygen atom into a substrate while reducing the other to water.

questions.text: 4. Mention Two importance of Glucuronic acid
questions.explanation: Glucuronic acid conjugation increases compound solubility for elimination; it also forms part of glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans. Its pathway can feed xylulose into pentose metabolism.
questions.modelAnswer:
Detoxification of some compounds e.g. Steroids, bilirubin and Aspirin.
a component of the glycosaminoglycans & proteoglycans.
Glucuronic acid is converted to L-Xylulose then to D-Xylulose which can enter HMP pathway.

questions.text: Which of the followings are not lipotropic agents
questions.explanation: Biotin is not a typical lipotropic factor; choline, methionine, and some vitamins support phospholipid synthesis or hepatic fat export.
options: Essential fatty acids Vitamin A.C and E

questions.text: 4. What is the relation of Cytochrome P450 to carcinogens? Mention one reason.
questions.explanation: Some CYP enzymes bioactivate procarcinogens, such as smoke-derived polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, into DNA-reactive metabolites.
questions.modelAnswer:
Convert inert inactive metabolite into active “Prodrug into active compound”.
In the lung, pro-carcinogens polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon “PAHs” inhaled by smoking are converted to active carcinogens.

questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is involved in the Glucuronidation reactions?
questions.explanation: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase transfers glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronic acid to bilirubin, drugs, and other compounds to aid excretion.

questions.text: Activation of xenobiotics can be ___ or ___ which can lead to the formation of ___ From an inert precursor.
questions.explanation: Phase-I activation can be beneficial or harmful: bioactivation may convert an inert xenobiotic into a reactive carcinogen.

questions.text:
Cytochrome P450 is involved in some normal physiological processes as 
synthesis of___ And ___
Vit D
Steroid hormones
questions.explanation: Cytochrome P450 enzymes support vitamin D activation and steroid hormone synthesis as well as xenobiotic metabolism, using oxygen and reducing equivalents.

questions.text: Which of the following statement is incorrect about conjugation reaction?
questions.explanation: Conjugation generally adds a polar group and increases water solubility; it does not decrease xenobiotic polarity.
options: The reaction can occur after phase 1 reaction.
Most of the reaction take place in the liver.
After conjugation, most of the compounds are considered non toxic.
The polarity of xenobiotics decreased after conjugation.

questions.text: BIO6: Which of the following is true regarding cytochrome P 450?
questions.explanation: Most CYP isoforms are inducible by drugs or other xenobiotics, allowing enzyme levels to rise with repeated exposure.
options: NADH acts as a cofactor for it.
Most cytochrome P 450 isoform are inducible.
It catalyzes the introduction of 2 oxygen atom into the substrate.
Not all cytochrome P 450 isoform are hemoproteins.

questions.text: The biochemical basis of AFLD is due to decreased NADH/NAD+ ratio
questions.explanation: Alcohol metabolism raises the hepatic NADH/NAD+ ratio, promoting triglyceride synthesis and impairing fatty-acid oxidation. Thus a decreased ratio is not the biochemical basis of AFLD.

questions.text: Phenyl acetate is conjugated with amino acid ___ to give___
questions.explanation: Phenylacetate conjugates with glutamine to form phenylacetylglutamine, which is more water-soluble and excreted in urine.

questions.text: The hydroxylated products of phase 1 are converted to soluble metabolites by coupling with polar agents in phase 2 of detoxification reactions by a process called Conjugation. Which of the following is not a conjugating agent
questions.explanation: Phase II conjugation uses acetate, sulfate, glutathione, or glucuronate; bicarbonate is not a typical activated conjugating donor.

questions.text: Early stages of fatty liver are asymptomatic and reversible.
questions.explanation: Early hepatic steatosis often produces no symptoms and can improve when its cause is addressed. Persistent injury may progress to inflammation, fibrosis, or cirrhosis.

questions.text: 3. Define Lipotropic Factors and mention Two examples:
questions.explanation: Lipotropic factors help package and export hepatic fat by supporting phospholipid synthesis; examples include choline and methionine.
questions.modelAnswer:
These are factors that stimulate synthesis of phospholipids and avoid fatty liver.
Examples: 1) Methyl donors for choline: S-adenosyl Methionine and Casein. 2) Choline, inositol, serine and ethanolamine. 3) B12, folic acid, pantothenic acid (Trans-methylation reactions). 4) Essential FA (Unsaturated FA). 5) Estrogen inhibit HMG COA reductase. 6) Antioxidants like Vit. E and Selenium

questions.text: The enzyme catalyzing the conjugation of glutathione with xenobitics is ___
questions.explanation: Glutathione S-transferases attach glutathione to electrophilic xenobiotics, increasing water solubility and facilitating detoxification or excretion.

questions.text: Sulfation Is an Important method of detoxification of foreign compounds. Which of the following acts as a source of sulfate?
questions.explanation: Sulfotransferases use PAPS, 3′-phosphoadenosine-5′-phosphosulfate, as the activated sulfate donor for conjugation reactions.

questions.text: Cytochrome P450 needs ___ As a cofactor.
questions.explanation: Cytochrome P450 reactions require NADPH as the electron donor, delivered through the NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase system.

questions.text: For the patient, who take Isoniazid for TB, which of the following using in conjugation for excretion
questions.explanation: Isoniazid is primarily acetylated by NAT2; inherited slow or rapid acetylator status changes its metabolism and adverse-effect risk.

questions.text: 1. Mention Two main categories of Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease:
questions.explanation: Fatty liver develops when fatty-acid delivery and synthesis exceed oxidation and export. Raised plasma free fatty acids and impaired lipoprotein production are two contributing mechanisms.
questions.modelAnswer:
Raised levels of plasma free fatty acids.
Metabolic block in the production of plasma lipoproteins

questions.text: Compounds enhance breakdown of fat during metabolism in the body are called ___ such as ___ and___
questions.explanation: Lipotropic factors such as choline and folate/B₁₂ support phospholipid production and export of triglyceride from liver, limiting fatty accumulation.

questions.text: The active form of glucuronic acid is
questions.explanation: UDP-glucuronic acid is the activated glucuronate donor used by glucuronosyltransferases in phase II conjugation.

questions.text: What is the fate of compound activation which can occur during detoxification?
questions.explanation: Phase I metabolism can activate an inactive prodrug or create a harmful reactive metabolite, such as a carcinogenic intermediate. Activation is therefore beneficial or harmful depending on the substrate.
questions.modelAnswer:
it can desirable, as Activation of a prodrug to the active form.
Also it can be undesirable, like formation of a carcinogen from an inert precursor (converting inactive polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons by hydroxylation in the lung into active carcinogens).

questions.text: Which of the following reactions is considered as an index for liver function?
questions.explanation: Hippuric acid formation from benzoate and glycine is used as a liver detoxification-function test.

questions.text: Aspirin which is used as analgesic and antipyretic is conjugated by ___
questions.explanation: Aspirin can undergo glucuronidation, forming acyl and phenolic glucuronides that enhance elimination.

questions.text: 6. Mention one active compound used in conjugation, its enzyme and its use.
questions.explanation: Conjugation uses activated donors such as UDP-glucuronic acid, PAPS, acetyl-CoA, or SAM and matching transferases to increase solubility or alter biological activity.
questions.modelAnswer:
Table columns: Glucuronidation | Sulfation | Glycine | Acetylation | Methylation
Active donor: UDP-Glucuronic | PAPS “3’phsphoadenosyl 5’ Phospho-sulfate” | Glycine | Acetyl CoA | SAM “S-Adenosyl Methionine”
Enzyme: glucuronyl transferase | sulfotransferase | Glycine transferase | Acetyl transferase | Methyltransferase
One use: bilirubin, salicylic acids from Aspirin | Steroids and alcoholic compounds | Benzoic acid → give hippuric acid | Histamine & Isoniazid (INH) drug | Nicotinamide.

questions.text: Ethanol metabolism is carried out by two enzymes ___ and ___ Which yield high level of ___ (coenzyme) in the reduced state.
questions.explanation: Alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases oxidize ethanol to acetate, reducing NAD⁺ to NADH at both steps.

questions.text: Conjugation of foreign compounds with glycine results in the formation of
questions.explanation: Glycine conjugation of benzoic acid forms hippuric acid, a water-soluble product excreted in urine.

questions.text: Metabolism of xenobiotics can be mainly detoxification or___
questions.explanation: Xenobiotic metabolism can detoxify a compound for elimination or bioactivate it into a more reactive product, sometimes creating toxicity.

questions.text: 3. Increase the dose of anticoagulant for patients who take phenobarbital, Why? mention one cause.
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital induces hepatic CYP enzymes, accelerating warfarin breakdown and lowering anticoagulant effect; a higher dose may therefore be needed.
questions.modelAnswer: phenobarbital is an inducer for Cytochrome P-450 “increased 3-4 folds in 4 days”, so the patient catabolism warfarin more rapidly.

questions.text: Conjugation of foreign compounds with glycine results in the formation of
questions.explanation: Hippuric acid is produced when glycine conjugates benzoate; this pathway helps eliminate aromatic organic acids.

questions.text: If a patient is taking phenobarbital with warfarin, the doctor should ___ the dose of warfarin.
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital induces hepatic enzymes that metabolize warfarin faster, lowering its anticoagulant effect. Clinicians may need to increase the dose and monitor INR.

questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about cytochrome p450?
questions.explanation: Cytochrome P450 enzymes are monooxygenases: they incorporate one oxygen atom into substrate and reduce the other to water, so they are not dioxygenases.
options: They can be inhibited by drugs.

questions.text: at which carbon UDP glucoronate result from oxidation of UDP glucose
questions.explanation: UDP-glucose is oxidized at carbon 6 to UDP-glucuronate, providing activated glucuronic acid for conjugation reactions.

questions.text: 1. Mention two pathological effects of xenobiotics on human cells.
questions.explanation: Reactive xenobiotics can bind DNA and cause mutations or bind proteins and create antigenic complexes, leading to carcinogenesis or immune reactions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Bind to DNA, cause mutation & may be carcinogenic if mutation occur in tumor suppressor gene.
May be antigenic after binding to protein & stimulate antibodies formations.

questions.text:
The hydroxylated products of phase 1 are converted to a more soluble metabolite by conjugation with a polar
compounds in phase 2 of detoxification reaction. Which of the following is NOT a conjugating agent?
questions.explanation: Active sulfate, SAM, glucuronate, and acetate can donate conjugating groups; bicarbonate is not a phase-II conjugation donor.

questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is involoved in glucuronidation reaction?
questions.explanation: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase transfers glucuronate from UDP-glucuronic acid to substrates, increasing their aqueous solubility.

questions.text: The consequences of shifting the redox state of the liver; high (NADH/NAD+) are all except:.
questions.explanation: A high hepatic NADH/NAD+ ratio favors triglyceride production and lipogenesis, but it causes lactic acidosis rather than metabolic alkalosis.
options: availability of acetyl CoA for lipogenesis.
increase rate of lipogenesis and decrease the rate of FFA oxidation.

questions.text: 30. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the biochemical basis of non alcoholic fatty liver (NAFLD)?
questions.explanation: Reduced hepatic lipoprotein/VLDL production limits triglyceride export, allowing fat to accumulate in hepatocytes in fatty liver.
options: Decrease FFAs uptake by the liver
Decrease lipoprotein production by the liver
Impaired TAG synthesis in the liver
Eating excess unsaturated fatty acids in diet

questions.text: The hydroxylated products of phase.1 are converted to soluble metabolites by coupling with polar agents in phase .2 of detoxification reactions by a process called Conjugation. Which of the following is not a conjugating agent?
questions.explanation: Bicarbonate is not a usual phase II conjugating agent; acetyl, sulfate, glutathione, and glucuronate are common activated donors.

questions.text: Sulphation is an important reaction in conjugation. The source of Sulphur is ___
questions.explanation: Sulfation uses activated sulfate in PAPS, synthesized from sulfate and ATP. Sulfotransferases transfer that sulfate group to substrates.

questions.text: Ethanol can increase the carcinogenesis occurring due to tobacco smoking.
questions.explanation: True: ethanol can increase tobacco-related carcinogenesis by facilitating carcinogen penetration and adding acetaldehyde and oxidative injury.

questions.text: 5. Mention three physiological substrates of mitochondrial Cytochrome P450.
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial CYP enzymes participate in steroid hydroxylation, bile-acid synthesis, and vitamin D activation; their substrates are physiologic rather than xenobiotic.
questions.modelAnswer:
Hydroxylation in Steroid Hormones synthesis in steroidogenic tissues.
Bile acid synthesis in liver.
Vit D3 hydroxylation and activation in kidney.

questions.text: 4. Increase NADH/NAD ratio leads to Alcoholic fatty liver disease (AFLD) Mention two causes.
questions.explanation: Alcohol-derived NADH suppresses fatty-acid oxidation and shifts intermediates toward glycerol-3-phosphate and lactate. More triglyceride synthesis and less export promote fatty liver.
questions.modelAnswer:
Inhibit FA oxidation.
Shift oxaloacetate to malate, so inhibit Krebs’s cycle. (Accumulate acetyl CoA).
↑ Acetyl CoA with increase FA synthesis.
Shift Dihydroxyacetone Phosphate (DHAP) to glycerol 3-P
Fatty acids + Glycerol 3-P → ↑ TAG synthesis.
Shift pyruvate to lactate → lactic acidosis.

questions.text: Question 4: Give an account on the clinical forms of mucocutaneous candidiasis. (June 2013)
questions.explanation: Mucocutaneous candidiasis ranges from oral thrush to vulvovaginal and intertriginous skin or nail-fold infection. Moisture, diabetes, antibiotics, infancy, and immunosuppression increase risk.
questions.modelAnswer:
The clinical forms are:
1. Oral thrush or moniliasis :
  • White curd like patches on tongue, gums, palate.
  • Occurs in:
     a) Premature infants.
     b) Babies on antibiotics.
     c) Immunosuppressed patients on long-term antibiotics.
     d) Immune deficiency syndrome.

2. Vulvovaginitis :
  • Thick yellow discharge, burning sensation, curd like patches on vaginal mucosa.
  • Predisposed by:
     a)  Diabetes
     b)  Antibiotic therapy
     c)  Contraceptive pills
     d)  Pregnancy

3. Cutaneous candidiasis :
  •  Affects skin especially in obese, diabetics, infants (napkin dermatitis). Usually at the
    moist and warm parts of body. e.g. axilla, groin, intergluteal or inframammary folds.
  •  Appear as red, moist lesions that may develop into vesicles.
  • Also can affect nails (onychomycosis) when fingers are repeatedly immersed in water
  painful swelling and erythema of nail fold  may destroy the nail.

For the first 2 days after onset of symptoms

subQuestions.explanation: Reflux esophagitis shows basal-zone hyperplasia, elongated lamina propria papillae, and inflammatory cells crossing the epithelium; severe injury may erode or ulcerate.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the possible complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Fibrotic narrowing follows chronic ulceration, while Barrett metaplasia reflects intestinal-type replacement of distal squamous epithelium after reflux.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Peptic ulcer, fibrotic stricture and Barrett metaplasia.

subQuestions.text: d. Enumerate causes of dysphagia?
subQuestions.explanation: Dysphagia can arise from luminal obstruction, congenital webs or stenosis, inflammatory scarring, motility disorders such as achalasia, tumors, or external compression.
