subQuestions.modelAnswer: Focal mucosal erosions/hemorrhage; acute peptic ulcers may be multiple small rounded brown-black lesions with normal adjacent mucosa and no scar.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the microscopic findings likely to be presentin a gastric biopsy?
subQuestions.explanation: NSAID injury reduces mucosal prostaglandins and causes acute erosive hemorrhagic gastritis, with neutrophilic inflammation, mucosal erosion, and hemorrhage on biopsy.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Neutrophilic inflammation, mucosal erosion/hemorrhage; severe ulcers may extend into deep layers with serositis.

subQuestions.text: d. List other causes of hematemesis.
subQuestions.explanation: Hematemesis can result from varices, erosive gastritis, peptic ulcer, upper-GI cancer, or bleeding disorders; the source is any lesion that bleeds into the upper tract.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Oesophageal varices, carcinoma, peptic ulcer or rupture of aortic aneurysm into oesophagus; acute/chronic gastritis, gastroduodenal peptic ulcer, gastric carcinoma and drug-induced erosions; generalized bleeding diseases such as purpura, leukaemia, haemophilia and scurvy.

questions.text: Helicobacter pylori are:
questions.explanation: H. pylori is a curved or S-shaped, motile gram-negative bacillus adapted to the gastric mucus layer.

questions.text: PAT4: The etiology of chronic atrophic gastritis involving the fundus and associated with pernicious anaemia is:
questions.explanation: Autoimmune gastritis targets parietal cells and intrinsic factor in body/fundus, causing achlorhydria and vitamin B12 deficiency with pernicious anemia.

questions.text: 9- The following is NOT a feature of chronic gastritis:
questions.explanation: Chronic gastritis commonly causes glandular atrophy, metaplasia, and chronic inflammation, sometimes with active neutrophils or dysplasia. Glandular hypertrophy is not typical.

questions.text: 45.Acute erosive gastritis is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Acute erosive gastritis produces multiple superficial mucosal erosions, unlike deep chronic ulcers with a fibrotic base.
options: superficial multiple ulcerations of gastric mucosa
a deep ulcer of the stomach with a scarred base
a frequent association with gastric cancer

questions.text: 49.What is the significance of intestinal metaplasia in the stomach or colon?
questions.explanation: Gastric intestinal metaplasia signals chronic mucosal injury and raises risk for dysplasia and adenocarcinoma, though risk depends on extent and subtype.
options: It is frequently associated with mildly precancerous inflammatory disease.
It is usually associated with heterotopic pancreas.

questions.text: 18. The premalignant change In chronic gastritis is :
questions.explanation: Intestinal metaplasia replaces gastric epithelium with intestinal-type cells during chronic injury and is a premalignant step in the gastric carcinogenesis sequence.

questions.text:
22. The most characteristic criteria for diagnosis of neoplastic adenomatous gastric polyp is
       :
questions.explanation: Dysplasia, with disordered growth and cytologic atypia, defines a gastric adenomatous polyp and signals neoplastic potential.

questions.text:
66.A normal level of gastric acidity following administration of histamine would tend to
exclude which of the following?
questions.explanation: Atrophic gastritis destroys acid-producing parietal cells, so a normal acid response to histamine argues against advanced atrophy.

questions.text: Pathogenicity of Helicobacter pylori is due to:
questions.explanation: Helicobacter pylori produces urease, generating ammonia that buffers local acid and supports gastric colonization. Adhesins and toxins also contribute to injury.

questions.text:
29. A 54-year-old man has complained for 5 months of upper abdominal pain accompanied
by nausea. Microscopic examination of gastric biopsies reveals acute and chronic mucosal
inflammation along with the presence of Helicobacter pylori organisms. The presence of these
organisms is most likely to be associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: H. pylori infection is strongly associated with duodenal peptic ulceration, often through antral inflammation and increased acid delivery.
options: Development of large B cell lymphoma

questions.text:
40) Gastric biopsies from patients with dyspeptic symptoms reveal inflammatory
 infiltration in the foveolar areas, consisting mainly of lymphocytes, with few neutrophils
 and eosinophils. Glandular atrophy is insignificant. Which of the following diagnoses is
 most compatible with these histologic features?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes with few neutrophils and preserved glands indicate chronic superficial gastritis rather than acute inflammation or established atrophy.

questions.text:
(1006) Choose the correct answer:
Pathogenicity of Helicobacter pylori is due to:
questions.explanation: H. pylori urease generates ammonia from urea, buffering gastric acid and helping the organism colonize the gastric mucus layer.

questions.text:
(1070) Choose the correct answer:
A patient taking aspirin for many years. Now he is complaining of hematemesis. The most possible diagnosis.
questions.explanation: Long-term aspirin use impairs prostaglandin-mediated mucosal defense, increasing risk of gastric peptic ulceration and bleeding.

questions.text:
10) A 45-year-old man has had vague abdominal pain and nausea for the past 3 years.
He has no difficulty in swallowing and no heartburn following meals. Upper Gi
endoscopy reveals antral mucosal erythema, but no ulcerations or masses. Biopsies
are taken, and microscopically there is a chronic non-specific gastritis. Which of the

following conditions most likely to be present in this man?
questions.explanation: H. pylori colonization and chronic mucosal inflammation are strongly associated with duodenal ulceration, often through increased acid delivery.

questions.text: Activity in chronic gastritis means:
questions.explanation: Chronic gastritis is “active” when neutrophils infiltrate the chronic inflammatory background; lymphocytes and plasma cells define chronic inflammation itself.

questions.text:
39) Endoscopic biopsy performed in a patient with gastric hypochlorhydria reveals chronic
 atrophic gastritis, involving the fundus and sparing the antral region. Which of the
 following pathogenetic mechanisms. is involved in this form of gastritis?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune gastritis targets parietal cells in the body and fundus while often sparing the antrum, producing atrophy, hypochlorhydria, and intrinsic-factor deficiency.

questions.text: A 54-year-old man has complained for 5 months of upper abdominal pain accompanied by nausea. Microscopic examination of gastric biopsies reveals acute and chronic mucosal inflammation along with the presence of Helicobacter pylori organisms. The presence of these organisms is most likely to be associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: Antral chronic gastritis is usually associated with H. pylori infection, which is distinct from autoimmune pernicious anemia.
options: Development of large B cell lymphoma

questions.text:
20. Endoscopic biopsy perforated in a patient with gastric hypochlorhydiia reveals chronic
afrophic gastritis, involving the fundus and sparing the antral region. Which of the following
pathogenetic mechanisms is involved in this form of gastritis?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune injury to parietal cells causes fundus/body atrophy, hypochlorhydria, intrinsic-factor loss, and potential pernicious anemia while sparing antrum.

questions.text:
47.Which is/are seen with greater than usual frequency in patients exhibiting atrophic
gastritis?
questions.explanation: Atrophic gastritis reduces acid and intrinsic-factor production, increasing risk of pernicious anemia; chronic mucosal atrophy also raises gastric carcinoma risk.

questions.text: 21- Risk of development of adenocarcinoma is high with:
questions.explanation: Adenomatous gastric polyps contain dysplasia and carry greater malignant potential than inflammatory, hyperplastic, or fundic gland polyps.

questions.text:
16. A biopsy of the antrum of the stomach of an adult who presents with epigastric pain
reveals numerous lymphocytes and plasma cells within the lamina propria, which is of normal
thickness. « • There are also scattered neutrophils within the glandular epithelial cells. A
silver stain for this specimen reveals small, curved organisms. These histologic changes are
more consistent with infection by which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: Curved organisms on gastric silver stain with chronic active antral gastritis are characteristic of Helicobacter pylori infection.

questions.text:
(1004) Choose the correct answer:
The commonest cause of chronic gastritis is:
questions.explanation: Helicobacter pylori is the commonest cause of chronic gastritis worldwide. Autoimmune gastritis is a less common, corpus-predominant cause.

questions.text: 16- Pathogenesis of H- pylori gastritis include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: H. pylori colonizes the mucus layer; acid output varies by disease distribution, so increased secretion is not present in nearly every case.
options: The organism is found in the mucous layer of gastric epithelium
High acid production occurs almost in all cases
The acute inflammatory response is mediated by complement

questions.text:
(1000) Choose the correct answer:
Chronic atrophic gastritis is characterised by:
questions.explanation: Chronic atrophic gastritis means loss and thinning of gastric glands, often with intestinal metaplasia; muscle atrophy is not the defining lesion.

questions.text: 48.The occurrence of chronic non-specific gastritis is most strongly related to:
questions.explanation: Chronic nonspecific gastritis becomes more prevalent with age, partly reflecting cumulative Helicobacter pylori exposure and chronic mucosal injury.

questions.text:
(1623) Encircle True or False:
Gastrectomy leads to early iron deficiency anaemia and late megaloblastic anaemia. ( T - F )
questions.explanation: Gastrectomy can cause early iron deficiency and later vitamin B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anemia as body B12 stores decline.

questions.text: 46.Which is true concerning chronic non-specific gastritis?
questions.explanation: Chronic nonspecific gastritis is often linked to H. pylori and carries a modest later gastric-cancer risk through atrophy/metaplasia.
options: It is much more common in males.
It is most common in young adults.
It has a slight association with development of cancer

questions.text: 13- Common causes of acute gastritis include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Alcohol and NSAIDs directly injure gastric mucosa and can trigger acute gastritis. Autoimmune gastritis is typically chronic rather than an acute erosive cause.

questions.text:
(1001) Choose the correct answer:
Activity in chronic gastritis means:
questions.explanation: In chronic gastritis, activity means neutrophils are present within glands or epithelium, unlike chronic lymphocytes and plasma cells.

questions.text: Gastric biopsies are taken from a 54-year-old male who had complained for months of upper abdominal pain accompanied by nausea. The biopsies reveal the presence of Helicobacter pylori organisms.
questions.explanation: H. pylori causes chronic active gastritis; neutrophils indicate activity, while gland loss and mucosal thinning indicate atrophy, often with intestinal metaplasia. Autoimmune and reactive gastritis are other etiologic types.

subQuestions.text: a. These organisms are most likely associated with........
subQuestions.explanation: The organisms in the antral biopsy are H. pylori, which commonly causes chronic active gastritis with lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and neutrophils.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: H. pylori-associated chronic antral gastritis.

subQuestions.text: b. What are the other types of chronic gastritis recognized according to oetiology?
subQuestions.explanation: Autoimmune gastritis targets the body and fundus, while reactive gastritis can follow NSAIDs, chemicals, radiation, or bile reflux.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Autoimmune gastritis of body/fundus; reactive gastritis from chemicals/drugs/radiation/chronic bile reflux.

subQuestions.text: c. How to classify such condition according to the severity of inflammat- ion and atrophy?
subQuestions.explanation: “Active” denotes neutrophils superimposed on chronic inflammation, whereas atrophy means gland loss and mucosal thinning, often with metaplasia.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Active chronic gastritis means neutrophils in chronic inflammation; atrophic gastritis means mucosal thinning and gland loss, with intestinal metaplasia in established disease.

questions.text:
(1005) Choose the correct answer:
The following is NOT a feature of chronic gastritis:
questions.explanation: Chronic gastritis features chronic inflammation, activity, atrophy, metaplasia, and sometimes dysplasia. Glandular hypertrophy is not a characteristic feature.

questions.text:
34- A biopsy of the antrum of the stomach of an adult who presents with epigastric pain
reveals numerous lymphocytes and plasma cells within the lamina propria, which is of normal
thickness. There are also scattered neutrophils within the glandular epithelial cells. A silver
stain for this specimen reveals small, curved organisms. These histologic changes are more
consistent with infection by which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: Curved organisms on silver stain plus active antral inflammation are characteristic of Helicobacter pylori gastritis.

questions.text: complications of helicobacter gastritis include all ECEPT:
questions.explanation: H. pylori can cause peptic ulceration, gastric adenocarcinoma, and MALT lymphoma; carcinoid tumors are linked more to autoimmune atrophic gastritis.

questions.text:
5. A54-year-old man has complained for 5 months of upper abdominal pain accompanied by
nausea. Microscopic examination of gastric biopsies reveals acute and chronic mucosal
inflammation along with the presence of Helicobacter pylori organisms. The presence of
these organisms is most likely to be associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: H. pylori increases risk of duodenal peptic ulcer by altering gastrin and acid regulation, especially with antral-predominant infection.
options: Development of large B cell lymphoma

questions.text: 44.Chronic atrophic gastritis is characterized by all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Atrophic gastritis causes gland loss, parietal-cell depletion, intestinal metaplasia, and often autoantibodies, but not rigid gastric wall thickening.
options: gross and radiological rigidity of gastric wall
chronic inflammatory cells in gastric mucosa
frequent presence of serum antibodies to intrinsic factor

questions.text: The premalignant change in chronic gastritis is:
questions.explanation: Intestinal metaplasia replaces gastric epithelium with intestinal-type cells and is a premalignant step in the gastritis–metaplasia–dysplasia sequence.

questions.text:
(1002) Choose the correct answer:
The premalignant change in chronic gastritis is:
questions.explanation: Intestinal metaplasia is a premalignant epithelial change in chronic gastritis and can progress through dysplasia to gastric adenocarcinoma.

questions.text:
8.An endoscopic biopsy of gastric mucosa reveals small intestinal type epithelium. This
finding is most likely due to:
questions.explanation: Intestinal-type epithelium in the stomach usually represents metaplasia after chronic gastritis, rather than congenital tissue or a tumor.

questions.text:
32- A 45-year-old man has had vague abdominal pain and nausea for the past 3 years. He has
no difficulty in swallowing and no heartburn following meals. Upper GI endoscopy reveals
mucosal erythema in stomach fundus & body, but no ulcerations or masses. Biopsies are
taken, and microscopically there is a chronic nonspecific gastritis with atrophic mucosal
changes . Which of the following conditions most likely to be present in this man?
questions.explanation: Fundic atrophy with hypochlorhydria destroys parietal cells and intrinsic factor, impairing B12 absorption and causing pernicious anemia.

questions.text:
8) A 54-year-old man has complained for 5 months of upper abdominal pain accompanied
 by nausea. Microscopic examination of gastric biopsies reveals acute and chronic mucosal
 inflammation along with the presence of Helicobacter pylori organisms. The presence of
 these organisms is most likely to be associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: H. pylori-associated antral gastritis can increase acid output and predispose to duodenal ulceration. It is not a typical cause of pernicious anemia.
options: Development of large B cell lymphoma

questions.text: 57- Which of the following is not true about pathogenesis of peptic ulcer disease?
questions.explanation: Gastric peptic ulcers often reflect failure of mucosal defenses; excess acid is not generally more important than barrier breakdown.
options: A mucous-bicarbonate barrier is one of the defensive mechanism
Prostaglandin E increases blood flow & increases mucosal regeneration
High dose of corticosteroids suppress prostaglandin synthesis
In peptic ulcer of the stomach, hyperacidity is more important than breakdown of mucosal defense

questions.text:
(1064) Choose the correct answer:
A 50 years old male suffers from epigastric pain. Endoscopy shows a duodenal ulcer which is round, small with clear floor. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: A round, sharply demarcated duodenal crater is a peptic ulcer; histology and clinical setting distinguish it from infection or malignancy.

questions.text: 73.Which finding favors peptic ulcer over ulcerated carcinoma of the stomach?
questions.explanation: A benign peptic ulcer typically has mucosal folds radiating toward its sharply defined crater; heaped-up irregular margins suggest ulcerated carcinoma.

questions.text: 65.Acute superficial ulcers of the stomach or duodenum may occur in patients with:
questions.explanation: Severe burns and intracranial injury can trigger acute stress-related erosions and ulcers through ischemia and impaired mucosal protection.

questions.text:
(1010) Choose the correct answer:
The commonest cause of peptic ulcer is:
questions.explanation: H. pylori is a leading cause of peptic ulcer disease by damaging mucosal defenses; NSAIDs are another major cause.

questions.text:
15.The most common cause of upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage (hematemesis or
melena) is:
questions.explanation: Peptic ulcer disease is a common cause of upper-GI bleeding, presenting as hematemesis or melena when the ulcer erodes a vessel.

questions.text: The histologic features of peptic ulcer include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Peptic ulcers show necrosis, inflammation, granulation tissue, and fibrosis; smooth-muscle proliferation is not a defining histologic feature.
options: Proliferation of the smooth muscle fibres

questions.text:
(1244) Choose the correct answer:
Zollinger Ellison syndrome is characterised by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Zollinger–Ellison is gastrinoma-driven hypergastrinemia with acid hypersecretion and recurrent ulcers; diabetes is not a defining feature.

questions.text: 54.The most common site of chronic gastric peptic ulcer is:
questions.explanation: Chronic gastric peptic ulcers commonly occur along the lesser curvature near the antral-body junction, where acid exposure and mucosal defense interact.

questions.text:
11. Which of the following tumors is most likely to be present in a 55-year-
old woman who presents with painful chronic diarrhea, multiple
recurrent duodenal ulcers, and increased basal gastric acid output?
questions.explanation: A gastrin-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causes Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, with acid hypersecretion, ulcers, and diarrhea.
options: A gastrin-secreting tumor of the pancreas
A serotonin-secreting tumor of the ileum
A somatostatine-secreting tumor of the duodenum
An epinephrin-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla
An erythropoietin-secreting tumor of the liver

questions.text: Zollinger Ellison syndrome consists of:
questions.explanation: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome results from gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor causing severe gastric acid hypersecretion and recurrent peptic ulcers.

questions.text: After an episode of hematemesis, a 48-year-old male undergoes upper endoscopy, and a 1.5 cm sharply demarcated punched-out ulceration is noted in the gastric antrum. A biopsy of the adjacent gastric mucosa shows many Helicobacter pylori organisms.
questions.explanation: A punched-out H. pylori-associated gastric ulcer shows surface necrotic fibrin, acute inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and a fibrous scar base. It can bleed, perforate, penetrate adjacent organs, or heal with stenosis/deformity.

subQuestions.text: a. What is your diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: This is a chronic gastric peptic ulcer: the sharply punched-out antral defect explains the hematemesis, and adjacent mucosa contains H. pylori.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Chronic gastric peptic ulcer associated with H. pylori (historical antral-gastritis diagnosis incompletely answers the described ulcer).

subQuestions.text: b. What are the microscopic features seen during the active phase.
subQuestions.explanation: An active chronic ulcer has a necrotic fibrinous surface, neutrophilic zone, granulation tissue, and deep fibrous scar; vessels may be thrombosed.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Four layers: necrotic fibrinous surface, neutrophilic inflammation, granulation tissue and fibrous scar; base arterioles thrombosis/endarteritis.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the possible complications?
subQuestions.explanation: A chronic gastric ulcer can bleed, perforate into the peritoneum, penetrate adjacent organs, or heal with scar-related deformity and pyloric narrowing.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Hemorrhage, perforation/peritonitis, cicatricial pyloric stenosis/hourglass stomach, penetration and rare gastric malignant change.

questions.text: 56.Chronic peptic ulcer of the stomach occurs predominantly:
questions.explanation: Gastric ulcers often occur near the border of acid-secreting body mucosa, where impaired mucosal defenses permit acid-peptic injury.
options: on the acid-secreting portion of the gastric mucosa
in an area of the stomach that has undergone squamous metaplasia
on areas of the gastric mucosa adjacent to the acid secreting mucosa

questions.text: 15.  All of the following are the main complications of duodenal peptic ulcer EXCEPT :
questions.explanation: Duodenal ulcers may bleed, perforate, scar, or adhere to nearby structures, but malignant transformation is exceptionally not a typical complication.

questions.text: 12.Hematemesis is an indication of:
questions.explanation: Hematemesis is vomiting of blood and indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding, usually proximal to the ligament of Treitz.

questions.text: 17. Recurrent peptic ulcers suggests the possibility of:
questions.explanation: Gastrinoma causes recurrent peptic ulcers by raising gastrin and stimulating excessive gastric acid secretion.

questions.text:
6. A 38-year-old man has had upper abdominal pain for 3 months. For the past week he has
had nausea. On physical examination, a stool sample tested for occult blood is positive. An
upper GI endoscopy reveals no esophageal lesions, but there is a solitary, round, 2cm
diameter, shallow, sharply demarcated ulceration of the stomach. Which of the following

statements regarding this lesion is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A small, sharply demarcated gastric ulcer is commonly antral; gastric ulcers still require biopsy because benign appearance cannot exclude cancer.
options: It is probably located in the antrum
It is probably associated with increased gastric acid production
Because of its small size, a biopsy is not necessary
A gastrinoma of the pancreas is probably present

questions.text: 58.All of the following are frequent complications of chronic peptic ulceration except:
questions.explanation: Bleeding, perforation, and scar-related deformity are common peptic-ulcer complications. Carcinomatous change in a benign gastric ulcer is very uncommon.
options: scarring deformity of the involved organ upon healing

questions.text:
51.Multiple recurrent ulcers in proximal and distal duodenum for several years are likely
to be associated with:
questions.explanation: A pancreatic islet-cell gastrinoma can produce severe acid hypersecretion and recurrent ulcers beyond the usual proximal duodenum.

questions.text: 65- All of the following conditions may be associated with melena except:
questions.explanation: Melena usually reflects upper-GI bleeding because digested blood darkens stool; hemorrhoidal bleeding is typically bright red, not tarry.

questions.text: 165.The most common fatal complication of chronic peptic ulcer of the stomach is:
questions.explanation: Perforation of a gastric ulcer can spill contents into the peritoneum, causing peritonitis and sepsis; it is a major fatal complication.

questions.text: List causes of Hematemesis
questions.explanation: Hematemesis may arise from esophageal varices, mucosal erosions, peptic ulcers, tumors, or systemic bleeding disorders.
questions.modelAnswer:
Diseases of the esophagus:
a.  Esophageal varices.
b.  Carcinoma of esophagus.
c.   Peptic ulcer of esophagus.
d.  Rupture of aortic aneurysm into the esophagus.
Diseases of the stomach and duodenum:
e.  Acute and chronic gastritis.
f.    Peptic ulcer.
g.   Gastric carcinoma.
h.   Gastric erosion following ingestion of some drugs e.g. aspirin.
Generalized disease: such as purpura, leukaemia, haemophilia and scurvey.

questions.text: 50.Choose the best statement concerning the pathogenesis of peptic ulcer.
questions.explanation: Peptic ulcers require acid-peptic activity, but acid need only be present, not elevated; mucosal-defense failure also drives ulceration.
options: Acid must be at least normal in amount.

questions.text: 14. The following are the sites of peptic ulcer EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Peptic ulcers can occur in the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel diverticulum, but not the ascending colon.

questions.text: 125.Chronic peptic ulcer of the stomach occurs predominantly:
questions.explanation: Chronic gastric ulcers often occur near the transition between acid-secreting mucosa and the antral region.
options: on the acid secreting portion of the gastric mucosa
in an area of the stomach that has undergone squamous metaplasia
on areas of the gastric mucosa adjacent to the acid secreting mucosa

questions.text:
20) A 51-year-old man presents with epigastric pain that is lessened whenever he
eats. A gastroscopy is performed to evaluate these gastric symptoms and a solitary
gastric ulcer, is seen. Which one of the listed gross findings, if present, would be
most suspicious for the lesion being a malignant ulcer?
questions.explanation: Raised, heaped-up ulcer margins with irregular base and interrupted rugae raise concern for gastric carcinoma rather than a benign peptic crater.

questions.text:
123.A bus driver has a long history of epigastric pain related to meals. The x-ray reveals an
area of gastric ulceration with a Hampton’s line. The least likely complication is:
questions.explanation: A Hampton line supports a benign gastric ulcer. Such ulcers may bleed, perforate, or scar, but malignant transformation of a benign ulcer is least likely.

questions.text: A 38-year-old man has had upper abdominal pain for 3 months. For the past week he has had nausea. On physical examination, a stool sample tested for occult blood is positive. An upper GI endoscopy reveals no esophageal lesions, but there is a solitary 2cm diameter shallow, sharply demarcated ulceration of the stomach.
questions.explanation: Microscopy of a chronic gastric ulcer shows surface necrosis, inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and fibrous scar at its base.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: Chronic gastric ulcer is a persistent acid-peptic mucosal defect with fibrosis and inflammation; relation to meals can help localize but is not diagnostic alone.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Chronic gastric peptic ulcer.

subQuestions.text: b. Which part of the stomach is most frequently affected by this ulcer?
subQuestions.explanation: The usual gastric peptic-ulcer site is the lesser curvature near the junction of the antrum and body.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Usually antrum at lesser curvature.

subQuestions.text: c. If a biopsy is taken, what are the features which can be seen on microscopic examination?
subQuestions.explanation: Chronic peptic ulcer bases contain necrotic debris, inflammation, granulation tissue, and fibrosis from repeated injury and repair.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Necrotic fibrinous surface, neutrophilic infiltrate, granulation tissue, dense fibrocollagenous scar, and arteriolar thrombosis/endarteritis at base.

questions.text:
131.A bus driver has a long history of epigastric pain related to meals. The x-ray reveals an
area of gastric ulceration with a Hampton’s line. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Hampton’s line is a thin radiolucent line at a benign gastric ulcer crater; radiating folds support a chronic peptic ulcer diagnosis.

questions.text: 10- The histologic features of peptic ulcer include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A chronic peptic ulcer shows inflammatory exudate, granulation tissue, and fibrosis beneath the crater. Smooth-muscle proliferation is not a defining layer.

questions.text: The edges of acute peptic ulcer are:
questions.explanation: Acute peptic ulcers have sharply demarcated, clear-cut margins rather than undermined or everted edges.

questions.text: 13.Melena is an indication of:
questions.explanation: Melena indicates digested blood, most often from an upper-GI source, though sufficiently slow lower bleeding can also darken stool.

questions.text: Peptic ulcer does NOT occur in the:
questions.explanation: Peptic ulcers occur in stomach, duodenum, distal esophagus, and ectopic gastric mucosa, but the large intestine lacks the acid-peptic setting.

questions.text:
(1013) Choose the correct answer:
Complications of duodenal peptic ulcer do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Duodenal ulcers can bleed, perforate, or scar and obstruct, but malignant transformation is not a typical complication.

questions.text: 14.  The following are the sites of peptic ulcer EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Peptic ulcers commonly affect stomach, proximal duodenum, distal esophagus, and Meckel diverticulum with ectopic acid mucosa, not ascending colon.

questions.text:
(1086) Encircle True or False:
Duodenal peptic ulcer never turn malignant. (T - F )
questions.explanation: Duodenal peptic ulcers are not considered premalignant; unlike gastric ulcers, they do not undergo malignant transformation.

questions.text:
30- A 40-year-old man has had mid epigastric pain and nausea for the past 2 months. On
    physical examination he has no abnormal findings. On upper GI endoscopy, a solitary
   sharply demarcated 2-cm shallow gastric antral ulcer is seen. Which of the following is
   most likely to be present in this man?
questions.explanation: Antral gastric ulceration is commonly associated with H. pylori infection, which damages mucosal defenses and promotes inflammation.

questions.text:
128.A bus driver has a long history of epigastric pain related to meals. The x-ray reveals an
area of gastric ulceration with a Hampton’s line. The most likely diagnostic histologic
feature of the stomach is:
questions.explanation: A chronic peptic ulcer shows mucosal destruction with chronic inflammation and fibrosis; invasive atypical glands would instead suggest carcinoma.

questions.text:
8. A 40-year-old man has had mid epigastric pain and nausea for the past 2 months. On
physical examination he has no abnormal findings. On upper GI endoscopy, a solitary sharply
demarcated 2- cm shallow gastric antral ulcer is seen. Which of the following is most likely to

be present in this man?
questions.explanation: H. pylori is common in patients with gastric antral ulcers and causes chronic active gastritis that weakens mucosal defenses.

questions.text: 58- Common sites of peptic ulcer disease include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The ileocecal valve is not a usual peptic-ulcer site; common locations include proximal duodenum and stomach.

questions.text:
62.Among the following, chronic peptic ulcer of the duodenum is best characterized as a
lesion that:
questions.explanation: Duodenal ulcers are associated with intact or increased gastric acid exposure; acid-pepsin injury exceeds mucosal protective mechanisms.
options: frequently develops carcinoma as a complication
is related to intrinsic factor deficiency
occurs in patients with high levels of gastric acidity
is the result of cytotoxic antibodies to duodenal epithelial antigen
is due to focal infarction of the duodenal mucosa

questions.text:
60.In a patient with a chronic peptic ulcer of the stomach, the chance that carcinoma will
develop in the ulcer is:
questions.explanation: Malignant transformation of a benign chronic gastric ulcer is very uncommon; many apparent “malignant ulcers” are cancers ulcerating from the outset.

questions.text:
(1012) Choose the correct answer:
The edges of acute peptic ulcer are:
questions.explanation: Clean-cut edges are typical of acute peptic ulcers; raised, irregular margins raise concern for malignant ulceration.

questions.text:
(1009) Choose the correct answer:
Peptic ulcer does NOT occur in the:
questions.explanation: Large intestine is not a typical acid-peptic ulcer site, unlike stomach, proximal duodenum, distal esophagus, or acid-secreting Meckel diverticulum.

questions.text: 18- Causes of acute gastric ulceration include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Stress, Curling, and Cushing ulcers are acute gastric lesions. Zollinger–Ellison syndrome more characteristically causes recurrent acid-peptic ulcers rather than acute stress ulceration.

questions.text: Which of the following types of hemorrhage is MOST commonly associated with duodenal ulcers?
questions.explanation: Upper GI bleeding from a duodenal ulcer may produce melena as blood is digested during intestinal transit.

questions.text: 59.Which of the following is most clearly predisposing to acute stress ulcers?
questions.explanation: Extensive burns cause stress-related mucosal ischemia and acute gastric/duodenal ulcers (Curling ulcers), sometimes with bleeding or perforation.

questions.text: 16.  The most common complication of gastric ulcer is:
questions.explanation: Hemorrhage is a frequent complication of gastric ulcer because acid-peptic injury can erode submucosal vessels.

questions.text:

questions.text: A 30-year-old male banker complains of mid-epigastric boring pain for the last week. The pain is worse at night and is somewhat better immediately after he eats. He has not had any fever, nausea, or vomiting; but he had taken approximately one 500-mg acetaminophen tableta week ago for headache. Upper endoscopy reveals a 2cm. mucosal defect in the antrum of the stomach. There is mild edema in the adjacent mucosa, but there is no thickening of the edges of the ulcer.
questions.explanation: Meal-relieved epigastric pain and an antral crater suggest chronic peptic ulcer; acid-pepsin injury overcomes mucosal defenses, often with H. pylori/NSAIDs. It may bleed, perforate, or scar; other sites include duodenum, distal esophagus, jejunum with gastrinoma, and Meckel diverticulum.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: The long-standing punched-out gastric lesion is a chronic gastric peptic ulcer, typically related to H. pylori or NSAID-associated loss of mucosal protection.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Chronic gastric peptic ulcer.

subQuestions.text: b. What are complications from this condition?
subQuestions.explanation: Peptic ulcers may bleed, perforate, penetrate adjacent organs, or scar and obstruct; chronic gastric ulcers also warrant malignancy exclusion.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Hemorrhage, perforation/peritonitis, pyloric stenosis/hourglass contraction, penetration and rare gastric malignant change.

subQuestions.text: c. What is the most likely mechanism of this condition? (pathogenesis)
subQuestions.explanation: Chronic peptic ulceration reflects acid-pepsin injury overcoming mucus, bicarbonate, epithelial restitution, blood flow, and prostaglandin defenses.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Imbalance of mucosal mucus/bicarbonate/epithelial/blood-flow/PG defense against acid-pepsin damage, notably H. pylori/NSAIDs; the isolated acetaminophen dose does not establish etiology.

subQuestions.text: d. Mention the other possible sites.
subQuestions.explanation: Peptic ulcers may occur in the first part of the duodenum, stomach, distal esophagus, gastrojejunal anastomosis, or ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel diverticulum.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Duodenal first part, lower oesophagus, gastroenterostomy margins, stomach/duodenum/jejunum with gastrinoma, and Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa.

questions.text: A 30-year-old man complains of mid-epigastric boring pain for the last week. The pain is worse at night and is sometimes better immediately after he eats. Upper endoscopy reveals a 2cm. round sharply punched out hole in the antrum of the stomach. There is mild oedema in the adjacent mucosa, but no thickening of the edge of the ulcer. The overlying serosa is thick & opaque.
questions.explanation: A chronic gastric ulcer shows a necrotic surface, neutrophils, granulation tissue, and scar; impaired mucus/bicarbonate/prostaglandin defenses permit acid injury and may lead to bleeding, perforation, penetration, or stenosis.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: The lesion described is a chronic gastric peptic ulcer, a persistent mucosal defect with a sharply demarcated crater and fibrotic base.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Chronic gastric peptic ulcer.

subQuestions.text: b. Describe the microscopic picture during the active phase.
subQuestions.explanation: An active chronic ulcer has surface fibrinoid necrosis, neutrophils, granulation tissue, and deeper fibrous scar, often with damaged vessels.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Four active zones: fibrinous necrotic surface, neutrophilic inflammation, granulation tissue and dense fibrous scar; base arterioles show thrombosis/endarteritis.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the complications of this condition?
subQuestions.explanation: Hemorrhage, perforation, and cicatricial pyloric stenosis are classic peptic-ulcer complications; scarring may obstruct gastric emptying.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Hemorrhage, perforation/peritonitis, pyloric stenosis/hourglass contraction, penetration into adherent organs and rare gastric malignant change.

subQuestions.text: d. What is the most likely mechanism of this disorder (pathogenesis)?
subQuestions.explanation: Peptic ulceration develops when acid-pepsin injury exceeds mucus-bicarbonate, epithelial, blood-flow, and prostaglandin defenses. H. pylori and NSAIDs are major causes.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Imbalance between mucus/bicarbonate/epithelial regeneration/blood-flow/prostaglandin defenses and damaging acid-pepsin forces; H. pylori, NSAIDs/aspirin, cigarettes/alcohol and impaired acid regulation impair defense or increase damage.

subQuestions.modelAnswer: Defective absorption of important nutrients. Luminal failure includes insufficient pancreatic digestive enzymes and deficient bile salts/micelles, impairing digestion and fat/fat-soluble-vitamin absorption. Intestinal failure includes loss or dysfunction of villous epithelial absorptive surface: gluten-triggered T-cell/antibody injury in celiac disease; Giardia villous irritation/dysfunction; capillarial villous atrophy; tuberculous ulcers and histiocyte/lymphatic compression; Whipple PAS-positive mucosal macrophages; Crohn intestinal disease.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the possible clinical complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Untreated celiac disease can cause abdominal distension, growth failure, anemia and deficiencies of calcium, vitamin D, folate/B12, and vitamin K due to malabsorption.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Abdominal distension; osteoporosis/rickets and low-calcium tetany; iron/folate/B12 anaemia; vitamin-K deficiency bleeding; cachexia and failure to thrive.

subQuestions.text: d. Enumerate other small bowel diseases presenting with the same complains as in this case.
subQuestions.explanation: Small-bowel differential diagnoses for malabsorption include celiac, Whipple, Crohn, intestinal tuberculosis, Giardia, and other enteric infections.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Other small-bowel diseases include celiac disease, Whipple disease, intestinal tuberculosis, Crohn disease, giardiasis, intestinal capillariasis and strongyloidiasis.

questions.text: 50. in whipples disease the mechanism of malabsorption include:
questions.explanation: In Whipple disease, PAS-positive macrophages fill the lamina propria and obstruct lacteals, impairing lymphatic transport of absorbed lipids.

questions.text: An 8-year-old boy complains of a chronic diarrhea. A stool fat collection indicates steatorrhea. Biopsy of the duodenum is performed. The biopsy reveals absence of villi, increased number of plasma cells and T lymphocytes of the lamina propria and hyperplastic appearing elongated crypts.
questions.explanation: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and lamina propria lymphocytes/plasma cells indicate celiac disease; gluten avoidance is treatment, and other intestinal causes include Whipple disease, TB, Crohn disease, and parasites.

subQuestions.text: a. What is your diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: Celiac disease is gluten-triggered injury of the small-intestinal mucosa, with villous atrophy and impaired absorption.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Celiac disease.

subQuestions.text: b. What is the indicated therapy?
subQuestions.explanation: The gluten-responsive flat-villus enteropathy is celiac disease; gluten withdrawal removes the trigger and permits mucosal recovery.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Gluten-free diet.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the other causes of intestinal-phase malabsorption?
subQuestions.explanation: Other intestinal-phase causes include Whipple disease, intestinal tuberculosis, Crohn disease, and infections such as giardiasis; each impairs mucosal absorption by a different mechanism.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Whipple disease and intestinal tuberculosis (mucosal surface loss, lymphatic/histiocyte involvement); Crohn disease causes malabsorption. Other current-book intestinal causes include giardiasis, intestinal capillariasis and strongyloidiasis.

questions.explanation: Celiac disease is a small-intestinal mucosal disorder causing villous injury and malabsorption, not a colonic or reflux condition.

asymptomatic disease of the left colon

defective fat digestion due to lipase deficiency

questions.text: 48. In celiac disease the mechanism of malabsorption include:
questions.explanation: Celiac disease damages the brush border and epithelial transport, so both terminal digestion and nutrient uptake contribute to malabsorption.

questions.text: 86.Celiac disease is best treated by:
questions.explanation: Celiac disease is treated with a strict gluten-free diet; supplements may be needed until iron, folate, and other deficiencies recover.
options: low fat and low protein diet with vitamin supplements
gluten free diet and vitamin supplements
high protein diet and vitamin supplements

questions.text: 141.Responds to antibiotics:

questions.text: 137.A cause of malabsorption:
questions.explanation: Both celiac disease and Whipple disease injure small-intestinal absorptive mucosa and can cause diarrhea, weight loss, and nutrient deficiencies.

questions.text: Which of the following microscopic features is associated with celiac disease?
questions.explanation: Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia together support celiac disease on small-bowel biopsy.

questions.text: 85.Weight loss, steatorrhea, and marked atrophy of villi in the jejunum are seen in:
questions.explanation: Celiac disease causes proximal small-bowel villous atrophy, reducing absorptive area and leading to weight loss and steatorrhea.

questions.text:

questions.explanation: Villous atrophy is the key tissue change in celiac disease: flattened villi and crypt changes reduce absorptive surface and produce malabsorption.

questions.explanation: Small-bowel biopsy demonstrates villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, the characteristic celiac pattern.
options: radiographic study of the upper intestinal tract

questions.text:

a cystic glandular polyp with totally denuded ulcerated surface and inflammatory change

questions.text:

provisional diagnosis was villous adenoma. A partial colectomy was performed. The

questions.explanation: Villous adenomas have a substantial risk of invasive carcinoma, especially when large; malignancy is found in roughly 25–50% of large lesions in classic series.

questions.text:

The most important premalignant change in the neoplastic polypi is:
questions.explanation: Dysplasia is the key premalignant change in an adenomatous polyp and reflects neoplastic epithelial growth.

questions.explanation: Juvenile polyps are usually hamartomatous with little malignant potential, unlike dysplastic adenomas or villous adenomas.

32.In the colon, which is benign and has no significant tendency to undergo malignant
transformation?
questions.explanation: A solitary juvenile polyp is a benign hamartomatous lesion with little malignant potential. Familial polyposis and adenomas carry substantial neoplastic risk.

questions.text:
(1028) Choose the correct answer:
The Salmonella typhi organisms multiply in the:
questions.explanation: Salmonella Typhi can multiply in Peyer patches and disseminate through macrophages to mesenteric nodes, liver, and spleen.

questions.text: 36.  Concerning colonic polyps, all of the following statements are false EXCEPT:

options: Villous adenoma is a pedunculated tumor.

Polyposis coli, is formed mainly of hyperplastic polyps.

questions.text: 44- All of the following are types of non-neoplastic colonic polyps except:
questions.explanation: Adenomatous polyps are dysplastic neoplasms and precursors to colorectal carcinoma; hyperplastic, hamartomatous, and bilharzial polyps are non-neoplastic.

questions.text:

   change?
questions.explanation: Villous adenomas have greater malignant potential than tubular adenomas, especially when large or dysplastic.

questions.text:

questions.explanation: Typhoid fever causes Peyer-patch necrosis and ileal ulceration; deep ulcers can perforate and cause peritonitis.

questions.explanation: Villous adenomas secrete abundant mucus and can cause watery, mucoid diarrhea. They also carry greater malignant risk than tubular adenomas.

questions.text: A 24-year-old male presents with ill-health, malaise, fever and vague abdominal pain. Further evaluation reveals enlarged spleen and tender abdomen. Laboratory examination reveals leucopenia with relative monocytosis. After a week, Widal agglutination test becomes positive.
questions.explanation: Fever, malaise, splenomegaly, abdominal tenderness, leukopenia, and a positive Widal test are compatible with enteric fever due to Salmonella Typhi.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: Longitudinal ileal ulcers, fever, leukopenia, and splenomegaly are characteristic of typhoid caused by Salmonella Typhi.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Typhoid fever.

subQuestions.text: b. Describe the pathogenesis of this disease.
subQuestions.explanation: After ingestion, Salmonella Typhi reaches ileal Peyer patches, enters macrophages, and spreads through lymph and blood to reticuloendothelial organs before returning to the intestine.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Ingested bacilli are phagocytosed and reach Peyer patches causing hyperplasia, then bacteremia via thoracic duct; multiply within mononuclear phagocytes of liver/spleen/nodes/patches/GB, with endotoxin release.

subQuestions.text: c. Give an account on the gross pathology of the involved organs.
subQuestions.explanation: Typhoid gross pathology includes swollen necrotic Peyer patches, longitudinal ulcers in ileum, and possible mesenteric-node and splenic enlargement.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Terminal ileal raised Peyer patches become long-axis oval necrotic ulcers; mesenteric nodes enlarged with necrotic typhoid nodules; spleen enlarged soft deep red; liver/bone marrow typhoid nodules.

subQuestions.text: d. Describe the microscopic findings in intestinal lesion.
subQuestions.explanation: Typhoid intestinal lesions show macrophages and necrotic lymphoid tissue, followed by ulceration and hemorrhage with little scar on healing.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Macrophages containing erythrocytes/debris; later confluent follicle necrosis, ulceration/hemorrhage; lack of neutrophils, healing with little fibrosis.

subQuestions.text: e. What are the expected complications in this case?
subQuestions.explanation: Typhoid can cause intestinal hemorrhage or perforation, toxemia, ileus, cholecystitis, osteomyelitis, and chronic gallbladder carriage.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Toxemia with ileus/fatty liver/Zenker necrosis, perforation/peritonitis/bleeding, cholecystitis/stones, osteomyelitis, leukopenia with monocytosis and carrier state.

questions.text: A 51-year-old man has a 1cm polyp on a narrow stalk located in the descending colon. Microscopic examination shows crowded, tubular, atypical colonic-type glands. The stalk of the polyp is covered with normal colonic epithelium. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.text: Enumerate ulcers of small, and large intestine
questions.explanation: Small-bowel ulcers include peptic (duodenal, Meckel ectopic mucosa, or Zollinger–Ellison jejunal), typhoid, tuberculosis, Crohn, and malignant ulcers. Colonic ulcers include dysenteric, bilharzial, inflammatory-bowel, ischemic, stercoral, and malignant lesions.
questions.modelAnswer: Small-intestinal ulcers: typhoid, tuberculous and Crohn ulcers; peptic ulcers may affect jejunum in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and Meckel diverticulum containing ectopic gastric mucosa. Large-intestinal ulcers: bacillary and amoebic dysentery, ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease, malignant ulceration and stercoral ulcers above obstruction. Include peptic ulcer of the first part of duodenum (commonest peptic site) in small-intestinal ulcers and bilharzial dysentery/ulceration in large-intestinal ulcers.

questions.text:

 as well as sacral edema for the past month. Diffuse rales are present in all lungs fields. He is

questions.text: compare types of IBD
questions.explanation: Crohn disease is often transmural and patchy, with granulomas, fistulas, strictures, and malabsorption; UC is continuous and mucosa-limited.
questions.modelAnswer: Crohn disease versus ulcerative colitis: ileum/colon (potentially any GIT segment) versus colon/rectum; skip lesions versus continuous extension proximally from rectum; thick wall/stricture versus thin wall with dilatation and pseudopolyps; deep fissuring ulcers and transmural inflammation versus superficial mucosal/submucosal inflammation; prominent fibrosis, lymphoid reaction and noncaseating granulomas versus crypt distortion and crypt abscesses without granulomas; fistulas and malabsorption versus toxic megacolon; increased cancer risk in both, emphasized for ulcerative colitis. Crohn complications include strictures, fistulas, malabsorption, bleeding/perforation; ulcerative colitis complications include bleeding, toxic megacolon, rare perforation and colonic cancer. Comparison table: Crohn strictures, thick wall, no dilatation, mild-to-moderate pseudopolyps, marked lymphoid reaction/fibrosis/serositis, granulomas in about 35%, fistulas/sinuses and fat/vitamin malabsorption; UC rare strictures, thin wall, dilatation, marked pseudopolyps, moderate lymphoid reaction, mild-to-no fibrosis, no serositis/granulomas/fistulas or fat/vitamin malabsorption. Crohn malignant potential rare and surgical response poor; UC malignant potential common and surgical response good. Crohn clinical course includes intermittent diarrhoea, fever, abdominal pain and weight loss; UC bloody/mucoid diarrhoea, lower pain and cramps. Both have extraintestinal manifestations; toxic megacolon is UC rather than Crohn.

questions.explanation: Patchy transmural inflammation with skip lesions and granulomas supports Crohn disease rather than continuous, mucosa-limited ulcerative colitis.

subQuestions.explanation: The case is Crohn disease, a relapsing inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any GI segment and often causes transmural injury.

weight loss. Colonoscopy revealed a friable, diffusely red mucosa involving the rectum and
