to involve most of the entire colon, but not the ileum. Many years later, a colonic biopsy
shows high grade epithelial dysplasia. The most likely diagnosis at this time is:
questions.explanation: Long-standing ulcerative colitis can develop high-grade dysplasia, a precursor to colorectal adenocarcinoma.

questions.text:
7- Which of the following intestinal ulcer has a higher risk for malignant

transformation:
questions.explanation: Long-standing ulcerative colitis increases risk of colorectal dysplasia and carcinoma; the other listed ulcer types are not similarly premalignant.

questions.text: 161.Chronic ulcerative colitis usually starts in the:
questions.explanation: Ulcerative colitis usually starts in rectum and extends proximally through rectosigmoid colon.

questions.text: A 54-year-old healthy man presents with sudden severe painless bleeding per rectum. He tells his physician that he had no colonic troubles before. Colonoscopy reveals the presence of mucosal herniation through the muscular layers of the colon at different spots.
questions.explanation: Colonic diverticula can bleed when mucosal vessels are stretched at their necks; painless rectal bleeding is a common presentation.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: The described lesion is colonic diverticular disease, in which mucosa and submucosa herniate through weak points in the muscular wall.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Colonic diverticular disease.

subQuestions.text: b. What are the microscopic features in colonic biopsy?
subQuestions.explanation: Colonic diverticula are thin-walled mucosal/submucosal outpouchings through muscularis propria; biopsy may show flattened mucosa, compressed submucosa, and attenuated muscle, with fibrosis if chronically inflamed.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Thin wall with flattened mucosa, compressed submucosa and attenuated muscularis mucosa, continuous with surface mucosa; chronic diverticulitis gives fibrous wall thickening.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the possible complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Diverticular disease can cause bleeding, inflammation, perforation, fistula, or obstruction; severity depends on location and infection.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Perforation/peritonitis and chronic fibrotic intestinal obstruction.

questions.text: 19.Mucosal necrosis is an essential part of:
questions.explanation: Pseudomembranous colitis produces superficial mucosal necrosis with fibrin, mucus, and neutrophils forming adherent pseudomembranes.

questions.text: 43- One of the pathological features of diverticular disease of the colon:
questions.explanation: Colonic diverticula are acquired pseudodiverticula: mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscularis propria.
options: It is most common in the rectum
The pouch is formed of mucosa & submucosa only
The pouch protrude on the mesenteric border

questions.text: 97.Colonic diverticula are associated with all of the following complications, except:
questions.explanation: Diverticula may bleed or become inflamed, but they do not themselves cause carcinoma.

questions.text:
145.Diverticula in the colon may be associated with all of the following complications
except:
questions.explanation: Colonic diverticula can bleed, inflame, obstruct, or form fistulas. They do not cause Crohn disease, which is a separate inflammatory disorder.

questions.text:
96.At which of the following ages would you expect colonic diverticula to be most
common?
questions.explanation: Diverticula become increasingly common with age as colonic wall structure and intraluminal pressure change.

questions.text: 41- All of the following are true about diverticular disease of the colon except:
questions.explanation: Colonic diverticulosis is an acquired disease of older adults, associated with wall weakness and increased intraluminal pressure.
options: It is a disease of young infants
It occurs due to weakness in the intestinal wall
Chronic constipation may be a cause
The condition remains silent until inflammation develops

questions.text:
(1089) Encircle True or False:
Diverticulitis may give symptoms simulating appendicitis. ( T -F)
questions.explanation: Sigmoid diverticulitis can cause left-lower-quadrant pain and fever, mimicking appendicitis on the opposite side of the abdomen.

questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with increasing left side abdominal pain for the past days, with bright blood in his stools. Physical examination reveals low-grade fever and fresh blood on rectal examination. Colonoscopy reveals hundreds of inflamed mucosal holes, with flask- like mucosal herniations through the muscular layers of distal colon. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his G.I.T. bleeding?
questions.explanation: Inflamed colonic diverticula can bleed from adjacent vessels and cause hematochezia in an older patient.

questions.text: 42- Diverticular disease of the colon commonly affects
questions.explanation: The sigmoid colon is commonly affected because its relatively narrow lumen experiences higher pressure.

questions.text: A 34-year-old male presents with diarrhea, tenesmus with passage of blood and mucus. He noticed the appearance of piles during straining. The physician recommends colonoscopy. The findings include necrotic ulcerated mucosa, partially covered by thin clera-white pseudomembrane.
questions.explanation: Bloody mucoid diarrhea with a fibrinous pseudomembrane suggests Shigella bacillary dysentery. Biopsy shows necrotic mucosa, fibrin, neutrophils, and edematous submucosa; complications include toxemia, rare perforation, and reactive arthritis/urethritis/conjunctivitis.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: The pseudomembrane over necrotic, ulcerated colonic mucosa with bloody mucoid diarrhea supports bacillary dysentery (typically Shigella infection).
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Bacillary dysentery.

subQuestions.text: b. What is the cause of this disease?
subQuestions.explanation: Shigella is acquired from contaminated food or water and causes invasive bacillary dysentery with fever and bloody diarrhea.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Shigella organisms ingested in contaminated food.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the microscopic findings?
subQuestions.explanation: Bacillary dysentery destroys superficial colonic mucosa, leaving fibrin, necrotic debris, neutrophils, and bacteria over an edematous congested submucosa.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Colonic mucosa destroyed and replaced by fibrin/necrotic tissue/polymorphs/pus cells and organism colonies; congested edematous submucosa.

subQuestions.text: d. What are the possible complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Reactive arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis may follow bacillary dysentery; severe disease can rarely cause perforation or peritonitis.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Marked acute toxaemia with sterile arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis; rare perforation with peritonitis.

questions.text:
127.Diverticula in the colon may be associated with all of the following complications,
except:
questions.explanation: Crohn disease is not a direct diverticular complication; fistula, hemorrhage, obstruction, and peridiverticulitis can follow diverticulosis.

questions.text: A 61-year-old woman presents with nausea, vomiting, and the sudden onset of left-sided abdominal pain. Physical examination finds a low grade fever, and laboratory evaluation finds increased numbers of neutrophils in her peripheral blood. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute left-sided abdominal pain, fever, and neutrophilia in an older adult are typical of diverticulitis, often from an inflamed sigmoid diverticulum.

questions.text:
20.Which of the following mechanisms most accurately describes how pseudo -
membranous colitis caused by Clostridium difficile is produced?
questions.explanation: C. difficile colonizes the colon and produces toxins that damage epithelium, causing pseudomembranous colitis.
options: elaboration of an enterotoxin following colonization of the colon
invasion and destruction of mucosa by the organism
host immune response to the organism

questions.text:
15) A 61-year-old woman presents with nausea, vomiting, and the sudden onset of left-
 sided abdominal pain. Physical examination finds a low grade fever, and laboratory
 evaluation finds increased numbers of neutrophils in her peripheral blood. Which of the
 following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Left-sided pain, fever, and neutrophilia in an older adult suggest acute diverticulitis.

questions.text: 119.The most common histological type of primary malignant tumor of the anus is:
questions.explanation: Most primary anal canal malignancies are squamous cell carcinomas because the distal canal is lined by squamous epithelium.

questions.text: 41.  Which of the following diseases predisposes to colonic carcinoma:
questions.explanation: Longstanding extensive ulcerative colitis increases colorectal dysplasia and carcinoma risk through chronic inflammation.

questions.text:
50- Familial adenosis polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutation

of:
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by inherited APC tumor-suppressor mutation, activating β-catenin signaling in colonic epithelium.

questions.text: 45. All of the following statements are true about patients with carcinoid tumors EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Most carcinoid tumors are localized and do not cause carcinoid syndrome; systemic serotonin effects usually emerge after hepatic metastases bypass first-pass metabolism.
options: They often have evidence o f serotonin production.
May produce dumb-bell lesion in the peribronchial tissue.
Caecum and appendix are of common sites of origin.

questions.text: A 39-year-old man is having a routine physical examination because of a history of colon cancer in his family. His stool is positive for occult blood. Colonoscopy reveals multiple polyps in the ascending colon, including small 5cm pendunculated tubular adenomas and 1cm tubulovillous adenomas. Also, few 2cm sessile villous adenoma was found in the cecum, containing a focus of well differentiated adenocarcinoma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Numerous adenomatous polyps with a carcinoma focus suggest familial adenomatous polyposis from inherited APC dysfunction.

questions.text:
3) A 39-year-old man is having a routine physical examination because of a history of colon
 cancer in his family. His stool is positive for occult blood. Colonoscopy reveals multiple
 polyps in the ascending colon, including small 5cm pendunculated tubular adenomas and
 lcm tubulovillous adenomas. Also, few 2cm sessile villous adenoma was found in the cecum,
 containing a focus of well differentiated adenocarcinoma. Which of the following is the
 most likely diagnosis?.
questions.explanation: Numerous adenomas with an early carcinoma focus and family history suggest familial adenomatous polyposis, an inherited APC-associated syndrome.

questions.text: 9-Classification of colorectal carcinoma depends of the degree of:
questions.explanation: Colorectal carcinoma staging depends on depth of wall invasion and spread to nodes or distant organs, as reflected in TNM/Dukes systems.

questions.text: 43.  Not characteristic of argentaffinoma (carcinoid) of the ileum:
questions.explanation: Ileal carcinoids produce serotonin and other peptides; catecholamine excretion is not the usual biochemical finding.
options: Brown -black cytoplasmic granules with silver stain.
Excretion of catecholamines in the urine.

questions.text: An 82-year-old female presents with bleeding per rectum. Physical examination reveals piles. Pelvic examination reveals enlarged right ovary. Colonoscopy reveals polypoidfungating mass in the rectum.
questions.explanation: A rectal fungating mass in an older patient with bleeding is most consistent with colorectal adenocarcinoma; an enlarged ovary may indicate spread.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: In the described older woman with rectal bleeding, a fungating rectal mass, and ovarian enlargement, colorectal adenocarcinoma with possible ovarian metastasis is likely.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Rectal/colorectal adenocarcinoma.

subQuestions.text: b. What is the pathogenesis?
subQuestions.explanation: Colorectal carcinogenesis follows adenoma–carcinoma and mismatch-repair pathways, with APC, KRAS, TP53, and DNA repair alterations.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Risks include low vegetable fibre, high refined carbohydrate and fat diet, pre-existing adenomas and UC. Pathways: APC/beta-catenin adenoma–carcinoma sequence (APC, KRAS and P53) and mismatch-repair deficiency/microsatellite instability.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the possible microscopic findings?
subQuestions.explanation: Colorectal carcinomas may be conventional gland-forming, mucinous, or signet-ring cell types.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Adenocarcinoma, mucoid carcinoma or signet-ring cell carcinoma.

subQuestions.text: d. What are the methods of spread?
subQuestions.explanation: Colorectal adenocarcinoma spreads locally, through regional lymphatics, and via blood—especially to liver and lung; ovarian deposits may form Krukenberg tumors.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Local invasion into intestinal wall/surrounding tissues, regional lymphatic spread, ovarian Krukenberg tumour and blood spread to liver, lungs, bones and brain.

subQuestions.text: e. Can you explain the right ovarian enlargement? What is the stage of the disease?
subQuestions.explanation: If an ovarian mass is a metastasis, it is distant M1 disease; the primary tumor's T and N stage need separate assessment.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Enlarged ovary may represent ovarian metastatic Krukenberg tumour. If this metastasis is established, it is distant metastatic disease (M1). T and N cannot be determined from the supplied findings.

questions.text:
163.An elderly male had rectal bleeding. A flat velvety mass was observed in the cecum.
The provisional diagnosis was villous adenoma. A partial colectomy was performed.
Invasion through the muscularis mucosae, but not into the muscularis propria, was
observed on paraffin sections. Therefore, the final diagnosis was:
questions.explanation: Invasion through muscularis mucosae into submucosa but not through muscularis propria is Dukes A colorectal carcinoma.

questions.text:
110.A man of advanced middle age or beyond with iron deficiency anemia must be
suspected of having:
questions.explanation: Iron-deficiency anemia in an older adult can result from occult bleeding by colorectal carcinoma and warrants investigation for a GI malignancy.

questions.text: A 52-year-old male presents with bleeding per rectum. Colonoscopy reveals the presence of innumerable polyps, exceeding 100 in number, The physician sends a lot for pathological examination and asks the pathologist for rapid report.
questions.explanation: Hundreds of colorectal polyps suggest familial adenomatous polyposis, driven by germline APC mutation and requiring urgent management.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis is a hereditary APC syndrome with numerous adenomas and near-certain cancer risk without colectomy.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Familial adenomatous polyposis.

subQuestions.text: b. Why does he ask for rapid report?
subQuestions.explanation: In familial adenomatous polyposis, hundreds of adenomas carry near-certain lifetime colorectal cancer risk; rapid pathology helps identify dysplasia or invasive carcinoma.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Virtually 100% adenocarcinoma progression risk; rapid assessment evaluates malignant change.

subQuestions.text: c. What is the microscopic picture of the polyps and what are the possible variants?
subQuestions.explanation: FAP polyps are dysplastic adenomas, most often tubular but also tubulovillous or villous; Gardner and Turcot are recognized variants.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Dysplastic adenomatous glands: mainly tubular, also tubulovillous/villous; Gardner variant with osteomas/cysts/thyroid/dental abnormalities; Turcot with CNS tumors.

subQuestions.text: d. Enumerate types of large intestinal polypi..
subQuestions.explanation: Large-intestinal polyps include adenomatous, hyperplastic, juvenile, hamartomatous, and inflammatory forms.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Neoplastic: tubular/villous/tubulovillous and serrated adenomas; nonneoplastic: bilharzial, hyperplastic, juvenile and Peutz-Jeghers hamartomatous, inflammatory polyps.

subQuestions.text: e. What are the possible complications in our case?
subQuestions.explanation: With familial adenomatous polyposis, adenomas can bleed, obstruct, or undergo malignant transformation; prophylactic colectomy reduces colorectal cancer risk but does not eliminate extracolonic tumors.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Ulceration/bleeding, intussusception and malignant transformation; prophylactic colectomy is curative for colonic risk but other-site neoplasia risk remains.

questions.text: 40.  The most common rectal malignant tum or is:
questions.explanation: Adenocarcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of rectum and arises from colorectal glandular epithelium.

questions.text:
109.Adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon is more likely than adenocarcinoma of the
sigmoid colon to:
questions.explanation: Right-colon cancers often grow as bulky masses and cause occult blood loss/anemia; left-sided tumors more often encircle and obstruct.
options: encircle the bowel, causing a stricture or obstruction

questions.text:
31.Which of the following characterizes the biologic nature of carcinoid tumors
(argentaffinomas)?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome usually appears after liver metastases release serotonin and other mediators into systemic circulation, causing flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm.
options: production of systemic symptoms when they metastasize to the liver
especially malignant when primary in the appendix
production of jejunal ulceration due to gastrin elaboration

questions.text:
(1076) Choose the correct answer:
All the following are features of carcinoid tumor EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome does not occur in every neuroendocrine tumor; it usually requires systemic mediator release, often after metastasis.
options: It can be located in any site of the gastrointestinal tract.
It can be located in the bronchi.
It is always associated with carcinoid syndrome.

questions.text: A 64-year-old man has noted a 5kg. weight loss, abdominal distention with lack of stool in the past two days. An abdominal CT scan reveals a mass involving the descending colon. Microscopically, the mass is found to be a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.
questions.explanation: This descending-colon mass is an adenocarcinoma causing weight loss and obstruction; colorectal tumors spread locally, through nodes, and via blood.

subQuestions.text: a. What are the risk factors?
subQuestions.explanation: Colorectal cancer risk rises with age, adenomas, inflammatory bowel disease, family history, inherited APC or mismatch-repair defects, and dietary or metabolic factors.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Age 60–70, male sex, low vegetable-fiber/high refined-carbohydrate/high-fat diet, APC/beta-catenin sequence or mismatch-repair deficiency, adenomas and ulcerative colitis.

subQuestions.text: b. What are the other possible microscopic types?
subQuestions.explanation: Signet-ring and mucinous adenocarcinomas are additional microscopic colorectal carcinoma types beyond conventional gland-forming adenocarcinoma.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Mucoid and signet-ring cell carcinoma.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the methods of spread?
subQuestions.explanation: Colorectal carcinoma spreads directly through the bowel wall, to regional lymph nodes, and hematogenously, especially to liver; ovarian deposits occur.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Direct wall/surrounding invasion, regional-node spread, Krukenberg ovarian spread and blood spread to liver/lung/bone/brain.

subQuestions.text: d. Mention the possible effects and complication.
subQuestions.explanation: Colorectal cancer can cause occult bleeding and anemia, altered bowel habits, obstruction, pain, and symptoms from metastases, especially in liver or lung.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Occult bleeding/iron-deficiency anemia, bowel-habit changes, obstruction, cramps and symptoms of metastases.

questions.text:
26.In which of the following segments of the gastrointestinal tract is primary carcinoma
least common?
questions.explanation: Primary carcinoma is least common in the small intestine compared with esophagus, stomach, colon, and mouth.

questions.text: A 70-year-old previously healthy man notes blood streaked stool. A colonoscopy is performed, and there is an area of obstruction from an encircling mass with superficial ulceration that is located at 20cm above the anal verge. Which of the following factors was most likely to have been present for development of this lesion?
questions.explanation: High-fat diets are associated with colorectal cancer risk; diet joins age, family history, and adenomas among risk factors.

questions.text: 23.Carcinoid tumors (argentaffinomas) are characterized by all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Appendiceal carcinoids are common but usually have low malignant potential; ileal carcinoids are more likely to metastasize and cause systemic disease.
options: many are multiple especially in the ileum
can occur in alimentary, biliary and respiratory tracts
may produce systemic symptoms when accompanied by liver metastases
appendix is the most common site
appendiceal types have greatest malignant potential

questions.text: 22.The carcinoid syndrome is likely to occur with carcinoid tumors:
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome is uncommon with a localized appendix or ileum primary because portal blood carries serotonin to liver for metabolism; systemic spread is typical.

questions.text: Which of the following is not among Risk factors for Colorectal cancer
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B is not an established colorectal cancer risk factor; obesity and diets high in processed or red meat are associated risks.

questions.text:
106.Which of the following factors is most valuable in predicting the biologic behavior of
carcinoma of the colon?
questions.explanation: Lymph-node involvement is a major prognostic factor in colon cancer because it indicates regional spread and affects stage.

questions.text: 102.Familial polyposis of the colon is associated with:
questions.explanation: Familial colonic polyposis is associated with colorectal carcinoma because adenomas accumulate mutations and progress over time.

questions.text:
(1121) Encircle True or False:
Malignant melanoma never occurs in the anal canal. ( T - F )
questions.explanation: Anal canal melanoma can occur, though it is rare and aggressive. The statement that it never occurs is therefore false.

questions.text:
112.Persistent elevation of serum carcinoembryonic antigen following surgical resection of
a carcinoma of the colon suggests:
questions.explanation: Persistent CEA after resection can indicate residual or recurrent colorectal cancer, including distant metastases, and prompts further evaluation.

questions.text: 113.Which would be the most encouraging findings in a patient with colon carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Absence of regional lymph-node metastases is favorable because nodal involvement signals more advanced colorectal cancer.
options: normal liver function tests and normal liver biopsy
short duration of symptoms at the time of diagnosis
absence of tumor in regional lymph nodes

questions.text:
(1096) Encircle True or False:
Carcinoid tumor never metastasize. ( T - F )
questions.explanation: Carcinoid tumors can metastasize, especially when larger or invasive; distant spread can produce systemic carcinoid syndrome.

questions.text: 8- The most important prognostic factor in colorectal carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: Depth of bowel-wall invasion is a major prognostic factor because it tracks local extension and risk of regional or distant spread.

questions.text:
TRUE & FALSE:
34.The commonest peritoneal tumor is metastatic tumors
questions.explanation: Metastases are the commonest tumors involving the peritoneum, often originating from abdominal or pelvic malignancies.

questions.text: 51- The affected gene in FAP is a member of:
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by inherited loss of APC, a tumor-suppressor gene that regulates beta-catenin signaling.

questions.text:
44. C arcinoid tumor arises from :
a .Glandular epithelial'cells;
questions.explanation: Intestinal carcinoid tumors arise from enterochromaffin (argentaffin) neuroendocrine cells that store serotonin and related amines.
options: Argentaffin cells. e: Vascular endothelial cells.

questions.text: 34.The commonest peritoneal tumor is metastatic tumors
questions.explanation: Metastatic deposits are more common in the peritoneum than primary peritoneal tumors because many intra-abdominal cancers seed the serosal surfaces.

questions.text: 48- Regarding the lymphomas of the GIT, which of the following is incorrect:
questions.explanation: Primary GI lymphomas commonly involve stomach and small intestine; colon involvement is less frequent, making the first statement incorrect.
options: More common in colon than the small intestine

questions.text: Which of the following molecular alterations is commonly seen in the carcinoma of colon and rectum?
questions.explanation: APC loss activates β-catenin signaling and initiates the common adenoma–carcinoma pathway in colorectal epithelium.

questions.text:
9) A-20-year-old man is healthy but,has a family history of colon cancer at a young age. He
 undergoes colonoscopy and there are over 200 tubular adenomas ranging in size from 0.2
 to 1 cm. which of the following diseases is he most likely to have?
questions.explanation: Hundreds of colorectal adenomas plus a family history of early colon cancer are characteristic of familial adenomatous polyposis caused by APC-pathway dysfunction.

questions.text:
(1060) Choose the correct answer:
The most important prognostic factor in colorectal carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: Depth of tumor invasion into bowel wall is a major determinant of colorectal cancer stage and prognosis, reflected in the T category.

questions.text:
(1095) Encircle True or False:
Lymphoma of the large intestine is more common than adenocarcinoma. ( T - F)
questions.explanation: Large-intestinal lymphoma is uncommon; adenocarcinoma is far more frequent, so the statement is false.

questions.text: Which of the following molecular alterations is commonly seen in the carcinoma of colon and rectum?
questions.explanation: The adenoma-carcinoma sequence commonly begins with APC loss and altered beta-catenin/WNT signaling, followed by additional mutations during progression.

questions.text:
52- What is the suspected modified Dukes stage of a case of colonic carcinoma extending
into the muscularis propria with positive metastatic lymph node?
questions.explanation: Dukes C1 describes invasion into muscularis propria with regional lymph-node metastasis; C2 extends through the bowel wall.

questions.text: 24.Primary carcinoma is least common in:
questions.explanation: Primary carcinoma is least common in the small intestine, whose tumor incidence is lower than that of colon, stomach, or esophagus.

questions.text:
(1039) Choose the correct answer:
Carcinoid syndrome occurs in:
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome usually occurs after hematogenous spread to the liver, allowing secreted serotonin and peptides to reach systemic circulation.
options: Carcinoid tumor with lymph node metastases

questions.text: A 39-year-old male is having a routine physical examination because of a history of colon cancer in his family. Colonoscopy is performed. There are innumerable adenomatous polyps in the colon.
questions.explanation: Numerous colorectal adenomas suggest familial adenomatous polyposis, an inherited APC-associated syndrome with high cancer risk.

subQuestions.text: a. What is your diagnosis? And what is the risk of progression to adenocarcinoma?
subQuestions.explanation: FAP stems from germline APC mutation and untreated patients have a near-certain lifetime progression to colorectal carcinoma.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Familial adenomatous polyposis; virtually 100% colorectal adenocarcinoma progression.

subQuestions.text: b. What are the other possible complications of this condition?
subQuestions.explanation: Adenomatous polyps can ulcerate, bleed, or cause intussusception; familial polyposis also carries extracolonic tumor risks that remain after colectomy.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Ulceration, bleeding and intussusception; extraintestinal neoplasia risk remains after colectomy.

subQuestions.text: c. Enumerate non-neoplastic polyps which might occur in the colon.
subQuestions.explanation: Even with numerous adenomas suggesting FAP, other non-neoplastic colonic polyps include hyperplastic, juvenile, inflammatory, hamartomatous, and bilharzial types.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Bilharzial, hyperplastic, juvenile/retention, Peutz-Jeghers hamartomatous and inflammatory polyps.

questions.text:
(1036) Choose the correct answer:
Carcinoid tumor arises from:
questions.explanation: Carcinoid neuroendocrine cells are argentaffin/enterochromaffin cells, especially in intestinal crypts.

questions.text:
114.In contrast to carcinoma of the right colon, carcinoma of the left colon tends to be
associated with:
questions.explanation: Left-sided colorectal cancers tend to grow circumferentially in a narrowed lumen, causing altered bowel habits and obstruction; right-sided tumors more often bleed occultly.

questions.text: 108.Colonic neoplasms tend to metastasize most frequently to:
questions.explanation: Colonic venous drainage enters the portal system, so the liver is the most common first site of hematogenous metastasis.

questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a family history of colon cancer undergoes a screening colonoscopy. No invasive carcinomas are identified. But two small pedunculated tubular adenomas are removed and one villous adenoma measuring 5mm in diameter is biopsied.
questions.explanation: Three adenomas alone do not establish FAP; a family history raises concern, but the source criterion is at least 100 adenomas.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: The described lesions are colorectal adenomas; tubular and villous architecture distinguishes their growth pattern and malignancy risk.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Colorectal adenomas: two tubular and one villous adenoma as described.

subQuestions.text: b. What is the syndrome that could predispose this individual to colon cancer?
subQuestions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis is one inherited colorectal cancer syndrome; hundreds of adenomas support it, while a few alone do not establish it.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Familial adenomatous polyposis is a possible predisposing syndrome (APC mutation; virtually complete carcinoma risk). These three adenomas do not establish FAP: the book requires at least 100 colonic adenomas.

subQuestions.text: c. What other dietary factors could play a role in the development of colon cancer?
subQuestions.explanation: Low vegetable-fiber intake and diets rich in refined carbohydrates and fat are associated with higher colorectal cancer risk.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Low vegetable-fibre intake and high refined-carbohydrate/high-fat diets increase colorectal-cancer risk.

subQuestions.text: d. Enumerate other non-neoplastic colonic polyps.
subQuestions.explanation: Non-neoplastic colonic polyps include hyperplastic, inflammatory, bilharzial, and hamartomatous types such as juvenile and Peutz–Jeghers polyps.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Bilharzial, hyperplastic, hamartomatous juvenile/retention and Peutz–Jeghers polyps, and inflammatory polyps.

questions.text: Which of the following molecular alterations is commonly seen in the carcinoma of colon and rectum?
questions.explanation: APC loss stabilizes beta-catenin and drives the adenoma–carcinoma sequence in many colorectal cancers.

questions.text:
25.Which is most characteristic of carcinoma of the cecum or right colon (in contrast to
carcinoma of the rectum)?
questions.explanation: Right-colon carcinoma more often causes occult bleeding and anemia; rectal tumors more often cause visible blood or tenesmus.

questions.text: 107.Which of the following is most strongly predisposing to colon cancer?
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis produces numerous adenomas and near-certain colorectal carcinoma without prophylactic management, making it a major inherited risk.

questions.text:
150.A 76-year-old male was admitted for symptoms including constipation, change in stool
character and weight loss. Colonoscopy revealed multiple polyps in the rectosigmoid area.
An adenomatous polyp was removed. Another colonic tumor was seen in the same patient
which was flat with irregular “shaggy rug” surface. A biopsy showed frond-like glandular
architecture. Atypical epithelial cells in clusters were seen beneath the muscularis
mucosae. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Atypical glands beneath muscularis mucosae have invaded submucosa, establishing adenocarcinoma arising in a villous adenoma.
options: focus of adenocarcinoma arising in villous adenoma

questions.text: 14.Occult fecal blood may be an indication of:
questions.explanation: Fecal occult blood may originate from upper or lower GI bleeding; the test does not localize its source.

questions.text:
111.Tumors of the ascending colon in comparison to tumors of the descending colon are
more likely to:
questions.explanation: Right-colon cancers grow in a roomy lumen and can become bulky before causing obstruction; left-sided lesions more often constrict the bowel.

questions.text:
(1119) Encircle True or False:
High vegetable intake can protect against colonic cancer. ( T - F)
questions.explanation: Vegetable fiber may reduce colorectal cancer risk through stool dilution, faster transit, and a diet pattern associated with lower carcinogen exposure.

questions.text: 16.Occult fecal blood test would be helpful in discovering:
questions.explanation: Colorectal carcinoma may bleed microscopically, so fecal occult-blood testing can reveal an otherwise silent lesion.

questions.text:
(1075) Choose the correct answer:
The most important prognostic factor in colorectal cancer is:
questions.explanation: Depth of invasion and spread to lymph nodes or distant organs are the strongest prognostic factors in colorectal cancer, not size or grade alone.

questions.text:
(1037) Choose the correct answer:
The metastatic potential of carcinoid tumor depends mainly on:
questions.explanation: Carcinoid metastatic potential depends strongly on primary site: appendiceal tumors are often indolent, while ileal tumors more often metastasize.

questions.text:
28) A 2-week-Old neonate presents with regurgitation and persistent, severe, projectile
 vomiting. An olive-like epigastric mass is felt during physical examination. A chest x-ray
 does not reveal the presence of bowel gas in the chest cavity. The infant's mother did not
 had any. troubles during pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate

questions.explanation: Projectile nonbilious vomiting with an olive-like epigastric mass suggests hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; pyloromyotomy relieves obstruction.
options: Surgery to cut a hypertrophic band at the pylorus
Surgery to remove a mass of the adrenal gland
Surgery to resect an aganglionic section of the intestines.

questions.text: 4.A two-week-old boy develops persistent projectile vomiting. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Projectile nonbilious vomiting beginning in early infancy is typical of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which obstructs gastric emptying.

questions.text:
9.A male infant, who was normal for the first three weeks of life, develops projectile
vomiting after feeding. The likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Projectile vomiting beginning at a few weeks of age is typical of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which obstructs gastric emptying.

questions.text:
(999) Choose the correct answer:
Congenital pyloric stenosis is due to:
questions.explanation: Congenital pyloric stenosis results from hypertrophy of the pyloric circular smooth muscle, narrowing gastric outlet.

questions.text:
(1040) Choose the correct answer:
The cause of Hirschsprung's disease is:
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest-derived enteric ganglion cells to populate a distal bowel segment, causing functional obstruction.

questions.text:

Meckel's diverticulum is a blind pouch lined by mucosa, submucosa and muscle layer. ( T - F )
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum containing mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria, usually from persistent vitelline duct.

questions.text: Congenital pyloric stenosis is due to:
questions.explanation: Hypertrophied pyloric smooth muscle narrows the channel and causes forceful nonbilious vomiting in young infants.

questions.text: 11.Absence of ganglion cells is an essential diagnostic feature of:
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease is diagnosed by absence of enteric ganglion cells in the affected distal bowel, unlike pyloric stenosis.

questions.text: 1-Meckel's diverticulum is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum is a blind pouch that opens into the ileal lumen; its persistence does not leave it isolated from bowel.
options: It is due to persistence of the vitelline duct.
It is a mucosa-lined blind pouch.
Its lumen does not communicate with the intestinal lumen.
It may contain heterotrophic gastric tissue.

questions.text: 29- Features of Hirschsprung disease include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease causes constipation and distension from distal aganglionosis; severe diarrhea is not typical.
options: It is a disease of children less than one year
Due to congenital absence of the ganglionic cells in the mesenteric plexus
Manifested by severe diarrhea & abdominal distension
The aganglionic segment is narrow & the segment proximal to it is markedly dilated

questions.text: 63.Ulcers of the ileum with massive hemorrhage are usually associated with:
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum may contain ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates adjacent ileum, causing severe bleeding in children.

questions.text:
9. A 23-year-old primigravida gives birth at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy to a
male infant with no apparent congenital anomalies. At 4 weeks of age, the infant begins to
exhibit forceful vomiting after each meal. The infant had been fine previously and gaining
weight normally. Which of the following conditions is the probable cause for his vomiting?
questions.explanation: Forceful non-bilious vomiting around four weeks of age suggests hypertrophic pyloric stenosis from thickening of pyloric circular muscle.

questions.text: 10.The treatment of Hirschsprung’s disease typically involves:
questions.explanation: Definitive Hirschsprung treatment removes the aganglionic segment and connects normally innervated bowel to the anus.
options: avoidance of surgical intervention, if possible

questions.text:

Meckel's diverticulum is a:
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum is a congenital remnant of the vitelline duct on the antimesenteric ileum, so it is not a perforation, fistula, or sinus.
options: Congenital anomaly in the large intestine

questions.text:
6.An 8-month-old boy is reported by his mother to have had several episodes of “colic”
and she has noticed blood in his stools. Your examination is negative except for slight
abdominal tenderness and moderate anemia. Which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum may contain ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates adjacent ileum, causing bleeding and intermittent colicky pain.

questions.text: A 3 months old infant has marked abdominal distention along with infrequent bowel movements. A radiograph reveals marked colonic dilatation.
questions.explanation: A contracted aganglionic distal segment causes functional obstruction and megacolon proximally in this infant.

subQuestions.text: a. What pathologic finding would be most likely found in this setting?
subQuestions.explanation: The clinical setting of congenital megacolon is most consistent with Hirschsprung disease, caused by aganglionosis of the distal bowel.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Congenital aganglionosis (Hirschsprung disease) is the most likely finding.

subQuestions.text: b. What is the pathogenesis of this condition?
subQuestions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from failed neural crest migration, leaving distal bowel aganglionic and unable to relax.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Arrested proximal-to-distal neural-crest migration leaves distal bowel without ganglion cells, causing functional obstruction and proximal dilation.

subQuestions.text: c. Describe the gross and microscopic features?
subQuestions.explanation: Histology shows absent ganglion cells in contracted distal bowel, with proximal dilation from retained stool and pressure.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Rectum always involved with possible proximal extension; aganglionic segment remains contracted and proximal colon is dilated. Microscopy shows transmural absence of ganglion cells in affected segment.

subQuestions.text: d. Mention other possible causes of colonic obstruction in children.
subQuestions.explanation: Childhood bowel obstruction can result from intussusception, meconium ileus, malrotation, congenital stenosis, or Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead point.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Other childhood causes include ileocaecal intussusception (more common in children), inspissated meconium in newborns and Meckel-diverticulum-associated intussusception.

questions.text: 3.Each of the following applies to Hirschsprung’s disease except:
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease is treated by pull-through removal of the aganglionic distal segment; resecting only the dilated proximal bowel misses the cause.
options: absence of ganglion cells in myenteric plexus
treated by removal of distended segment of bowel
narrow, more distal segment exhibits characteristic deficiency of development

questions.text:
(1041) Choose the correct answer:
The colon proximal to the segment affected by Hirschsprung's disease shows:
questions.explanation: The bowel proximal to an aganglionic segment dilates because peristaltic contents meet distal functional obstruction.

questions.text: A 3-day- old male infant was born at term. His mother has noted marked abdominal enlargement along with infrequent bowel movements. Abdominal radiograph reveals marked colonic dilation. What pathologic finding is most likely to be present in this infant?
questions.explanation: A neonate with abdominal distension, infrequent stool, and colonic dilation likely has an aganglionic distal segment that fails to relax in Hirschsprung disease.

questions.text:
28. A 23-year-old primigravida gives birth at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy to a
male infant with no apparent congenital anomalies. At 4 weeks of age, the infant begins to
exhibit forceful vomiting after each meal. The infant had been fine previously and gaining
weight normally. Which of the following conditions is the probable cause for his vomiting?
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes projectile post-feed vomiting in young infants because a thickened pylorus blocks gastric outflow.

questions.text:

The length of Meckel's diverticulum varies from 10 - 15 cm. ( T - F)
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum is usually only a few centimeters long; 10–15 cm is longer than the typical lesion.

questions.text: 28- The following feature is not true about Meckel’s diverticulum:
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum is a blind pouch on the antimesenteric border of ileum, arising from a persistent vitelline duct and sometimes containing ectopic mucosa.

It is a blind pouch present on the mesenteric border of the small intestine
Located 2-3 feet from the ilieocecal junction
May get inflamed and present as acute abdomen

questions.explanation: An olive-like pyloric mass and projectile vomiting indicate hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, treated with pyloromyotomy to split the muscle.

questions.text: 38.  In congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung's disease) the essential lesion is:
questions.explanation: Congenital megacolon reflects loss of ganglion cells in a distal segment, causing functional obstruction and upstream dilation.

Weakness, of taeniae coli and circular muscle.

questions.text:
5.Which congenital abnormality of the gastrointestinal tract most characteristically has its
clinical onset at 2 to 4 weeks of age and has a strong male preponderance?
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically presents at 2–4 weeks with nonbilious projectile vomiting and is more common in boys.

questions.text:
(1098) Encircle True or False:
Hirschsprung's disease is due to absence of ganglion cells in the wall of the small intestine. ( T - F)

questions.text:

include
questions.explanation: Intestinal atresia is a congenital mechanical blockage that usually causes vomiting in the first days after feeding begins.

options: narrowed segment distal to the dilated segment

questions.text:
(1025) Choose the correct answer:
Meckel's diverticulum may cause peptic ulcer manifestations because of:
questions.explanation: Ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel diverticulum can secrete acid and ulcerate adjacent ileum, producing bleeding or ulcer-like pain.
options: Diverticulitis simulating symptoms of peptic ulcer

questions.text: 54. A 2-year-old girl with a history of chronic constipation since birth is brought to the emergency room because of nausea and vomiting. Physical examination shows marked abdominal distension. Abdominal radiography reveals distended bowel loops with a paucity of air in the rectum. A rectal biopsy shows an absence of ganglion cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Constipation from birth, abdominal distension, absent rectal ganglion cells, and proximal dilation indicate Hirschsprung disease.

questions.text:
(1024) Choose the correct answer:
Meckel's diverticulum is characterised by all EXCEPT:

options: It is due to persistence of the vitelline duct
It is a mucosa-lined blind pouch
Its lumen does NOT communicate with the intestinal lumen
It may contain heterotropic gastric tissue

questions.text:
25. A n elderly man who has had several attacks of coronary disease is admitted to hospital for
    incipient gangrene of one leg a n d found on admission to have symptoms of intestinal
    obstruction. What is the most probable cause of the latter ?
questions.explanation: Severe peripheral vascular disease may accompany mesenteric arterial thrombosis, causing intestinal ischemia and acute obstruction-like symptoms.

questions.text: 29.  All the following : are effects of small bowel obstruction EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Ascites is not a usual direct effect of small-bowel obstruction; distension, vomiting, fluid loss, renal failure, or strangulation may follow.

questions.text: An 8-year-old healthy boy suffers from severe abdominal colicky pain, distension, vomiting which is bile-stained. He starts losing much fluid and becomes dehydrated. Further investigations reveal an oblong non- neoplastic mass at the iliocecal mass.
questions.explanation: A child with an ileocecal mass, colic, distension, and bilious vomiting likely has intussusception: one bowel segment telescopes into another. Vomiting and fluid sequestration cause dehydration; ischemia may progress to hemorrhagic infarction, gangrene, renal failure, and shock.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: Intussusception telescopes one bowel segment into another, obstructing the lumen and impairing venous drainage.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Intussusception causing acute intestinal obstruction.

subQuestions.text: b. What is the pathogenesis of this iliocecal mass in such age?
subQuestions.explanation: Intussusception is telescoping of bowel, commonly near the ileocecal region in children, and can form an obstructing mass.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Invagination of one intestinal loop into another forms an obstructing mass, most often at ileocaecal valve and more commonly in children.

subQuestions.text: c. Explain the cause of dehydration.
subQuestions.explanation: Repeated bilious vomiting and poor intake cause substantial water and electrolyte loss; intestinal obstruction can also sequester fluid in bowel and worsen dehydration.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Marked fluid loss with the stated vomiting causes dehydration/electrolyte imbalance.

subQuestions.text: d. What are other possible complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Intussusception can strangulate mesenteric vessels, causing hemorrhagic infarction, necrosis, peritonitis, and shock.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Haemorrhagic infarction followed by gangrene, renal failure and shock; intestinal obstruction may also produce stercoral ulceration and acute-on-chronic worsening.

questions.text:
88.The following are associated with intestinal obstruction. Which is/are a cause rather
than a result of intestinal obstruction?
questions.explanation: Intussusception and chronic diverticulitis can each cause mechanical obstruction, so both listed conditions qualify.

questions.text: (1125) Match the statement on the right side with the related one on the left side:
questions.explanation: Paralytic ileus is cessation of bowel movement; volvulus twists a loop and obstructs its lumen; intussusception telescopes one segment into another, risking obstruction and ischemia.

subQuestions.text: Complete cessation of the intestinal movement
subQuestions.explanation: Paralytic ileus is functional cessation of peristalsis without a physical blockage, commonly after surgery or severe illness.

subQuestions.text: Twisting of a loop of intestine with obstruction of its lumen
subQuestions.explanation: Volvulus is twisting of bowel and mesentery that obstructs the lumen and may compromise blood supply.

subQuestions.text: Invagination of a loop of intestine into aNOTher part
subQuestions.explanation: Intussusception is telescoping of one bowel segment into another, producing obstruction and possible ischemia if untreated.

questions.text: 138.A cause of intestinal obstruction:
questions.explanation: Celiac disease and Whipple disease cause malabsorption rather than mechanical obstruction; neither is a usual obstructive lesion.

questions.text: 31- All of the following are causes of chronic intestinal obstruction except:
questions.explanation: A strangulated hernia causes an acute obstruction with threatened blood supply, whereas Crohn stricture, carcinoma, and Hirschsprung disease can produce chronic obstruction.

questions.text: 21.Infarction of the bowel may be caused by:
questions.explanation: Volvulus twists bowel and mesentery, while mesenteric arterial thrombosis blocks blood flow; either can infarct bowel.

questions.text: Gall stone ileus results when:
questions.explanation: Gallstone ileus occurs when a calculus enters bowel through a biliary-enteric fistula and lodges at a narrow point.
options: There is empyema of the gall bladder.
Cholesterol stone obstruct the common bile duct.
A calculus migrates through a fistulous tract.

questions.text:
(1077) Choose the correct answer:
An atherosclerotic patient presented with severe colicky abdominal pain and vomiting. On operation, A loop of intestine was gangrenous. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Atherosclerosis can occlude mesenteric arteries, causing ischemia and gangrene of bowel. Sudden severe pain with a necrotic loop supports vascular occlusion.

questions.text: 87.In children, the most common site of intussusception is:
questions.explanation: The ileocecal region is the commonest site of childhood intussusception, often involving ileum telescoping through the ileocecal valve.

questions.text: 116.The most common area for volvulus is:
questions.explanation: Sigmoid colon is the commonest site of volvulus, particularly with redundancy and chronic constipation.

questions.text: A 3-year-old girl presents with the abrupt onset of colicky abdominal pain, abdominal distension with blood and mucus in stools. Physical examination reveals a slightly tender, sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant of her abdomen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Colicky pain, blood and mucus, and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass in a young child are classic for intussusception.

questions.text: 30- One of the functional causes of acute intestinal obstruction is:
questions.explanation: Paralytic ileus is functional obstruction caused by absent peristalsis, unlike mechanical obstruction from adhesions or hernia.
options: Thrombosis or embolism of mesenteric artery

questions.text: A 47-year-old female presents with chronic constipation. She tells her physician that she is always suffering a problem during defaecation as if something is preventing complete evacuation of her intestine. Further investigations reveal asymmetrically enlarged, distorted uterus by multiple leiomyomata.
questions.explanation: A large fibroid uterus can externally compress the colon and cause chronic partial obstruction with incomplete evacuation.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: Large uterine leiomyomata can compress the bowel and cause chronic intestinal obstruction, fitting the long-standing constipation and incomplete evacuation.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Chronic intestinal obstruction.

subQuestions.text: b. What is relation between her uterus and her complain?
subQuestions.explanation: A large leiomyomatous uterus can compress the colon externally, slowing passage and contributing to obstructive symptoms.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Enlarged leiomyomatous uterus compresses colon from outside.

subQuestions.text: c. What are other possible causes that may lead to the same problem in other individuals?
subQuestions.explanation: Other mechanical obstruction causes include colorectal cancer, adhesions, healed strictures, megacolon, ovarian masses, and uterine compression.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Colonic carcinoma, healed intestinal-ulcer strictures, interloop adhesions, megacolon, large ovarian cyst or uterine leiomyoma.

subQuestions.text: d. What are the effects and complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Obstruction can cause dehydration, electrolyte loss, renal injury, and shock; strangulation may cause infarction, while chronic obstruction can produce pressure ulcers.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Infarction/gangrene, dehydration/electrolyte imbalance, renal failure/shock, stercoral ulcers above obstruction and acute-on-chronic obstruction from impacted stool or inflammation.

questions.text: A 45-year-old male presents with severe abdominal colicky pain, distension and vomiting which is at first bile-stained, then faecal. He suffers from dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. He is known to have inguinal hernia.
questions.explanation: A known inguinal hernia can trap bowel and cause mechanical obstruction, with bilious then feculent vomiting as contents accumulate.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: A strangulated inguinal hernia can cause acute mechanical obstruction and threaten bowel viability through impaired blood flow.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Acute intestinal obstruction, most likely from strangulated inguinal hernia.

subQuestions.text: b. What is the possible cause in this case, describe the pathogenesis?
subQuestions.explanation: A trapped hernia compresses venous outflow first, causing edema; rising pressure then compromises arterial inflow and can progress to ischemia and gangrene.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Hernial strangulation obstructs venous return; further swelling of trapped loop increases strangulation.

subQuestions.text: c. What are other possible causes or mechanisms that may lead to the same presentation in other individuals?
subQuestions.explanation: Other obstruction mechanisms include impacted stool, parasites, gallstones, volvulus, intussusception, ileus, and mesenteric ischemia.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Impacted hard faeces, ball of Ascaris, gallstone or inspissated neonatal meconium; volvulus; intussusception; postoperative paralytic ileus; mesenteric thrombosis or embolism.

subQuestions.text: d. What are the effects and complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Obstruction can cause hemorrhagic infarction/gangrene, fluid and electrolyte loss, dehydration, renal failure, and shock.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Haemorrhagic infarction/gangrene; marked fluid loss with dehydration/electrolyte imbalance; renal failure/shock; stercoral ulcers above obstruction; acute-on-chronic obstruction from impacted faeces or inflammatory oedema.

subQuestions.text: e. Can you explain the cause of dehydration?
subQuestions.explanation: Repeated vomiting and fluid sequestration proximal to the obstruction reduce circulating volume and electrolytes, producing dehydration.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Marked fluid loss, including repeated vomiting explicitly stated in the stem, causes dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

questions.text: 32- Pathological features of chronic intestinal obstruction include:
questions.explanation: In chronic obstruction, bacteria liquefy retained food and generate gas in the dilated proximal segment.
options: There is collapse of the proximal segment
The lumen contains liquefied food & gases by the action of the bacteria
Hypertrophy and thickening of the wall of the distal segment

questions.text: An 18-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain; localized to the right lower quadrant, nausea, vomiting, mild fever and leucocytosis. An appedecectomy is performed. Which of the following statements best describes the expected microscopic appearance of the appendix?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils infiltrating the muscularis propria support acute suppurative appendicitis rather than normal appendix or isolated lymphoid hyperplasia.
options: Lymphoid hyperplasia within the muscular wall
A dilated lumen, filled with mucus
A yellow tumor nodule at the tip of appendix.

questions.text: 35.Pseudomyxoma peritonii occurs only in mucinous tumors
questions.explanation: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is accumulation of mucinous ascites from mucin-producing neoplasms, classically appendiceal mucinous tumors; the statement limits it too narrowly.

questions.text: 46. Commonest site for carcinoid is:
questions.explanation: Appendix is a frequent site of gastrointestinal neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors, many discovered incidentally after appendectomy.

questions.text: A 32-year-old man has had lower abdominal pain for the past 12 hours. On physical examination there is tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant. Laparoscopic appendectomy is performed. On microscopic examination of the resected appendix by the pathologist, all the inflammation is limited to the serosa. What should the pathologist most strongly suspect in this case?
questions.explanation: Inflammation limited to appendiceal serosa suggests secondary serositis from peritonitis; the finding alone is not specific for PAN.

questions.text: 94.Of the following, the most definitive morphologic finding of acute appendicitis is:
questions.explanation: Neutrophils extending into the muscularis propria are the key histologic criterion for acute appendicitis; luminal obstruction alone is not diagnostic.
options: obstruction of the lumen by a fecalith
congestion and margination of polys in the serosa

questions.text:
(1288) Encircle True or False:
Pseudomyxoma peritoneii occurs only in ovarian tumors. ( T - F)
questions.explanation: Pseudomyxoma peritonei most often arises from mucinous appendiceal neoplasms, though ovarian mucinous tumors can also be associated.

questions.text:
(1283) Encircle True or False:
Acute suppurative appendicitis may be fatal due to suppurative peritonitis. ( T - F)
questions.explanation: Suppurative appendicitis may perforate, spreading infection through the peritoneum and causing life-threatening peritonitis.

questions.text: 49- The following are known predisposing factors of acute appendicitis except:
questions.explanation: Fecaliths and lymphoid hyperplasia can obstruct the appendix and precipitate acute inflammation. Senility is not a predisposing factor.

questions.text:
(1038) Choose the correct answer:
The commonest site of carcinoid tumor is:
questions.explanation: Appendix is a common site for GI neuroendocrine tumors, many of which are small and found incidentally.

questions.text:
A 20 year old male presented with sudden lower right abdominal pain. Appendectomy was done. Microscopic
examination revealed mucosal ulceration and transmural inflammatory infiltrate rich in neutrophils and pus cells. This
condition can be complicated by:
questions.explanation: Transmural suppurative appendicitis can seed portal veins and cause pyaemia, including septic thrombosis or liver abscess.

questions.text: A 26-year-old man returns home from playing foot-ball, complaining of midline abdominal pain. He denies being hit or suffering any other trauma. Over the next few hours, the pain does not remit but becomes more severe and is localized to the lower right quadrant. He also develops nausea and vomiting, but without diarrhea. Over the next 24 hours, the pain worsens and he develops fever and chills. On examination, he has a temperature of 38.8 C (102 F) and appears ill. The abdomen is diffusely tender to palpation, particularly in the right lower quadrant.
questions.explanation: Migrating pain with right-lower-quadrant fever/tenderness suggests acute suppurative appendicitis, often after luminal obstruction by a fecalith or lymphoid hyperplasia. Histology shows transmural neutrophils and suppurative serositis; complications include perforation, abscess, peritonitis, and portal pyaemia.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: Acute suppurative appendicitis features neutrophils through the wall and can progress to perforation or periappendiceal abscess.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Acute suppurative appendicitis.

subQuestions.text: b. What are the possible predisposing factors?
subQuestions.explanation: Fecaliths, food, parasites, or rarely tumors can obstruct the appendix, leading to stasis, bacterial growth, and inflammation.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Luminal obstruction from fecalith/food/seeds, less often gallstone/tumor/worms; impaired drainage/ischemia with bacterial proliferation.

subQuestions.text: c. Describe its microscopic picture.
subQuestions.explanation: Acute appendicitis shows transmural neutrophils, mucosal ulceration, luminal pus, edema, and suppurative serositis; gangrene appears in severe cases.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Necrotic luminal material/neutrophils/pus, mucosal ulceration and lymphoid hyperplasia, transmural neutrophils, subserosal edema/congestion and suppurative serosal exudate.

subQuestions.text: d. What are the expected effects and complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Perforated appendicitis may cause peritonitis or abscess; portal venous spread can rarely lead to pylephlebitis and hepatic abscess.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Perforation/generalized peritonitis, appendicular mass/abscess/subphrenic spread, portal pyaemia and fistulas.

questions.text:
30.Carcinoid tumors have a varied malignant potential. The most benign are located in
the:
questions.explanation: Small localized appendiceal neuroendocrine tumors are usually indolent and have low metastatic potential.

questions.text: 47- The commonest site of carcinoid tumor:
questions.explanation: Older classifications often list the appendix as the commonest site of carcinoid tumor, while adult distributions vary and small-intestinal primaries are also frequent.

questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents with sudden development of nausea, vomiting and Right lower abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals local tenderness, mild fever and leucocytosis. She lies down in bed for rest, but over the next 24 hours, the pain worsens and she develops fever, chills and clinical signs of acute abdomen.
questions.explanation: Appendiceal inflammation with neutrophils throughout the wall can spread through portal veins and cause pylephlebitis.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: Right-lower-quadrant pain, fever, neutrophilia, and pus-filled transmural inflammation indicate acute suppurative appendicitis.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Acute suppurative appendicitis, possibly complicated by perforation and peritonitis.

subQuestions.text: b. Describe both gross and microscopic picture of such lesion?
subQuestions.explanation: Acute appendicitis produces a swollen, congested appendix with purulent lumen and neutrophils through the wall; gangrenous cases show friable green-black necrosis.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Gross: swollen congested appendix with fibrinopurulent serosa, purulent lumen, focal wall abscesses and possible mucosal ulcers. Gangrenous disease gives soft friable wall and greenish-black necrosis. Microscopy: luminal necrotic material with neutrophils and pus cells, ulcerated mucosa/lymphoid hyperplasia, neutrophils throughout wall, congested oedematous subserosa with suppurative exudate.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the other possible complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Acute appendicitis may progress to perforation, abscess, diffuse peritonitis, portal pyaemia, or fistula formation.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Generalized suppurative peritonitis from perforation, appendicular inflammatory mass/abscess, subphrenic abscess, portal pyaemia and fistulas to abdominal wall or bladder.

subQuestions.text: d. If this condition occurs with the same sequence of events but on the left side, what is the possible diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: A left-sided episode with similar symptoms suggests sigmoid diverticulitis, the common left-colon inflammatory mimic of appendicitis.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: A possible left-sided counterpart is sigmoid diverticulitis, which may perforate and cause peritonitis.

questions.text: 93.Which neoplasm is most FREQUENTLY found in the appendix?
questions.explanation: Neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors are the most frequent primary neoplasm of the appendix, often discovered incidentally after appendectomy.

questions.text:
A 20 year old male presented with sudden lower right abdominal pain. Appendectomy was done. Microscopic
examination revealed mucosal ulceration and transmural inflammatory infiltrate rich in neutrophils and pus cells. This
condition can be complicated by:
questions.explanation: Transmural neutrophilic inflammation with mucosal ulceration defines acute appendicitis; portal pyaemia is a recognized complication.

questions.text:
(1278) Choose the correct answer:
Peritoneal extension of the following carcinoma may be associated with pseudomyxoma peritonei:
questions.explanation: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is mucinous ascites and peritoneal implants, most often from an appendiceal mucinous neoplasm.

questions.text:
TRUE & FALSE:
35.Pseudomyxoma peritonii occurs only in mucinous tumors

questions.text: A 32-year-old male presents with attacks of flushing of the face, watery diarrhea and dyspnea as if he is asthmatic. Further work up and investigations reveal appendicular mass.

questions.text: 16- Budd-Chiari syndrome is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Budd–Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow obstruction, usually from hepatic vein thrombosis, leading to congestion and fibrosis.
options: Prolonged obstruction of extrahepatic bile ducts
Chronic venous congestion of the liver
Thrombosis of hepatic veins followed by fibrosis & cirrhosis
Toxic alkaloids in some plants producing fibrosis of hepatic veins followed by cirrhosis

questions.text: 14) Cirrhosis is a reversible condition.
questions.explanation: Established cirrhosis is generally irreversible because fibrosis and regenerative nodules distort architecture, although early fibrosis can sometimes regress when injury is removed.

questions.text: 27- A 57-year old man presents with fatigue, weight loss for several months without any GIT symptoms. Careful history reveals past history of car accident with blood transfusion. On examination, the patient has jaundice, firm nodular liver and mild ascites. Lab studies reveal elevated liver enzymes, raised bilirubin and decreased albumin.
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis after transfusion may reflect chronic viral hepatitis; nodular liver, jaundice, low albumin, and ascites indicate decompensation.

subQuestions.text: a. What is your most likely diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: The transfusion history, jaundice, low albumin, and firm nodular liver indicate cirrhosis; the exposure suggests viral risk but does not identify the cause.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Liver cirrhosis. Transfusion suggests viral exposure without identifying a virus.

subQuestions.text: b. Enumerate four other possible etiologies of this disorder?
subQuestions.explanation: Cirrhosis can follow autoimmune injury, alcohol or steatohepatitis, chronic biliary disease, and metabolic disorders.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Autoimmune; alcohol/NASH; biliary; metabolic disease.

subQuestions.text: c. What are the possible mechanisms for ascites in such case?
subQuestions.explanation: Portal hypertension increases hydrostatic pressure while hypoalbuminemia and renal sodium retention expand ascites in cirrhosis.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Portal hypertension, hypoproteinemia and sodium/water retention.

subQuestions.text: d. What are the possible complications?
subQuestions.explanation: Cirrhosis can cause variceal bleeding, ascites, hypersplenism, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, liver failure, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Varices with fatal bleeding, splenomegaly/hypersplenism, ascites, hypoproteinemia, hormonal effects, clotting-factor deficiency, liver failure/encephalopathy and HCC in specified etiologies.

questions.text: The most dangerous complication of portal hypertension is:
questions.explanation: Esophageal variceal hemorrhage is the most dangerous portal-hypertension complication because bleeding can be sudden and fatal.

questions.text: compare 1ry. 2ry biliary cirrhosis
questions.explanation: Primary biliary cholangitis is autoimmune small-duct destruction with AMA and granulomas; secondary biliary cirrhosis follows prolonged extrahepatic obstruction.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary biliary cholangitis: chronic progressive autoimmune granulomatous destruction of small/medium intrahepatic ducts; typically middle-aged women, high AMA; ductopenia, lymphoplasmacytic duct destruction/noncaseating granulomas, cholestasis, portal fibrosis and eventual micronodular green cirrhotic liver. Secondary biliary cirrhosis: prolonged extrahepatic obstruction from stones, biliary/pancreatic malignancy, postoperative strictures or compressive lymphadenopathy causes cholestatic liver damage ending in cirrhosis.

questions.text: 5- A 25-year-old man noted abdominal cramps for four weeks. His stool was positive for mucus and blood. Ultrasound reveals a cystic lesion in the liver. Aspirate of the cyst reveals pasty greyish-brown material with streaks of blood.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the most likely diagnosis?

subQuestions.modelAnswer: Amoebic liver abscess.

subQuestions.text: b. List the possible complications of this cyst?
subQuestions.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess may rupture into the peritoneum or adjacent hollow organs, pleura, or pericardium, causing peritonitis, fistulae, or pleural/pericardial complications.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Rupture into peritoneum causing peritonitis; rupture into colon/stomach, pleura/pericardium; pleural effusion and systemic organ spread.

subQuestions.text: c. What is the cause of abdominal pain and its relation to the liver cyst?
subQuestions.explanation: Amoebic colitis causes bloody diarrhea; Entamoeba reaches the liver through portal blood and causes a necrotic abscess that can produce right upper abdominal pain.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Amoebic colonic infection causes intestinal symptoms; amoebae reach liver through portal blood and enzymes cause necrosis.

subQuestions.text: d. State another cystic lesion in the liver and mention 2 differences between the 2 cysts.

questions.explanation: This is hereditary hemochromatosis: excess iron absorption causes bronze skin, diabetes, and hemosiderin deposition in hepatocytes and Kupffer cells.

subQuestions.text: a. What is the possible diagnosis?

In-born error in iron metabolism in which absorption of iron exceeds
body needs

subQuestions.text: c. What is the pathological effect on the liver?
subQuestions.explanation: Iron overload causes oxidative hepatocyte injury and fibrogenesis, which can progress to cirrhosis and liver failure.

subQuestions.text: d. What is the cause of diabetes in this case?

questions.text: Give an account on Pancreatic carcinoma.
questions.explanation: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is a desmoplastic, infiltrative cancer, often in the head, where biliary obstruction causes early jaundice; pain, perineural invasion, metastases, and Trousseau thrombosis reflect its aggressive spread.
questions.modelAnswer: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma arises from ductal epithelium/PanIN; peak 60–80 years. Risks: diabetes, chronic pancreatitis, smoking, familial incidence. Head 60%, body 15%, tail 5%, diffuse 20%. Gritty gray hard infiltrative mass; moderately/poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with perineural/peripancreatic invasion. Pain is often first symptom; head tumors obstruct CBD/ampulla causing jaundice, body/tail tumors present late. Spread to retroperitoneum, nerves, nodes, lung/bone. questions.explanation: Sucralfate forms a protective barrier over ulcer bases in acidic conditions and promotes local prostaglandin, mucus, and bicarbonate effects; constipation is common.
questions.modelAnswer: In acid, sulfated sucrose binds ulcer-base proteins to coat against acid/bile/pepsin and increases PG/mucus/bicarbonate. Adverse effects nausea/vomiting/dry mouth, flatus/constipation and phosphate chelation causing osteomalacia/encephalopathy in renal disease.

questions.text: Compare between sucralfate and bithmus
questions.explanation: Sucralfate forms an acid-dependent barrier over ulcers and binds bile salts; bismuth also coats mucosa but adds anti-H. pylori activity and can darken stool or tongue.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sucralfate: an aluminium salt of sulfated sucrose. In an acid medium, its negatively charged sulfate groups bind positively charged proteins in the ulcer base to form a barrier against acid, bile and pepsin; it also inactivates bile and pepsin and increases prostaglandins, mucus and bicarbonate. It is used as a mucosal protective in peptic-ulcer treatment. Adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, dry mouth, flatulence and constipation; aluminium toxicity and phosphate chelation can cause osteomalacia and encephalopathy in renal disease. Give on an empty stomach, four doses daily: three between meals and one before sleep. Separate antacids or H2 blockers by at least one hour because acid is required for activity, and drugs it binds (for example tetracycline) by at least two hours.

Colloidal bismuth subcitrate: its main effect is anti-H. pylori activity. It also chelates proteins in the ulcer base, forming a protective coat against acid and pepsin, inactivates pepsin, and increases mucosal bicarbonate, mucus and prostaglandins. It is used in anti-H. pylori therapy, including ranitidine-bismuth citrate. Adverse effects are teeth and tongue discoloration, black stools that can be confused with bleeding, and encephalopathy/neurotoxicity, especially in renal disease. Do not give for more than two months or restart within one year.

questions.explanation: Clonidine activates alpha-2 receptors, reducing enteric acetylcholine release and gut motility; this can help selected refractory or withdrawal-associated diarrhea.

questions.text: What is the difference between loperamide & diphenoxylate
questions.explanation: Both are peripheral opioid antimotility drugs; loperamide has minimal CNS penetration, while diphenoxylate is paired with atropine to deter misuse and reduce spasm.
questions.modelAnswer: Both peripheral opioid-related antimotility agents. Loperamide least BBB penetration with lower abuse potential; diphenoxylate spasmogenic effect and is combined with atropine; overdose CNS/respiratory depression/ileus.

questions.text: 4-Diagnosis of H. pylori infections can be done in both noninvasive and invasive methods compare between them
questions.explanation: Biopsy enables rapid urease testing, histology, or culture; stool antigen and urea-breath testing detect active infection without endoscopy and can confirm cure.
questions.modelAnswer: Invasive: endoscopic gastric biopsy (definitive strategy) for rapid urease test in indicator urea broth, histopathology/microscopy and culture. Noninvasive: stool antigen detection and labelled-urea breath testing are useful both initially and for treatment follow-up; serology for IgG is of limited use. PCR can detect nucleic acid in gastric juice/biopsy or faeces. Urea breath testing detects labelled CO2 produced by bacterial urease after oral labelled urea.

questions.text: A patient was admitted to the hospital because of bleeding duodenal ulcer. Culture at 37°C grew oxidase positive, urease-positive curved bacteria. What is the most likely causative agent?

questions.text: Diagnosis of H. pylori infections can be done in both non invasive and invasive methods, compare between them
questions.explanation: Biopsy permits direct histology, rapid urease testing, or culture, while breath and stool antigen tests detect active infection without endoscopy; serology cannot confirm eradication.
questions.modelAnswer: Invasive: endoscopic gastric biopsy (definitive strategy) for rapid urease test in indicator urea broth, histopathology/microscopy and culture. Noninvasive: stool antigen detection and labelled-urea breath testing are useful both initially and for treatment follow-up; serology for IgG is of limited use. PCR can detect nucleic acid in gastric juice/biopsy or faeces. Urea breath testing detects labelled CO2 produced by bacterial urease after oral labelled urea.

questions.text: 5- Concerning isolation of H. pylori, describe the used media & mention the microscopic apperance and BRs of the organism

Microscopy shows pale-staining curved Gram-negative bacilli with S/gull-wing forms. They are oxidase and catalase positive, rapidly urease positive and do not utilize sugars.

Urease hydrolyses urea to ammonia and CO2, neutralizing local acid; ammonia plus inflammatory cytokine release contributes to mucosal injury. Adhesins bind epithelial membrane lipids/carbohydrates.
