questions.explanation: Microsporidia are transmitted by environmentally resistant spores, which inject their contents into host cells through a polar tube.

questions.text: Cryptosporidiosis is severe in AIDS patients.
questions.explanation: Without effective T-cell immunity, Cryptosporidium can produce prolonged, profuse watery diarrhea and life-threatening dehydration in AIDS.
questions.modelAnswer:
Because Cryptosporidium is an opportunistic parasite → severe & prolonged diarrhea in
immunocompromised patients → Cholera-like & life threatening

questions.text: Cryptosporidium is:
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium can be zoonotic, waterborne, opportunistic in immunocompromised hosts, and causes watery diarrhea, so all listed features apply.

questions.text: Habitat of Cryptosporidium is:
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium occupies an intracellular but extracytoplasmic niche at the intestinal brush border, bounded by host membrane.
options: brush border of small intestine intracellular extracytoplasmic
brush border of small intestine intracellular intracytoplasmic
brush border of small intestine extracellular extracytoplasmic
brush border of small intestine extracellular intracytoplasmic

questions.text: What is the infective stage of Cyclospora ?
questions.explanation: Cyclospora oocysts need external sporulation and become infective with two sporocysts, each containing two sporozoites.

questions.text: Which of the following parasites / is or are opportunistic
questions.explanation: Strongyloides, Cryptosporidium, and Cyclospora can cause severe or prolonged disease when cell-mediated immunity is impaired.

questions.text: Infective stage of Cystoisospora is:
questions.explanation: Cystoisospora oocysts become infective after sporulation into two sporocysts, each containing four sporozoites.

questions.text: What is the habitat of Cryptosporidium ?
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium occupies an apical parasitophorous vacuole at the brush border, sequestered within the cell membrane but outside cytoplasm.
options: Brush border of small intestine Intracellular extracytoplasmic
Brush border of small intestine intracellular intracytoplasmic
Brush border of small intestine extracellular extracytoplasmic
Brush border of small intestine extracellular intracytoplasmic

questions.text: Outbreaks of cryptosporidiosis may be linked to swimming pools.
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium oocysts are immediately infectious and chlorine tolerant, so a contaminated pool can transmit infection despite routine chlorination.
questions.modelAnswer: Because infected children with Cryptosporidium may pass mature infective oocyst in water of swimming pool with their stool infecting other people b. Also Cryptosporidium oocyst is resistant to chlorinated water of swimming pools.

questions.text: Cryptosporidium parvum oocyst is:
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium oocysts are not packaged in sporocysts; each contains four sporozoites.

questions.text: Which of the following protozoa affecting small intestine is opportunistic?
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium, Cystoisospora, and microsporidia can cause opportunistic small-intestinal disease, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

questions.text: Which of the following protozoa affecting small intestine has polar filament to inject spore contents into host cell?
questions.explanation: Microsporidia spores use a polar filament to pierce host cells and inject the infectious sporoplasm.

questions.text: the modified trichrome stain is used for diagnosis of
questions.explanation: Modified trichrome staining highlights microsporidial spores in clinical specimens, helping diagnose microsporidiosis.

questions.text: What is the infective & diagnostic stage of Cryptosporidium ?
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium oocysts are infectious when shed and contain four sporozoites without sporocysts, making the oocyst both diagnostic and infective.

questions.text: What is the diagnostic stage of Cyclospora ?
questions.explanation: Cyclospora is shed as an immature unsporulated oocyst; it becomes infective only after sporulation in the environment.

questions.text: All the following parasite infect human through eating fish except
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium is usually acquired from contaminated water or fecal exposure, whereas the other listed parasites can be fish-borne.

questions.text: the infective stage of Cyclospora is
questions.explanation: Cyclospora oocysts sporulate into two sporocysts, each with two sporozoites; the mature disporocystic, disporozoic oocyst is infective.

questions.text: There is autoinfection in Cryptosporidium not in Cystoisospora.
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium oocysts are already infective when passed, allowing external autoinfection; Cystoisospora oocysts mature outside the host first.
questions.modelAnswer: Because oocyst of Cryptosporidium pass mature & infective in stool while oocyst of Cystoisospora passes immature & needs about two weeks outside man to be mature & infective to other person.

questions.text: Give reason/interpret the following statements (1mark each): Cor-pulmonale is caused by Schistosoma mansoni bilharziasis.
questions.explanation: S. mansoni eggs may lodge in pulmonary vessels and provoke granulomas and fibrosis, raising pulmonary vascular resistance and causing right-heart strain.
questions.modelAnswer: Schistosoma eggs embolize to pulmonary vessels; granulomas and fibrosis thicken and occlude pulmonary arteries (endarteritis obliterans), causing pulmonary hypertension and consequent right-sided heart failure (cor pulmonale).

questions.text: Which of the following is untrue about concomitant immunity in schistosomiasis?
questions.explanation: Concomitant immunity limits new schistosomula while established adult worms evade elimination; the claim that it cannot attack new invaders is therefore false.
options: Immune complexes are formed in early egg laying stages
Delayed hypersensitivity reactions cause the main pathology

questions.text: Which of the following is a mechanism of egg penetration of blood vessels to lumen of viscus?
questions.explanation: Schistosome eggs use spines, secreted enzymes, and pressure to traverse venule walls and reach the intestinal or bladder lumen.
options: Tearing action of spine of eggs
Histolytic enzymes secreted from penetrating glands of miracidium

questions.text:
PAR15: In chronic complicated cases of schistosomiasis mansoni, the most likely cause of repeated negative stool
examination is:
questions.explanation: Colonic fibrosis can trap eggs and obstruct their passage through the bowel wall, reducing egg shedding into stool despite chronic intestinal infection.
options: Migration of adult worms out of intestine.
Non sexual maturity of adult worms.

questions.text: The infective stage of schistosomes is:
questions.explanation: Schistosome cercariae have a forked tail (furcocercous) and directly penetrate human skin from contaminated water.

questions.text: Schistosomiasis may be associated with anemia.
questions.explanation: Schistosome egg-related intestinal bleeding and variceal hemorrhage can cause chronic blood loss; portal hypertension and hypersplenism may add cytopenias.
questions.modelAnswer: Anaemia results from blood loss as eggs pass with stool and from oesophageal-variceal haemorrhage; liver failure adds a bleeding tendency. Hypersplenism can produce pancytopenia, including anaemia.

questions.text:
PAR15: In chronic complicated cases of schistosomiasis mansoni, the most likely cause of repeated negative stool
examination is:
questions.explanation: Fibrosis of the colon can prevent eggs from reaching the lumen, explaining repeatedly negative stool examinations in complicated intestinal schistosomiasis.
options: Non sexual maturity of adult worms.
Migration of adult worms out of intestine.

questions.text: Oxamniquine may used as alternative drug in treatment of:
questions.explanation: Oxamniquine is an alternative antischistosomal drug for Schistosoma mansoni; it is not used for the other listed parasites.

questions.text: Schistosoma adults can evade the host immune response because:
questions.explanation: Adult schistosomes evade immunity by acquiring host molecules, mimicking host antigens, renewing their tegument, and modulating immune effectors.
options: Parasite can acquire host antigen on its surface
Parasite can rapidly change its tegument
Parasite can inactivate or down-regulate immune effectors

questions.text: Schistosoma eggs can escape to perivascular tissue then to lumen of viscus.
questions.explanation: Schistosome eggs cross vessel and bowel walls through the combined effects of their spine, local pressure, tissue motion, and miracidial secretions.
questions.modelAnswer: Eggs pass through the vessel and organ wall aided by the tearing action of the egg spine, pressure of venules, and lytic secretions from the miracidium. They enter perivascular tissues and then the bowel lumen to pass with faeces.

questions.text: PAR14: About Schistosoma mansoni, all are true except:
questions.explanation: S. mansoni has separate male and female worms; it is not hermaphroditic, unlike many other trematodes.
options: The adult worm has oral and ventral suckers.
The adult worm lives in the inferior mesenteric vein.
The intermediate host is Biomphalaria alexandrina snail.

questions.text: S. mansoni may be associated with oesophageal varices & haematemesis.
questions.explanation: Egg granulomas and periportal fibrosis raise portal pressure in chronic S. mansoni infection, leading to esophageal varices and hematemesis.
questions.modelAnswer: Due to deposition of eggs in portal circulation in chronic stage with formation of granuloma around them → portal hypertension → oesophageal varices & haematemesis.

questions.text: Which of the following is / are character (s) of Schistosoma mansoni egg?
questions.explanation: S. mansoni eggs are diagnostic when found in stool and have a lateral spine; they are not the infective stage for humans.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of cercarial penetration to the skin ?
questions.explanation: Cercariae use tail movement, chemical/thermal cues, and lytic penetration-gland secretions to attach to and penetrate skin.
options: Lytic secretions by penetration glands of cercaria
Surface tension of water around cercariae

questions.text: Acute schistosomiasis is named open lesion.
questions.explanation: Acute intestinal schistosomiasis is called an open lesion because eggs penetrate the bowel wall and pass into stool.
questions.modelAnswer: Because in acute schistosomiasis, eggs can penetrate wall of intestine & can pass with stool.

questions.text: Schistosoma adult can evade the host immune response.
questions.explanation: Adult schistosomes evade immunity through host-like surface antigens and tegumental changes that reduce immune recognition and attack.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Parasite can acquire host antigen on its surface (antigenic mimicry).
- Parasite can produce host-like antigen.
- Parasite can rapidly change its tegument.
- Parasite can inactivate or down-regulate immune effectors.

questions.text: Habitat of Schistosoma japonicum is:
questions.explanation: Adult S. japonicum inhabit mesenteric venous plexuses draining the small intestine, especially the superior mesenteric system.

questions.text: Amphibian snail is:
questions.explanation: Oncomelania is an amphibious snail host of S. japonicum; it survives on land and in water, complicating control.

questions.text: Mechanism of egg penetration of blood vessels to lumen of viscus:
questions.explanation: Egg passage into the bowel lumen reflects several cooperating forces: spine-mediated tissue injury, miracidial lytic secretions, venous pressure, and organ movement.
options: Tearing action of spine of eggs
Histolytic enzymes secreted from penetrating glands of miracidium

questions.text: The intermediate host of Schistosoma japonicum is:
questions.explanation: Oncomelania snails are the intermediate host of S. japonicum; Biomphalaria and Bulinus transmit other schistosome species.

questions.text: The normal habitat for adult Schitosoma mansoni is:
questions.explanation: Adult S. mansoni pairs occupy inferior mesenteric venules draining the large intestine, with eggs passing through bowel wall into stool.
options: Pelvic and vesical plexus of veins.

questions.text: What is the habitat of Schistosoma mansoni?
questions.explanation: Adult S. mansoni worms inhabit the inferior mesenteric venous plexus draining the large intestine; eggs then pass through the bowel wall.

questions.text: Serology is useful in diagnosis of schistosomiasis.
questions.explanation: Serology can detect low-intensity or chronic schistosomiasis when egg output is sparse or lesions block eggs from reaching stool or urine.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Diagnosis of mild infection.
- Diagnosis of chronic infection (closes lesion) where eggs cannot pass in urine or stool.

questions.text: 16. A 40-year-old farmer presented to the hospital suffering from three attacks of vomiting blood. He gave a history of repeated attacks of diarrhea with mucous and blood in stool. By clinical examination, liver and spleen were enlarged. Stool examination revealed no parasitic ova or cyst. The most probable cause of liver enlargement in this case is:
questions.explanation: Repeated bloody diarrhea with variceal bleeding indicates chronic hepatosplenic schistosomiasis, where egg granulomas cause periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension.
options: Cyst filled with fluid that enlarges slowly

questions.text: Which of the following is true about intestinal schistosomiasis?
questions.explanation: S. mansoni eggs passed in stool are mature and bear a characteristic lateral spine, unlike operculated trematode eggs.

questions.text: Ectopic schistosomiasis ( brain & spinal cord lesions) occur mostly in S.japonicum
questions.explanation: S. japonicum lays many small, relatively rounded eggs that can embolize beyond the bowel and cause large CNS granulomas.
questions.modelAnswer: S. japonicum produces large numbers of relatively rounded eggs without prominent spines, facilitating embolization. Heavy egg deposition and large granulomas in circumscribed brain or spinal-cord areas cause tumour-like lesions, raised intracranial pressure and focal neurological signs.

questions.text: Schistosoma japonicum is difficult to be controlled.
questions.explanation: S. japonicum is difficult to control because many mammals act as reservoirs and its amphibious Oncomelania snail is hard to eliminate.
questions.modelAnswer:
a-has many reservoir hosts as dog, horse, sheep, pig & cattle transmitting infection to man.
b-its snail intermediate host Onchomelania is amphibious.

questions.text: Schistosomiasis may be associated with core-pulmonale.
questions.explanation: Egg-induced pulmonary granulomas and fibrosis can obstruct pulmonary vessels, causing pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure.
questions.modelAnswer: Due to granuloma around trapped eggs in lung which leads to fibrosis & occlusion of pulmonary vessels this leads to pulmonary hypertension & right side heart failure.

questions.text: What is the Intermediate host of Schistosoma japonicum ?
questions.explanation: S. japonicum develops in Oncomelania snails before cercariae emerge and infect people through skin contact with freshwater.

questions.text: The most difficult type of schistosomes to be controlled is:
questions.explanation: S. japonicum has multiple mammalian reservoirs and an amphibious snail host, allowing transmission to persist despite human-focused control.

questions.text:
PAR15: In chronic complicated cases of schistosomiasis mansoni, the most likely cause of repeated negative stool
examination is:
questions.explanation: Colonic fibrosis can block egg passage into feces, producing repeatedly negative stool tests in chronic complicated S. mansoni disease.
options: Migration of adult worms out of intestine.
Non sexual maturity of adult worms.

questions.text: Which of the following snails amphibian ?
questions.explanation: Oncomelania is amphibious and serves as the S. japonicum intermediate host; the other listed snails are aquatic species.

questions.text: Furcocercus cercaria can penetrate human or animal skin.
questions.explanation: Furcocercous cercariae penetrate skin using tail-driven motion, temperature cues, and lytic secretions from penetration glands.
questions.modelAnswer:
1- Thermal tropism.
2- Lytic secretions by penetration glands of cercaria.
3- Surface tension of water around cercariae.
4- Mechanical movement of tail.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about intestinal schistosomiasis?
questions.explanation: Intestinal schistosome eggs are mature when passed and have a spine; S. mansoni has a lateral rather than terminal spine.

questions.text: Mechanism of cercarial penetration to the skin:
questions.explanation: Cercariae attach using environmental cues and tail movement, then penetrate skin with proteolytic secretions from penetration glands.
options: Lytic secretions by penetration glands of cercaria
Surface tension of water around cercariae

questions.text: Serology can be useful in diagnosis of schistosomiasis.
questions.explanation: Serology can support diagnosis when egg detection is negative, especially in light or closed disease; antibodies may persist after cure, limiting active-infection interpretation.
questions.modelAnswer: Antigen detection can help diagnose mild or closed intestinal infection with negative stool examinations. Antibody tests have limitations: antibodies may persist after cure and cannot distinguish resolved from active infection in repeatedly infected/treated patients.

questions.text: S. mansoni may be associated with esophageal varices
questions.explanation: Egg-driven periportal fibrosis raises portal pressure, which can produce esophageal varices and risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
questions.modelAnswer: Due to deposition of eggs in portal circulation with fibrosis → portal hypertension

questions.text: Schistosoma japonicum is more dangerous than other type of schistosomes.
questions.explanation: S. japonicum produces many small rounded eggs with limited spine injury; wider embolization increases ectopic granulomas and neurologic complications.
questions.modelAnswer:
Because its eggs can spread all over the body (Ectopic Lesions) due to:
1- Eggs are small in size & has rounded contour → Egg embolism
2- Eggs are without spine.
3- Eggs are deposited by female in large number.

questions.text: The main pathogenesis of schistosomiasis is due to:
questions.explanation: Schistosome eggs trapped in tissues drive granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis; adult worms cause little direct damage compared with retained eggs.
options: Penetration of the wall of intestine by spinated eggs
Penetration of the skin by cercaria
Retained eggs in tissues surrounded by granulomas
Adults of schistosomes in blood vessels

questions.text: Schistosomiasis may be associated with anaemia.
questions.explanation: Intestinal blood loss, variceal bleeding, impaired hepatic function, and hypersplenism can each contribute to anemia in chronic schistosomiasis.
questions.modelAnswer:
1- Blood loss with stool, hematemesis & melena.
2- Complicated oesophageal varices.
3- Bleeding tendency due to liver cell failure.
4- Pancytopenia due to hypersplenism.

questions.text: What is the diagnostic stage of Schistosoma Japonicum ?
questions.explanation: S. japonicum eggs are small and have a subtle lateral knob or curved tubercle, unlike the prominent spines of other intestinal schistosomes.

questions.text: Concentration techniques are important in diagnosis of light infection with Shistosome
questions.explanation: Light schistosome infection sheds few eggs, so stool concentration increases recovery compared with a single direct wet mount.
questions.modelAnswer: Wet-mount stool examination is insensitive when few eggs are shed. Concentration techniques increase the likelihood of finding eggs in light infection.

questions.text:
Indirect immunological (Serological) methods are used for diagnosis of chronic
schistosomiasis.
questions.explanation: When fibrosis traps eggs in the bowel wall and stool shedding falls, serology can support diagnosis even when egg detection is difficult.
questions.modelAnswer:
As eggs cannot penetrate wall of intestine due to granuloma & fibrosis (closed lesion) →>
cannot pass with stool

questions.text: Tissue proliferation & fibrosis due to egg retention are responsible for the following complications?
questions.explanation: Egg granulomas and fibrosis can obstruct portal flow, cause variceal bleeding, and form fistulae; pulmonary egg disease can lead to cor pulmonale.

questions.text: Shistosomular migration is responsible for which of the following manifestations?
questions.explanation: Migrating schistosomula can pass through the lungs and provoke transient eosinophilic pneumonitis, termed verminous pneumonia.

questions.text: Furococercus cercaria emerges from the following snail:
questions.explanation: Biomphalaria alexandrina is the freshwater snail intermediate host for Schistosoma mansoni, releasing the infective cercarial stage.

questions.text: Schistosoma eggs can penetrate blood vessels to lumen of the intestine.
questions.explanation: Egg spines, miracidial lytic secretions, and venular pressure help eggs traverse bowel-vessel walls into the intestinal lumen for excretion.
questions.modelAnswer:
1- Tearing action of spine of eggs
2- Lytic secretion from miracidium inside eggs
3- Pressure within the venules

questions.text: Diagnostic stage of Schistosoma japonicum is:
questions.explanation: S. japonicum eggs have a small lateral knob or curved tubercle, unlike the prominent terminal or lateral spines of other species.

questions.text: Serological diagnosis is very important in chronic schistosomiasis.
questions.explanation: Chronic intestinal fibrosis may trap eggs and reduce their passage into stool, making antibody-based tests useful adjuncts to direct egg detection.
questions.modelAnswer: Because in chronic schistosomiasis, eggs cannot penetrate wall of intestine & are retained in tissues due to granuloma & cannot pass with stool.

questions.text: Discoid snail is:
questions.explanation: Biomphalaria alexandrina is a discoid snail and the intermediate host of S. mansoni in Egypt.

questions.text: Which larval stage is not found in life cycle of schistosomes ?
questions.explanation: Schistosomes develop through sporocysts in the snail but have no redia stage; cercariae leave the snail and penetrate human skin.

questions.text: Oviposition in tissue is responsible for which of the following manifestations?
questions.explanation: Egg deposition in intestinal tissues causes dysentery, while eggs reaching the portal system can provoke Katayama syndrome; swimmer’s itch is cercarial skin penetration.

questions.text: The major pathology in schistosomiasis is due to:
questions.explanation: Schistosome eggs trapped in tissues provoke granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis, causing most chronic organ pathology.

questions.text: What is the infective stage of schistosomes ?
questions.explanation: The human-infective stage is the fork-tailed furcocercous cercaria, which penetrates skin in contaminated freshwater.

questions.text: Immune response against Schistosome can lead to pathological consequences
questions.explanation: Schistosome eggs release antigens that provoke granulomas; subsequent fibrosis in bowel, liver, or lungs causes the major chronic complications.
questions.modelAnswer: Trapped eggs release soluble egg antigen, eliciting eosinophil, lymphocyte and macrophage infiltration and granulomas. Subsequent fibrosis causes colonic ulceration, polyps/strictures/fistulae, periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension, and pulmonary vascular fibrosis/occlusion with pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

questions.text: PAR14: About Schistosoma mansoni, all are true except:
questions.explanation: S. mansoni is dioecious; the male and female worms pair in mesenteric veins, so “hermaphrodite” is the false statement.
options: The adult worm has oral and ventral suckers.
The intermediate host is Biomphalaria alexandrina snail.
The adult worm lives in the inferior mesenteric vein.

questions.text: Immune response induced by adult Shistosomes prevents new infection
questions.explanation: Newly invading schistosomula lack the acquired host molecules that camouflage adult worms, so existing immunity may damage them.
questions.modelAnswer: It destroys newly formed cercaria(shistosomula) as they aren't coated with host molecules

questions.text: Katayama fever occurs more in S.japonicum
questions.explanation: S. japonicum typically produces a heavier egg burden, so greater egg-antigen release can make acute Katayama fever more prominent.
questions.modelAnswer: due to greater number of eggs

questions.text: PAR14: About Schistosoma mansoni, all are true except:
questions.explanation: Schistosomes have separate sexes; S. mansoni is not hermaphroditic despite sharing other listed traits.
options: The adult worm has oral and ventral suckers.
The intermediate host is Biomphalaria alexandrina snail.
The adult worm lives in the inferior mesenteric vein.

questions.text: Schistosoma adults can evade the host Immune response by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Schistosome adults can mask themselves with host antigens, change their tegument, and suppress immune effectors, allowing long-term survival.
options: Acquire host antigen on its surface

questions.text: Intestinal schistosomiasis is caused by:
questions.explanation: S. mansoni and S. japonicum primarily cause intestinal schistosomiasis; S. haematobium is associated with urinary disease.

questions.text: Which of the following is untrue about Shistosoma japonicum compared to S.mansoni ?
questions.explanation: S. japonicum is harder to control because many animal reservoirs sustain transmission; it also causes more ectopic disease and Katayama fever.
options: Less tearing action on blood vessels
More liable to cause neurological signs
More liable to cause Katayama fever

questions.text: 2nd phase( Acute) schistosomiasis is called open lesion.
questions.explanation: Eggs traverse intestinal mucosa and enter stool in acute intestinal schistosomiasis, creating an “open” lesion.
questions.modelAnswer: As eggs can penetrate wall of intestine &pass in stool.

questions.text: Swimming or bathing in canals should be avoided.
questions.explanation: Schistosome cercariae emerge from freshwater snails and penetrate intact skin during contact with contaminated water.
questions.modelAnswer:
To avoid infection with furcocercus cercaria of schistosomes which penetrate
human skin while swimming or bathing in contaminated water.

questions.text: Furcocercus cercaria are responsible for which of the following manifestations?
questions.explanation: Furcocercous cercariae penetrate skin and can cause cercarial dermatitis, commonly called swimmer’s itch.

questions.text: Praziquantel is the drug of choice in treatment of schistosomiasis.
questions.explanation: Praziquantel is active against major schistosome species; oxamniquine has narrower activity, mainly against S. mansoni.
questions.modelAnswer:
as it kills all types of schistosomes (S. haematobium, japonicum) ,
while oxamniquine kills only S. mansoni.

questions.text: Which of the following is a quantitative method used to determine severity of Shistosomiasis?
questions.explanation: Kato-Katz quantifies eggs per gram of stool, helping estimate intestinal schistosomiasis intensity and monitor infection burden.
options: Detection of specific Ags or Abs in serum

questions.text: Schistosoma mansoni egg:
questions.explanation: S. mansoni eggs pass in stool and have a prominent lateral spine; they are diagnostic, not the human infective stage.

questions.text: The adult schistosoma evade the human immunity by:
questions.explanation: Adult schistosomes evade immunity by acquiring host antigens, producing host-like antigens, renewing their tegument, and down-regulating immune effectors.
options: parasite can acquire the host antigen
parasite can produce host like antigen

questions.text: What is the habitat of Schistosoma japonicum ?
questions.explanation: Adult S. japonicum inhabit the superior mesenteric venous plexus draining the small intestine, where eggs can enter the gut wall.

questions.text: Which of the following is the main pathogenesis of schistosomiasis ?
questions.explanation: Eggs retained in tissues trigger granulomas and fibrosis; cercarial penetration and adult worms contribute less to chronic pathology.
options: Penetration of the wall of intestine by spinated eggs
Penetration of the skin by cercaria
Retained eggs in tissues surrounded by granulomas
Adults of schistosomes in blood vessels

questions.text: Which of the following methods can be used to diagnose closed lesions of Shistosomiasis?
questions.explanation: Rectal biopsy can reveal trapped eggs in closed disease, while serum antigen or antibody tests may aid diagnosis when stool is negative.
options: Detection of specific Ags or Abs in serum

questions.text: The larval stage which is not found in life cycle of schistosomes is:
questions.explanation: Schistosomes develop through miracidia, sporocysts, cercariae, and schistosomula; they have no redia stage in the snail.

questions.text: Enterobiasis can cause family or mass infection
questions.explanation: Enterobius eggs spread easily from fingers and contaminated surfaces after nocturnal itching; light eggs also disperse in household dust.
questions.modelAnswer: Eggs lodge beneath nails after scratching and contaminate fingers, bedding, clothing, toys, door handles and toilet seats. Light eggs disperse with air currents and become infective within hours, enabling family/institutional group infection.

questions.text: House cleaning & vacuuming around beds is important to prevent enterobiasis.
questions.explanation: Enterobius eggs spread on hands and household surfaces; cleaning and vacuuming reduce environmental eggs and reinfection.
questions.modelAnswer: To prevent enterobiasis because infected child with Enterobius can contaminate different objects as door knobs, toilet seats with eggs from his contaminated hands infecting other people using these objects.

questions.text: Oxyuriasis is caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Oxyuriasis is another name for enterobiasis, caused by the pinworm Enterobius vermicularis.

questions.text: Stool examination is not good method for diagnosis of
questions.explanation: Female pinworms lay eggs on perianal skin, so the tape test is more sensitive than routine stool examination for enterobiasis.

questions.text: Autoinfection occurs in:
questions.explanation: Enterobius eggs can be transferred from the perianal area to the mouth by scratching, causing autoinfection.

questions.text: Double bulbed oesphagus is a characteristic feature of:
questions.explanation: Enterobius has a double-bulbed esophagus, a characteristic feature of the adult pinworm.

questions.text: Patient with Enterobius infection may suffer from nocturnal enuresis.
questions.explanation: Nocturnal pinworm migration can cause intense itching and, rarely, genital or urinary tract irritation that contributes to enuresis.
questions.modelAnswer: In females, worms may reach urethra/bladder, causing urethritis and cystitis with nocturnal enuresis.

questions.text: Children infected with Enterobius must wear tight fitting trousers.
questions.explanation: Tight clothing reduces scratching and dispersal of perianal eggs, limiting hand contamination and reinfection in children.
questions.modelAnswer: Tight trousers limit perianal scratching/contamination and help control egg spread and hand-to-mouth autoinfection.

questions.text: Pruritis ani and nocturnal enuresis may be caused by infection with:
questions.explanation: Female pinworms migrate to perianal skin at night, causing itching and disturbing sleep; nocturnal scratching may contribute to enuresis.

questions.text: Treatment of Enterobius should be applied to all members of community.
questions.explanation: Treat close contacts together and repeat hygiene measures to interrupt household reinfection from persistent eggs and asymptomatic carriers.
questions.modelAnswer: To overcome autoinfection & reinfection.

questions.text: What is/are the infective stage(s) of Enterobius?
questions.explanation: Enterobius infection follows ingestion of embryonated eggs containing larvae; eggs become infective after developing outside the host.

questions.text: Loeffler's syndrome occurs with the following except:
questions.explanation: Enterobius remains in the gut and does not migrate through lungs, so it does not cause Loeffler syndrome.

questions.text: Female patient with Enterobius may suffer from vaginal mucoid discharge.
questions.explanation: Female pinworms may migrate into the vagina and cause vulvovaginitis with mucoid discharge, especially during nighttime egg laying.
questions.modelAnswer: Due to vaginitis caused by migrating female Enterobius through the vaginal opening of the infected patient to deposit eggs at night while the patient is asleep.

questions.text: Un-washable clothes should be exposed to sun light.
questions.explanation: Sunlight helps inactivate environmentally persistent Enterobius eggs on clothes that cannot be laundered.
questions.modelAnswer: To kill Enterobius eggs which are the infective stage of enterobiasis.

questions.text: Eggs of Enterobius vermicularis is sticky to perianal skin.
questions.explanation: Gravid female pinworms deposit sticky eggs on perianal skin at night, promoting adherence and easy transfer to fingers and bedding.
questions.modelAnswer: Because eggs are glued to perianal skin

questions.text: All perianal swabs for diagnosis of enterobiasis must be done early in the morning before defecation or bathing.
questions.explanation: Female pinworms lay eggs on perianal skin overnight; sampling before bathing or defecation preserves eggs for detection.
questions.modelAnswer: To avoid washing of Enterobius females & eggs deposited on perianal skin at night.

questions.text: Boil under wears, night wears & bed linen are important to prevent Enterobius.
questions.explanation: Boiling or hot laundering kills pinworm eggs on underwear, sleepwear, and bedding, reducing reinfection after treatment.
questions.modelAnswer: To kill Enterobius eggs which are the infective stage of enterobiasis.

questions.text:

questions.text:
A minimum of 4-6 consecutive negative perianal swabs is required to rule out infection

questions.text: Stool examination is not recommended in the diagnosis of:
questions.explanation: Enterobius deposits eggs on perianal skin rather than usually in stool, so the tape test is preferred for diagnosis.

questions.text: Nocturnal enuresis & vaginitis are caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Enterobius females migrate to perianal skin and sometimes the vulva, causing nocturnal itching, vaginitis, or urinary symptoms.

questions.text: Retrofection occurs in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Retrofection occurs when Enterobius eggs hatch near the anus and larvae migrate back through the anus into the intestine.

questions.text:
Disinfection of Toilet seats & door handles/ House cleaning & vacuuming around beds is
Important to prevent enterobiasis.

questions.text: A patient is suffering from pruritis ani & insomnia + nocturnal enuresis. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nocturnal perianal itching, insomnia, and occasional enuresis are classic consequences of Enterobius egg-laying and migration.

questions.text: PAR16: Scotch tape method can detect the eggs of:

questions.text: The eggs that may be found in the urine of female patient is that of:

questions.text: Adults of Enterobius are called pinworms.

questions.text: The most reliable method for diagnosis of enterobiasis is:

questions.text: Eggs which may be found in urine are eggs of which of the following?

questions.text: Ingestion of larvae is the mode of infection of all these nematode, except:

questions.text: It is very difficult to control Enterobius

questions.explanation: Swallowing eggs from contaminated hands causes external autoinfection; larvae hatching around the anus can re-enter the bowel by retrofection.
questions.modelAnswer: Two types of autoinfection: external by ingestion of eggs in contaminated hands of the same child & internal (retro infection) as eggs may hatch in perianal area liberating larvae that migrate back to anus of the same child then LI to become adults.

questions.text: Double bulbed oesphagus is a characteristic feature of:
questions.explanation: Enterobius vermicularis has the characteristic double-bulbed esophagus, a useful morphologic clue for identifying the adult worm.

questions.text: Oxyuriasis is caused by:
questions.explanation: Oxyuriasis is the older name for pinworm infection caused by Enterobius vermicularis.

questions.text: Stool analysis is not of great value in diagnosis of which of the following?

questions.text: Ingestion of Entamoeba trophozoites does not cause infection.
questions.explanation: Trophozoites are fragile and are destroyed by gastric acid; the mature quadrinucleate cyst survives passage and initiates infection.
questions.modelAnswer: Because they are digested in gastric juice as they have thin wall while mature quadrinucleated cyst has thick cyst wall so it represents the only infective stage.

questions.text: E. histolytica trophozoite, tissue form is the form that may be found in:
questions.explanation: Invasive E. histolytica trophozoites may be present in colonic ulcers and spread via portal blood to liver, lung, or brain.

questions.text: Infective stage of Entamoeba histolytica is:
questions.explanation: The mature four-nucleate E. histolytica cyst survives outside the host and is the infective stage swallowed in contaminated food or water.

questions.text: Autoinfection must be considered in control programs of parasitic infections.
questions.explanation: Autoinfection sustains infection within one host and enables recurrence, so prevention must interrupt internal development or self-reingestion routes.
questions.modelAnswer: Autoinfection sustains parasitic transmission within the same host, as exemplified by pinworm finger-to-mouth and retroinfection; treating individuals without interrupting these routes permits recurrent infection.

questions.text: Diagnostic stage of Entamoeba histolytica in acute amoebic dysentery:
questions.explanation: Trophozoites are shed in fresh dysenteric stool and represent the key diagnostic stage in acute invasive amoebiasis.

questions.text: What parasitic stage can be seen microscopically in the aspirate material obtained by sigmoidoscopy?
questions.explanation: Amoebic ulcers contain invasive E. histolytica trophozoites in aspirated material; cysts are primarily passed in formed stool.

questions.text: Amoebic dysentery is more dangerous than balantidial dysentery.
questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica can invade blood vessels and spread to organs such as the liver, while Balantidium usually remains in the intestine.
questions.modelAnswer: Entamoeba may spread through portal blood and cause liver, lung, brain and cutaneous disease. Balantidium is usually confined to intestine because its large trophozoites rarely enter vessels; this explains the greater extraintestinal danger.

questions.text: Which of the following is untrue about bacillary dysentery ?
questions.explanation: Shigella causes superficial inflammatory mucosal lesions; longitudinally oriented ulceration is not its defining feature, making that option the exception.
options: Ulcers along the longitudinal axis of the colon

questions.text: Entamoeba lesion in colon may be mistaken as tumor.
questions.explanation: Amoeboma is a mass-like granulomatous response around chronic amoebic ulceration and can resemble a colonic tumor.
questions.modelAnswer: Because Entamoeba may be complicated by formation of amoeboma which is amoebic granuloma around the ulcer that may be mistaken as tumor.

questions.text: The diagnostic stage mainly found in severe amoebic dysentery is:
questions.explanation: In acute amoebic dysentery, trophozoites that have ingested red blood cells indicate invasive E. histolytica infection.
options: Trophoziote with RBCs in its cytoplasm.

questions.text: Bloody dysentry is seen in Egyptian patients infected with:
questions.explanation: E. histolytica invades the colon and causes bloody dysentery; other listed organisms do not typically cause amoebic dysentery.

questions.text: Amoebic dysentery is characterized by:
questions.explanation: RBCs and Charcot–Leyden crystals in stool support amoebic dysentery; severe diffuse tenderness is not required, so the feature is the stool finding.
options: Generalized tenderness over the whole abdomen.
Stool examination reveals numerous RBCs & Charcot Leyden crystals.

questions.text: Acute cases of Entamoeba are of little significance in transmission of the disease.
questions.explanation: Acute diarrheal cases mainly pass fragile trophozoites, which die outside the host and are not the environmentally resistant infective stage.
questions.modelAnswer: Because they pass trophozoites in their diarrheic stool & trophozoites are not the infective stage

questions.text: Entamoeba histolytica cysts can be found in:
questions.explanation: Cysts form in the intestinal lumen and are passed in formed stool; tissue abscesses contain trophozoites rather than cysts.

questions.text: Sigmoidoscopy & proctoscopy are important in diagnosis of Entamoeba histolytica.
questions.explanation: Endoscopy can reveal characteristic ulcers and intact mucosa between lesions, and allows sampling of ulcer-edge material for trophozoites.
questions.modelAnswer: To take biopsy, aspirate materials, to see ulcers & intact mucosa in-between ulcers.

questions.text: What is the diagnostic stage of Entamoeba histolytica in acute dysentery ?
questions.explanation: Fresh dysenteric stool commonly contains motile E. histolytica trophozoites; cysts are more typical of formed stool or chronic carriage.

questions.text: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites move by which of the following organ(s)?
questions.explanation: E. histolytica uses pseudopodia for amoeboid movement and phagocytosis; it has neither cilia nor flagella.

questions.text: Diagnostic stage of Entamoeba histolytica in chronic amoebic dysentery is:
questions.explanation: In chronic intestinal amoebiasis, formed stool commonly contains cysts; trophozoites are more likely in fresh diarrheal stool.

questions.text:
Stool sample must be fresh & examined within 20 mints for diagnosis of amoebic
dysentery.
questions.explanation: Motile trophozoites rapidly lose motility after collection; prompt examination preserves the features used to identify invasive amoebiasis.
questions.modelAnswer: A fresh wet mount within 20 minutes demonstrates motile trophozoites containing RBCs, which are diagnostic of amoebic dysentery; delay compromises this motility-based observation.

questions.text: Entamoeba histolytica moves by
questions.explanation: Amoeboid pseudopodia extend and retract to propel E. histolytica across intestinal tissue.

questions.text:
Carriers especially food handlers represent an important source of infection of Entamoeba
histolytica.
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic carriers shed infective cysts without illness, allowing food contamination and transmission more readily than acute trophozoite-rich dysentery.
questions.modelAnswer: Asymptomatic carriers pass mature infective cysts without ulcerative disease, and food handlers can contaminate food; they are active transmission sources requiring detection and treatment.

questions.text: What is the diagnostic stage of Entamoeba histolytica in chronic dysentery ?
questions.explanation: In chronic or formed stool, resistant E. histolytica cysts are more likely to be found than fragile trophozoites.

questions.text: Entamoeba histolytica cause ulcers in the mucosa of large intestine.
questions.explanation: Trophozoites adhere to and lyse colonic cells, then invade the mucosa to form characteristic undermined flask-shaped ulcers.
questions.modelAnswer: Trophozoites adhere to target intestinal cells, lyse them through ionophore/proteolytic action and destroy tissue, producing characteristic flask-shaped ulcers.

questions.text: Entamoeba cyst passers must be excluded from the working staff in restaurants.
questions.explanation: Restaurant workers who pass infective Entamoeba cysts can contaminate food with unwashed hands and spread infection to many people.
questions.modelAnswer: Because working staff in restaurants may have Entamoeba & pass cyst with their stool & can contaminate their hands by autoinfection & infect other people.

questions.text: Ulcers of Entamoeba infection occur usually in ileocaecal & sigmoidorectal regions.
questions.explanation: Ulcers are common in the cecum and rectosigmoid regions, where slower transit can prolong mucosal exposure to invasive amoebae.
questions.modelAnswer: Due to low colonic flow in these areas.

questions.text: Trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica are found in the floor of ulcers.
questions.explanation: Trophozoites concentrate at the ulcer floor where viable host cells remain; necrotic tissue above is less suitable for feeding.
questions.modelAnswer: To be at the junction between dead & healthy tissue to feed on living cells.

questions.text: What is the habitat of Entamoeba histolytica ?
questions.explanation: E. histolytica trophozoites colonize the large intestine and may invade its mucosa, producing ulcers or disseminating to the liver.

questions.text: Mode of infection of E. histolytica is ingestion of infective stage through:
questions.explanation: Entamoeba cysts are acquired through contaminated food or water, and hand-to-mouth autoinfection can also occur; the listed routes are all possible.

questions.text: Diagnostic stage of Entamoeba histolytica in acute amoebic dysentery:
questions.explanation: Fresh dysenteric stool most often contains invasive E. histolytica trophozoites; cysts predominate in formed stool.

questions.text: Give reason/interpret the following statements (1mark each): Both proctoscopy and sigmoidoscopy are used for diagnosis of parasitic diseases.
questions.explanation: Proctoscopy and sigmoidoscopy permit direct visualization and sampling of rectal or colonic lesions, including parasite eggs or trophozoites.
questions.modelAnswer: Proctoscopy permits a rectal snip to find Schistosoma eggs in closed lesions with repeatedly negative stool, and can show Trichuris adults attached to inflamed mucosa in heavy infection. Proctoscopy/sigmoidoscopy visualize amoebic lesions and permit aspiration or biopsy, while Balantidium trophozoites/cysts may be identified in ulcer scrapings taken through sigmoidoscopy.

questions.text: Entamoeba infection may be associated with thickening of the colon
questions.explanation: Chronic amoebiasis can form an amoeboma, an inflammatory mass with fibrosis that thickens the colonic wall and may mimic cancer.
questions.modelAnswer: Chronic amoebic lesions can produce a chronic inflammatory mass with fibrosis in the colonic wall (amoeboma), causing localized thickening. Healing by fibrosis can also produce an annular stricture. This is a book-supported explanation for possible thickening, rather than a claim that every case has an amoeboma.

questions.text: Diagnostic stage of Entamoeba histolytica in acute dysentery is:
questions.explanation: Acute amoebic dysentery is diagnosed by finding trophozoites in fresh bloody stool, rather than mature cysts.

questions.text:
Acute cases of Entamoeba Infection are of little significance in transmission of the
disease.
questions.explanation: Acute dysenteric trophozoites are fragile and usually destroyed by stomach acid; asymptomatic carriers shed hardy infective cysts.
questions.modelAnswer: The major transmission stage is the mature cyst passed by carriers; trophozoites in acute dysenteric stool are not the usual infective stage and are destroyed by gastric juice.

questions.text: As regards diagnosis of intestinal amoebiasis:
questions.explanation: Stool is the main specimen; fresh examination preserves trophozoite motility, and Charcot–Leyden crystals may accompany eosinophilic parasitic inflammation.
options: Charcot Leyden crystals in stool is present.
To visualize the trophozoites stool sample should be fresh.
Stool is the specimen of choice.

questions.text: The diagnostic stage in stools in chronic intestinal amoebiasis is:
questions.explanation: Chronic luminal infection sheds cysts into formed stool; tissue trophozoites are more typical of acute invasive disease.

questions.text: What is/are the pathogenic stage(s) of Entamoeba histolytica ?
questions.explanation: E. histolytica trophozoites invade tissue and cause ulcers; cysts are the transmissible environmental stage.

questions.text: Sigmoidoscopy & proctoscopy are Important in diagnosis of Entamoeba infection.
questions.explanation: Endoscopy can show characteristic colonic ulcers and obtain material from their edges or base for microscopy and confirmation.
questions.modelAnswer: These endoscopic methods visualize lesions and allow aspirate or biopsy to confirm infection; sample ulcer floor at the diseased/healthy junction for trophozoites.

questions.text: Infective stage(s) of Entamoeba histolytica is/are:
questions.explanation: The mature quadrinucleate cyst survives gastric passage and is the infective stage transmitted by contaminated food or water.

questions.text:
Entamoeba histolytica carriers rather than amoebic dysentery patients constitute a public
health problem.
questions.explanation: Carriers shed mature infective cysts in formed stool, while trophozoites in dysentery stool are fragile and less important for transmission.
questions.modelAnswer: Carriers discharge mature infective cysts while dysenteric trophozoites are destroyed by gastric juice, making carriers a major transmission hazard.

questions.text: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites move by the following organ(s):
questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites move by extending pseudopodia, which also help them engulf host cells.

questions.text: What is/are the infective stage(s) of Entamoeba histolytica ?
questions.explanation: The mature quadrinucleate cyst is the infective form; ingested cysts excyst in the intestine and release trophozoites.

questions.text: Habitat of Entamoeba histolytica is:
questions.explanation: E. histolytica normally inhabits the large intestine, where trophozoites may remain luminal or invade the mucosa.

questions.text: Diagnostic stage of Entamoeba histolytica in chronic dysentery is:
questions.explanation: In chronic amoebiasis, formed stool more often contains resistant cysts than fragile motile trophozoites.

questions.text: The pathogenic stage in E. histolytica is:
questions.explanation: Tissue trophozoites invade and destroy host cells, causing colitis and extraintestinal abscesses; cysts are transmissible but not tissue-invasive.

questions.text: Entamoeba carriers rather than amoebic dysentery patients constitute a public health problem.
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic carriers continue to pass hardy infective cysts, whereas acute patients mainly shed fragile trophozoites that do not survive gastric passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Because Entamoeba carriers don't have any symptoms & pass infective cysts in their stool & infect other people while patients with amoebic dysentery suffer from diarrhea & dysentery & pass trophozoites in their stool & trophozoites are not infective so, don't constitute a public health problem.

questions.text: Which of the following stages are commensals form of E.histolytica that feeds on starch & mucus secretions?
questions.explanation: Lumen trophozoites feed on starch and mucus without invading tissue; tissue forms are associated with invasive disease.

questions.text: All about bacillary dysentery is true except:
questions.explanation: Bacillary dysentery is characterized by frequent small stools, tenesmus, and superficial mucosal inflammation; longitudinal-axis ulcers are not typical.
options: Ulcers along the longitudinal axis of the colon

questions.text: Examination of stool using concentration techniques for diagnosis of amoebiasis, all are true except:
questions.explanation: Stool concentration helps recover cysts in chronic intestinal amoebiasis but cannot diagnose an extraintestinal liver abscess.
options: Useful in diagnosis of Liver abscess.
Increase the chance of finding cysts.
Zinc sulphate one of this concentration methods.

questions.text: What is the infective stage?
questions.explanation: The mature quadrinucleate E. histolytica cyst is the environmentally resistant infective stage swallowed by a new host.

questions.text: Diagnostic stage(s) of Entamoeba histolytica is/are:
questions.explanation: Cysts are expected in formed stool, whereas fresh diarrheic stool may contain trophozoites; this explains the combined a-and-d answer.

questions.text: There may be thickening of the colon in case of Entamoeba infection.
questions.explanation: Chronic amoebic inflammation can cause tissue repair, granulation, and fibrosis, thickening the colonic wall and sometimes forming an amoeboma.
questions.modelAnswer: Due to continuous tissue regeneration, proliferation & fibrosis.

questions.text:
Treatment of asymptomatic cases of amoebiasis is very important/ Entamoeba cyst
passers must be excluded from the working staff in restaurants.
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic cyst passers shed infective cysts and can transmit amoebiasis, so treatment and food-handling exclusion help prevent spread.
questions.modelAnswer: Asymptomatic cyst passers remain active sources of infection; finding and treating carriers is a community measure to interrupt spread.

questions.text: What is/are the diagnostic stage(s) of Entamoeba histolytica?
questions.explanation: E. histolytica cysts occur in formed stool and trophozoites in diarrheic stool, so both specimen patterns are diagnostic.

questions.text: Most cases of Entamoeba histolytica complain of:
questions.explanation: Most E. histolytica infections are asymptomatic; dysentery, pain, tenesmus, and frequent stools occur only in symptomatic invasive disease.

questions.text: Periodic health examination for food handlers must be done.
questions.explanation: Food handlers may shed mature infective cysts while asymptomatic; screening and hygiene reduce fecal–oral transmission.
questions.modelAnswer: Because they are asymptomatic & pass mature infective quadrinucleated cyst in their stool & transmit infection to other people by their contaminated hands.

questions.text: Ingestion of trophozoites or precysts of Entamoeba does not cause Infection.
questions.explanation: Trophozoites and precysts are destroyed by gastric acid; the resistant mature quadrinucleate cyst must be swallowed to establish infection.
questions.modelAnswer: Trophozoites and precysts are destroyed by gastric juice; infection requires the resistant mature quadrinucleate cyst.

questions.text: Pathogenic stage(s) of Entamoeba histolytica is/are:
questions.explanation: Trophozoites invade tissue and cause amoebic ulcers; cysts are chiefly the infectious stage transmitted between hosts.

questions.text: Charcot-Leyden crystals may appear in stool samples of:
questions.explanation: Amoebic dysentery can produce Charcot–Leyden crystals from eosinophil breakdown during parasitic inflammation.

questions.text: Most cases infected with E. histolytica may be
questions.explanation: Most E. histolytica infections remain asymptomatic because luminal colonization does not necessarily progress to invasive mucosal disease.

questions.text: The intestinal protozoa with extraintestinal hematological spread is:
questions.explanation: E. histolytica can invade through colonic mucosa into portal blood and spread to liver or other organs, unlike noninvasive intestinal protozoa.

questions.text: Entamoeba histolytica tissue trophozoite can be found in the following organs except:
questions.explanation: Tissue trophozoites invade the colonic wall and may spread to organs, but the small-intestinal lumen is not a tissue site.

questions.text: Serological tests can’t be used to follow up treatment of amoebic abscess
questions.explanation: Antibodies can remain detectable long after an amoebic liver abscess resolves, so serology cannot reliably monitor treatment response or cure.
questions.modelAnswer: Specific antibodies are sensitive/specific for diagnosis but persist long after cure, so serology cannot assess cure.

questions.text: Entamoeba histolytica tissue trophozoite can not be found in which of the following organs ?
questions.explanation: E. histolytica tissue trophozoites invade the large bowel and may spread hematogenously, but the small-intestinal lumen is not their tissue site.

questions.text: Elevated right dome of diaphragm occurs with which of the following?
questions.explanation: A right-lobe amoebic liver abscess can elevate the right hemidiaphragm because of its location beneath it.

questions.text: All about amoebic liver abscess is true except:
questions.explanation: Amoebic abscesses contain necrotic “anchovy-sauce” material; trophozoites are usually found at the viable advancing margin, not the necrotic center.
options: in right lobe of the liver
tissue trophozoite is present in center of abscess

questions.text: Extraintestinal amoebiasis occurs mostly in:
questions.explanation: Portal venous spread from the colon makes liver the most common site of extraintestinal amoebiasis and amoebic abscess.

questions.text: CBC is important in diagnosis of amoebic liver abscess.
questions.explanation: Neutrophilic leukocytosis on CBC supports a pyogenic-appearing inflammatory process such as amoebic liver abscess, though it is not species-specific.
questions.modelAnswer: CBC demonstrates polymorphonuclear leucocytosis supporting amoebic liver abscess.

questions.text: What is the diagnostic stage in biopsy from amoebic liver abscess ?
questions.explanation: Tissue biopsy near the abscess margin may reveal invasive E. histolytica trophozoites; cysts remain in the intestinal lumen.

questions.text: Diffuse amoebic hepatitis is diagnosed by which of the following methods?
questions.explanation: Diffuse amoebic hepatitis may not form a focal abscess; serology supports invasive amoebiasis when stool tests are negative.

questions.text: Entamoeba histolytica may invade skin.
questions.explanation: E. histolytica can extend from a liver abscess to adjacent skin or perianal tissue, producing destructive cutaneous ulcers.
questions.modelAnswer: Cutaneous amoebiasis can form ulcers on the abdominal wall after liver-abscess aspiration or in perianal skin.

questions.text: Diagnostic stage in biopsy from amoebic liver abscess:
questions.explanation: Trophozoites at the viable lesion edge are the tissue stage of invasive amoebiasis and may be identified in biopsy material.

questions.text: All about amoebic liver abscess is true except:
questions.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess contains necrotic “anchovy-sauce” material; viable trophozoites, when found, are usually at the advancing abscess margin.
options: Occurs mainly in right lobe of the liver
Tissue trophozoite is present in center of abscess

questions.text: Diffuse amoebic hepatitis is diagnosed by:
questions.explanation: Serology is useful for diffuse amoebic hepatitis because antibodies reflect invasive extraintestinal infection even when stool studies are negative.

questions.text: Elevation of right dome of diapharm in x rays occurs in
questions.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess enlarges the right hepatic dome and can elevate the right hemidiaphragm on chest imaging.

questions.text: Stool examination is not suitable for diagnosis of amoebic liver abscess.
questions.explanation: Liver abscess is extraintestinal and stool may be negative; serum antibodies and imaging are more useful than stool microscopy for diagnosis.
questions.modelAnswer: Because stool examination is positive in only about 30% of cases of amoebic liver abscess.

questions.text: Entamoeba trophozoites are present at the edge of the amoebic liver abscess.
questions.explanation: Trophozoites concentrate at the abscess margin where viable tissue and necrotic material meet, allowing them to feed on living cells.
questions.modelAnswer: To be at the junction between dead & healthy tissue to feed on living cells.

questions.text: Pain of amoebic liver abscess increase with deep inspiration & cough.
questions.explanation: Deep inspiration moves the diaphragm downward and stretches inflamed tissues over the liver abscess, worsening pleuritic right-upper-quadrant pain.
questions.modelAnswer: Because with deep inspiration there is distention of the lung by air pushing diaphragm downward pressing the amoebic liver abscess causing more pain.

questions.text: PAR18: Extraintestinal amoebiasis occurs mostly in:
questions.explanation: Amoebic trophozoites reach the liver through portal blood, so the liver is the commonest extraintestinal site.

questions.text: X-Ray is important in diagnosis of amoebic liver abscess.
questions.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess may elevate the right diaphragmatic dome or create a dense hepatic shadow on imaging.
questions.modelAnswer: Radiography may show a dense hepatic shadow and abnormal elevation of the right diaphragmatic dome, supporting a right-lobe abscess.

questions.text: Extra-intestinal complications mainly occurs in
questions.explanation: The liver is the most common site of extraintestinal amoebiasis because trophozoites reach it through portal venous drainage from colon.

questions.text: PAR17: The intestinal protozoa with extra-intestinal hematological spread is:
questions.explanation: E. histolytica invades the colon and can enter portal circulation, spreading to the liver and occasionally other organs.

questions.text: Diffuse amoebic hepatitis is best diagnosed by:
questions.explanation: Serologic tests detect antibodies associated with invasive amoebic hepatitis and are useful when diffuse liver involvement lacks a discrete abscess.
options: Stool examination for Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite.

questions.text: What is the most common site of extraintestinal amoebiasis ?
questions.explanation: Portal spread carries E. histolytica from the colon to the liver, the most frequent extraintestinal site.

questions.text: During amoebic abscess aspiration, sample is taken from the border of the abscess.
questions.explanation: Viable E. histolytica trophozoites feed at the interface of living and necrotic tissue, so aspiration samples the abscess edge.
questions.modelAnswer: To detect tissue trophozoites of Entamoeba which are present at the border of the amoebic liver abscess to be at the junction between dead & healthy tissue to feed on living cells.

questions.text: The pathogenic protozoon with extra-intestinal spread through blood is:
questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica can invade intestinal tissue and spread through portal blood, especially to the liver.

questions.text: What is the intestinal protozoa with extraintestinal hematological spread ?
questions.explanation: E. histolytica invades intestinal tissue and can spread through portal blood to liver and other organs.

questions.text: Which of the following is untrue about amoebic liver abscess ?
questions.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess usually contains necrotic debris; trophozoites are typically located at the periphery, not the center.
options: In right lobe of the liver
Tissue trophozoite is present in center of abscess

questions.text: 7. A male patient presented to the outpatient clinic with acute upper abdominal pain. The pain increases with deep breathing and coughing. On examination he had earthy look, high fever, tinge of jaundice and enlarged tender liver. The reliable diagnostic method is:
questions.explanation: Serologic antibody testing supports amoebic liver abscess when pain, fever, and liver findings suggest invasive extraintestinal disease.
options: Direct examination of fresh faecal smear

questions.text: occupational protozoa is
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is associated with pig exposure, so infection is occupationally linked to pig farming, slaughter, and animal handling.

questions.text: Balantidium coli moves by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is the only ciliated protozoan parasite of humans; coordinated cilia propel it through the intestinal contents.

questions.text: Balantidium coli moves by:
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is the large ciliated protozoan; cilia provide its motility.

questions.text: The infective stage of Balantidium coli:
questions.explanation: The mature binucleate cyst survives outside the host and is the infective form swallowed in contaminated food or water.

questions.text: Balantidium coli reproduce sexually by:
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli reproduces sexually by conjugation, exchanging genetic material between paired trophozoites.

questions.text: Balantidium coli reproduce asexually by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli reproduces asexually by transverse binary fission across the cell body.

questions.text: Balantidium coli reproduce sexually by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli exchanges genetic material during conjugation, a sexual process distinct from its usual binary fission.

questions.text: The largest protozoan parasite that infect man is:
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is the largest protozoan parasite of humans, a ciliated organism that may cause colitis.

questions.text: Special care in people work in pig farm is important to control
questions.explanation: Pig-farm workers have occupational exposure to Balantidium coli because pigs shed infective cysts in feces.

questions.text: All about Balantidium coli are true except:
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is zoonotic, with pigs as major reservoirs; it is not strictly anthroponotic, while cyst and trophozoite stages can be diagnostic.

questions.text: What is/are the diagnostic stage(s) of Balantidium ?
questions.explanation: Both trophozoites and cysts can be found in stool, so either stage may support diagnosis of balantidiasis.

questions.text: Balantidiasis coli is a zoonotic & occupational disease
questions.explanation: Pigs are reservoirs for Balantidium; close contact with pig feces increases occupational exposure and zoonotic transmission.
questions.modelAnswer: Pigs are reservoir hosts; people in close contact in farms/slaughterhouses are more often infected, so balantidiasis is zoonotic and occupational.

questions.text: All the following are complications of Balantidium except:
questions.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess is caused by E. histolytica, not Balantidium, which usually causes colitis and may perforate bowel.

questions.text: Avoid close contact with pigs & their stool is important in prevention of:
questions.explanation: Pigs are an important reservoir for Balantidium coli; ingestion of cysts from contaminated hands or food transmits infection.

questions.text: Occupational protozoa is:
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is associated with pig exposure and farm or slaughterhouse work, making it an occupational protozoan.

questions.text: There must be special care for people working in pig farms or slaughter houses.
questions.explanation: Pig handlers encounter feces contaminated with Balantidium cysts, increasing occupational exposure to this zoonotic intestinal protozoan.
questions.modelAnswer: Because these people working in close contact with pigs & their stool & may be infected with Balantidium coli infection.

questions.text: What is the infective stage of Balantidium ?
questions.explanation: The binucleated Balantidium cyst survives outside the host and is swallowed to initiate intestinal infection.

questions.text: The Protozoa which invade the mucosa of the large intestine is:
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli invades the large-intestinal mucosa and can cause ulcers and dysentery.

questions.text: What is/are the pathogenic stage(s) of Balantidium ?
questions.explanation: The trophozoite invades intestinal mucosa and causes balantidial colitis; the cyst mainly enables transmission.

questions.text: Diagnostic stage(s) of Balantidium is/are:
questions.explanation: Balantidium cysts and trophozoites may be passed in stool and both can be diagnostic.

questions.text: Extra-intestinal lesion is rare in balantidiasis coli.
questions.explanation: Balantidium trophozoites are large and rarely enter blood vessels, so extraintestinal spread is uncommon.
questions.modelAnswer: Due to large size of trophozoites of Balantidium coli that cannot pass easily into blood vessels.

questions.text: Occupational protozoa is:
questions.explanation: Pig-associated Balantidium infection is occupationally important among people who handle pigs or their waste.

questions.text: Balantidium coli multiplies sexual by
questions.explanation: Balantidium reproduces sexually by conjugation; simple transverse binary fission is its asexual multiplication.

questions.text: We must avoid close contact with pigs & their stool
questions.explanation: Pig feces can contaminate food or water with Balantidium cysts; avoiding direct exposure reduces zoonotic infection risk.
questions.modelAnswer: Pigs are reservoir hosts and faecal contamination carries infective cysts into food/water; avoid close pig/faecal contact to prevent zoonotic infection.

questions.text: All about Balantidium coli are true except:
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli has animal reservoirs, especially pigs, so calling it anthroponotic is the false statement.

questions.text: The following are common complications of balantidiasis, except:
questions.explanation: Balantidiasis can cause ulceration, hemorrhage, perforation, and peritonitis; liver abscess is characteristic of amoebiasis instead.

questions.text: The infective stage of Balantidium is:
questions.explanation: The binucleated Balantidium cyst survives outside the host and is the infective stage swallowed in contaminated material.

questions.text: 43. The TRUE statement regarding Balantidium coli infection is that:
questions.explanation: Balantidium is transmitted from pigs and other animals and is associated with occupational exposure; it infects the large intestine.
options: Typical stage in feces is tetrasporozoic oocyst
It is a zoonotic occupational disease

questions.explanation: A ciliated organism in stool with colonic ulceration points to Balantidium coli, the only ciliated protozoan parasite of humans.

questions.explanation: Balantidium trophozoites multiply asexually by binary fission; conjugation is a separate sexual exchange process.

questions.explanation: Conjugation is a sexual exchange process characteristic of Balantidium coli among the listed intestinal protozoa.

questions.text: Avoid close cintact with pigs is important to prevent
questions.explanation: Pigs carry Balantidium cysts and are the main reservoir, so avoiding contaminated pig contact prevents balantidiasis.

questions.text: Extra-intestinal lesions are rare in balantidiasis coli.
questions.explanation: Balantidium trophozoites are large and usually remain in the intestinal lumen or mucosa, making hematogenous spread and extraintestinal disease uncommon.
questions.modelAnswer: Large trophozoites cannot easily pass into blood vessels, so extraintestinal lesions are rare.

questions.text: the largest protozoa is
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is the largest protozoan parasite infecting humans, with a large ciliated trophozoite.

questions.text: Special care for people working in pig farms or slaughter houses is important in prevention of:
questions.explanation: Pig-associated Balantidium transmission makes hygiene and protective care important for pig-farm and slaughterhouse workers.

questions.text: Which of the following is an occupational protozoa ?
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is zoonotic and linked to pig exposure, distinguishing it from the other listed intestinal protozoa.

questions.text: The largest protozoa is:
questions.explanation: The ciliated Balantidium coli is a conspicuously large intestinal protozoan and can be identified by its size and cilia.

questions.text: What is the drug of choice in treatment of Balantidium coli ?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is used to treat Balantidium coli infection by targeting the anaerobic protozoan.

questions.text: Avoiding close contact with pigs & their stool is important in prevention of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Pigs shed Balantidium cysts in feces; avoiding contaminated pig waste reduces exposure to this zoonotic parasite.

questions.text: Which of the following isn't a complication of Balantidium ?
questions.explanation: Balantidiasis can cause colitis, bleeding, secondary infection, or perforation; amoebic liver abscess belongs to E. histolytica.

questions.text: The largest protozoa is:
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is the largest protozoan parasite of humans, recognizable by its cilia and large trophozoite.

questions.text: Pathogenic stage(s) of Balantidium is/are:
questions.explanation: Balantidium trophozoites invade and damage the colonic mucosa; cysts are mainly the resistant, infective transmission stage.

questions.text: What is the largest protozoa?
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is the largest protozoan that infects humans and may invade the colonic mucosa.

questions.text: A 50-year-old patient presents with a deviated tongue on protrusion after a recent surgery. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles; injury causes deviation toward the weak side on protrusion.

questions.text: Which cranial nerve carries special sensory (taste) fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
questions.explanation: Taste from the anterior two-thirds travels with the chorda tympani branch of CN VII; the lingual nerve carries general sensation there.
options: Facial nerve (CN VII) via chorda tympani
Trigeminal nerve (CN V) via lingual nerve

questions.text: Which group of lymph nodes receives the lymphatic drainage from the tip of the tongue ?
questions.explanation: The tongue tip drains bilaterally to submental nodes, which also receive lymph from the central lower lip and floor of mouth.

questions.text: Special visceral afferent nerve fibers transmitting taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travel via which nerve ?
questions.explanation: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels with chorda tympani, a facial-nerve branch that joins the lingual nerve.

questions.text: Injury to which cranial nerve can result in loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve carries taste from the anterior tongue through chorda tympani; the lingual nerve carries touch and pain.

questions.text: Which nerve carries general sensory sensation from the tip of the tongue?
questions.explanation: General sensation from the anterior two-thirds, including the tip of the tongue, travels in the lingual nerve (V3).

questions.text: Which of the following nerves carries taste sensation from anterior 2/3 of tounge
questions.explanation: Chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; general sensation travels separately via the lingual nerve.

questions.text: Loss of taste And general sensation from posterior 1/3 of tongue indicates which of the following ?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies both taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue.

questions.text: To which lymph-node group does the tongue tip drain bilaterally?
questions.explanation: The central tip of the tongue drains to submental lymph nodes, often bilaterally across the midline.

questions.text: Which nerve carries taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
questions.explanation: Facial nerve taste fibers from the anterior tongue pass through chorda tympani before joining the lingual nerve.

questions.text: Which nerve carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve, a mandibular trigeminal branch, carries touch, pain, and temperature from the anterior tongue.

questions.text: Which muscle of the soft palate gives rise to the palatine aponeurosis?
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini aponeurosis fans into the soft palate and forms its fibrous framework.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles is NOT affected by injury to the cranial accessory and vagus nerves?
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini is supplied by the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve, not the vagus or accessory nerve.

questions.text: What is the main function of the palatoglossus muscle?
questions.explanation: Palatoglossus narrows the oropharyngeal isthmus and elevates the posterior tongue, helping close communication between mouth and oropharynx.
options: Closes off the oral cavity from the oropharynx

questions.text: Which nerve carries taste sensation from the soft palate?
questions.explanation: Taste fibers from the soft palate travel with the greater petrosal nerve, joining the facial nerve pathway to the geniculate ganglion.

questions.text: Which palate component is movable, muscular and separates the nasopharynx from the oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The soft palate is a movable muscular curtain that elevates to close the nasopharynx during swallowing.

questions.text: Which palatal muscle is supplied by the mandibular nerve rather than cranial accessory fibers joining the vagus?
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini is supplied by V3 via the nerve to medial pterygoid; most other palatal muscles receive vagal fibers through the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.text: Which nerve carries taste sensation from the soft palate?
questions.explanation: Greater petrosal nerve carries taste from the palate through the facial nerve; palatine nerves mainly convey general sensation.

questions.text: What is the length of the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The adult esophagus is about 25 cm long from the pharynx to the stomach.

questions.text: Where does the pharynx begin?
questions.explanation: The pharynx extends from the skull base to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage around C6.

questions.text: Which muscle functions as a physiological sphincter at the lower end of the pharynx to prevent the suction of air into the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus forms the upper esophageal sphincter and maintains tonic closure to prevent air entering the esophagus.

questions.text: The esophagus extends vertically through the neck and thorax between which two vertebral levels?
questions.explanation: The esophagus begins at C6 and passes through the diaphragm at about T10.

questions.text: Which muscle helps prevent air from entering the esophagus during respiration?
