questions.explanation: Cricopharyngeus forms the upper esophageal sphincter and maintains tone during breathing to prevent air from entering the esophagus.

questions.text: Which nerve passes between the middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles?
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and passes between the middle and inferior constrictors with superior laryngeal vessels.

questions.text: An injury affecting the cranial root of the accessory nerve impacts various pharyngeal and laryngeal structures, but which of the following muscles is typically unaffected?
questions.explanation: Tensor veli palatini is innervated by V3, so it is spared by injury to vagal or accessory-related pharyngeal motor fibers.

questions.text: What is the approximate vertebral extent of the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The esophagus begins at C6 and passes through the diaphragm around T10 before joining the stomach.

questions.text: What are the approximate vertebral levels of the esophagus, from its beginning to its passage through the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The esophagus begins at C6 and traverses the diaphragm at T10, giving the approximate C6-to-T10 course.

questions.text: Which pharyngeal muscle acts as a sphincter preventing suction of air into the esophagus between swallows?
questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus forms the upper esophageal sphincter and prevents air entering the esophagus between swallows.

questions.text: Which pharyngeal muscle originates from the medial surface of the styloid-process base and inserts at the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage?
questions.explanation: Stylopharyngeus arises from the styloid process and inserts into the pharyngeal wall and thyroid cartilage; CN IX supplies it.

questions.text: Which nerve supplies sensation to the mucosa of the laryngopharynx?
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies sensation above the vocal folds, including laryngopharyngeal mucosa.

questions.text: Which structure crosses behind the esophagus at T5 and then ascends on its left side?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct crosses behind the esophagus near T5 and then ascends along its left side.

questions.text: Which nerve passes with the superior laryngeal artery between the middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors?
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal vessels, passing between middle and inferior constrictors.

questions.text: Loss of sensation in the oropharyngeal mucosa most directly indicates injury to which nerve?
questions.explanation: Glossopharyngeal nerve carries general sensation from the oropharynx; internal laryngeal sensation is primarily in the laryngopharynx.

questions.text: Which vertebral levels mark the esophageal beginning and diaphragmatic passage, respectively?
questions.explanation: The esophagus begins at C6 and traverses the diaphragm at T10.

questions.text: The book places the beginning of the esophagus at C6 and its termination at T10.
questions.explanation: The esophagus begins behind the cricoid cartilage at C6 and passes through the diaphragm at T10, matching the stated extent.

questions.text: The parotid duct opens into the oral cavity opposite which tooth?
questions.explanation: The parotid duct pierces buccinator and opens opposite the upper second molar; the point of piercing and the oral opening are distinct landmarks.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man suffered of swelling in the parotid region. After investigation, he was diagnosed, and the surgeon decided to remove the gland. Which of the following is at risk of injury during this operation?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve passes through the parotid gland and divides into terminal branches, making it vulnerable in parotid surgery.

questions.text: Opposite to which tooth does the parotid duct open into the vestibule of the oral cavity?
questions.explanation: The parotid duct pierces buccinator and opens into the vestibule opposite the upper second molar.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most superficial structure within the parotid gland ?
questions.explanation: Within the parotid, the facial nerve is most superficial, followed deeper by the retromandibular vein and external carotid artery.

questions.text: Which muscle is located on the posteromedial surface of the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: The posterior belly of digastric lies along the posteromedial surface of the parotid gland.

questions.text: A patient undergoes surgery involving the parotid gland and develops weakness of the muscles of facial expression on the affected side. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve traverses the parotid gland and branches to facial-expression muscles; injury can cause ipsilateral facial weakness.

questions.text: A 35-year-old patient undergoes an intraoral examination of the opening of the parotid duct. At which location does the parotid duct normally open into the oral cavity after piercing the buccinator muscle?
questions.explanation: The duct crosses the cheek, pierces buccinator, then opens at the papilla opposite the upper second molar.

questions.text: Which of the following structures is related to the posteromedial surface of the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: The posterior belly of digastric lies along the posteromedial parotid surface and is an important deep relation.

questions.text: Which muscle is attached to the medial surface of the mastoid process in the posteromedial relations of the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: The posterior belly of digastric attaches to the mastoid notch and lies posteromedial to the parotid gland.

questions.text: Which structure is the most superficial major structure within the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: Within the parotid, the facial nerve is most superficial, followed deeper by the retromandibular vein and external carotid artery.

questions.text: Which muscle is related to the posteromedial surface of the parotid gland at the mastoid process?
questions.explanation: The posterior belly of digastric arises from the mastoid notch and forms a medial relation of the parotid gland.

questions.text: Which nerve traverses the parotid gland, dividing it into superficial and deep parts and forming the pes anserinus?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve traverses the parotid and branches into the pes anserinus, dividing the gland into superficial and deep surgical planes.

questions.text: Opposite which tooth does the parotid duct open into the oral vestibule?
questions.explanation: Stensen duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the maxillary second molar.

questions.text: Due to multiple stones in the submandibular duct, the submandibular gland of a 45-year-old patient was surgically removed. What major artery directly related to the gland was of special concern to the surgeon?
questions.explanation: The facial artery grooves the submandibular gland and must be considered during excision; its branches supply the face.

questions.text: Which nerve is most likely to be injured during surgery for a submandibular gland stone?
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve loops around the submandibular duct and lies close to it during stone removal.

questions.text: Which muscle separates the submandibular region into superficial and deep parts?
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid forms the muscular floor of the mouth and separates the superficial and deep portions of the submandibular gland.

questions.text: Which nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that join the lingual nerve and relay in the submandibular ganglion?
questions.explanation: Chorda tympani carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the facial nerve; they join the lingual nerve and synapse in the submandibular ganglion.

questions.text: During removal of a submandibular duct stone, which nerve is particularly at risk because it hooks around the duct from lateral to medial?
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve hooks around the submandibular duct from lateral to medial, putting it at risk during duct surgery.

questions.text: Which of the following is an origin to internal oblique muscle?
questions.explanation: Internal oblique arises partly from the lateral inguinal ligament, in addition to thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and related aponeuroses.

questions.text: Fascia transversalis attaches to the iliac crest between transversus abdominis and which muscle?
questions.explanation: Fascia transversalis attaches to the iliac crest between transversus abdominis and iliacus, defining its lateral lower abdominal relationship.

questions.text: Which anatomical landmark forms the lower free border of the posterior wall of the rectus sheath?
questions.explanation: The arcuate line marks where the posterior rectus sheath ends below; beneath it, all aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus abdominis.

questions.text: The inferior epigastric artery and superior epigastric artery form an important arterial anastomosis of the anterior abdominal wall. From which arteries do these two vessels respectively arise?
questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac; the superior epigastric continues from the internal thoracic artery.
options: External iliac artery and internal thoracic artery
Internal iliac artery and axillary artery
External iliac artery and axillary artery
Femoral artery and internal thoracic artery

questions.text: The umbilicus corresponds approximately to which spinal nerve dermatome?
questions.explanation: The umbilicus is classically at the T10 dermatome, useful as a surface landmark for spinal sensory levels.

questions.text: Which spinal nerve supplies the pyramidalis muscle?
questions.explanation: The pyramidalis is supplied by the subcostal nerve, the anterior ramus of T12.

questions.text: Which landmark forms the arched lower border of the aponeurotic posterior rectus sheath?
questions.explanation: Below the arcuate line, the aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus abdominis, so the posterior sheath ends at this curved margin.

questions.text: Which artery supplies the inferior epigastric artery?
questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery branches from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles forms the roof of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: Arching fibers of internal oblique contribute to the roof of the inguinal canal.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles is supplied by genital branch of genitofemoral nerve?
questions.explanation: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster muscle and carries its motor fibers.

questions.text: Which anatomical structure forms part of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon, formed by internal oblique and transversus aponeuroses, reinforces the medial posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

questions.text: The inguinal ligament is formed by which anatomical structure?
questions.explanation: The inguinal ligament is the rolled, thickened inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis.
options: Tendon of the rectus abdominis muscle
Aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle

questions.text: Which of the following statements about the inguinal canal is correct?
questions.explanation: Internal oblique fibers contribute to the anterior wall laterally, while the external oblique aponeurosis forms it along the full canal.
options: The external oblique aponeurosis forms its posterior wall
The transversalis fascia forms its anterior wall
The internal oblique muscle forms its posterior wall
The internal oblique muscle forms part of its anterior wall
The inguinal ligament forms its roof

questions.text: Which muscle contributes to the roof and also, through the conjoint tendon, the posterior wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: Internal oblique contributes arching fibers to the canal roof and joins transversus aponeurosis in the conjoint tendon.

questions.text: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal along its whole length?
questions.explanation: The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal throughout its length.

questions.text: Which abdominal-wall muscle gives rise to the cremaster muscle?
questions.explanation: Cremaster fibers arise mainly from the internal oblique as it passes through the inguinal canal with the spermatic cord.

questions.text: Which structure reinforces the weak medial part of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon reinforces the medial posterior wall, where the transversalis fascia is weakest.

questions.text: Which of the following gastrointestinal structures is retroperitoneal?
questions.explanation: The ascending colon is secondarily retroperitoneal, unlike the jejunum, ileum, transverse colon, and sigmoid colon.

questions.text: Which one of the following organs divides the peritoneal cavity into greater and lesser [sac]?
questions.explanation: The stomach forms the key connection between greater and lesser sacs through the lesser omentum and epiploic foramen arrangement.

questions.text: Which one of the following organs is not a retroperitoneal organ?
questions.explanation: The first part of the duodenum is mostly intraperitoneal; kidneys, IVC, and ascending/descending colon are retroperitoneal.

questions.text: Which of the following structures is completely covered by peritoneum?
questions.explanation: The first inch of the duodenum is intraperitoneal and mobile; the remaining duodenum is largely retroperitoneal.
options: First inch of the first part of the duodenum

questions.text: Which of the following abdominal organs is primarily retroperitoneal?
questions.explanation: Most of the duodenum is secondarily retroperitoneal; stomach, jejunum, spleen, and transverse colon are intraperitoneal.

questions.text: How is the hepatic artery proper positioned within the right free border of the lesser omentum?
questions.explanation: In the hepatoduodenal ligament, the bile duct lies anterior-right and hepatic artery anterior-left of the posterior portal vein.
options: Posterior to bile duct and right of portal vein
Posterior to both portal vein and bile duct
Anterior to portal vein and right of bile duct
Posterior to portal vein and right of bile duct
Anterior to portal vein and left of bile duct

questions.text: To which liver landmark are the margins of the lesser omentum attached?
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum attaches to the liver at the porta hepatis and fissure for the ligamentum venosum.

questions.text: The upper part of the greater curvature of the stomach gives attachment to the gastrosplenic ligament.
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament attaches to the upper part of the stomach’s greater curvature and contains short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels.

questions.text: The posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen is the free edge of the lesser omentum enclosing the portal vein.
questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen’s anterior boundary is the free edge of the lesser omentum; the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava.

questions.text: Within the right free margin of the lesser omentum, the portal vein lies anterior to the hepatic artery.
questions.explanation: False: in the hepatoduodenal ligament, the portal vein lies posterior to the hepatic artery and bile duct.

questions.text: The portal vein lies in the right free margin of the lesser omentum, which forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
questions.explanation: The portal triad lies in the free edge of the lesser omentum, forming the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.

questions.text: Which artery follows a tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas, posterior to the lesser sac and stomach?
questions.explanation: The splenic artery follows a tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas toward the spleen.

questions.text: Which arteries arise near the end of the splenic artery and pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to the gastric fundus?
questions.explanation: Short gastric arteries arise near the splenic artery’s termination and pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the fundus.

questions.text: Which arteries supply the fundus of the stomach?
questions.explanation: Short gastric arteries from the splenic artery supply the fundus, anastomosing with branches of the left gastric artery.

questions.text: Which arterial trunk supplies the foregut, including the stomach?
questions.explanation: The celiac trunk supplies foregut derivatives, including stomach, liver, spleen, and proximal duodenum.

questions.text: Which artery lies anterior to the third part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery crosses anterior to the third part of the duodenum and can compress it if the mesenteric angle narrows.

questions.text: Which vessels are a posterior relation of the descending second part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The right renal vessels lie behind the descending second part of the duodenum, along with the right kidney and IVC.

questions.text: An ulcer penetrating the posterior wall of the first duodenal part may erode which immediately related artery?
questions.explanation: The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum, so posterior ulcer penetration can cause severe hemorrhage.

questions.text: Which peritoneal fold attaches to the anterior border of the pancreatic body?
questions.explanation: The transverse mesocolon attaches along the anterior border of the pancreatic body, separating supracolic and infracolic compartments.

questions.text: Which artery gives numerous small branches to the pancreatic neck, body and tail?
questions.explanation: The splenic artery runs along the superior border of the pancreas and sends branches to its neck, body, and tail.

questions.text: Which structure is lodged in a groove on, or embedded within, the posterior aspect of the pancreatic head?
questions.explanation: The common bile duct descends in a groove on or through the posterior pancreatic head before joining the duodenum.

questions.text: The entire duodenum is retroperitoneal, including the first inch of its first part.
questions.explanation: False: the proximal first inch of the duodenum is intraperitoneal; the rest is mostly secondarily retroperitoneal.

questions.text: Which duodenal segment is completely covered by peritoneum and therefore movable?
questions.explanation: The proximal inch of the duodenal bulb is intraperitoneal and mobile; the remainder is fixed secondarily retroperitoneally.
options: First inch of the first part
Second inch of the first part

questions.text: The philtrum of the upper lip develops from:
questions.explanation: The philtrum forms where the medial nasal processes merge, derivatives of the frontonasal prominence.

questions.text: Which embryological structure contributes to the formation of the secondary palate?
questions.explanation: The secondary palate forms from the paired palatal shelves of the maxillary processes, which fuse in the midline.

questions.text: Deficiency in which of the following causes bilateral cleft lip
questions.explanation: Bilateral cleft lip results when both maxillary prominences fail to fuse with the intermaxillary segment formed by medial nasal prominences.

questions.text: Which peritoneal fold between liver and stomach develops from the ventral mesogastrium?
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum develops from ventral mesogastrium and connects liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum.

questions.text: Which structure marks the junction of the foregut and midgut within the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla marks the foregut–midgut boundary and receives bile and pancreatic secretions.

questions.text: The secondary palate develops from the intermaxillary segment that forms the primary palate.
questions.explanation: The secondary palate forms from paired lateral palatine shelves, not the intermaxillary segment that forms the primary palate.

questions.text: Which embryological junction accounts for the dual celiac and superior mesenteric supply of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The duodenal transition from foregut to midgut marks the shift in arterial supply from celiac to superior mesenteric branches.

questions.text: The falciform ligament develops from the dorsal mesogastrium.
questions.explanation: False: the falciform ligament develops from the ventral mesogastrium, not the dorsal mesogastrium.

questions.text: A cleft anterior to the incisive foramen may involve a unilateral or bilateral lateral cleft lip from deficient mesenchyme in the maxillary prominence or intermaxillary segment.
questions.explanation: Clefts anterior to the incisive foramen involve the lip/alveolus and arise from failed fusion of maxillary and medial nasal components.

questions.text: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes obstruction and vomiting through hypertrophy of the circular fibers of the pyloric sphincter.
questions.explanation: Congenital pyloric stenosis results from hypertrophy of the pyloric circular muscle, narrowing the outlet and causing projectile vomiting.

questions.text: Which vein is formed behind the pancreatic neck by union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins?
questions.explanation: The portal vein forms behind the pancreatic neck where the superior mesenteric and splenic veins unite.

questions.text: The caudate lobe lies between the gallbladder fossa and the fissure for ligamentum teres.
questions.explanation: The caudate lobe lies between the fissure for ligamentum venosum and the IVC; the gallbladder fossa and ligamentum teres bound the quadrate lobe.

questions.text: Which gastric vein drains directly into the portal vein?
questions.explanation: The left gastric vein drains directly into the portal vein, while short gastric and left gastroepiploic veins drain to the splenic vein.

questions.text: Which structure forms the left boundary of the quadrate lobe?
questions.explanation: The fissure for the ligamentum teres forms the left boundary of the quadrate lobe.

questions.text: Which pair of veins unites behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein?
questions.explanation: The portal vein forms behind the pancreatic neck from the union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins.
options: Superior rectal and left colic veins
Left gastric and right gastric veins

questions.text: Which pair of veins unites behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein?
questions.explanation: The portal vein typically forms behind the pancreatic neck by union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
options: Inferior mesenteric and left gastric veins

questions.text: The portal vein is formed anterior to the neck of the pancreas.
questions.explanation: False: the portal vein forms posterior to the pancreatic neck, not anterior to it.

questions.text: Which rectal vein contributes to the portal side of the portosystemic anastomosis in the rectal wall?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal vein drains to the inferior mesenteric and portal systems; middle and inferior rectal veins drain systemically.

questions.text: The uncinate process develops from which embryonic source?
questions.explanation: The ventral pancreatic bud rotates posteriorly and forms the uncinate process and inferior pancreatic head.

questions.text: Which venous connection is responsible for the lower esophageal portosystemic anastomosis?
questions.explanation: The left gastric vein drains into the portal system and connects with esophageal veins draining to the azygos system.
options: Superior rectal and middle rectal veins

questions.text: Which embryonic source gives rise to the uncinate process of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The ventral pancreatic bud rotates posteriorly and forms the uncinate process and inferior head of the pancreas.

questions.text: Which venous connection accounts for esophageal varices in portal hypertension?
questions.explanation: The left gastric vein communicates with esophageal veins draining to the azygos system, creating the portosystemic route for varices.
options: Superior rectal with middle and inferior rectal veins
Colonic veins with posterior abdominal-wall veins
Left gastric with azygos esophageal tributaries

questions.text: Which duct is formed by union of the right and left hepatic ducts before it joins the cystic duct?
questions.explanation: The right and left hepatic ducts unite to form the common hepatic duct, which later joins the cystic duct.

questions.text: Which developmental process contributes to formation of the hepatic blood sinusoids?
questions.explanation: Hepatic sinusoids develop as vitelline and umbilical venous channels are remodeled within the expanding hepatic cords.
options: Persistence of the pars hepatica stem

questions.text: Breaking down of the vitelline veins contributes to formation of the liver sinusoids.
questions.explanation: Vitelline veins remodel into hepatic sinusoids and portal venous channels during liver development.

questions.text: Which two ducts unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla opening at the major duodenal papilla?
questions.explanation: The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, opening at the major papilla.
options: Cystic duct and common hepatic duct
Right hepatic duct and left hepatic duct
Accessory pancreatic duct and cystic duct
Common bile duct and main pancreatic duct
Common hepatic duct and accessory pancreatic duct

questions.text: Which duct is formed when the cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct?
questions.explanation: The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct, which descends toward the duodenum.

questions.text: The cystic artery supplying the gallbladder is usually a branch of which artery?
questions.explanation: The cystic artery usually branches from the right hepatic artery within the hepatocystic triangle.

questions.text: Which artery supplies the ileum and the other midgut derivatives?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut from the distal duodenum through the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.

questions.text: Which intestinal segment lies in the territory of the superior mesenteric artery?
questions.explanation: The ileum is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery; sigmoid and descending colon and most rectum belong to inferior mesenteric territory.

questions.text: Occlusion of which arterial supply directly threatens perfusion of the ileum?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, including most of the small intestine and the ileum.

questions.text: Which appendix position is most common?
questions.explanation: The retrocecal position is the most common location of the vermiform appendix.

questions.text: Which structure descends into the pelvis behind the apex of the sigmoid mesocolon root?
questions.explanation: The left ureter descends behind the root of the sigmoid mesocolon toward the pelvic cavity.

questions.text: Following the three taeniae coli to their convergence identifies the tip of the appendix.
questions.explanation: The three taeniae coli converge at the base of the appendix; tracing them helps locate its origin, not its tip.

questions.text: The lower third of the female rectum lies anterior to the middle part of the vagina.
questions.explanation: False: the lower rectum lies posterior to the vagina; the middle vagina is anterior to the rectum.

questions.text: The rectum bears appendices epiploicae along its outer surface.
questions.explanation: Rectum lacks the appendices epiploicae and taeniae coli that characterize the colon.

questions.text: Which rectal segment is covered by peritoneum anteriorly and on both sides?
questions.explanation: The upper third of the rectum is covered by peritoneum anteriorly and laterally; lower portions lose lateral or all peritoneal covering.

questions.text: Which structure belongs to the posterior relations of the male rectum?
questions.explanation: The sacrum lies posterior to the male rectum; seminal vesicles, vas deferens ampullae, prostate, and bladder are anterior relations.

questions.text: Which developmental error is responsible for imperforate anus in the book?
questions.explanation: The anal membrane normally ruptures to establish the anal opening; failure of rupture can cause imperforate anus.
options: Faulty formation of the urorectal septum
Absence of autonomic plexuses in a colonic segment

questions.text: Which embryonic structure forms the lower ectodermal part of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The anal canal’s lower ectodermal portion develops from the proctodeum, while its upper part derives from hindgut endoderm.

questions.text: Incomplete midgut rotation limited to 90 degrees places the small intestine on the left and the large intestine on the right.
questions.explanation: False: a 90-degree rotation leaves small intestine predominantly on the right and large intestine on the left, opposite the statement.

questions.text: Which part of the gastrointestinal tract bears the Meckel diverticulum caused by persistence of the vitellointestinal duct?
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of the vitellointestinal duct on the antimesenteric ileum.

questions.text: Meckel diverticulum is a persistent remnant of the vitellointestinal duct.
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum is a persistent vitelline duct remnant, usually on the antimesenteric border of ileum.

subjects.name: Physiology
lectureNames: Physiology Of Digestive System & Regulation of GIT Functions
Physiology Of Gastric Mucosa & Phases of Gastric Secretion
Physiology Of Gall Bladder& Bile Salts
Physiology Of Absorption in Small Intestine
Physiology Of Diarrhea & Large Intestine and Constipation

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes propulsive movement in the gastrointestinal tract?
questions.explanation: Esophageal propulsive waves move food faster than small-intestinal transit, which allows time for digestion and absorption.
options: Is faster in the esophagus than in the small intestine.
Is presented by intestinal segmentation movement.

questions.text: In intestinal smooth muscle cells, peak of slow wave potential becomes away from threshold by which of the following factors?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine hyperpolarizes intestinal smooth muscle and reduces slow-wave peaks, moving them farther from threshold and lowering contraction likelihood.
options: presence of food in the alimentary canal.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the composition of salivary secretion?
questions.explanation: As saliva flows through ducts, sodium and chloride are reabsorbed while potassium and bicarbonate are secreted; at higher flow bicarbonate rises.
options: It is watery following sympathetic stimulation.
It is initially isotonic but later becomes hypertonic.
It is rich in enzymes following parasympathetic stimulation.
It has more Na⁺ concentration than plasma during resting conditions.
The secondary secretion has more HCO₃⁻ concentration than plasma.

questions.text: The reabsorption of sodium and secretion of potassium during the ductal modification of saliva are primarily regulated by which hormone?
questions.explanation: Aldosterone increases ductal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in salivary glands, making final saliva potassium-rich and sodium-poor.

questions.text: Which neurotransmitter causes the slow-wave potential of gastrointestinal smooth muscle to move further away from the threshold, thereby reducing the likelihood of action potentials?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine inhibits enteric excitability and hyperpolarizes smooth muscle, making slow waves less likely to trigger action potentials.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the bicarbonate concentration in saliva compared with plasma?
questions.explanation: Salivary ducts secrete bicarbonate, and its concentration can exceed plasma, especially with stimulated flow.
options: It is always lower than plasma
It is approximately equal to plasma
It is higher only during fasting

questions.text: During resting conditions, how is saliva compared with plasma?
questions.explanation: Salivary ducts reabsorb sodium and chloride more than they secrete potassium and bicarbonate, producing hypotonic saliva at rest.
options: Equal in electrolyte concentration to plasma

questions.text: Choose the correct statement about saliva
questions.explanation: Aldosterone alters salivary duct electrolyte transport; increased bicarbonate relative to chloride can make final saliva more alkaline.

questions.text: Choose the correct answer about peristalsis
questions.explanation: Esophageal peristalsis rapidly propels a bolus; small-intestinal contractions move contents more slowly and also mix them.
options: peristalsis is faster in stomach than esophagus
peristalsis is faster in intestine than esophagus
peristalsis is faster in esophagus than intestine
peristalsis considers as apart of mixing food in intestine
peristalsis is done by adding Ach to previous segment for relaxation

questions.text: Which of the following neurotransmitters is released by inhibitory motor neurons in the myenteric plexus to cause relaxation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: Enteric inhibitory motor neurons release nitric oxide to relax gastrointestinal smooth muscle, including the LES.

questions.text: Which of the following mechanisms explain the slow onset of contraction in smooth muscle compared to skeletal muscle ?
questions.explanation: Smooth-muscle myosin ATPase hydrolyzes ATP more slowly than skeletal-muscle myosin, delaying cross-bridge cycling and contraction.
options: Slow release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Slow binding of Ca2+ to calmodulin
Slow dephosphorylation of myosin light chain by phosphatase
Slow splitting of ATP by myosin ATPase activity
Slow removal of Ca2+ from the cytoplasm

questions.text: Which type of activity is responsible for the pacemaker function of gastrointestinal smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: Interstitial cells of Cajal and smooth muscle generate rhythmic slow waves intrinsically, making gastrointestinal pacing myogenic.

questions.text: During gastrointestinal smooth muscle contraction, the binding of intracellular calcium to calmodulin initiates cross-bridge cycling by activating which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Calcium binds calmodulin, activating myosin light-chain kinase, which phosphorylates myosin and enables contraction.

questions.text: Which primary neurotransmitter acts on gastrointestinal smooth muscle and enteric neurons to decrease motility and tone?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine from sympathetic fibers inhibits enteric activity and reduces gastrointestinal motility and tone.

questions.text: Which electrophysiological feature is characteristic of the esophageal smooth muscle in a patient with a motility disorder?
questions.explanation: Esophageal smooth muscle has a resting membrane potential between contractions; action potentials occur with excitatory stimulation rather than continuously at rest.
options: Depolarization during the entire resting phase

questions.text: What is one important function of chewing?
questions.explanation: Chewing breaks food into smaller particles and mixes it with saliva, forming a bolus that is easier to swallow.

questions.text: Regarding gastrointestinal propulsive movements, how does the movement of contents through the esophagus compare to that in the small intestine?
questions.explanation: Esophageal peristalsis rapidly moves a bolus to the stomach, whereas small-intestinal transit is slower to permit digestion and absorption.
options: Content transit is faster in the small intestine than in the esophagus
Content transit is identical in speed throughout both organs
Segmentation contractions propel food faster in the small intestine than in the esophagus
Propulsive motility occurs exclusively in the small intestine
Transit through the esophagus is rapid, whereas content movement in the small intestine is slow

questions.text: Which electrical event in gastrointestinal smooth muscle occurs when slow-wave potentials reach threshold, directly resulting in muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: When slow waves reach threshold, spike potentials open calcium channels and trigger gastrointestinal smooth-muscle contraction.

questions.text: Which feature explains the slow onset of smooth-muscle contraction compared with skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: Smooth-muscle myosin ATPase turns over ATP slowly, producing slower cross-bridge cycling and a delayed contraction compared with skeletal muscle.
options: Slow ATP splitting by myosin ATPase
Calcium pumping back into extracellular fluid

questions.text: Which autonomic mediator decreases gastrointestinal smooth muscle excitability through sympathetic influence?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic norepinephrine reduces enteric excitability and inhibits gastrointestinal smooth-muscle activity.

questions.text: Which intracellular complex activates myosin light chain kinase during gastrointestinal smooth muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: The calcium–calmodulin complex activates myosin light-chain kinase, initiating cross-bridge cycling in smooth muscle.

questions.text: Which transmitter released by excitatory intrinsic enteric neurons stimulates smooth-muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine from excitatory enteric motor neurons depolarizes gastrointestinal smooth muscle and promotes contraction.

questions.text: Which intrinsic enteric neuronal mediator relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide is an inhibitory enteric transmitter that relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle, including sphincters.

questions.text: The slow-wave potentials generated by interstitial cells of Cajal are action potentials.
questions.explanation: False: interstitial cells of Cajal generate slow waves; action potentials occur only when slow waves reach threshold.

questions.text: Norepinephrine increases gastrointestinal smooth-muscle excitability and favors contraction.
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine generally inhibits gastrointestinal smooth-muscle excitability and motility, so the statement is false.

questions.text: Autoregulatory escape results from local metabolic vasodilation overriding sympathetic vasoconstriction.
questions.explanation: Local metabolites can dilate vessels enough to overcome sympathetic vasoconstriction, maintaining flow in active tissue.

questions.text: At low salivary flow under resting conditions, which composition best describes saliva reaching the mouth?
questions.explanation: At low flow, ductal modification is prolonged, so sodium concentration falls below plasma and saliva becomes hypotonic.
options: Isotonic, with sodium at plasma concentration
Isotonic, with potassium below plasma concentration
Hypotonic, with bicarbonate below plasma concentration
Hypotonic, with sodium below plasma concentration
Hypotonic, with sodium above plasma concentration

questions.text: Which change in salivary duct transport is described with excess aldosterone?
questions.explanation: Aldosterone increases ductal sodium reabsorption and bicarbonate secretion, changing saliva toward a more alkaline, potassium-rich composition.
options: Decreased sodium absorption and bicarbonate secretion
Increased chloride secretion and potassium absorption
Decreased potassium secretion and sodium absorption
Increased sodium secretion and bicarbonate absorption
Increased sodium absorption and bicarbonate secretion

questions.text: Which paired ionic change occurs while primary saliva passes through the ducts?
questions.explanation: Salivary ducts reabsorb sodium from primary saliva and secrete bicarbonate; this modification makes final saliva hypotonic.

questions.text: Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter is mediated by which of the following neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide released by inhibitory enteric neurons relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter during swallowing.

questions.text: Which of the following occurs during the pharyngeal stage of swallowing?
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal swallow reflex closes the vocal folds and laryngeal inlet to protect the airway while food passes into the esophagus.
options: Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter

questions.text: One of the following chemical released for relaxing of lower esophageal sphincter
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide released by inhibitory neurons relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter during swallowing.

questions.text: Which of the following esophageal disorders is characterized by an increased resting tone of the lower esophageal sphincter during swallowing ?
questions.explanation: Achalasia features impaired LES relaxation and increased resting tone, causing dysphagia and esophageal retention.

questions.text: Which structure closes over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing to prevent food from entering the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: The epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing, directing the bolus away from the airway.

questions.text: What two voluntary motor processes occur in the oral cavity and pharynx to mechanically prepare food and propel it toward the esophagus
questions.explanation: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces and mixes it with saliva; swallowing propels the bolus from mouth and pharynx toward the esophagus.

questions.text: Which surgical procedure still allows tube feeding directly into the esophagus as it does not affect 2ry esophageal peristalsis?
questions.explanation: Vagotomy disrupts primary swallowing-related peristalsis but leaves enteric secondary peristalsis relatively intact, so tube feeding through the esophagus can continue.

questions.text: Which of the following occurs during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing?
questions.explanation: During the pharyngeal phase, laryngeal elevation and glottic closure protect the airway as the bolus moves through the pharynx.

questions.text: Which condition is characterized by the failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing?
questions.explanation: Achalasia reflects failed LES relaxation and absent or impaired peristalsis, often from loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons.

questions.text: What is the primary stimulus that triggers secondary esophageal peristalsis?
questions.explanation: Local distension of the esophageal wall triggers secondary peristalsis through enteric reflexes without requiring a new swallow.
options: Voluntary tongue movement against the hard palate
Deglutition center activation in the medulla
Localized distension of the esophageal wall
Acid stimulation in the oral cavity

questions.text: The pharyngeal stage of swallowing is an involuntary reflex that moves food through the pharynx into the esophagus.
questions.explanation: Once triggered, the pharyngeal phase is involuntary and rapidly propels food through the pharynx into the esophagus.

questions.text: A large sticky bolus remains after primary esophageal peristalsis. What initiates the secondary peristaltic wave?
questions.explanation: Distension of the esophageal wall by retained bolus activates stretch reflexes that initiate secondary peristalsis.
options: Release of nitric oxide at the lower sphincter

questions.text: Slow esophageal transit provides time for nutrient digestion and absorption before food reaches the stomach.
questions.explanation: False: esophageal transit mainly propels swallowed material to the stomach; nutrient digestion and absorption occur largely downstream.

questions.text: Which mediator released by inhibitory enteric neurons helps relax the lower esophageal sphincter during swallowing?
questions.explanation: Inhibitory enteric neurons release nitric oxide to relax the lower esophageal sphincter during a swallow.

questions.text: Which movement of the epiglottis occurs during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing?
questions.explanation: During swallowing, the epiglottis tilts downward over the laryngeal inlet to direct food away from the airway.
options: Contracts to propel food through the esophagus
Relaxes to open the upper esophageal sphincter
Moves downward over the closed glottis
Elevates to close the posterior nasal passages
Moves forward to press food against the hard palate

questions.text: Which neurons mediate secondary esophageal peristalsis without involving the swallowing center?
questions.explanation: Enteric neurons detect esophageal distension and coordinate secondary peristalsis without engaging the medullary swallowing sequence.
options: Vagal efferent neurons from the swallowing center
Hypoglossal motor neurons to the tongue

questions.text: Which center is temporarily inhibited during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing?
questions.explanation: The swallowing reflex briefly inhibits the respiratory center, creating a short apnea that prevents simultaneous breathing and swallowing.

questions.text: After the vagus nerves supplying the esophagus are cut, the myenteric plexus can produce strong secondary peristaltic waves after several days.
questions.explanation: After vagotomy, intrinsic myenteric circuits can recover and generate secondary peristalsis in response to esophageal distension.

questions.text: Which action directly closes the glottis during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing?
questions.explanation: Adduction of the vocal folds closes the glottis and protects the airway during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing.
options: Relaxation of the upper esophageal sphincter

questions.text: Which type of gastric motility is primarily responsible for the mixing of food with gastric juices to form chyme ?
questions.explanation: Antral peristaltic waves churn food with gastric secretions and propel it toward the pylorus, forming chyme.

questions.text: Activation of which of the following receptor types by agents like apomorphine is primarily responsible for stimulating the vomiting center?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine stimulates dopamine D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, activating the vomiting center.

questions.text: Which of the following is an important event during vomiting?
questions.explanation: Vomiting requires contraction of the diaphragm and abdominal wall to raise intra-abdominal pressure and expel gastric contents.
options: Contraction of the diaphragmatic and abdominal muscles
Contraction of the lower esophageal sphincter
Relaxation of the pyloric sphincter only

questions.text: Which gastrointestinal hormone, released by cells of the upper small intestine in response to fat and protein digestion products, is the most potent inhibitor of stomach motility and evacuation?
questions.explanation: Fat and amino acids trigger CCK release from the small intestine; CCK slows gastric emptying, giving the intestine time to digest and absorb the incoming nutrients.

questions.text: Which of the following gastrointestinal hormones promotes gastric emptying by increasing gastric motility?
questions.explanation: Gastrin increases gastric motility and promotes emptying, whereas CCK, secretin, GIP, and somatostatin inhibit it.

questions.text: Which hormone promotes gastric motility and increases the rate of gastric emptying?
questions.explanation: Gastrin promotes gastric motility; CCK, secretin, GIP, and somatostatin generally inhibit gastric emptying.

questions.text: Mixing of food with gastric juice occurs by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Antral peristaltic waves churn food against a closed pylorus, mixing it with gastric juice and grinding particles.
options: Peristaltic contractions at the gastric body.

questions.text: Which of the following promotes gastric emptying?
questions.explanation: Antral gastrin promotes gastric motility and emptying; duodenal hormones and sympathetic reflexes generally slow delivery when chyme enters.
options: Gastric release of gastrin from antral G cells
Release of secretin from the duodenum
Release of cholecystokinin (CCK) from the duodenum
Increased sympathetic stimulation of the stomach

questions.text: Which hormone participates in the increased gastric motility produced by stomach distension?
questions.explanation: Gastric distension stimulates gastrin release and vagovagal reflexes, increasing antral motility and promoting emptying.

questions.text: During vomiting, which action supplies a major force for expulsion of gastric contents?
questions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm and abdominal muscles raises intra-abdominal pressure, providing force to expel stomach contents.
options: Contraction of the stomach as the main pump
Opening of the glottis during expulsion
Contraction of the lower esophageal sphincter

questions.text: What provides the major force expelling gastric contents during vomiting?
questions.explanation: Diaphragmatic and abdominal contractions create the pressure that expels stomach contents during vomiting.
options: Contraction of esophagus and gastric fundus
Contraction of upper and lower esophageal sphincters
Contraction of stomach and lower esophageal sphincter
Contraction of diaphragm and abdominal muscles
Contraction of gastric fundus and pyloric sphincter

questions.text: Which gastric motor event mixes food with secretion by propelling it toward a closed pylorus and back into the antrum?
questions.explanation: Strong antral peristalsis drives chyme toward the partly closed pylorus; retropulsion back into the antrum mixes and grinds food.

questions.text: A man sustains an area-postrema lesion in an accident. Which vomiting response remains possible despite this lesion?
questions.explanation: Motion sickness reaches the vomiting center through vestibular pathways. Area-postrema damage reduces responses to blood-borne triggers but does not abolish vestibular vomiting.

questions.text: Which effect of prostaglandins contributes to their inhibition of gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Prostaglandins inhibit parietal-cell acid secretion partly by lowering intracellular cAMP and also strengthen mucosal defenses.

questions.text: Which prostaglandin decreases gastric HCl secretion?
questions.explanation: PGE₂ inhibits parietal-cell acid secretion and supports mucosal protection through reduced cAMP and increased mucus/bicarbonate.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most potent physiological stimulus for gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Food in the stomach activates neural, gastrin, and histamine pathways, making it a strong physiological stimulus for acid secretion.
options: Presence of food in the stomach

questions.text: Which of the following acts as a paracrine inhibitor of gastric acid secretion ?
questions.explanation: Somatostatin released from gastric D cells acts locally to inhibit gastrin and histamine signaling and reduce acid secretion.

questions.text: Which of the following would lead to an increase in gastric HCl secretion?
questions.explanation: Loss of inhibitory D-cell somatostatin removes restraint on gastrin and parietal cells, increasing gastric acid secretion.

questions.text: Which dietary constituent is the most potent chemical stimulus for increasing gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Peptides and partially digested proteins stimulate gastrin release and strongly increase gastric acid secretion.

questions.text: Which paracrine agent directly stimulates gastric parietal cells to increase acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Enterochromaffin-like cell histamine directly activates parietal-cell H2 receptors, increasing cAMP and acid secretion.

questions.text: Which mediator inhibits parietal-cell acid secretion through a Gi-mediated decrease in intracellular cyclic AMP?
questions.explanation: PGE₂ activates Gi-coupled receptors on parietal cells, lowering cAMP and reducing acid secretion.

questions.text: Which locally acting secretion from enterochromaffin-like gastric cells stimulates parietal cells?
questions.explanation: Histamine released by enterochromaffin-like cells acts locally on H2 receptors of parietal cells to increase acid secretion.

questions.text: Gastric secretion evoked by chewing and tasting food before it enters the stomach belongs to the gastric phase.
questions.explanation: Chewing and tasting food activate the cephalic phase through vagal pathways before food enters the stomach; the statement is false.

questions.text: Which event initiates the gastric phase that accounts for most secretion after a meal?
questions.explanation: Food entering the stomach initiates the gastric phase through distension and peptides, accounting for most post-meal acid secretion.

questions.text: Which local mediator inhibits parietal-cell acid secretion through Gi and reduced cAMP?
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin E2 activates Gi-coupled receptors on parietal cells, lowering cAMP and inhibiting acid secretion.

questions.text: Histamine stimulates parietal-cell H2 receptors by raising intracellular calcium rather than cyclic AMP.
questions.explanation: Histamine activates H2 receptors mainly through Gs and cAMP, not by raising intracellular calcium; the statement is false.

questions.text: Which transport mechanism secretes hydrogen ions through the parietal-cell luminal H+-K+ ATPase?
questions.explanation: The parietal-cell H⁺/K⁺ ATPase directly hydrolyzes ATP to exchange luminal potassium for hydrogen, so acid secretion is primary active transport.

questions.text: Somatostatin released from gastric D cells acts locally as a paracrine inhibitor of acid secretion.
questions.explanation: True: D-cell somatostatin diffuses locally and suppresses gastrin release and parietal-cell acid secretion.

questions.text: Gastric distension is a more potent gastric-phase secretory stimulus than protein peptide fragments.
questions.explanation: Protein peptides stimulate gastrin and acid secretion; gastric distension contributes but is not the stronger secretory stimulus in this comparison.

questions.text: Which vitamin becomes malabsorbed when atrophic gastritis reduces intrinsic factor secretion?
questions.explanation: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, required for ileal vitamin B12 uptake; atrophic gastritis can therefore cause B12 deficiency.

questions.text: Loss of gastric parietal cells in atrophic gastritis leads to pernicious anemia by reducing secretion of which substance?
questions.explanation: Gastric parietal cells produce intrinsic factor; its loss prevents vitamin B12 absorption and can cause pernicious anemia.

questions.text: Deficiency of which pancreatic digestive enzyme most directly impairs triglyceride digestion and produces steatorrhea?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes triglyceride ester bonds into absorbable fatty acids and monoglycerides; deficiency leaves fat in stool.

questions.text: Reducing bile-salt and lecithin secretion relative to cholesterol keeps more cholesterol dissolved in bile.
questions.explanation: Bile salts and lecithin solubilize cholesterol; reducing them relative to cholesterol raises supersaturation and promotes gallstone precipitation.

questions.text: Loss of bile salts after terminal ileal removal increases gallstone risk through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Ileal loss reduces the bile-salt pool and cholesterol solubilization, allowing cholesterol to precipitate and form gallstones.
options: Precipitation of cholesterol in the gall bladder
Increased micellar transport of dietary fat
Increased intestinal absorption of bile salts
Increased solubility of cholesterol in bile

questions.text: Which hormone is the principal stimulus for gallbladder contraction and emptying after a fatty meal?
questions.explanation: Cholecystokinin is released by fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum and contracts the gallbladder while relaxing the sphincter of Oddi.

questions.text: Bile salts help prevent cholesterol precipitation by keeping cholesterol soluble in micelles.
questions.explanation: Bile salts form micelles that keep cholesterol dissolved in bile, lowering the chance of crystal formation.

questions.text: Which hormone stimulates the smooth muscle of the gallbladder?
questions.explanation: Cholecystokinin contracts gallbladder smooth muscle and helps expel bile after a fatty meal.

questions.text: Most bile salts return to portal blood by passive diffusion from the proximal small intestine.
questions.explanation: Most bile salts are actively reclaimed in the terminal ileum, then returned to the liver through portal blood for reuse.

questions.text: A choleretic increases bile secretion by stimulating hepatocytes.
questions.explanation: A choleretic increases bile formation by the liver; bile salts and secretin are physiological stimuli of bile secretion.

questions.text: Bile-salt emulsification increases the exposed fat surface available to pancreatic lipase.
questions.explanation: True: bile salts emulsify fat into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area accessible to pancreatic lipase.

questions.text: Which bile constituent undergoes extensive enterohepatic recycling after assisting intestinal fat absorption?
questions.explanation: Bile salts are secreted into bile, aid micelle formation in the intestine, and are largely recycled through enterohepatic circulation.

questions.text: Which hormone is a potent physiological cholagogue that contracts and empties the gall bladder?
questions.explanation: CCK is released by duodenal fat and amino acids; it contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi to expel bile.

questions.text: Which bile component helps maintain cholesterol in solution by incorporating it into micelles?
questions.explanation: Bile salts form micelles that keep cholesterol soluble in bile and help transport lipids toward the intestinal surface.

questions.text: Bile salts digest triglycerides by hydrolyzing their ester bonds.
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify dietary fat and form micelles; pancreatic lipase, not bile salt, hydrolyzes triglyceride bonds.

questions.text: Which substance is the most potent physiological choleretic, stimulating hepatic bile secretion after enterohepatic reabsorption?
questions.explanation: Reabsorbed bile salts return to the liver through enterohepatic circulation and stimulate further bile secretion, making them potent choleretics.

questions.text: Which fasting motor pattern clears the stomach and small intestine of food remnants, mucosal debris and bacteria?
questions.explanation: The migrating motor complex sweeps residual food, debris, and bacteria through the stomach and small bowel during fasting.

questions.text: Which intestinal movement consists of alternating ring-like contractions that thoroughly mix luminal chyme?
questions.explanation: Segmentation alternates local circular-muscle contractions to mix chyme with digestive secretions and expose it to mucosa.

questions.text: Which enzyme embedded in the duodenal luminal membrane initiates conversion of trypsinogen to trypsin?
questions.explanation: Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border cleaves trypsinogen to active trypsin, which then activates other pancreatic zymogens.

questions.text: Which ion is cotransported with dipeptides and tripeptides by intestinal PepT1?
questions.explanation: PepT1 cotransports dipeptides and tripeptides with hydrogen ions across the intestinal brush border.

questions.text: By which mechanism is fructose absorbed across the intestinal epithelium?
questions.explanation: Fructose crosses the luminal membrane via GLUT5-mediated facilitated diffusion, moving down its concentration gradient without sodium coupling.

questions.text: Which basolateral enterocyte transporter exports absorbed iron into blood?
questions.explanation: Ferroportin exports iron across the basolateral enterocyte membrane into blood, where transferrin carries it to tissues.

questions.text: How does increased circulating iron regulate ferroportin-mediated iron exit from enterocytes?
questions.explanation: High iron increases hepcidin, which binds ferroportin and promotes its internalization and degradation, reducing iron export from enterocytes.
options: Decreased hepcidin blocks ferroportin-mediated iron exit
Increased hepcidin activates ferroportin-mediated iron exit

questions.text: By which mechanism does fructose enter small intestinal epithelial cells at the luminal membrane?
questions.explanation: Apical GLUT5 transports fructose by facilitated diffusion; unlike glucose and galactose, it does not use sodium cotransport.

questions.text: During intestinal water absorption, where does actively transported sodium accumulate to draw water osmotically before it enters capillaries?
questions.explanation: Sodium transport draws water into lateral intercellular spaces; it then moves into capillaries, while lacteals absorb dietary lipid.

questions.text: Chylomicrons pass directly from intestinal enterocytes into the hepatic portal blood.
questions.explanation: False: chylomicrons enter intestinal lymphatics and reach systemic blood via the thoracic duct, bypassing the portal vein.

questions.text: Which transport mechanism supports glucose-and-salt oral rehydration therapy during cholera diarrhea?
questions.explanation: Sodium-glucose cotransport remains functional in cholera and carries sodium and glucose together, drawing water absorption and making oral rehydration effective.

questions.text: Which luminal condition increases absorption of inorganic dietary iron?
questions.explanation: Acid and vitamin C keep iron more soluble and reduce ferric iron to the absorbable ferrous form.
options: A high body iron store with reduced erythropoiesis
Acidity with hydrochloric acid and vitamin C
Increased intestinal ferric relative to ferrous iron

questions.text: Which involuntary muscular event is part of the defecation reflex?
questions.explanation: The defecation reflex contracts the sigmoid colon and rectum to propel contents toward the anal canal.
options: Contraction of sigmoid colon and rectum
Contraction of the internal anal sphincter
Relaxation of the rectum and sigmoid colon

questions.text: Lactase deficiency leaves lactose in the intestinal lumen. Which mechanism produces the resulting diarrhea?
questions.explanation: Unabsorbed lactose raises luminal osmolality and retains water in the bowel, producing osmotic diarrhea and sometimes gas from fermentation.

questions.text: Which mechanism explains diarrhea in lactose intolerance?
questions.explanation: Undigested lactose remains in the lumen and raises osmotic pressure, retaining water and causing diarrhea and gas.
options: Toxin-induced secretion of fluid by intestinal crypts
Impaired sacral reflex delaying fecal evacuation
Osmotic retention of fluid by undigested lactose
Excess colonic water absorption during delayed transit
Rapid transit caused by increased intestinal motility

questions.text: Sympathetic innervation is excitatory to the internal anal sphincter.
questions.explanation: True: sympathetic activity contracts the internal anal sphincter and helps maintain continence.

questions.text: Acid reaches the duodenum and triggers a marked increase in watery bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion. Which hormone mediates this response?
questions.explanation: Duodenal acid stimulates S cells to release secretin, which drives bicarbonate-rich pancreatic duct secretion to neutralize chyme.

questions.text: Products of protein digestion stimulate cholecystokinin release more strongly than fat in the duodenum.
questions.explanation: Fat is a particularly strong stimulus for CCK release; protein can stimulate it too, so the stated comparison is reversed.

questions.text: Fat in the duodenum strongly stimulates release of which hormone controlling pancreatic enzyme secretion?
questions.explanation: Cholecystokinin is released in response to duodenal fat and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.

subjects.name: Histology
lectureNames: Histology of Taste bud, palate and pharynx

questions.text: The masticatory mucosa is characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Masticatory mucosa on gingiva and hard palate is protected by stratified squamous keratinized epithelium against friction.
options: It is found on the gums and the soft palate.
It is covered by stratified squamous keratinized epithelium.
It has numerous minor salivary glands.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the anatomical distribution of fungiform papillae on the tongue?
questions.explanation: Fungiform papillae are scattered over the anterior tongue, especially the tip and lateral margins, and contain taste buds.
options: They are arranged in a V-shape near the sulcus terminalis.
They are restricted entirely to the posterior third of the tongue.
They are scattered predominantly across the tips and edges of the tongue.
They form large leaf-like folds along the lateral borders.
They lack taste buds entirely and function purely as mechanoreceptors.

questions.text: Which histological feature is characteristic of the vermilion zone of the lip?
questions.explanation: The vermilion zone has tall connective-tissue papillae with abundant capillary loops close to the surface, giving the lips their red color.
options: Thick keratinized epidermis with deep dermal glands
High dermal papillae with numerous capillary loops
Presence of hair follicles throughout the surface

questions.text: Which type of lingual papillae is associated with numerous nerve endings involved in general sensory sensation?
questions.explanation: Filiform papillae are heavily innervated for general sensation and grip; unlike fungiform, foliate, and circumvallate papillae, they lack taste buds.

questions.text: Which type of lingual papillae are large, dome-shaped structures arranged in a V-shaped row immediately anterior to the sulcus terminalis of the tongue?
questions.explanation: Circumvallate papillae are large, trench-surrounded structures arranged in a V just anterior to the sulcus terminalis.

questions.text: Which of the following statements best characterizes the tongue?
questions.explanation: Tongue skeletal muscle runs in three perpendicular planes, allowing complex movements for speech, chewing, and swallowing.
options: Filiform papillae contain numerous taste buds
The Tongue consists of  skeletal muscle fibers arranged in three perpendicular directions
The ventral surface is lined by simple columnar epithelium
The posterior one-third of the dorsal surface contains abundant filiform papillae
Circumvallate papillae are the most numerous papillae in humans

questions.text: Which histological characteristic describes the vermilion zone (free red margin) of the lip?
questions.explanation: The thin vermilion epithelium lets underlying capillaries show through; numerous tall vascular dermal papillae give the lip its red color.
options: Transparent epidermis with highly vascular dermal papillae
Thickly keratinized epidermis with coarse hair follicles

questions.text: The free red margin of the lip has transparent epidermis, deep vascular papillae and no hair follicles, sebaceous glands or sweat glands.
questions.explanation: The vermilion border has thin translucent epithelium and tall vascular papillae but lacks hair follicles and glands, giving lips their red color.

questions.text: The vermilion border contains hair follicles and sweat glands beneath its transparent epidermis.
questions.explanation: False: vermilion skin lacks hair follicles and sweat glands, so it is prone to drying and appears red through superficial capillaries.

questions.text: The skeletal muscle bundles of the tongue are arranged in vertical, horizontal and longitudinal directions.
questions.explanation: Tongue muscle bundles run in three planes—vertical, transverse/horizontal, and longitudinal—allowing complex shape changes.

questions.text: The vermilion zone has transparent epidermis over numerous deep vascular dermal papillae.
questions.explanation: The vermilion is thin and translucent over highly vascular papillae, without hair follicles, sweat glands, or sebaceous glands.

questions.text: Where are circumvallate papillae mainly located?
questions.explanation: Circumvallate papillae form a V-shaped row just anterior to the sulcus terminalis at the boundary of the posterior tongue.
options: At the tongue tip and edges
Across anterior dorsum in oblique rows

questions.text: The dermal papillae of the vermilion zone are numerous, deep and highly vascular.
questions.explanation: Deep vascular papillae bring capillaries close to the thin vermilion epithelium, creating its characteristic red appearance.

questions.text: Which feature characterizes filiform papillae?
questions.explanation: Filiform papillae provide friction and tactile sensation but lack taste buds, unlike fungiform, foliate, and circumvallate papillae.
options: No taste buds, but touch nerve endings
Occasional taste buds and a broad rounded apex
Numerous taste buds and a surrounding trench
Numerous taste buds in parallel lateral ridges
Taste cells arranged as barrel-shaped organs

questions.text: Which of the following histological features is characteristic of the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: The parotid is enclosed by a well-developed capsule and contains conspicuous striated ducts among its serous acini.
options: Poorly developed capsule and absence of striated ducts
Well-developed capsule and prominent striated ducts
Predominantly mucous acini with no ducts
Lack of connective tissue septa and ducts
Presence of Brunner’s glands within the gland

questions.text: Under routine light microscopy, which histological characteristic distinguishes mucous acini from serous acini in salivary and digestive glands?
questions.explanation: Mucous acini look pale and foamy because mucin washes out during routine staining; distinct cell borders and flattened nuclei are common.
options: Dense apical zymogen granules and dark basophilic cytoplasm
Pale, vacuolated cytoplasm with distinct intercellular cell boundaries
Spherical, centrally located nuclei with prominent nucleoli
Abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum in basal regions

questions.text: Which of the following statements best describes the striated duct ?
questions.explanation: Striated ducts have basal infoldings with interdigitating mitochondria, which support active ion transport and modify saliva.
options: Lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells surrounded by myoepithelial cells
Composed of pyramidal cells containing apical acidophilic zymogen granules
It appears more prominent in the sublingual gland  than other glands
Composed of cuboidal cells containing pale basophilic foamy cytoplasm
Composed of columnar cells with basal infoldings interdigitating with elongated mitochondria

questions.text: Which of the following histological features is characteristic of the parotid salivary gland ?
questions.explanation: Parotid tissue is composed of serous acini and has well-developed intercalated and striated ducts.
options: Predominantly mucous acini with serous demilunes
Formed of pure serous acini and prominent striated duct
The main duct opens on the floor cavity of the mouth
Less developed intercalated and striated ducts
Presence of diffuse intraepithelial goblet cells

questions.text: Which histological feature is characteristic of the submandibular salivary gland?
questions.explanation: Submandibular glands are mixed, predominantly serous, and contain serous demilunes within a lobulated gland enclosed by connective tissue.
options: Pure serous acini with prominent fat cells in the stroma
Predominantly mucous acini lacking striated ducts
A thick connective tissue capsule with presence of serous demilunes
Absence of an outer connective tissue capsule

questions.text: The intercalated ducts of salivary glands are lined by:
questions.explanation: Intercalated ducts are the smallest salivary ducts and are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium.

questions.text: Which microscopic feature distinguishes mucous acini from serous acini in salivary glands?
questions.explanation: Mucous acini have pale cells with distinct boundaries and flattened basal nuclei; serous acini are darker with rounded nuclei.
options: Pyramidal cells with a narrow apex
Distinct cell boundaries and flat basal nuclei
Indistinct cell boundaries and rounded nuclei
Small diameter with a narrow lumen

questions.text: Which ultrastructural feature accounts for the basal striations in salivary striated-duct cells?
questions.explanation: Basal membrane infoldings and aligned mitochondria power ion transport and create the striped appearance of salivary striated ducts.
options: Apical zymogen granules above basal rough endoplasmic reticulum
Contractile processes containing actin and myosin
Basal membrane folds containing elongated mitochondria
Mucin granules above flattened basal nuclei
Intracellular canaliculi lined by numerous microvilli

questions.text: The submandibular gland has a thick capsule and is a mixed gland with predominantly serous acini.
questions.explanation: Submandibular glands are mixed but predominantly serous and are enclosed by a dense connective-tissue capsule.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the histological features of the upper third of the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The upper esophagus has mucous glands in the submucosa and an adventitia because most of the organ lies outside the peritoneal cavity.
options: Submucosa contains serous glands, and the outer layer is serosa
Submucosa contains mucous glands, and the outer layer is adventitia
Submucosa lacks glands, and the outer layer is serosa
Submucosa contains mucous glands, and the outer layer is serosa
Submucosa contains serous glands, and the outer layer is adventitia

questions.text: Which of the following is part of serosa ?
questions.explanation: The outer serosal surface is covered by mesothelium; the other listed structures belong to deeper gut-wall layers.

questions.text: Which layer of the gastrointestinal tract is the outermost layer when the organ is covered by peritoneum?
questions.explanation: Serosa is the outer visceral peritoneal covering; where peritoneum is absent, adventitia anchors the organ to nearby tissues.

questions.text: Which epithelial covering distinguishes serosa from adventitia in the digestive tract?
questions.explanation: Serosa is covered by mesothelium, a simple squamous epithelium; adventitia lacks this outer epithelial covering.

questions.text: In the upper third of the esophagus, which layer contains the scattered mucous esophageal glands?
questions.explanation: Esophageal submucosa contains mucous glands that lubricate the lumen; the upper third of the muscularis externa is striated muscle.

questions.text: Mucous glands in the esophageal submucosa lubricate swallowed food.
questions.explanation: Submucosal esophageal glands secrete mucus that lubricates the lumen and protects epithelium during swallowing.

questions.text: Active parietal cells are characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Active parietal cells expose extensive microvilli-lined intracellular canaliculi where acid secretion occurs.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the structural characteristics of pyloric glands?
questions.explanation: Pyloric glands are branched and coiled tubular glands, rich in mucus-producing and gastrin-secreting cells.

questions.text: Which feature is characteristic of an active parietal cell in the stomach?
questions.explanation: Active parietal cells develop intracellular canaliculi with microvilli, expanding the apical surface for acid secretion.

questions.text: Which histological feature is characteristic of enterochromaffin cells?
questions.explanation: Enterochromaffin cells store peptide or amine secretions in basal granules and release them toward nearby vessels and target cells.

questions.text: Which of the following cells secretes acidic mucous ?
questions.explanation: Mucous neck cells secrete a soluble, relatively acidic mucus, whereas surface mucous cells make thicker protective mucus.

questions.text: Which gastric cells are microscopically similar to cells of the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: Chief cells and parotid serous cells both synthesize protein secretions. Abundant basal rough ER produces basophilia, while apical zymogen granules store their enzymes.

questions.text: In which structural region of the gastric mucosa are parietal (oxyntic) cells most abundant and numerous?
questions.explanation: Oxyntic glands of the fundus and body contain abundant parietal cells; the pyloric region is rich in mucous and endocrine cells.
options: Body and fundus of the stomach

questions.text: Compared to fundic glands, which of the following is true about the pyloric glands ?
questions.explanation: Pyloric glands have deep gastric pits that occupy a larger proportion of the mucosa than fundic pits.
options: They are very crowded and long
They are simple branched tubular glands
They are perpendicular to the surface
They occupy most of the thickness of the mucosa

questions.text: Which of the following histological features is characteristic of the gastric mucosa of the fundus and body?
questions.explanation: Fundic and body glands contain mucous neck cells along with chief and parietal cells; Brunner glands and Paneth cells belong to intestine.

questions.text: A patient with vitamin B12 deficiency is found to have impaired gastric acid secretion due to dysfunction of gastric parietal cells. Which specialized structure is present within these cells and is involved in HCl secretion?
questions.explanation: Intracellular canaliculi increase apical membrane area for HCl secretion; parietal cells also make intrinsic factor for B12 absorption.

questions.text: Which structural feature is prominently seen in an active, acid- secreting gastric parietal cell?
questions.explanation: During acid secretion, parietal cells expand intracellular canaliculi lined with microvilli to increase the secretory surface.
options: Extensive intracellular canaliculi lined with microvilli

questions.text: Which ultrastructural change accompanies active hydrochloric acid secretion by a parietal cell?
questions.explanation: Active acid secretion inserts proton pumps into canalicular membranes: microvilli expand while cytoplasmic tubulovesicles are depleted.
options: Fewer canalicular microvilli with fewer tubulovesicles
More canalicular microvilli with fewer tubulovesicles
Fewer canalicular microvilli with more tubulovesicles
More canalicular microvilli with more tubulovesicles

questions.text: Compared with fundic glands, the gastric pits in the pyloric region occupy approximately what fraction of mucosal thickness?
questions.explanation: Pyloric pits are relatively deep, occupying about half the mucosal thickness, with shorter glands below them.

questions.text: Which paired ultrastructural change indicates an actively secreting parietal cell?
