questions.explanation: Active parietal cells recruit tubulovesicles to the canalicular membrane, increasing microvilli and exposing proton pumps.

questions.text: Which gastric wall layer consists of loose connective tissue covered by a single layer of mesothelial cells?
questions.explanation: Serosa is loose connective tissue covered by a mesothelial cell layer; it is the stomach’s outer peritoneal coat.

questions.text: Which specialized structure in parietal cells provides extensive surface area for hydrochloric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Parietal-cell canaliculi have microvilli and provide a large membrane surface where proton pumps secrete hydrochloric acid.

questions.text: Where are the secretory granules of gastric enteroendocrine cells concentrated?
questions.explanation: Enteroendocrine granules accumulate basally for release toward the lamina propria and nearby capillaries.

questions.text: Which gastric cell secretes acidic soluble mucus and is situated in the neck of the fundic gland?
questions.explanation: Mucous neck cells sit in the neck of fundic glands and release soluble acidic mucus into the gland lumen.

questions.text: Which gastric cell secretes both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?
questions.explanation: Parietal cells produce both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells secrete pepsinogen instead.

questions.text: Which intestinal region is characterized by Peyer patches extending from lamina propria into submucosa?
questions.explanation: Peyer patches are aggregates of lymphoid nodules characteristic of the ileum, often extending into the submucosa.

questions.text: Which tissue layers form the plicae circulares of the small intestine?
questions.explanation: Plicae circulares are permanent folds of mucosa and submucosa that increase surface area and slow chyme passage.

questions.text: Which enterocyte feature prevents luminal food from entering between adjacent epithelial cells?
questions.explanation: Apical tight junctions seal adjacent enterocytes, restricting uncontrolled movement of luminal contents between cells.

questions.text: Which structure is a distinctive aggregate of lymphatic nodules in the ileum, often extending from lamina propria into submucosa?
questions.explanation: Peyer patches are organized aggregates of lymphoid nodules in the ileum that sample intestinal antigens.

questions.text: In which intestinal segment are Brunner glands present in the submucosa?
questions.explanation: Brunner glands lie in the duodenal submucosa and secrete alkaline mucus to protect against acidic gastric contents.

questions.text: Solitary lymphatic nodules can be detected in the colonic submucosa.
questions.explanation: Solitary lymphoid nodules occur in colonic mucosa and may extend into the submucosa as part of gut-associated lymphoid tissue.

questions.text: Solitary lymphatic nodules may be found in the submucosa of the colon.
questions.explanation: True: solitary lymphoid nodules may extend into the colonic submucosa as part of mucosal immune surveillance.

questions.text: Bile canaliculi are lined by fenestrated endothelial cells.
questions.explanation: Bile canaliculi are narrow channels formed between adjacent hepatocytes, not endothelial-lined vascular spaces; the statement is false.

questions.text: Which liver cell stores vitamin A in fat and can differentiate into collagen-synthesizing myofibroblasts?
questions.explanation: Ito (hepatic stellate) cells store vitamin A in lipid droplets and can become collagen-producing myofibroblasts during fibrosis.

questions.text: Which stored material characterizes the Ito cells that can become collagen-producing myofibroblasts during hepatic fibrosis?
questions.explanation: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells store vitamin A in lipid droplets and can become collagen-producing myofibroblasts during fibrosis.

questions.text: Which functional hepatic unit is diamond-shaped and extends between two portal tracts and the nearest central veins?
questions.explanation: The liver acinus is a diamond-shaped functional unit between portal tracts and central veins, organized by oxygen and nutrient gradients.

questions.text: Which cells in the space of Disse store vitamin A and secrete extracellular matrix?
questions.explanation: Ito cells reside in the space of Disse, store vitamin A, and synthesize extracellular matrix when activated.

questions.text: Which cells line hepatic sinusoids adjacent to the space of Disse and possess fenestrae without diaphragms?
questions.explanation: Fenestrated sinusoidal endothelial cells line the liver sinusoids and permit exchange with the space of Disse.

questions.text: In which organ are mucin-secreting glands specifically described within its neck region?
questions.explanation: Mucin-secreting glands in the gallbladder neck contribute mucus to bile and can be prominent around the cystic duct region.

questions.text: Centroacinar cells represent the beginning of which pancreatic component?
questions.explanation: Centroacinar cells are the beginning of intercalated ducts within pancreatic acini and contribute bicarbonate-rich fluid.

questions.text: Which cell is the invaginated initial intercalated duct cell within a pancreatic acinus?
questions.explanation: Centroacinar cells are pale ductal cells that begin the intercalated ducts within pancreatic acini.

questions.text: Which cell is found within pancreatic acinar lumina and represents the invaginated beginning of the intercalated duct?
questions.explanation: Centroacinar cells sit within pancreatic acini and mark the beginning of the intercalated duct system.

questions.text: Both the parotid gland and the exocrine pancreas contain prominent striated ducts.
questions.explanation: Parotid glands have prominent striated ducts, but the exocrine pancreas lacks them; its centroacinar cells lead into intercalated ducts.

questions.text: Which gland contains centroacinar cells and lacks striated ducts?
questions.explanation: The exocrine pancreas has centroacinar cells and ducts but lacks the striated ducts found in salivary glands.

questions.text: Which nutritional deficiency disorder is characteristically associated with edema?
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor is severe protein deficiency with relative calorie intake and low albumin, causing edema; marasmus primarily reflects total energy deficiency.

questions.text: According to standard nutritional guidelines, carbohydrates should typically account for what percentage of total daily caloric intake in a balanced human diet?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates generally supply 45–65% of daily calories in standard nutritional guidance, with the rest from fat and protein.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes HFCS-55?
questions.explanation: HFCS-55 is a sweetener mixture containing about 55% fructose and 45% glucose, not a chemically linked disaccharide.
options: A disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose

questions.text: The disaccharide sucrose is composed of which two monosaccharide units?
questions.explanation: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose linked by their anomeric carbons.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the energy yield of macronutrients ?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate yields about 4 kcal per gram; fat yields 9, protein 4, and alcohol 7 kcal per gram.
options: 1 gram of carbohydrates produces 4 Kcal of energy
1 gram of fats produces 7 Kcal of energy
1 gram of proteins produces 7 Kcal of energy
1 gram of alcohol produces 9 Kcal of energy
1 gram of proteins produces more energy than that of alcohol

questions.text: Complete oxidation of 1g of dietary fats produces ........... of energy
questions.explanation: Fat provides about 9 kcal per gram because its reduced carbon chains yield more energy on oxidation than carbohydrate or protein.

questions.text: In an elderly man with an increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD), which type of fatty acid should be limited in the diet because of its association with increased LDL cholesterol?
questions.explanation: Palmitic acid is a saturated fat that can raise LDL cholesterol; unsaturated oleic and linoleic acids generally have more favorable lipid effects.

questions.text: Which dietary fatty acid is associated with a decreased incidence of coronary heart disease (CHD)?
questions.explanation: Alpha-linolenic acid is an essential omega-3 fatty acid; replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats is associated with lower coronary risk.

questions.text: Marasmus differs from Kwashiorkor in that Marasmus results from?
questions.explanation: Marasmus reflects combined energy and protein deficiency, causing severe wasting without the edema typical of kwashiorkor.
options: Deficiency in both protein and energy/carbohydrates
Pure protein deficiency with adequate carbohydrate intake
Deficiency of essential fatty acids only

questions.text: In which of the following situations or conditions is a positive nitrogen balance typically observed ?
questions.explanation: Growing children retain nitrogen to build new tissue, producing positive nitrogen balance; severe illness or protein deficiency causes negative balance.
options: an individual with inadequate dietary protein intake
a patient during acute stress or surgery
a non-pregnant woman maintaining stable weight

questions.text: Which type of malnutrition occurs when protein deficiency is greater than calorie deficiency ?
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor reflects severe protein deficiency relative to energy intake and commonly causes edema from hypoalbuminemia.

questions.text: Which of the following laboratory findings is characteristic of Kwashiorkor syndrome?
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor commonly causes hypoalbuminemia from severe protein deficiency, contributing to edema.

questions.text: Which metabolic effect on plasma lipoproteins is produced by dietary trans fatty acids
questions.explanation: Trans fatty acids worsen lipoproteins by raising LDL cholesterol and lowering HDL, increasing atherosclerotic risk.
options: Increasing total cholesterol and increasing HDL-C
Decreasing plasma total cholesterol and decreasing TAGs
Suppressing cardiac arrhythmias without altering lipoprotein levels

questions.text: Which physiological state normally involves positive nitrogen balance?
questions.explanation: Growing children retain nitrogen to build new tissue, creating a positive nitrogen balance.

questions.text: Which dietary fatty acid belongs to the omega-3 group associated in the book with reduced coronary heart disease incidence and reduced sudden cardiac death risk?
questions.explanation: Alpha-linolenic acid is an essential omega-3 fatty acid that can be converted to longer-chain omega-3 products.

questions.text: Marasmus usually results from a diet deficient in both calories and protein.
questions.explanation: Marasmus reflects chronic deficiency of both calories and protein, causing severe wasting without the edema typical of kwashiorkor.

questions.text: Which dietary fatty acid is saturated and associated with increased coronary heart disease incidence?
questions.explanation: Palmitic acid is a saturated fatty acid; higher intake of saturated fats can raise LDL cholesterol and coronary risk.

questions.text: Dietary carbohydrate supplies the same energy per gram as dietary fat.
questions.explanation: False: carbohydrate provides about 4 kcal per gram, while fat provides about 9 kcal per gram.

questions.text: Which LDL/HDL pattern is associated with dietary trans fatty acids?
questions.explanation: Dietary trans fats raise LDL while lowering HDL, a particularly unfavorable pattern for coronary risk.
options: Increased LDL with little HDL effect

questions.text: Edematous malnutrition is the term used for marasmus rather than kwashiorkor.
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor is edematous protein-energy malnutrition; marasmus is severe wasting without the characteristic edema.

questions.text: Which enzyme plays the most crucial regulatory role in intracellular lipolysis within adipose tissue?
questions.explanation: Hormone-sensitive lipase mobilizes stored triacylglycerol in adipocytes during fasting or catecholamine stimulation.

questions.text: Activation of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is mediated by which of the following?
questions.explanation: cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates hormone-sensitive lipase and associated lipid-droplet proteins to promote fat mobilization.

questions.text: Which of the following actions happens in obesity
questions.explanation: Adiponectin levels generally fall with obesity and insulin resistance, removing an insulin-sensitizing and anti-inflammatory signal.

questions.text: What is the primary biochemical function of hormone- sensitive lipase (HSL) in human adipose tissue?
questions.explanation: HSL hydrolyzes stored adipose triacylglycerol, releasing fatty acids for oxidation and glycerol for hepatic metabolism.
options: Synthesis of triacylglycerols from fatty acids and glycerol
Hydrolysis of triacylglycerols (TAG) stored in adipose tissue
Transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix
Phosphorylation of free glycerol during gluconeogenesis
Cleavage of dietary chylomicrons in capillary endothelial walls

questions.text: Lipogenesis in adipose tissue depends on the presence of which of the following in appropriate amounts in blood?
questions.explanation: Adipocytes need glucose to generate glycerol-3-phosphate for esterifying fatty acids into stored triglyceride.

questions.text: During TAG synthesis in the well-fed state, adipose tissue relies on the reduction of the glycolytic intermediate DHAP to form glycerol- 3-phosphate. Which of the following best explains why adipocytes cannot directly utilize free glycerol for this process ?
questions.explanation: Adipocytes lack glycerol kinase, so they cannot efficiently phosphorylate free glycerol; they use glycolytic DHAP to make glycerol-3-phosphate.
options: Glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase is inactive in the presence of insulin
Free glycerol cannot penetrate the cell membrane of adipocytes
Adipocytes lack fatty acyl-CoA synthetase enzyme
High intracellular glucose levels competitively inhibit glycerol absorption

questions.text: Which hormonal change is associated with decreased body weight?
questions.explanation: Leptin falls as fat mass and body weight decrease, reducing satiety signaling and contributing to compensatory appetite.

questions.text: Which endocrine alteration characteristically occurs in obesity as body weight increases?
questions.explanation: Leptin secretion generally rises with adipose mass; obesity often includes resistance to its appetite-suppressing signal.
options: Blood levels of free fatty acids decrease
Gluteal fat mobilization rates exceed visceral lipolysis rates

questions.text: As body weight increases, blood leptin levels increase.
questions.explanation: Adipocytes release more leptin as fat mass increases, although resistance to its appetite-suppressing signal is common in obesity.

questions.text: Which change accompanies increasing body weight?
questions.explanation: As adipose mass increases, leptin secretion generally rises because leptin reflects energy stores.

questions.text: How does cyclic AMP promote activation of hormone-sensitive lipase?
questions.explanation: cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates hormone-sensitive lipase and lipid-droplet proteins, initiating lipolysis.
options: Inhibition of adenyl cyclase and reduction of cyclic AMP
Activation of lipase phosphatase and dephosphorylation of lipase
Activation of phosphodiesterase and degradation of cyclic AMP
Activation of protein kinase and phosphorylation of lipase
Stimulation of insulin and dephosphorylation of lipase

questions.text: As body weight increases, the blood leptin concentration decreases.
questions.explanation: Greater adipose mass usually raises circulating leptin; leptin resistance, rather than a lower level, can sustain appetite in obesity.

questions.text: Which glycolytic intermediate is reduced to form glycerol-3-phosphate for triacylglycerol synthesis in adipose tissue?
questions.explanation: Dihydroxyacetone phosphate is reduced to glycerol-3-phosphate, providing the backbone for triacylglycerol synthesis in adipocytes.

questions.text: Which enzyme initiates mobilization of stored triacylglycerol in adipose tissue?
questions.explanation: Hormone-sensitive lipase helps release fatty acids from stored adipose triglycerides after phosphorylation by protein kinase A.

questions.text: Which vitamin is required as a cofactor for hydroxylation reactions during collagen synthesis?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, stabilizing collagen triple helices during synthesis.

questions.text: What is the primary function of vitamin E in the body?
questions.explanation: Vitamin E is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects polyunsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes from oxidative damage.

questions.text: Which of the following used as a coenzyme in carboxylation reaction?
questions.explanation: Biotin carries activated carbon dioxide in carboxylation reactions, including pyruvate and acetyl-CoA carboxylases.

questions.text: Deficiency in vitamin C can cause ?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C reduces ferric iron to ferrous iron in the gut, improving nonheme iron absorption.
options: defect in reducing of vitamin B

questions.text: Which of the following vitamins serves as an essential coenzyme required for carboxylation reactions ?
questions.explanation: Biotin serves as a coenzyme for carboxylases that transfer carbon dioxide in metabolic reactions.

questions.text: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is a required for the activity of which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD derived from riboflavin as a cofactor while oxidizing succinate in the TCA cycle.

questions.text: A patient with a diet deficient in a particular water-soluble vitamin develops dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Which vitamin is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation: Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, classically dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.

questions.text: Which two water-soluble vitamins serve as key coenzymes (FMN/FAD and NAD/NADP) in cellular electron transfer and redox reactions?
questions.explanation: Riboflavin forms FMN and FAD, while niacin forms NAD and NADP; these coenzymes carry electrons in redox reactions.
options: Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid) and Vitamin B7 (Biotin)
Vitamin B5 (Pantothenic acid) and Folic acid

questions.text: Which of the following clinical features is a characteristic sign of riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency?
questions.explanation: Riboflavin deficiency can inflame the mouth and lips, causing angular stomatitis, cheilosis, or glossitis.

questions.text: Which enzyme uses FAD as a hydrogen acceptor in the tricarboxylic acid cycle?
questions.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD as an electron acceptor while oxidizing succinate to fumarate in the TCA cycle.

questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency causes pellagra, characterized by dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia?
questions.explanation: Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, classically marked by dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.

questions.text: Which vitamin supports hydroxylation of proline and lysine in procollagen?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is required for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases that stabilize collagen by hydroxylating procollagen residues.

questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency produces angular stomatitis and dermatitis?
questions.explanation: Riboflavin forms FMN and FAD; deficiency can produce angular stomatitis, cheilosis, glossitis, and dermatitis.

questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency is associated with angular stomatitis and dermatitis?
questions.explanation: Riboflavin deficiency can cause angular stomatitis and dermatitis because epithelial tissues require flavin-dependent metabolism.

questions.text: Which vitamin is covalently bound to enzymes as a prosthetic group for carboxylation reactions?
questions.explanation: Biotin is covalently attached to carboxylases and carries activated CO2 during enzymatic carboxylation.

questions.text: Riboflavin supplies NAD and NADP, whereas niacin supplies FMN and FAD.
questions.explanation: Riboflavin is the precursor of FMN and FAD, whereas niacin supplies NAD and NADP; the statement reverses their coenzymes.

questions.text: Which nutrient has the main function of preventing nonenzymatic oxidation of biologically important cell components?
questions.explanation: Vitamin E interrupts lipid peroxidation and protects membranes and other biologically important cell components from oxidation.

questions.text: Which trace element is a constituent of the metalloenzymes RNA and DNA polymerase?
questions.explanation: Zinc is a structural and catalytic component of many DNA- and RNA-polymerizing enzymes.

questions.text: Which metal is a constituent of RNA and DNA polymerases?
questions.explanation: Zinc coordinates catalytic sites in many DNA and RNA polymerases and helps stabilize their structure.

questions.text: Phosphorus is important for pH regulation and is a component of ATP, nucleic acids and phospholipids.
questions.explanation: True: phosphate buffers intracellular and extracellular pH and is part of ATP, nucleic acids, and phospholipids.

questions.text: Which trace element is a constituent of xanthine oxidase?
questions.explanation: Xanthine oxidase contains molybdenum in its catalytic center for purine oxidation to uric acid.

questions.text: Which trace element is important for glutathione peroxidase and cooperates with vitamin E to prevent peroxide injury?
questions.explanation: Selenium is incorporated into glutathione peroxidase, which reduces peroxides and works with vitamin E antioxidant defenses.

questions.text: Which trace metal is a constituent of xanthine oxidase?
questions.explanation: Molybdenum is part of the molybdenum cofactor used by xanthine oxidase in purine degradation.

questions.text: Complete absence of glucuronyl transferase with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia describes which book category?
questions.explanation: Complete UDP-glucuronosyltransferase absence causes severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in Crigler–Najjar type I.

questions.text: In hemolytic jaundice, excessive erythrocyte destruction increases unconjugated bilirubin in the blood.
questions.explanation: Accelerated red-cell breakdown releases heme that becomes unconjugated bilirubin, exceeding the liver’s conjugation capacity.

questions.text: Common bile duct obstruction prevents bilirubin passage into the intestine. Which blood bilirubin change is described?
questions.explanation: Bile-duct obstruction prevents conjugated bilirubin excretion into the intestine, causing conjugated bilirubin to reflux into blood.
options: No rise in either bilirubin fraction

questions.text: Which congenital jaundice has complete absence of glucuronyl transferase activity?
questions.explanation: Crigler–Najjar type I reflects near-total absence of bilirubin-conjugating UGT1A1 activity; type II retains some enzyme function.

questions.text: Bile salts are more effective detergents than bile acids because of their enhanced amphipathic properties.
questions.explanation: Conjugated bile salts are more water-soluble and amphipathic than bile acids, making them more effective detergents in micelles.

questions.text: Hepatic 7-alpha-hydroxylase catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step in bile-acid synthesis from cholesterol.
questions.explanation: True: hepatic cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase catalyzes the rate-limiting first step in the classic bile-acid synthesis pathway.

questions.text: Uridine administration improves the anemia and decreases urinary orotate excretion in orotic aciduria.
questions.explanation: Uridine bypasses the UMP-synthesis block in hereditary orotic aciduria, restoring pyrimidine supply and reducing excess orotate.

questions.text: Which enzyme catalyzes the regulated carbamoyl-phosphate-forming step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis?
questions.explanation: CPS II catalyzes the regulated cytosolic entry step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis by producing carbamoyl phosphate from glutamine.

questions.text: Which enzyme catalyzes the regulated first step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Cytosolic carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II catalyzes the regulated first committed step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

questions.text: Hydroxyurea suppresses DNA synthesis by directly inhibiting which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides; hydroxyurea blocks this step and limits DNA synthesis.

questions.text: Which pyrimidine-pathway end product inhibits carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II?
questions.explanation: UTP feedback-inhibits CPS II, slowing pyrimidine synthesis when nucleotide supply is adequate.

questions.text: Which purine nucleotide is structurally mimicked by 6-mercaptopurine in the book’s description?
questions.explanation: 6-Mercaptopurine resembles IMP and inhibits purine synthesis after conversion to active nucleotide metabolites.

questions.text: What change produced by alcohol metabolism contributes to alcoholic fatty liver?
questions.explanation: Alcohol metabolism raises the hepatic NADH/NAD+ ratio, suppressing fatty-acid oxidation and favoring triglyceride accumulation.

questions.text: S-adenosylmethionine is a lipotropic methyl donor for choline synthesis that helps prevent fatty liver.
questions.explanation: S-adenosylmethionine donates methyl groups for phosphatidylcholine synthesis, supporting VLDL export and reducing hepatic fat accumulation.

questions.text: Choline promotes fatty liver by blocking the synthesis of phospholipids.
questions.explanation: False: choline is needed to synthesize phosphatidylcholine and export hepatic triglyceride in VLDL; deficiency can promote fatty liver.

questions.text: Methionine’s lipotropic action results from reduced hepatic phospholipid synthesis.
questions.explanation: Methionine supports phosphatidylcholine synthesis through methyl donation, helping export fat from liver; reduced phospholipid synthesis would worsen steatosis.

subjects.name: Pathology
lectureNames: Diseases & tumors of the oral cavity
Diseases and tumors of salivary glands
Infectious Diseases of Small Intestine & intestinal polyps
Congenital anomalies of small & large intestine

questions.text: How is oral leukoplakia best classified in pathology?
questions.explanation: Oral leukoplakia is a potentially malignant white plaque that cannot be otherwise classified; biopsy assesses dysplasia or carcinoma.

questions.text: What is the most common type of cancer in the oral cavity?
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of the oral cavity because the mucosa is lined by squamous epithelium.

questions.text: Which of the following oral mucosal lesions is clinically defined as a white patch or plaque that cannot be scraped off ?
questions.explanation: Leukoplakia is a persistent, non-scrapable white oral plaque after other specific causes are excluded; it may harbor dysplasia.

questions.text: A 58-year-old male smoker presents for a routine oral examination. The dentist identifies a well-demarcated, firm white mucosal patch along the lateral border of his tongue. The clinician attempts to scrape the patch off using a tongue depressor, but it cannot be detached or wiped away. What is the clinical term for this white mucosal lesion?
questions.explanation: A persistent non-scrapable white plaque in a smoker, especially on the lateral tongue, is leukoplakia until biopsy excludes dysplasia.

questions.text: Which histological type characterizes carcinoma arising from the oral mucosal lining?
questions.explanation: Oral mucosal lining gives rise to squamous cell carcinoma, the dominant histologic type of oral cancer.

questions.text: Which oral lesion is defined as a white plaque that cannot be scraped off and cannot be characterized as another disease?
questions.explanation: Leukoplakia is a non-scrapable white lesion not otherwise classifiable; candidiasis often wipes away, while erythroplakia is red.

questions.text: The recurrence of pleomorphic adenoma is attributed to:
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma can recur when pseudopod-like tumor buds extend beyond its capsule and are left behind during excision.
options: Budding of tumor cells beyond the capsule.

questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with a painless mass in the parotid gland. Biopsy and histological examination reveal a neoplastic proliferation consisting of a mixture of mucous cells, epidermoid (squamous-like) cells, and intermediate cells forming sheets and small mucinous cysts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma contains mucous, intermediate, and epidermoid cells and is a common malignant salivary gland tumor.

questions.text: In a condition characterized by xerostomia and keratoconjunctivitis sicca, which microscopic finding is typically seen in the affected glands?
questions.explanation: Sjögren syndrome causes lymphocytic and plasma-cell infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands, progressively destroying secretory tissue.
options: Diffuse neutrophilic infiltration with abscess formation
Lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration forming lymphoid follicles
Extensive eosinophilic infiltration with granuloma formation
Proliferation of adipocytes replacing the glandular tissue
Fibroblastic proliferation with dense collagen deposition

questions.text: Which condition is characteristically associated with xerostomia (dry mouth) due to autoimmune destruction of salivary glands?
questions.explanation: Sjögren syndrome is autoimmune lymphocytic destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands, causing xerostomia and dry eyes.

questions.text: Which is the most common site of pleomorphic adenoma?
questions.explanation: The parotid is the most common site of pleomorphic adenoma because it is the largest salivary gland.

questions.text: A 42-year-old female presents with a slow-growing, painless mass in the right parotid gland. Biopsy reveals epithelial ductal structures intermixed with myxoid and chondroid stroma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma has mixed epithelial and myoepithelial elements in chondromyxoid stroma, the classic benign parotid tumor pattern.

questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with a slow-growing, painful mass in her submandibular salivary gland. A fine-needle aspiration biopsy is performed, and histological examination reveals tumor cells arranged in nest-like patterns surrounding round, cyst-like spaces filled with mucinous material, creating a cribriform pattern. What’s the diagnosis ?
questions.explanation: A painful submandibular mass with cribriform nests and perineural invasion suggests adenoid cystic carcinoma.

questions.text: Which benign salivary gland tumor is histologically characterized by papillary projections into cystic spaces lined by oncocytes, surrounded by a dense lymphoid stroma?
questions.explanation: Warthin tumor shows oncocytic epithelium lining cystic spaces with papillary projections and a lymphoid stroma.

questions.text: What is the natural host of the mumps virus?
questions.explanation: Humans are the natural reservoir for mumps virus; transmission occurs through respiratory droplets and saliva.

questions.text: A 7-year-old unimmunized boy presents with low-grade fever, malaise, and painful bilateral swelling over the angle of the jaw causing upturned ear lobules. Which pathogen is the most common cause of this presentation ?
questions.explanation: Mumps virus classically causes painful bilateral parotitis with jaw-angle swelling and upward displacement of the earlobes.

questions.text: A patient presents with fever, headache, and painful bilateral swelling of the parotid glands. Which antibody is most useful for diagnosing an acute mumps infection?
questions.explanation: Mumps-specific IgM supports a current or recent infection; IgG alone does not diagnose acute mumps. A negative IgM result, especially after vaccination, does not exclude infection.

questions.text: Pleomorphic adenoma most commonly affects the sublingual gland.
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma most often arises in the parotid gland; sublingual tumors are uncommon and have a higher malignancy likelihood.

questions.text: Which is the commonest primary malignant tumor of the salivary glands according to the book?
questions.explanation: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common primary malignant salivary-gland tumor in many textbook series.

questions.text: Which salivary tumor shows cystic spaces with papillary projections lined by columnar oncocytes and underlying lymphoid stroma?
questions.explanation: Warthin tumor has papillary oncocytic epithelium overlying lymphoid stroma, often forming cystic spaces.

questions.text: In Sjögren syndrome, which microscopic finding accompanies destruction of lacrimal and salivary gland architecture?
questions.explanation: Sjögren syndrome produces focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with lymphoid follicles and progressive glandular destruction.
options: Ductal and myoepithelial cells in myxoid stroma
Lymphocytes and plasma cells forming follicles
Mucous, epidermoid and intermediate tumor cells

questions.text: Which salivary gland malignancy has a classic cribriform, Swiss-cheese microscopic pattern?
questions.explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma shows cribriform architecture with pseudocystic spaces, the classic “Swiss-cheese” pattern.

questions.text: A salivary tumor is encapsulated and contains epithelial/myoepithelial elements in myxoid stroma with chondroid islands. Which tumor is it?
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma combines epithelial and myoepithelial cells with myxoid or chondroid stroma and is usually encapsulated.

questions.text: Humans are the only natural hosts of mumps virus.
questions.explanation: Mumps circulates among humans, with no established nonhuman natural reservoir, so the statement is true.

questions.text: Autoimmune destruction of both lacrimal and salivary glands produces dry eyes and xerostomia. Which syndrome best fits?
questions.explanation: Sjögren syndrome targets salivary and lacrimal glands, producing the paired symptoms of dry mouth and dry eyes.

questions.text: Detection of IgM by ELISA is a laboratory method used in the diagnosis of mumps.
questions.explanation: True: mumps-specific IgM by ELISA supports diagnosis of acute infection, especially when collected near symptom onset.

questions.text: Which virus is specifically named in the book as a cause of sialadenitis?
questions.explanation: Mumps virus infects salivary glands and is a classic cause of acute sialadenitis, especially parotitis.

questions.text: Which parotid tumor combines epithelial/myoepithelial elements with myxoid tissue containing chondroid islands?
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma mixes epithelial and myoepithelial cells with myxoid or chondroid stroma, creating its varied histology.

questions.text: Which condition is classically characterized by chronic heartburn and inflammatory mucosal changes just above the gastro-esophageal junction?
questions.explanation: GERD causes chronic heartburn and inflammatory mucosal changes at the distal esophagus near the gastroesophageal junction.

questions.text: A patient with a history of recurrent chronic vomiting develops sudden hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals longitudinal mucosal lacerations at the gastroesophageal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful vomiting; it causes hematemesis without full-thickness rupture.

questions.text: A patient develops repeated forceful vomiting followed by sudden upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Endoscopy reveals a mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mallory–Weiss syndrome is a mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful retching; Boerhaave is a full-thickness rupture.

questions.text: A 55-year-old male with a long history of chronic GERD undergoes esophageal biopsy, which reveals replacement of the normal stratified squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar mucosa in the lower esophagus. Which of the following is the most significant clinical outcome associated with this condition ?
questions.explanation: Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia from chronic reflux and increases the risk of distal esophageal adenocarcinoma.
options: Increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
Loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus
Increased risk of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma
Longitudinal mucosal tears at the esophagogastric junction

questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive difficulty swallowing both solid foods and liquids, accompanied by nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food and weight loss. Esophageal manometry reveals incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and aperistalsis in the smooth- muscle body of the esophagus. Barium swallow shows smooth 'bird's-beak' tapering at the gastroesophageal junction. What’s the likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation: Achalasia combines impaired LES relaxation with absent esophageal peristalsis, causing dysphagia to solids and liquids and a bird-beak appearance.

questions.text: Loss of myenteric ganglion cells causing failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation is characteristic of which disorder?
questions.explanation: Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons, so the LES fails to relax and esophageal peristalsis is impaired.

questions.text: Failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation on swallowing, aperistalsis and increased resting sphincter tone most strongly indicate which disorder?
questions.explanation: Achalasia combines failed LES relaxation, aperistalsis, and elevated resting sphincter tone due to enteric neuron loss.

questions.text: Barrett esophagus increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.
questions.explanation: Barrett metaplasia replaces distal esophageal squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar mucosa, increasing adenocarcinoma risk.

questions.text: Which esophageal condition is caused by reduced lower esophageal sphincter tone allowing acidic gastric contents to reflux?
questions.explanation: Reduced LES tone permits acid reflux into the esophagus, causing reflux esophagitis and mucosal injury.

questions.text: Severe vomiting is followed by longitudinal mucosal tears at the esophagogastric junction. Which condition is described?
questions.explanation: Mallory–Weiss syndrome is a longitudinal mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful vomiting or retching.

questions.text: What is the most common site of esophageal squamous cell carcinomas?
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma classically occurs in the middle third of the esophagus, while adenocarcinoma favors the distal third.

questions.text: A mass arising in the middle third of the esophagus is most likely to show which histological feature?
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma is common in the middle esophagus and may show keratinization; adenocarcinoma is more typical distally.

questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss. Endoscopy reveals an ulcerated mass in the lower third of the esophagus, associated with Barrett’s esophagus. What is the most likely type of malignancy?
questions.explanation: Lower esophageal adenocarcinoma is associated with chronic reflux and Barrett metaplasia, whereas squamous carcinoma is more common in the upper esophagus.

questions.text: Which esophageal tumor is most commonly located in the middle third and associated with tobacco and alcohol use?
questions.explanation: Tobacco and alcohol are major risks for esophageal squamous carcinoma, which commonly arises in the middle esophagus.

questions.text: The lower third is the most common esophageal site for squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.explanation: Esophageal SCC often arises in the middle third, while adenocarcinoma is more common in the lower third.

questions.text: The commonest cause of chronic gastritis is:
questions.explanation: Helicobacter pylori is the most common cause of chronic gastritis because persistent colonization drives long-term mucosal inflammation.

questions.text: Which condition can cause vitamin B12 deficiency anemia?
questions.explanation: Chronic atrophic gastritis can destroy parietal cells and intrinsic-factor production, impairing B12 absorption and causing pernicious anemia.

questions.text: Which mucosal change in chronic gastritis is considered precancerous ?
questions.explanation: Chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia is a precancerous change that can progress to dysplasia and gastric adenocarcinoma.
options: Basal cell hyperplasia of squamous epithelium
Smooth muscle hypertrophy of the pylorus

questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with fatigue, lower extremity paresthesias, and a smooth, painful red tongue (glossitis). Laboratory studies reveal macrocytic anemia and markedly reduced vitamin B12 levels. A gastric mucosal biopsy confirms chronic mucosal atrophy of the fundus and body with intestinal metaplasia. What is the underlying etiology of this condition?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells causes intrinsic-factor loss and vitamin B12 deficiency, producing glossitis and neurologic symptoms.
options: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells

questions.text: Which change in chronic gastritis is associated with increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma?
questions.explanation: Atrophy and intestinal metaplasia reflect chronic mucosal injury and create a premalignant pathway toward gastric adenocarcinoma.
options: Tubulovesicular expansion in resting parietal cells
Apical mucinogen storage in surface cells
Normal renewal by isthmus stem cells

questions.text: A patient has been taking NSAIDs regularly for chronic pain and develops epigastric discomfort. Endoscopy reveals a mucosal ulcer in the stomach. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A mucosal crater in a patient using NSAIDs is a peptic ulcer; COX inhibition reduces protective gastric prostaglandins.

questions.text: Which peptic ulcer location is listed first in descending order of frequency?
questions.explanation: The first part of the duodenum is the most common peptic-ulcer site among the listed locations.

questions.text: A peptic ulcer remains superficial to the muscularis mucosa.
questions.explanation: A peptic ulcer extends through the muscularis mucosa into submucosa or deeper; a superficial mucosal defect is an erosion.

questions.text: Gastrinoma is associated with gastric hypersecretion and peptic ulcerations that may involve the duodenum.
questions.explanation: Gastrinomas cause Zollinger–Ellison syndrome with marked acid hypersecretion and recurrent ulcers, often distal to the duodenal bulb.

questions.text: Linitis plastica means:
questions.explanation: Linitis plastica is diffuse infiltrating gastric carcinoma that stiffens and thickens the wall, reducing its ability to distend.
options: Diffuse infiltration of the gastric wall by malignancy.

questions.text: Which immunohistochemical marker is characteristically positive in most gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs)?
questions.explanation: Most GISTs express KIT (CD117), reflecting activating KIT or PDGFRA pathway mutations in interstitial-cell-of-Cajal lineage tumors.

questions.text: A patient presents with progressive early satiety, weight loss, and persistent epigastric discomfort. Endoscopy reveals a diffusely thickened, rigid stomach with reduced distensibility, giving it a characteristic “leather-bottle” appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Linitis plastica is diffuse infiltrative gastric carcinoma with desmoplastic stiffening, limiting distension and producing a leather-bottle stomach.

questions.text: Which pathological variant of gastric adenocarcinoma is characterized by discohesive tumor cells containing abundant intracellular mucin that compresses the nucleus to the periphery?
questions.explanation: Diffuse gastric carcinoma has discohesive signet-ring cells with intracellular mucin and infiltrates the wall rather than forming a glandular mass.
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the stomach

questions.text: The most important prognostic factor for gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors is their location.
questions.explanation: Carcinoid prognosis depends strongly on primary location because site predicts metastatic potential and outcome; the statement is true.

questions.text: A gastric tumor consists of discohesive signet-ring cells infiltrating the wall and provoking marked desmoplasia. Which carcinoma pattern is present?
questions.explanation: Diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma contains poorly cohesive signet-ring cells that infiltrate the wall and provoke desmoplasia.

questions.text: Which gross ulcer pattern supports a malignant gastric ulcer?
questions.explanation: Malignant gastric ulcers often have raised, everted edges and an indurated base, reflecting infiltrative tumor growth.
options: Superficial erosions with diffusely red mucosa
Flattened mucosa with loss of rugal folds
Longitudinal tear at the esophagogastric junction
Raised everted edges with an indurated base

questions.text: Which neoplasm is associated with a CDH1 mutation?
questions.explanation: Germline CDH1 loss impairs E-cadherin and predisposes to familial diffuse gastric carcinoma with discohesive signet-ring cells.

questions.text: The whole stomach is thickened and converted into a rigid, shortened tube without an intraluminal mass. Which tumor pattern accounts for this leather-bottle appearance?
questions.explanation: Diffuse carcinoma infiltrates the whole stomach wall, causing rigid thickening and the “leather bottle” appearance.

questions.text: c-KIT, a diagnostic marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors, encodes a cell-adhesion protein.
questions.explanation: False: c-KIT encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase, not a cell-adhesion protein; its expression helps identify GISTs.

questions.text: In a patient with small-intestinal malabsorption, PAS-positive mucosal macrophages containing acid-fast-negative bacilli suggest which disease?
questions.explanation: Whipple disease causes PAS-positive foamy macrophages containing Tropheryma whipplei in small-intestinal lamina propria, producing malabsorption.

questions.text: In a colonic biopsy showing superficial inflammation with crypt abscesses, what cells fill the dilated degenerated crypts?
questions.explanation: Crypt abscesses are dilated colonic crypts filled with neutrophils, reflecting active mucosal inflammation.

questions.text: Which inflammatory bowel disease has marked serositis and transmural inflammation?
questions.explanation: Crohn disease causes transmural inflammation and serositis, unlike ulcerative colitis, which is primarily mucosal and submucosal.

questions.text: Which inflammatory bowel disease causes intermittent diarrhea and may form fistulas to the urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: Transmural Crohn inflammation can fistulize from bowel into adjacent organs such as the urinary bladder, causing recurrent infection or pneumaturia.

questions.text: Ulcerative colitis can progress through epithelial dysplasia to malignant transformation in the colon.
questions.explanation: Longstanding ulcerative colitis increases colorectal cancer risk through chronic inflammation, dysplasia, and eventual carcinoma.

questions.text: Which of the following is an important factor affecting the prognosis of a gastrointestinal tumor?
questions.explanation: Tumor site affects symptoms, resectability, spread, and available treatment, making it an important prognostic factor.

questions.text: A low-fiber diet with a high fat content is a risk factor for colorectal adenocarcinoma in the book.
questions.explanation: High-fat, low-fiber dietary patterns are associated with colorectal cancer risk in the referenced teaching; fiber may dilute and speed transit of carcinogens.

questions.text: Which colonic condition carries a virtually 100% risk of progression to adenocarcinoma according to the book?
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis produces innumerable adenomas and near-certain colorectal cancer without prophylactic management.

questions.text: A patient with a family history of colorectal cancer and 200 colonic adenomas meets the polyp-count criterion for familial adenomatous polyposis.
questions.explanation: True: familial adenomatous polyposis is characterized by hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas in an affected patient.

questions.text: An appendiceal carcinoid can arise from argentaffin cells and appear as a circumscribed yellow nodule at the tip.
questions.explanation: Appendiceal neuroendocrine tumors often arise from argentaffin cells at the tip and appear as small yellow, circumscribed nodules.

questions.text: Ground-glass hepatocytes containing accumulated viral antigen most strongly support which viral hepatitis?
questions.explanation: HBsAg accumulation in hepatocytes produces the characteristic ground-glass cytoplasm of chronic hepatitis B.

questions.text: Fibrosis is a characteristic finding of acute viral hepatitis rather than chronic hepatitis.
questions.explanation: False: fibrosis develops in chronic hepatitis after ongoing injury and repair; acute viral hepatitis is usually not fibrotic.

questions.text: Chronic viral hepatitis shows hepatocyte steatosis, portal lymphoid infiltrates and bile-duct injury. Which virus is suggested by this histological combination?
questions.explanation: Chronic HCV commonly produces portal lymphoid aggregates, steatosis, and bile-duct injury, a characteristic biopsy pattern.

questions.text: Interface necrosis occurs at the junction of a central vein and the surrounding hepatic parenchyma.
questions.explanation: Interface hepatitis occurs at the limiting plate near portal tracts, not at the central vein; the central zone is a different location.

questions.text: Ground-glass hepatocytes caused by cytoplasmic viral antigen accumulation suggest which viral hepatitis?
questions.explanation: HBV surface antigen accumulation in hepatocyte cytoplasm produces the characteristic ground-glass appearance.

questions.text: Which condition involves bacterial inflammation of intrahepatic bile ducts with purulent bile after obstruction by a stone?
questions.explanation: A stone obstructing bile flow can permit bacterial ascent into intrahepatic ducts, producing purulent ascending cholangitis.

questions.text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis characteristically raises antimitochondrial antibody titres.
questions.explanation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with p-ANCA; antimitochondrial antibodies are characteristic of primary biliary cholangitis.

questions.text: Which chronic biliary disease has cholangiocarcinoma among its listed complications?
questions.explanation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis causes chronic bile-duct inflammation and strictures and increases cholangiocarcinoma risk.

questions.text: Which progressive disease produces patchy intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile-duct fibrosis and predisposes to cholangiocarcinoma?
questions.explanation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis causes progressive multifocal strictures and fibrosis of intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts and raises cholangiocarcinoma risk.

questions.text: Which antibody is characteristically increased in primary biliary cholangitis?
questions.explanation: Antimitochondrial antibody, especially against PDC-E2, is a characteristic serologic marker of primary biliary cholangitis.

questions.text: A liver biopsy shows iron deposits that stain blue with Prussian blue. Mutation of HFE reduces hepcidin and causes excessive intestinal iron absorption. Which inherited disease is described?
questions.explanation: HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis lowers hepcidin signaling, increases intestinal iron absorption, and deposits iron in tissues.

questions.text: Mutation of HFE and other genes reduces hepcidin and causes excessive intestinal iron absorption. Which inherited disease is described?
questions.explanation: HFE/hepcidin-pathway mutations increase intestinal iron absorption, producing hereditary hemochromatosis and progressive iron deposition.

questions.text: The book states that leptospirosis is usually diagnosed by serological detection of antibodies in the patient’s serum.
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis is commonly diagnosed by serum antibody tests, especially after the early bacteremic phase.

questions.text: A mutation in HFE leading to excess iron absorption is characteristic of which liver disorder?
questions.explanation: HFE mutation disrupts iron regulation and causes hereditary hemochromatosis with excess intestinal iron absorption.

questions.text: PAS-positive globules accumulated in hepatocytes suggest which inherited disorder?
questions.explanation: Misfolded alpha-1 antitrypsin accumulates in hepatocytes as PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules.

questions.text: Low serum ceruloplasmin, hepatic copper accumulation and Kayser-Fleischer rings suggest which inherited disorder?
questions.explanation: Wilson disease causes copper accumulation in liver and other tissues, low ceruloplasmin, and Kayser–Fleischer rings.

questions.text: Which exposure is particularly associated with hepatic adenoma in women of reproductive age?
questions.explanation: Prolonged oral contraceptive exposure is associated with hepatic adenomas, especially in women of reproductive age.

questions.text: Which liver tumor is associated with prolonged oral contraceptive use in women of reproductive age?
questions.explanation: Hepatic adenomas are associated with prolonged estrogen exposure, including oral contraceptives, and may bleed or rarely transform.

questions.text: Chronic hepatitis B is a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, and ulcerative colitis is a risk factor for colorectal carcinoma.
questions.explanation: Chronic HBV promotes hepatocellular carcinoma, while longstanding ulcerative colitis raises colorectal carcinoma risk through dysplasia.

questions.text: Control of hepatitis C infection addresses a viral risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.explanation: True: chronic HCV infection can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, so prevention and control reduce this risk.

questions.text: Exposure to a toxin from Aspergillus flavus in poorly stored grains can cause p53 mutations. Which liver tumor is associated with this exposure?
questions.explanation: Aflatoxin B1 from Aspergillus-contaminated grain can mutate TP53 and promote hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.text: How does a gallstone cause intestinal obstruction known as gallstone ileus?
questions.explanation: Gallstone ileus occurs when a stone passes through a cholecystoenteric fistula and lodges in the small bowel, often near the ileocecal valve.
options: Precipitation of bilirubin within the gall bladder
Impaction of a stone at the pancreatic ampulla
Obstruction of the cystic duct by a stone
Obstruction of the common bile duct by a stone

questions.text: Which pancreatic disease causes acute inflammation, fat necrosis, dystrophic calcification and hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis releases enzymes that cause autodigestion, fat necrosis, hemorrhage, and acute inflammation.

questions.text: Cancer in the head of the pancreas can obstruct the common bile duct embedded in that region.
questions.explanation: The pancreatic head surrounds the distal common bile duct; a tumor there can obstruct bile flow and cause jaundice.

questions.text: Which tumor is associated with raised CEA and CA 19-9, although these markers are not specific enough for screening?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma may raise CEA and CA 19-9; these markers support monitoring but lack screening specificity.

questions.text: Acute pancreatitis may cause epigastric pain radiating to the back, with pancreatic hemorrhage and fat necrosis.
questions.explanation: True: acute pancreatitis commonly causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and can produce hemorrhage and fat necrosis.

questions.text: Pancreatic head carcinoma may produce jaundice by obstructing the common bile duct.
questions.explanation: A pancreatic-head mass can compress the intrapancreatic common bile duct, causing obstructive jaundice.

questions.text: Pancreatic duct obstruction is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis.
questions.explanation: Alcohol and smoking are common causes of chronic pancreatitis; duct obstruction can cause it but is not the most common cause overall.

questions.text: A mass in the head of the pancreas causes obstructive jaundice. CEA and CA19-9 are elevated but are not considered specific screening tests. Which tumor best matches the book’s description?
questions.explanation: A pancreatic-head ductal carcinoma can obstruct the common bile duct and cause jaundice; CEA and CA19-9 support but do not screen reliably.

questions.text: Acute pancreatitis can cause fat necrosis with hemorrhage in and around the pancreas.
questions.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes released in acute pancreatitis digest peripancreatic fat, causing fat necrosis and hemorrhage.

questions.text: Pancreatic acinar injury is followed by release of amylase into the circulation, with increased serum and urinary levels. Which condition is specifically diagnosed by this finding in the book?
questions.explanation: Acinar injury in acute pancreatitis releases amylase into blood and urine, supporting diagnosis alongside symptoms and imaging.

subjects.name: Pharmacology
lectureNames: Pharmacology of Anti H. Pylori, Antacids & GERD

questions.text: A 24-year-old female used to have nausea and vomiting when traveling on a ship. Which of the following can be used to prevent motion sickness?
questions.explanation: First-generation H1 antihistamines cross the blood–brain barrier and suppress vestibular signaling, helping prevent motion sickness.

questions.text: Which of the following drugs can be used to treat vomiting due to motion sickness
questions.explanation: Dimenhydrinate blocks vestibular H1 signaling and is useful for motion-sickness nausea.

questions.text: Which antiemetic drug is associated with extrapyramidal side effects due to dopamine D₂ receptor blockade?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide blocks central D₂ receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone; this antiemetic action can also cause extrapyramidal effects.

questions.text: A 28-year-old traveler applies a transdermal patch behind her ear 4 hours prior to embarking on a boat trip to prevent motion sickness and sea nausea. What active anticholinergic drug is formulated in this patch?
questions.explanation: Scopolamine blocks muscarinic signaling in vestibular pathways and is delivered transdermally for motion-sickness prevention.

questions.text: Which drug is preferred as a prophylactic antiemetic for motion sickness during a flight ?
questions.explanation: Hyoscine (scopolamine) blocks muscarinic signaling from the vestibular system and is commonly used before travel for motion-sickness prevention.

questions.text: Which antiemetic agent can cause extrapyramidal side effects, including parkinsonism, due to central dopamine D2 receptor blockade?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide enters the CNS and blocks dopamine D₂ receptors, so it can cause dystonia, akathisia, or parkinsonism.

questions.text: Which receptor class is selectively blocked by ondansetron to produce its antiemetic action?
questions.explanation: Ondansetron selectively blocks 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and in vomiting pathways to prevent nausea and emesis.

questions.text: Which listed antiemetic is an H1 antagonist used prophylactically for motion sickness?
questions.explanation: Dimenhydrinate is a first-generation H1 antihistamine that suppresses vestibular pathways and prevents motion-sickness nausea.

questions.text: Domperidone causes more extrapyramidal reactions than metoclopramide because it readily crosses the blood-brain barrier.
questions.explanation: Domperidone penetrates the blood–brain barrier poorly and causes fewer central extrapyramidal effects than metoclopramide.

questions.text: Which antiemetic is listed as an H1 antagonist used prophylactically for motion sickness?
questions.explanation: Dimenhydrinate is a first-generation H1 antagonist with anticholinergic effects that help prevent motion sickness.

questions.text: Which antiemetic with central D2 antagonism can cause extrapyramidal reactions such as parkinsonism?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide blocks central D2 receptors and can cause acute dystonia, akathisia, or parkinsonian extrapyramidal effects.

questions.text: Which antiemetic is specifically described as better tolerated when supplied as a transdermal patch for motion sickness?
questions.explanation: The hyoscine patch provides sustained antimuscarinic prophylaxis for motion sickness and is described as better tolerated than other formulations.

questions.text: Which of the following are adverse effects of dimenhydrinate ?
questions.explanation: Dimenhydrinate commonly causes CNS sedation and drowsiness because it crosses the blood–brain barrier.

questions.text: Which condition is commonly treated with second- generation antihistamines?
questions.explanation: Second-generation H1 antihistamines relieve allergic rhinitis and urticaria with less CNS sedation than first-generation agents.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the pharmacokinetics of Famotidine?
questions.explanation: Famotidine is cleared substantially by the kidneys, so renal impairment requires dose adjustment to avoid accumulation.
options: It has a long t1/2 (taken once/day).
It needs dose adjustment in renal failure.
It is a less potent H2 blocker.

questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding Omeprazole
questions.explanation: Omeprazole is taken before meals so absorbed drug is present when meal-stimulated proton pumps become active.
options: It is a strong base ionized in the acidic medium of the stomach
It requires an acidic medium to be absorbed
It should be given 30-60 minutes before meals
It should not be taken on an empty stomach
It is metabolized in the kidney

questions.text: Which of the following has been proposed as a possible mechanism contributing to rebound gastric acid hypersecretion after discontinuation of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)?
questions.explanation: After chronic acid suppression, gastrin may rise; stopping PPIs can reactivate upregulated acid-secretory pathways and cause transient rebound hypersecretion.
options: Decreased gastrin secretion and permanent proton-pump inhibition
Increased gastrin levels with reactivation of proton pumps
Increased somatostatin secretion with reduced acid secretion

questions.text: Why are H₂-receptor antagonists generally less preferred than proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) for acid suppression?
questions.explanation: H₂ blockers suppress acid less potently than PPIs because they block histamine signaling but do not inhibit the final H⁺/K⁺ pump.
options: They have a higher risk of severe hepatotoxicity
They completely inhibit gastric mucus secretion
They have lower efficacy in suppressing gastric acid secretion than PPIs
They irreversibly damage gastric parietal cells
They have no effect on histamine-mediated acid secretion

questions.text: A 54-year-old male went to the hospital presenting with epigastric pain and was diagnosed with a peptic ulcer. The doctor prescribed him Drug X. After 4 months, he returned to the hospital complaining of severe bone pain. Investigations confirmed that he had developed osteoporosis. Which of the following best represents Drug X ?
questions.explanation: Lansoprazole suppresses gastric acid by inhibiting the H+/K+-ATPase and treats peptic ulcer disease.

questions.text: Which of the following adverse effects may occur with rapid IV infusion of ranitidine ?
questions.explanation: Rapid IV H2-blocker administration can cause bradycardia and hypotension, likely through cardiovascular effects of abrupt high plasma levels.

questions.text: To achieve optimal clinical efficacy and maximal inhibition of active gastric H+/K+-ATPase pumps, when should oral proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) be administered relative to food intake?
questions.explanation: PPIs bind most effectively when pumps are activated by a meal, so dosing 30–60 minutes beforehand aligns drug absorption with pump activation.
options: At bedtime on a full stomach

questions.text: Famotidine, cimetidine, and ranitidine suppress gastric acid secretion by acting through which pharmacologic mechanism?
questions.explanation: Famotidine, cimetidine, and ranitidine block histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells, reducing gastric acid secretion.

questions.text: Compared with H₂-receptor blockers, what is a characteristic feature of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)?
questions.explanation: PPIs inhibit the final H+/K+-ATPase step and suppress acid more completely than H2 blockers, which block only histamine signaling.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the pharmacokinetics of famotidine?
questions.explanation: Famotidine is cleared largely by the kidneys; dose reduction is needed in renal impairment to avoid accumulation.
options: It has a long t1/2 (taken once/day)
it needs dose adjustment in renal failure
lt is a less potent H2 blocker

questions.text: Which of the following mechanisms best explains why prolonged therapy with Proton Pump Inhibitors can cause diarrhea as an adverse effect ?
questions.explanation: Long-term acid suppression can permit microbial overgrowth in the stomach and intestine, contributing to diarrhea.
options: Direct stimulation of D2 receptors in CTZ
Inactivation of pepsinogen via alkalinization of the pancreatic secretions
Destruction of gastric parietal cells and loss of intrinsic factor
Hyperplasia of the basal cell layer of esophageal squamous epithelium
Marked hypochlorhydria leading to microbial overgrowth

questions.text: What is the approximate oral bioavailability of famotidine?
questions.explanation: Famotidine is incompletely absorbed orally, with bioavailability around one-half; renal impairment can prolong exposure.

questions.text: Which medication increases the risk of Clostridium difficile colitis due to marked suppression of gastric acid?
questions.explanation: PPIs reduce gastric acid and are associated with increased risk of C. difficile infection compared with less potent acid suppression.

questions.text: Which drug can increase C. difficile infection risk through potent proton-pump suppression of gastric acidity?
questions.explanation: Lansoprazole suppresses gastric acid and has been associated with increased susceptibility to enteric infections such as C. difficile.

questions.text: Rapid intravenous administration of an H2-receptor blocker can cause hypotension and bradycardia.
questions.explanation: Rapid IV H2 blockade can produce bradycardia and hypotension, so administer these drugs slowly when given intravenously.

questions.text: Which proton-pump inhibitor is described in the book as having the most potent anti-H. pylori effect?
questions.explanation: Lansoprazole is identified in the book’s regimen as having strong anti-H. pylori activity; eradication still requires combination therapy.

questions.text: What oral bioavailability is stated for famotidine?
questions.explanation: Famotidine has oral bioavailability of about 50%, reflecting incomplete absorption after dosing.

questions.text: Compared with H2 antagonists, what combination of efficacy and duration characterizes proton pump inhibitors?
questions.explanation: PPIs inhibit active pumps for a prolonged period and provide stronger acid suppression than reversible H2-receptor antagonists.
options: Lower efficacy and more prolonged effect
Higher efficacy and more prolonged effect

questions.text: For an enteric-coated proton-pump inhibitor, which administration instruction best matches the book?
questions.explanation: Enteric-coated PPIs should be taken before a meal so the drug is absorbed before meal-stimulated proton pumps become active.
options: Use without any relation to food or pump activity
Take immediately after a meal to preserve the coating
Take during the meal to maximize bioavailability
Crush the coating and take with acidic food

questions.text: When should an enteric-coated proton pump inhibitor generally be taken relative to a meal?
questions.explanation: Enteric-coated PPIs are generally taken 30–60 minutes before a meal so absorption precedes pump activation.

questions.text: Which mechanism contributes to osteoporosis during prolonged PPI therapy?
questions.explanation: Reduced gastric acidity may impair calcium absorption, a proposed mechanism linking prolonged PPI use with fracture risk; evidence is not fully settled.
options: Reduced calcium absorption with reduced acidity
Improved collagen cross-linking from high homocysteine

questions.text: Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E2 analogue that decreases gastric acid secretion.
questions.explanation: False: misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue, not PGE2.

questions.text: Which antiulcer drug is contraindicated in pregnancy because it may cause uterine contractions and abortion?
questions.explanation: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analogue that stimulates uterine contractions and can cause pregnancy loss.

questions.text: Which ulcer-protective drug is an aluminum salt of sulfated sucrose that forms a protective barrier in an acidic medium?
questions.explanation: Sucralfate is a sulfated sucrose–aluminum complex that polymerizes in acid and adheres to ulcerated mucosa as a barrier.

questions.text: Which cytoprotective drug is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue used for NSAID-induced gastric ulcers?
questions.explanation: Misoprostol is a PGE1 analogue that replaces protective prostaglandin effects and reduces NSAID-related gastric injury.

questions.text: Which mucosal protective drug has anti-H. pylori activity as its main effect and can cause black stools with teeth and tongue discoloration?
questions.explanation: Bismuth protects mucosa and has anti-H. pylori activity; it can harmlessly darken stool, tongue, and teeth.

questions.text: Anti-H. pylori eradication regimens include an acid suppressant because antibiotic treatment alone is ineffective.
questions.explanation: Antibiotics eradicate H. pylori, while acid suppression improves treatment conditions and ulcer healing; regimens use both.

questions.text: Which agent used for bleeding esophageal varices inhibits release of peptides, such as glucagon, that contribute to the hyperdynamic circulation?
questions.explanation: Octreotide suppresses glucagon and other gut peptides, reducing splanchnic flow and portal pressure during variceal bleeding.

questions.text: After liver transplantation, which original indication prevents routine corticosteroid withdrawal after 3–6 months in the book’s criteria?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune disease may recur in the graft, so the cited transplant criteria retain corticosteroids longer rather than routinely withdrawing them early.

questions.text: Which drug lowers ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy by acidifying colonic contents and producing an osmotic laxative effect?
questions.explanation: Lactulose is fermented to acids that trap ammonia as ammonium and retains water osmotically, lowering ammonia while increasing stool passage.

questions.text: Adding intravenous nitroglycerin to intravenous vasopressin decreases systemic vasoconstriction and accentuates portal hypotension.
questions.explanation: True: nitroglycerin offsets vasopressin’s systemic vasoconstriction and can further lower portal pressure.

questions.text: Why are opioid antimotility agents contraindicated in acute gastroenteritis in infants and children?
questions.explanation: Opioid antimotility drugs can cause ileus and respiratory depression in children, and slowing transit may worsen infectious or toxin-mediated illness.
options: Fluid retention and proximal muscle wasting

questions.text: Atropine is combined with diphenoxylate partly to relieve its spasmogenic effect.
questions.explanation: Atropine reduces intestinal spasm and cramping from diphenoxylate; a separate deterrent effect discourages misuse.

questions.text: Which constipation intervention supplies indigestible dietary fiber that adsorbs water and increases stool bulk?
questions.explanation: Bran is indigestible fiber that absorbs water and increases stool bulk, helping low-volume constipation.

questions.text: Which laxative works by unabsorbed fibers adsorbing water to increase stool bulk and stimulate peristalsis?
questions.explanation: Bran is insoluble fiber that absorbs water, increases stool bulk, and stimulates peristalsis.

questions.text: How does loperamide reduce intestinal peristalsis?
questions.explanation: Loperamide activates peripheral opioid receptors in the myenteric plexus, reducing acetylcholine release and slowing propulsive motility.
options: Activates presynaptic opioid receptors and reduces acetylcholine release
Blocks enkephalinase and inhibits secretion without changing motility
Activates alpha-2 receptors to inhibit motor activity
Reduces prostaglandin synthesis through its salicylate component

questions.text: Metronidazole’s poor intestinal absorption makes it primarily a luminal amoebicide.
questions.explanation: False: metronidazole is well absorbed systemically and treats tissue trophozoites; poorly absorbed drugs are used as luminal amoebicides.

questions.text: Which drug is the book first-choice luminal amoebicide for asymptomatic intestinal cyst passers?
questions.explanation: Diloxanide remains in the intestinal lumen and is used to clear cysts in asymptomatic E. histolytica carriers.

questions.text: Which tissue amebicide is cardiotoxic and is given in hospital with ECG monitoring?
questions.explanation: Emetine is a tissue amebicide with serious cardiotoxicity, so its historical use required hospital supervision and ECG monitoring.

questions.text: Helicobacter pylori possess ________ that helps to neutralize stomach acid.
questions.explanation: H. pylori urease converts urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide, buffering the acidic microenvironment around the organism.

questions.text: Which of the following culture media is most appropriate for the isolation of Helicobacter pylori from a gastric biopsy specimen?
questions.explanation: H. pylori is fastidious and grows on enriched selective blood media under microaerophilic conditions.

questions.text: Which virulence factor allows Helicobacter pylori to neutralize gastric acid and survive within the stomach?
questions.explanation: H. pylori urease converts urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, buffering acid around the organism and enabling gastric colonization.

questions.text: Which of the following is a non-invasive method used for the initial diagnosis of Helicobacter pylori infection?
questions.explanation: A stool antigen test detects active H. pylori infection without endoscopy and can also confirm eradication.

questions.text: Which of the following is an important virulence factor of Helicobacter pylori?
questions.explanation: CagA is delivered into gastric epithelial cells and alters signaling; it contributes to inflammation, ulcer disease, and cancer risk.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the fecal antigen test for H.pylori ?
questions.explanation: Stool antigen is noninvasive and detects active H. pylori, making it useful both for initial diagnosis and confirmation after treatment.
options: A non-invasive test that relies on radioactively labeled urea
An invasive test performed using a phenol red indicator
A non-invasive test that is effective in the definitive diagnosis of H. pylori
A non-invasive test that is effective for initial diagnosis and treatment follow-up
An invasive test that detects bacterial DNA in feces

questions.text: Helicobacter Pylori Possess ........... that helps to neutralize stomach acidic medium
questions.explanation: Urease breaks down urea to produce ammonia, helping H. pylori survive the acidic stomach environment.

questions.text: A patient with H. pylori infection is exposed to the highly acidic environment of the stomach. Which bacterial enzyme helps H. pylori survive by neutralizing gastric acid?
questions.explanation: Urease hydrolyzes urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, buffering the local acid around H. pylori.

questions.text: Which enzyme produced by Helicobacter pylori enables its survival in the acidic gastric lumen by neutralizing local acid?
questions.explanation: Urease produces ammonia from urea, creating a locally less acidic environment that helps H. pylori survive in the stomach.

questions.text: Which non-invasive test detects H. pylori material in feces and is useful for diagnosis and treatment follow-up?
questions.explanation: Fecal antigen testing detects H. pylori material in stool and is useful for diagnosis and post-treatment confirmation.

questions.text: H. pylori urease helps the organism survive gastric acidity by converting urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: Urease hydrolyzes urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide; ammonia buffers acid and protects the bacterium near gastric epithelium.

questions.text: Which enzyme allows H. pylori to survive gastric acidity by generating ammonia from urea?
questions.explanation: Urease generates ammonia by hydrolyzing urea, buffering the local acid around H. pylori.

questions.text: Which Helicobacter pylori virulence factor alters the host cytoskeleton and triggers oncogenic signals?
questions.explanation: CagA enters host cells through a type IV secretion system and alters cytoskeletal and oncogenic signaling pathways.

questions.text: H. pylori infection is associated with gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma.
questions.explanation: Chronic H. pylori-driven lymphoid stimulation can produce gastric MALT lymphoma, and eradication may regress early lesions.

questions.text: Which noninvasive H. pylori follow-up test detects microbial material in feces?
questions.explanation: Stool antigen testing detects current H. pylori infection and is suitable for follow-up after treatment.

questions.text: Which serological marker is most useful for diagnosing acute hepatitis B during the window phase when neither HBsAg nor anti-HBs is detectable?
questions.explanation: Anti-HBc IgM remains detectable in the HBV window period after HBsAg disappears and before anti-HBs appears.

questions.text: The hepatitis A vaccine used for active immunization is a live attenuated virus vaccine.
questions.explanation: The standard hepatitis A vaccine is inactivated, not live attenuated; it induces protective anti-HAV antibodies.
