questions.text: Which hepatitis B marker’s presence is associated with high infectivity?
questions.explanation: HBeAg indicates active HBV replication and is associated with high infectivity.

questions.text: Which hepatitis virus is specifically associated with high mortality among pregnant women?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis E can cause fulminant disease and high mortality in pregnancy, especially with genotype 1 infection.

questions.text: Which hepatitis virus depends on HBV for productive infection and may be acquired simultaneously with it?
questions.explanation: HDV depends on HBV surface antigen for its envelope and can be acquired with HBV coinfection or as superinfection.

questions.text: Hepatitis A does not produce a chronic infection or carrier state.
questions.explanation: True: hepatitis A is an acute, self-limited infection and does not establish a chronic carrier state.

questions.text: Which condition is explicitly described as having no chronic infection, carriers or predisposition to hepatocellular carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Classic teaching describes hepatitis E as an acute infection without chronic carriers or HCC risk; chronic infection can occur in immunosuppressed patients.

questions.text: Which HBV marker indicates high infectivity during the acute illness?
questions.explanation: HBeAg reflects active HBV replication and correlates with higher viral load and infectivity during acute infection.

questions.text: Which bacterium produces a preformed heat-stable food toxin causing abrupt nausea and vomiting 2-4 hours after ingestion, with little or no fever?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus produces preformed heat-stable enterotoxin, causing abrupt vomiting within a few hours of ingestion.

questions.text: Which organism causes gastroenteritis after raw or undercooked seafood and grows in 8% sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: V. parahaemolyticus is halophilic and associated with raw seafood; growth in high salt helps distinguish it from other enteric bacteria.

questions.text: Which diarrheagenic E. coli group uses bundle-forming pili and produces attachment-and-effacement of intestinal microvilli?
questions.explanation: EPEC uses bundle-forming pili for attachment and causes attaching-and-effacing lesions that disrupt intestinal microvilli.

questions.text: Which foodborne bacterium can continue replicating in refrigerated food because it grows at 4°C?
questions.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes can grow at refrigeration temperatures and contaminate chilled foods.

questions.text: Watery diarrhea with cramps and little vomiting develops 8-16 hours after a reheated meat dish. Which organism best fits the book description?
questions.explanation: C. perfringens produces enterotoxin after sporulating in the intestine, causing cramps and watery diarrhea after reheated meat.

questions.text: After a contaminated meal, severe nausea, vomiting and diarrhea begin abruptly within 2–4 hours, with little or no fever. Which organism best fits this food-intoxication pattern?
questions.explanation: Rapid vomiting within hours without fever suggests preformed, heat-stable Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin rather than invasive infection.

questions.text: Which effect distinguishes ETEC heat-labile toxin from its heat-stable toxin?
questions.explanation: ETEC heat-labile toxin activates adenylate cyclase and raises cAMP; its heat-stable toxin raises cGMP instead.
options: Heat-labile toxin requires uptake into macrophages
Heat-labile toxin produces intestinal mucosal invasion
Heat-labile toxin causes bloody inflammatory diarrhea

questions.text: Which intestinal disturbance is attributed to Vibrio cholera toxin in the book?
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin persistently activates adenylate cyclase, driving crypt chloride and water secretion that causes profuse watery diarrhea.
options: Excess crypt secretion of electrolytes and water
Osmotic retention of fluid by magnesium sulfate
Retention of undigested lactose in the lumen

questions.text: Which intracellular mediator is increased by the heat-labile toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli?
questions.explanation: ETEC heat-labile toxin activates adenylate cyclase through ADP-ribosylation of Gs, raising cAMP and driving intestinal secretion.

questions.text: Which organism produces toxins associated with antimicrobial-associated pseudomembranous enterocolitis?
questions.explanation: Clostridioides difficile toxins A and B damage colonic epithelium and cause antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous enterocolitis.

questions.text: Bloody diarrhea follows ingestion of an undercooked hamburger contaminated with E. coli O157:H7. What is the action of its verocytotoxin?
questions.explanation: EHEC verocytotoxin inactivates the 60S ribosome and stops protein synthesis, damaging intestinal and renal endothelial cells.

questions.text: Which bacterium can cause mesenteric adenitis clinically resembling acute appendicitis?
questions.explanation: Yersinia enterocolitica invades terminal ileum and mesenteric nodes, producing fever and right-lower-quadrant pain that mimic appendicitis.

questions.text: Which E. coli group is associated with bloody diarrhea after undercooked hamburger ingestion?
questions.explanation: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli produces Shiga-like toxins and can cause bloody diarrhea after contaminated or undercooked food.

questions.text: Bloody diarrhea caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 can be complicated by hemolytic uremic syndrome.
questions.explanation: Shiga-like toxin can damage renal microvascular endothelium after bloody diarrhea, producing hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.

questions.text: Which organism is associated with bloody diarrhea after undercooked hamburger and can produce hemolytic uremic syndrome?
questions.explanation: EHEC in undercooked beef produces Shiga-like toxin, causing hemorrhagic colitis and possible hemolytic uremic syndrome.

questions.text: Bloody diarrhea follows ingestion of undercooked hamburger. The implicated organism produces verocytotoxins and may cause hemolytic uremic syndrome. Which is it?
questions.explanation: EHEC verocytotoxin can injure vascular endothelium, causing hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome.

questions.text: Which organism is described as causing bacillary dysentery?
questions.explanation: Shigella invades colonic mucosa and causes inflammatory bacillary dysentery with fever, blood, mucus, and tenesmus.

questions.text: Which virus is described as the most important cause of epidemic gastroenteritis in adults?
questions.explanation: Norovirus spreads efficiently through food, water, and person-to-person contact, driving many adult gastroenteritis outbreaks.

questions.text: In enteric bacteria, O antigen is somatic and H antigen is flagellar.
questions.explanation: True: Salmonella O antigen is part of the somatic lipopolysaccharide, while H antigen is associated with flagella.

questions.text: An enteric fever causes lymphoid hyperplasia in Peyer patches, followed by oval ulcers along the long axis of the terminal ileum. Which cause fits this pattern?
questions.explanation: S. Typhi invades Peyer patches and causes oval longitudinal ulcers along the terminal ileum after lymphoid necrosis.

questions.text: Which fluid enrichment medium is used before selective solid media for isolation of Salmonella from enteric-fever specimens?
questions.explanation: Selenite broth enriches Salmonella from specimens while inhibiting competing intestinal flora before plating on selective agar.

questions.text: During the third week of an enteric-fever illness, diarrhea with a typical pea-soup stool may develop. Which organism causes the principal form of this disease?
questions.explanation: Salmonella Typhi causes enteric fever, and intestinal ulceration in later illness can produce pea-soup diarrhea.

questions.text: Deoxycholate citrate agar is a selective solid medium listed for Salmonella culture.
questions.explanation: DCA inhibits many Gram-positive organisms and differentiates enteric bacteria, supporting selective isolation of Salmonella.

questions.text: Which Salmonella species causes the principal form of enteric fever?
questions.explanation: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi causes classic enteric (typhoid) fever and is transmitted from human cases or carriers.

questions.text: Which infection may produce typical pea-soup stool in its third week?
questions.explanation: Pea-soup stool during the third week is associated with Salmonella Typhi enteric fever and intestinal ulceration.

subjects.name: Parasitology
lectureNames: Trematodes of the liver (Fasciola species & Clonorchis sinensis)
Cestodes of the liver (Echinococcus granulosus & Echinococcus multilocularis)

questions.text: A patient presents with fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tender hepatosplenomegaly, and marked eosinophilia. The symptoms developed several weeks after consuming raw aquatic vegetables. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fasciola larvae migrate through liver parenchyma after ingestion of aquatic-plant metacercariae, causing fever, RUQ pain, and eosinophilia.

questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with fever and tender hepatomegaly, he had a history of eating unwashed vegetables from the freshwater canals. Ultrasound reveals inflammatory tracks in the liver parenchyma, and blood tests show marked eosinophilia Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute Fasciola larvae migrate through liver parenchyma after metacercariae on aquatic vegetables are ingested, causing fever and eosinophilia.

questions.text: Which of the following is an effective measure for the prevention of Fasciola infection ?
questions.explanation: Washing aquatic vegetables with vinegar can reduce Fasciola metacercariae before ingestion, interrupting plant-borne transmission.
options: Immersion of vegetables in a water with vinegar
Preventing dogs from entering slaughter houses

questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with high fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tender hepatomegaly, and pronounced peripheral blood eosinophilia. She reports frequently eating fresh, unwashed watercress harvested near a sheep pasture.This is characteristic of which parasitic infection?
questions.explanation: Watercress can carry Fasciola metacercariae; migrating immature flukes cause acute hepatic inflammation and marked eosinophilia.

questions.text: Which organ is primarily affected by Fasciola infection?
questions.explanation: Fasciola juveniles migrate through the liver, and adults inhabit bile ducts, so the liver and biliary tract are primary targets.

questions.text: Which helminth infection is documented to predispose to cholangiocarcinoma after chronic biliary injury?
questions.explanation: Chronic Clonorchis sinensis infection inflames bile ducts and increases cholangiocarcinoma risk.

questions.text: Fever, tender hepatomegaly and eosinophilia follow consumption of leafy vegetables. Which parasitic infection does this triad suggest?
questions.explanation: Fever, tender hepatomegaly, and eosinophilia after raw leafy vegetables suggest acute Fasciola migration through liver tissue.

questions.text: Which parasite causes an acute hepatic migratory phase through liver parenchyma before entering the bile ducts?
questions.explanation: Fasciola larvae traverse hepatic tissue before reaching bile ducts; this migratory phase distinguishes it from fish-borne biliary flukes.

questions.text: Which parasitic stage is passed in the stool of the canine definitive host rather than being produced in the stool of a human intermediate host?
questions.explanation: Dogs shed Echinococcus granulosus eggs in feces; humans are accidental intermediate hosts and develop hydatid cysts instead of shedding eggs.

questions.text: Serological detection of specific antibodies is used to confirm suspected hydatid disease.
questions.explanation: Hydatid serology detects antibodies to Echinococcus and supports diagnosis alongside imaging; sensitivity depends on cyst site and stage.

questions.text: Both Fasciolopsiasis and heavy hookworm infection can cause protein-losing enteropathy.
questions.explanation: Heavy hookworm causes intestinal blood and protein loss, while Fasciolopsis can damage mucosa and impair protein absorption.

questions.text: Heterophyes eggs may migrate to the brain and produce ectopic disease.
questions.explanation: True: small Heterophyes eggs may enter circulation and embolize to the brain, causing ectopic disease.

questions.text: Which trematode is acquired in Egypt from insufficiently cooked or salted Mugil and Tilapia fish?
questions.explanation: Heterophyes metacercariae encyst in Mugil and Tilapia fish; undercooked or salted fish can transmit infection in Egypt.

questions.text: A trematode acquired from inadequately cooked Tilapia produces eggs that may disseminate to the brain or spinal cord and cause vascular embolism. Which parasite is implicated?
questions.explanation: Heterophyes metacercariae in inadequately cooked fish develop in the intestine; small eggs can enter circulation and embolize to heart or CNS.

questions.text: Eggs from deeply embedded Heterophyes adults can enter blood vessels and cause embolic complications in the brain or spinal cord.
questions.explanation: True: small Heterophyes eggs can cross the intestinal wall, enter vessels, and embolize to the brain or spinal cord.

questions.text: Metagonimus infection is acquired through which route?
questions.explanation: Metagonimus infects people who eat fish containing encysted metacercariae; the adult fluke then inhabits the small intestine.
options: Ingestion of hydatid eggs from dogs
Ingestion of encysted metacercariae in fish
Ingestion of embryonated eggs on vegetables

questions.text: Heterophyes eggs reaching cardiac blood vessels can produce ectopic embolic lesions.
questions.explanation: Small Heterophyes eggs can penetrate intestinal vessels and embolize to cardiac tissues, producing ectopic lesions.

questions.text: Which intestinal helminth can produce macrocytic megaloblastic anemia by consuming large amounts of vitamin B12 and folic acid?
questions.explanation: Diphyllobothrium latum competes for intestinal vitamin B12 and can cause macrocytic megaloblastic anemia.

questions.text: Which drug produces temporary paralysis of Taenia solium, allowing expulsion of the intact parasite?
questions.explanation: Quinacrine can paralyze Taenia worms and facilitate expulsion; other cestocides act through different mechanisms or kill the parasite.

questions.text: Which agent is described as preferable in T. solium infection because temporary paralysis leads to expulsion of an intact worm?
questions.explanation: Quinacrine was historically preferred in T. solium because it paralyzed and expelled the worm intact, limiting egg release from segments.

questions.text: Taenia saginata requires one intermediate host, cattle, in its life cycle.
questions.explanation: True: humans acquire Taenia saginata from cysticerci in cattle, its single intermediate host.

questions.text: Aberrant migration of Taenia gravid segments can cause obstructive appendicitis.
questions.explanation: A migrating gravid Taenia segment can enter the appendix and obstruct its lumen, provoking appendicitis.

questions.text: Which tapeworm has eggs that are diagnostic in human feces and directly infective for its human intestinal cycle?
questions.explanation: H. nana eggs are shed in stool and are immediately infective, enabling direct human-to-human transmission and autoinfection.

questions.text: The eggs of Hymenolepis nana passed in stool can serve as both diagnostic and infective stages.
questions.explanation: True: mature H. nana eggs are passed in stool for diagnosis and are immediately infective when swallowed.

questions.text: Which tapeworm can complete a direct cycle in humans after ingestion of eggs, without a required animal intermediate host?
questions.explanation: H. nana can transmit directly from swallowed eggs and maintain itself through autoinfection without an obligatory animal intermediate host.

questions.text: Niclosamide (Yomesan) kills both adult Hymenolepis nana worms and their cysticercoid larvae.
questions.explanation: Niclosamide mainly kills adult H. nana in the intestinal lumen; cysticercoid larvae in villi may survive and require repeat treatment.

questions.text: Which cestode is transmitted by ingestion of eggs through contaminated hands, especially those of food handlers, and can complete development in one human host?
questions.explanation: Hymenolepis nana eggs can spread by contaminated hands and complete development in one human host through direct infection and autoinfection.

questions.text: The obstructive jaundice of ascariasis results from larval migration through the lungs.
questions.explanation: Ascaris-related biliary obstruction occurs when adult worms migrate from the intestine into ducts, not during larval lung migration.

questions.text: Which parasite can cause intestinal obstruction by congregation of adult worms into a mass?
questions.explanation: Ascaris adults can aggregate into a bolus in the small bowel, causing mechanical intestinal obstruction.

questions.text: Which parasite can cause acute intestinal obstruction when many adult worms aggregate into a mass?
questions.explanation: Ascaris adults may aggregate into a worm bolus that obstructs the intestine, especially when infection is heavy.

questions.text: Which ascariasis prevention measure directly addresses the use of human excreta as an agricultural fertilizer?
questions.explanation: Treating or safely composting human excreta before field use prevents Ascaris eggs from contaminating crops and soil.
options: Treating excreta by sunlight or raised temperature
Treating infected people in endemic areas

questions.text: An intestinal roundworm’s adult migrates into the common bile duct and causes obstructive jaundice. Which parasite is described?
questions.explanation: Ascaris adults can migrate from the small intestine into the common bile duct and obstruct bile flow.

questions.text: Which transmission route characterizes ascariasis?
questions.explanation: Ascariasis follows ingestion of embryonated eggs from contaminated soil or food; the eggs develop outside the host first.
options: Ingestion of fish containing plerocercoid larvae
Ingestion of embryonated eggs from contaminated soil
Skin penetration by third-stage filariform larvae

questions.text: Human excreta should be treated before agricultural use as part of ascariasis prevention.
questions.explanation: Ascaris eggs mature in soil, so treating human waste before fertilizer use interrupts environmental transmission.

questions.text: Both Ascaris lumbricoides infection and intestinal Entamoeba histolytica infection may cause appendicitis.
questions.explanation: Ascaris may enter the appendix, while amoebic colitis can ulcerate or perforate the bowel, allowing both to contribute to appendiceal inflammation.

questions.text: During which stage of hookworm infection can Loeffler syndrome develop?
questions.explanation: Hookworm larvae migrate through the lungs after skin penetration, and this pulmonary phase can trigger Loeffler eosinophilic pneumonitis.

questions.text: An intestinal nematode causes chronic blood and protein loss, with microcytic hypochromic anemia, hypoproteinemia and growth retardation. Which infection best matches this mechanism?
questions.explanation: Hookworms attach to intestinal mucosa and consume blood, causing chronic iron and protein loss that can impair growth.

questions.text: Iron supplementation in hookworm infection replaces iron depleted through intestinal blood loss.
questions.explanation: Hookworms attach to intestinal mucosa and feed on blood, depleting iron; replacement therapy treats the resulting deficiency.

questions.text: In the Ancylostoma duodenale life cycle, larvae migrate through the lungs before they are swallowed and mature in the small intestine.
questions.explanation: True: Ancylostoma filariform larvae penetrate skin, migrate through lungs, are swallowed, and mature in the small intestine.

questions.text: Which intestinal nematode infection causes blood loss by buccal-capsule attachment and may require iron replacement?
questions.explanation: Ancylostoma buccal capsules attach to intestinal mucosa and cause ongoing blood loss, often requiring iron replacement.

questions.text: A colorless oval helminth egg with rounded poles, a thin shell and an immature segmented ovum is detected in stool. Which egg does this describe?
questions.explanation: Hookworm eggs are colorless, oval, thin-shelled, and usually contain a segmented morula when passed in stool.

questions.text: Which laboratory approach is described as the most reliable for diagnosis of visceral larva migrans?
questions.explanation: Visceral larva migrans is caused by migrating Toxocara larvae, so serologic antibody detection supports diagnosis when human stool contains no eggs.
options: Human stool examination for adult-worm eggs

questions.text: Which zoonotic parasite causes visceral larva migrans in humans after ingestion of eggs from dog or cat sources?
questions.explanation: Toxocara eggs from dogs or cats infect people, but larvae migrate through tissues rather than mature in the human intestine.

questions.text: Visceral larva migrans is diagnosed by finding Toxocara eggs in human stool.
questions.explanation: Humans are accidental hosts for Toxocara; larvae migrate in tissue and do not mature to egg-producing adults in the intestine.

questions.text: Which infective stage is ingested in human toxocariasis?
questions.explanation: Humans acquire toxocariasis by ingesting embryonated eggs containing second-stage larvae from contaminated soil or hands.
options: Hydatid cyst in infected herbivore organs
Rhabditiform larva passed in human stool

questions.text: Tender hepatomegaly, persistent marked eosinophilia and hyperglobulinemia occur in a child with a history of pica. Which parasite best matches this combination?
questions.explanation: Pica exposes children to embryonated Toxocara eggs; tissue migration causes eosinophilia, hyperglobulinemia, and tender hepatomegaly.

questions.text: Intestinal Capillaria philippinensis infection can produce hypokalemia.
questions.explanation: Severe Capillaria diarrhea causes potassium loss in stool and can produce hypokalemia.

questions.text: Raw freshwater-fish ingestion is followed by severe watery diarrhea with weight loss and protein loss. Which nematode infection is most consistent with the book?
questions.explanation: Capillaria philippinensis is acquired from raw freshwater fish and can cause severe watery diarrhea, malabsorption, and protein loss.

questions.text: Raw fish ingestion is followed by severe watery diarrhea, wasting, edema and low potassium from protein-losing enteropathy. Which intestinal nematode best fits this pattern?
questions.explanation: Capillaria philippinensis is acquired from infected fish and can cause severe protein-losing enteropathy, wasting, edema, and electrolyte loss.

questions.text: Which process explains why Strongyloides infection may persist for decades without renewed outside exposure?
questions.explanation: Strongyloides larvae can become infective within the intestine and reinvade through mucosa or perianal skin, sustaining internal and external autoinfection.
options: Cysts survive on food before another ingestion
Adults accumulate in a ball that obstructs the intestine
Hydatid cysts rupture into adjacent cavities
Larvae become infective within the intestine and reinvade
Eggs mature after leaving the host and then require fish

questions.text: Autoinfection in Strongyloides requires larvae to develop in soil before reentering the host.
questions.explanation: False: Strongyloides autoinfection occurs inside the host as larvae mature and reinvade through intestinal or perianal tissues.

questions.text: Which stage is the principal diagnostic finding in stool examination for Strongyloides stercoralis?
questions.explanation: Rhabditiform larvae are usually passed in Strongyloides stool samples; filariform larvae are infective and more typical of disseminated infection.

questions.text: Wearing boots when walking on contaminated soil helps prevent Strongyloides infection through skin penetration.
questions.explanation: Filariform Strongyloides larvae penetrate skin from contaminated soil, so protective footwear blocks a major route of infection.

questions.text: Duodenal aspirate examination for Strongyloides eggs is recommended when suspected strongyloidiasis has negative stool examination and culture.
questions.explanation: False: Strongyloides eggs hatch in the intestine; duodenal aspirate is examined for larvae, not eggs.

questions.text: In suspected strongyloidiasis with negative stool examination and culture, duodenal aspirate may reveal rhabditiform larvae.
questions.explanation: Strongyloides larvae can be found in duodenal aspirates when stool tests are negative, so the statement is true.

questions.text: Which intestinal nematode can multiply in a free-living stage and produce larva currens through repeated autoinfection?
questions.explanation: Strongyloides has both free-living generations in soil and parasitic females in humans; autoinfection causes larva currens.

questions.text: Which protozoan infection may cause cholecystitis when trophozoites reach the gallbladder?
questions.explanation: Giardia trophozoites can ascend into the biliary tract and gallbladder, where inflammation may cause cholecystitis.

questions.text: Giardiasis may be complicated by cholecystitis when trophozoites reach the gallbladder.
questions.explanation: Giardia usually adheres to duodenal mucosa, but trophozoites can occasionally reach the biliary tract and cause cholecystitis.

questions.text: Which waterborne intestinal protozoan produces mature oocysts with two sporocysts, each containing four sporozoites?
questions.explanation: Cystoisospora belli oocysts contain two sporocysts, each with four sporozoites, and become infective after sporulation outside the host.

questions.text: Cryptosporidiosis is transmitted predominantly by direct person-to-person contact rather than contaminated water.
questions.explanation: False: contaminated water is a major route of Cryptosporidium spread, alongside person-to-person and animal-to-person transmission.

questions.text: A 38-year-old male farmer presents with recurrent abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. He has a history of frequent contact with fresh canal water, and investigations confirm schistosomiasis. Which of the following pathological findings on liver biopsy is most characteristic of this condition ?
questions.explanation: Schistosome eggs trapped in hepatic tissue provoke granulomas and periportal fibrosis, which can obstruct portal flow.
options: Granuloma formation around trapped eggs and periportal fibrosis
Mucosal ulcers and a hepatic abscess containing necrotic fluid
Biliary epithelial hyperplasia with fibrous thickening of bile duct walls
A cyst surrounded by a fibrous capsule containing brood capsules
Diffuse villous atrophy of the duodenal mucosa

questions.text: Which of the following parasitic organisms is most commonly diagnosed or screened using immunodiagnostic assays (such as ELISA detecting cathodic circulating antigens [CCA] or circulating anodic antigens [CAA] in serum or urine)?
questions.explanation: Schistosome circulating cathodic or anodic antigens can be measured immunologically, providing evidence of active infection.

questions.text: Which of the following events represents the fundamental primary driver in the pathogenesis of chronic schistosomiasis, leading to granuloma formation, severe tissue destruction, and fibrosis?
questions.explanation: Egg antigens trapped in tissue trigger granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis, which drive chronic schistosomiasis pathology.
options: Direct tissue invasion and destruction by adult schistosomula
Exotoxin release from mature adult male and female worms
Host immune reaction triggered by eggs trapped in tissue
Widespread intravascular hemolysis caused by circulating miracidia
Deposition of immune complexes within renal glomeruli during primary infection

questions.text: Which of the following drugs is used to treat Schistosoma mansoni infection?
questions.explanation: Oxamniquine is an antischistosomal drug active against S. mansoni; praziquantel is more widely used against several schistosome species.

questions.text: Furcocercous cercariae penetrate the snail host, where they develop into sporocysts.
questions.explanation: Schistosome cercariae leave the snail and penetrate human skin; miracidiae, not cercariae, penetrate the snail host.

questions.text: In intestinal schistosomiasis with repeatedly negative stool examination due to closed infection, which indirect method is specifically recommended?
questions.explanation: Parasite antigen detection can indicate active infection in chronic schistosomiasis when stool microscopy remains negative.
options: Antibody detection to determine current activity
Rectal biopsy for direct egg detection

questions.text: What drives the characteristic granuloma formation and subsequent fibrosis in intestinal schistosomiasis?
questions.explanation: Soluble egg antigens trigger granulomatous immune responses around retained schistosome eggs, driving fibrosis and organ damage.
options: Direct invasion by intestinal protozoal trophozoites
Intestinal blood loss from adult buccal attachment
Cellular reaction to soluble antigens from trapped eggs
Hepatic migration of newly excysted larvae

questions.text: For which infection is Graham's adhesive Scotch-tape swab of the perianal region used to recover eggs?
questions.explanation: The Graham tape test collects Enterobius eggs deposited on perianal skin overnight.

questions.text: Recovery of adult Enterobius worms emerging from the anus at night can support the diagnosis of enterobiasis.
questions.explanation: True: gravid female pinworms may migrate out of the anus at night and can be identified directly, supporting enterobiasis.

questions.text: In children with nocturnal pruritus ani, routine stool examination is more likely to detect Enterobius eggs than early-morning perianal swabbing.
questions.explanation: Enterobius eggs are deposited on perianal skin at night, so early-morning tape/swab sampling is more sensitive than routine stool examination.

questions.text: Which feature is characteristic of enterobiasis?
questions.explanation: Female Enterobius migrates to perianal skin at night to lay eggs, producing characteristic nocturnal itching.

questions.text: Which intestinal nematode infection may cause rectal prolapse in heavy infection?
questions.explanation: Heavy Trichuris infection inflames the rectum and causes straining, which can lead to rectal prolapse.

questions.text: Which helminth causes rectal prolapse in heavy infection and may cause acute appendicitis through invasion of the appendix?
questions.explanation: Heavy Trichuris infection can cause rectal prolapse, and worms in the caecum or appendix may contribute to appendicitis.

questions.text: A whipworm inhabits chiefly the caecum and may invade the appendix, causing appendicitis. Which organism is described?
questions.explanation: Trichuris trichiura is the whipworm; adults inhabit the cecum and colon and can extend into the appendix.

questions.text: The trophozoite is the invasive tissue stage of Entamoeba histolytica, whereas the mature cyst is the infective stage acquired by ingestion.
questions.explanation: True: trophozoites invade tissues in amoebiasis, while mature quadrinucleate cysts survive ingestion and initiate infection.

questions.text: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites release proteolytic enzymes that contribute to tissue destruction and flask-shaped intestinal ulcers.
questions.explanation: E. histolytica trophozoites secrete proteases and other cytotoxic factors that destroy mucosa, producing undermined flask-shaped ulcers.

questions.text: Which protozoan infection is described as a zoonotic occupational infection among people working in pig farms or slaughter houses?
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli is a zoonotic ciliate associated with pigs, so occupational contact with pig feces increases exposure risk.

questions.text: Which intestinal protozoan disease is a zoonotic occupational infection of workers in pig farms or slaughterhouses?
questions.explanation: Balantidiasis is a zoonotic occupational infection because pigs carry the parasite and transmit cysts through fecal contamination.
